speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Budget reflects fiscal discipline, strategic foresight and a continued commitment to strengthen our social compact in a more uncertain and fragmented world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It balances long-term investment with immediate support for Singaporeans and businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, in a mature economy like ours, the central question is no longer simply gross domestic product (GDP) growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What matters is whether growth translates into mobility, fairness and confidence across generations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Increasingly, confidence means this: first, can I sustain my earning power?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will address this life-cycle economic security of Singaporeans in three parts today.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But Mr Speaker, before that, however, it is important to note that we are navigating a changed and uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Geopolitical shifts are reshaping global trade and weakening the international order we have long relied on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, technological advances, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI), will profoundly reshape how we work, learn and live.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This reflects a deliberate choice to strengthen long-term capabilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the surplus reflects, in part, the volatility of the global environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unexpected developments, whether geopolitical tensions or trade disruptions, can quickly affect growth and revenue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond the immediate tariff impact, the deeper concern is the increasing unpredictability of global trade rules and how it could eventually impact global inflation, growth and business sentiment going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Globally, beyond the uncertainty of potential refunds, companies must now navigate the specific country- and sector-specific incidences of new import duties.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For Singapore, there is still the risk of the semiconductor and pharmaceutical sectors being imposed tariffs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is therefore prudent that we channel today’s windfall towards strengthening resilience for tomorrow, rather than locking in spending that may not be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also not make the mistake of assuming that the profit cycles will always remain in Singapore's favour.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am certain our People’s Action Party (PAP) Members of Parliament (MPs) are aware of the pain points on the ground and will be sharing their views and concerns in this Budget debate today and over the next few days.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In preparing for this debate, the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Finance and Trade and Industry have engaged widely through, for example, the PAP Policy Forum (PPF), resource panel discussions and industry engagements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Healthcare affordability, job security and retirement adequacy follow closely behind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From my ground engagements, additional concerns have surfaced: rising business costs for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), higher foreign manpower costs, housing affordability for future and current generations, AI-related job anxieties for all ages, including young job seekers, and dealing with carbon transition costs and pressures from an ageing population – as our society ages and in general, live longer, concerns about a comfortable life as one gets older comes with the accompanying concerns.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singaporeans are not only concerned about growth in the abstract.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are concerned about whether growth translates into real improvements in purchasing power and economic activity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Small business leaders remain cautiously optimistic, but are still concerned about structural cost pressures, rising foreign manpower costs and uneven gains from growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While these factors are partly external in nature, that is scant consolation for ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The fact is that every dollar is now yielding progressively diminishing returns.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This concern also overlaps with the issue of retirement adequacy – which I will touch on later.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we are to ensure that Singaporeans can retire with confidence, we must mitigate cost of living pressures on a structural level.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the main expenses for households and retirees is food.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a 50% to 100% increase in less than 10 years!

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This puts direct pressure on households, especially low-income groups and retirees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the food and beverage sector, it is imperative for us to strengthen transparency in rental arrangements and assess subletting practices, so that they do not contribute to unreasonable increases in food prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the long term, we need to ensure that the healthcare system remains affordable and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That being said, we must also recognise the Government's efforts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Structurally, we have also enhanced schemes like MediShield, introduced the Jobseeker Relief Scheme and made the GST Voucher Scheme permanent, in order to give peace of mind to households who need help with their expenses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition to structural support, Budget 2026 continues the trend of providing one-off temporary support – in the form of the Cost-of-Living Special Payment, Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers and utilities rebates – when our fiscal position allows us to do so. : Mr Speaker, I will now continue in English.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is not a crisis, but it is a structural signal.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we take a longer-term view, including insights from economists like Thomas Piketty, the challenge is that wealth compounds faster than wages.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And wealth generates optionality: the ability to take risks, invest in education, support transitions and access opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over time, opportunity can become linked to starting point.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have made good progress through schemes, such as KidSTART and ComLink+.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can consider publishing clearer mobility indicators, such as school readiness, attendance and literacy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should also strengthen our efforts in terms of access for lower-income youths through internships, mentoring and enrichment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But because mobility is not only about grades; it is about access.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The new Central Provident Fund (CPF) life-cycle investment scheme mentioned in Budget 2026 is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As this is rolled out, it will be important to ensure: first, simplicity; second, strong default options; third, low fees; and fourth, safeguards against behavioural risks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The next step is whether we can connect and strengthen them within a more explicit life-cycle mobility framework, with a modest asset-building element that compounds over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, Canada’s education savings system uses government top-ups, including targeted support for lower-income families, to help build education assets over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This principle is clear – to broaden access through compounding, while keeping support progressive and fiscally disciplined.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In our context, we can consider a Singapore Opportunity Account framework: a modest starting stake, progressive top-ups for lower-income households, a safe, low-cost investment structure and restricted uses, such as education, skills upgrading, housing support enhancements or CPF top-ups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A student from a lower-income household may have the ability to pursue a specialised course or industry attachment but lack the financial buffer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Later in life, the same individual may wish to transition into a growth sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And at key life stages, it could support housing stability or CPF top-ups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this way, we are not just supporting income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By integrating existing schemes, targeting support and using capped matching with long-term investment and possibly private sector involvement, we can achieve more impact per dollar.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is an area where further study could strengthen how we design mobility-enhancing policies going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This framework was introduced in Budget 2002 to cushion lower- and middle-income Singaporeans as we shifted towards indirect taxation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But that was more than two decades ago.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since then, median incomes have more than doubled, the GST has increased and cost structures have shifted materially.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As incomes rise while thresholds remain static, bracket creep occurs quietly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More lower- and middle-income earners enter the tax base, not because they are significantly better off but because the system has not been recalibrated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this way, we strengthen progressivity while maintaining fiscal discipline.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad and grateful for the Prime Minister's continued focus on the issue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among other things, the Government-supported increase in our seniors' CPF contribution rates and the top-up for seniors who have lower CPF balances will boost the nest eggs for our seniors to retire and age with dignity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These must be seen alongside the other moves that we have made in recent years to help Singaporeans grow their retirement funds, such as the Silver Support and the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is, what is the Government's assessment on whether the MRSS has been successful in achieving its outcomes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The new and exciting announcement is the planned option for CPF members to invest their funds in a Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as CPF introduces low-cost life-cycle investment products, behavioural design becomes critical.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If CPF members are nudged into life-cycle funds, those funds must: first, automatically de-risk; second, be globally diversified; third, have strict fee caps; and lastly, include switching safeguards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is because Singaporeans see their CPF balances, but many residents that I have spoken to do not understand what "adequacy" means.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This makes it more important for every Singaporean to be able to be clear on what is "adequate" for himself or herself.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I recognise that there are inherent difficulties with such a definition.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, we must take care of Singaporeans' later years by strengthening work longevity and ensuring that seniors can retire with dignity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we do these well, through Budget 2026 and future Budgets, this will not only support Singaporeans through today's pressures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It will also reinforce confidence in the Singapore model itself – a model where growth, fairness and mobility move in tandem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will speak on the broader geostrategic environment and its implications for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The PAP Government dissolved Parliament just days after the Trump administration's announcement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The political timing of the general elections was calculated to put the PAP in the most advantageous position, with tariff uncertainty serving as a rallying call for voters to back the tried-and-tested.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Since then, however, there has been remarkably little information of the sectoral tariffs and their actual impact on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Trump administration has determined that the US must re-jig, reset and in some cases, dismantled key pillars of the international system that delivered decades of peace and relative stability in the Asia Pacific.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the US, nonetheless, retains deep influence in the region through its military and economic ties with friends and allies – Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, South Korea, Australia, India, Japan and others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Trump or no Trump, these links will continue to take significant priority and shape the strategic calculations of countries across the region.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And as the US moves towards a more confrontational posture with China, temperatures in the Asia Pacific have risen and they look set to continue rising.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The comprehensive electoral victory of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and the growing domestic political appetite for a more normalised diplomatic and military posture suggest that Japan's pacifist constitution, held for around 80 years, will finally be set aside.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospect of Japan or even South Korea acquiring nuclear weapons to counterbalance China and North Korea, is now closer to a probability and not merely a possibility.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The increased militaristic signature reflects a regional circumstance unfamiliar to many middle-aged Singaporeans and it remains a source of concern for them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Closer to home, recent hostilities between the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) neighbours – Thailand and Cambodia – remind us that regional fraternity and camaraderie do not guarantee peace dividends.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The heightened security environment will keep the Government fully occupied.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But for Singapore, the challenge is not just about managing foreign policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is what these developments mean at home for our society and our cohesion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prime Minister Wong's remarks on the back of Prime Minister Takaichi's comments about Japan's interest in Taiwan's security in November 2025 are a case in point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A notable number of online voices in Hong Kong and China, including some Singaporeans, raised concern that the Prime Minister's comments were insensitive towards Chinese sentiments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This points to something we must address directly – more needs to be done to engage Singaporeans, new immigrants and citizens of all races alike in an interactive and open conversation about our national interests.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Without that, the phrase "national interest" risks becoming a shorthand to shut down a conversation rather than to start one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We are a multiracial, multicultural society, not proportioned equally with a growing stock of new immigrants, whose loyalties understandably will take time to root.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this context, building resilience in our psychological defence is more urgent than ever.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) in Parliament, reflecting the political diversity of our people, looks forward to playing a positive role in strengthening that sense of home and our unity as one people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have ended my last two Budget speeches with a call to support our men and women in uniform.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It appears that our cyber defence agencies have already tasted combat in their virtual trenches, even if that domain remains shrouded in operational secrecy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As in previous Budgets, Singaporeans will know there is non-partisan support for the defence-related priorities in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Uncharacteristically, one of the most politically significant statements this year to date did not come from the Budget, but from the Deputy Prime Minister Gan at his January media interview on the mid-term update of the Economic Strategy Review.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What this does is to put every job-related policy, initiative and scheme announced by this Government into sharper perspective than ever before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For each more so than before, Singaporeans deserve a well-publicised and detailed report card, one that distinguishes rhetoric about promises kept with measurable outcomes subject to Parliamentary and public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Progressive Wage Model is driving income gains for the lowest 20th percentile rather than productivity, how far should it constitute a criterion of the national bonus for the Ministers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Arising from this year's Budget initiatives, I would argue that the national bonus should be anchored to one objective outcome: good jobs for Singaporeans in the age of AI.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: AI dominated this year's Budget, the first of this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet more than three years after ChatGPT changed the world, AI remains an enigma for much of our workforce and many of our businesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the Budget speaks of employing AI to facilitate end-to-end business transformation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Multinational companies (MNCs) and companies, like DBS and Grab, have the resources to experiment, to sandbox ideas and even to absorb failure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: SMEs are not necessarily in the same position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some of them, navigating AI to improve productivity is not just challenging; it can feel impossible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to the actionable strategies from the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) on the Champions of AI programme and specifically, how SMEs will benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Promoters helped to set up shell or dormant companies solely to claim PIC benefits with false documentation or listing phantom employees to meet qualifying conditions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Other reports questioned how many genuine research and development (R&D) breakthroughs were operationalised for businesses through the PIC scheme and whether they moved the productivity needle in proportion to the subsidies that were paid out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We cannot repeat that mistake with taxpayers money with this latest productivity push through AI-related subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For workers, the redesign of the SkillsFuture website to make AI learning pathways clearer is a welcome step.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At an overarching and strategic level, the AI Council must take a special interest in ensuring that AI-related outcomes are scoped properly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because done right, this raises Singaporean businesses and workers to higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second point covers the phrase used by the Prime Minister, "Because we take care of our own." That was arguably to me the most significant line in the entire Budget speech when it came to AI's impact on workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Last week, both CNA and The Straits Times ran a Financial Times opinion piece by Sarah O'Connor in the online and print mediums, respectively, titled "We have to stop calling some jobs 'low-skilled'".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: She wrote that, nobody – not your teachers, not your parents, not even the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development's (OECD's) head of skills analysis – knows which skills will be most valuable tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If that is daunting for our students and parents, one can imagine how it feels for a mid-career worker worrying about the next mortgage payment and their family while trying to retrain for a world that appears to constantly shift beneath their feet.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is an age-old problem that manifests itself – workers take up courses, earn new certificates and qualifications, but still find jobs hard to come by.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Compounded with that now, is the requirement to master AI.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the merger of Workforce Singapore (WSG) and SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) into one agency, there is an opportunity to improve one-stop support for our workers, especially for those who have been retrenched or displaced, steering them towards areas of real opportunity, not just available courses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) Minister's comments about greater public sector involvement in supporting job placement for workers at a media interview on the mid-term update of the Economic Strategy Review some weeks back.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I welcome that and look forward to seeing developments in this area.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On that note, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) should present a report card on the Jobs-Skills Integrator initiative announced at Budget 2023.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These integrators were supposed to bridge the gap between industry needs, training providers and workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To my knowledge, Parliament has not received a full account of how many workers have benefited, what the shortcomings have been or how this initiative will evolve.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To round-up this section, I wish the Government, our businesses and our union leaders and workers every success in the undertaking of making AI work for Singapore and to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At Budget 2024, the Government announced plans to spend $40 billion on Forward Singapore initiatives through 2030, with $5 billion committed at that inaugural Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To my knowledge, there has been no well-publicised tracking of cumulative spending since then.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is real value in reporting such outcomes publicly, at minimum, through an occasional paper at the close of each RIE cycle.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such transparency allows MPs on both sides of this House to fulfil their duty in scrutinising public expenditure as part of their responsibilities as MPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It gives our people, and our youth in particular, a clearer picture of the opportunities ahead and helps attract the best minds to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is much work still to be done in demonstrating how efficaciously taxpayer dollars have been spent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Across most Budgets, there is a lack of easy-to-rack outcomes on the headlines that have been announced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government should be conscious of the public cynicism and detachment that grows when Singaporeans cannot see a clear accounting of how public funds are being used and communicated for ease of understanding and what results have been achieved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is not good for Singapore and it sits in contradiction with the participatory spirit that Forward Singapore was meant to embody.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak further on this sub-point during the MOM's Committee of Supply (COS) debate, with specific reference to the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS), a scheme that was due to end, but has since been extended in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There will be significant public interest in how these surpluses are ultimately deployed, especially given the pressures of an ageing population and the persistent concern over inequality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before I turn to address some specific measures in the Budget, it is worth noting the results of the National Trades Union Congress' 2026 Survey of Economic Sentiments released last month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are the lived concerns of working Singaporeans and they should shape how we evaluate what this Budget delivers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe more should be done to assuage cost-of-living concerns of Singaporean workers and families.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On cost of living, this Budget introduces yet another tranche of CDC vouchers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans can be forgiven for treating the scheme as a permanent one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was not originally conceived as such when CDC vouchers were set at $100 per household.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With another $500 tranche to be dispersed in 2027, the time has come to refine the CDC Vouchers Scheme to better help Singaporean families.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the vouchers are distributed on a per household basis, regardless of household size.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A household of two individuals receives the same as a household of five.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Retain the $500 base for all households of three members or fewer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For owner-occupied households with more than three members, provide an additional $150 per person.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Based on the average Singapore household size of 3.06 persons in 2025, this is a modest and practical refinement, one that better reflects the actual cost-of-living burden larger families carry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On families with children, this Budget raises the monthly household income threshold for student care fee assistance to $6,500.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the expansion in reach, but I ask the Government to also review the subsidy calculation framework in favour of greater subsidies as it reviews this sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before the Budget announcement, there were 11 subsidy tiers for households earning between $1,500 and less, and $4,500.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The top tier provides a 98% subsidy up to $295 per month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This can be simplified further, starting at the new Local Qualifying Salary figure of $1,800 and below, with perhaps two to three additional tiers to better support parents with school-going children, with the lowest tier receiving at least a 50% subsidy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Alternatively, the preschool subsidy framework provides all qualifying families with a meaningful base subsidy regardless of income, with additional support determined by income.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That design is both simpler and more reassuring to families navigating the system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I ask the Government to consider a similar approach for student care subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The redistributive cost is relatively modest, especially when we consider our chronically low total fertility rate (TFR), but the impact on families and their confidence that the system is always working for them would give the reassurance of a more generous helping hand.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this context, taking care of our own represents one standard by which all Government policies will be unpacked, measured and scrutinised by the WP in this term of government.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the past few years have not been calm for the world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have just emerged from the pandemic, yet global recovery has been hesitant.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Businesses have had to reorganise their supply chains and families have had to readjust the rhythms of daily life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just as many thought we were entering a new phase of stability, global politics suddenly shifted gears and circumstances changed rapidly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some commentators have even described this as a kind of "gangster-style" logic in international conduct.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Agreements can be signed and just as easily overturned.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is not the textbook version of globalisation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a more direct and raw contest of power.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Middle East remains tense, with the shadow of Iran still looming.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Small and middle powers are increasingly pressured to declare positions and choose sides.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When large waves crash against the shore, small boats feel the impact first.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When storms arise, we are among the first to feel them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But amidst the storms, what ships fear most is not only the external waves, but also internal friction.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unity cannot be merely a slogan; it is the prerequisite for maintaining strategic resolve in a complex world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, in such a world, this Budget is not merely about numerical balance, but national assurance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After the Budget Statement, over the past few days, I have heard some interesting comments.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the Government runs a deficit, it is criticised as fiscally irresponsible.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When it runs a surplus, it is said to have miscalculated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is like a person who brings an umbrella and is mocked for being excessive, and yet if he does not bring one and gets drenched, he is mocked for being foolish.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, our Budgets have not only met fiscal targets, we have won a larger battle.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, We have more "ammunition" to face the storms ahead.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It means that in an uncertain world, we planned using conservative assumptions and reality has turned out better than expected.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we had planned using optimistic assumptions instead and subsequently found ourselves unable to pay for healthcare, ageing and security, who would bear the cost?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the ancient saying goes: "One survives in adversity and perishes in comfort." When a budget aims to be "just enough", it often ends up being "slightly short".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In such a world, we must build strength and prepare in advance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The bow must be fully drawn and the arrows well supplied.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Healthcare spending does not fluctuate simply because one year is strong and another is weak.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Of course, no one says they enjoy paying taxes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But what would truly be unfair is not adjusting tax policy today, it would be having to raise taxes suddenly during a downturn tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The real question is not whether we can spend more in any particular year, but whether we can support Singaporeans sustainably over the coming decades.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore's fiscal philosophy has always been simple: plan early, act prudently, share gains when conditions allow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When conditions turn out better than expected, the Government returns support to citizens through various packages.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As an ancient text puts it: "Digging a well when thirsty is inferior to preparing before the rain." We would rather be called conservative today than be forced into hurried tax increases tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the world is uncertain, when great power rivalry intensifies, when supply chains and financial systems can shift overnight, a surplus is not a luxury.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If the next storm arrives, we will not need to borrow in haste, raise taxes suddenly, or cut social support.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Residents do not speak to us about macroeconomic indicators.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They worry about: (a) whether AI will replace their jobs; (b) whether prices will continue to rise; (c) whether shop rentals will increase again; and (d) whether families can sustain expenses over the long term.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, a Budget must be macro-sound and micro-relevant.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Children aged zero to six receive $500 in annual support, with additional essentials provided in partnership with businesses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From early childhood education to parent-child bonding and nutrition, we walk step by step with families.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These measures may not be large in scale, but they are concrete.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The meaning of policy lies not only in national figures, but in the small sigh of relief in everyday life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A Budget is not merely a fiscal document.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It paints a picture of the society we want.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yesterday was the seventh day of the Lunar New Year, we all did "lohei".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If the fish is not fresh, nothing else matters.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: AI adoption, enterprise transformation, and industry upgrading ensure that the fish remains fresh.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Future security comes from adaptable capabilities, not fixed positions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Support for families, seniors and the vulnerable ensures that society can move forward together over the long term.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Not "what do I get?" But "how far can we go together?" Each ingredient alone seems ordinary.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But combined together, they create the flavour of the New Year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fiscal discipline is like the golden crackers simple in appearance, yet holding the entire structure together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore has never grown amidst an environment of certainty.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the next wave rises, we will have the resources, societal trust and capable people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As long as we continue to move forward together, Singapore will continue to rise!

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today is the eighth Day of the Lunar New Year, I wish for favourable weather and good harvests and peace and prosperity for the country and its people. : Mr Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Budget covers a great many areas and as in previous years, supports Singaporeans in a range of thoughtful ways: providing support for young families who wish to have children, working adults who need support to get better jobs, seniors to have better healthcare and quality of life in their later years and businesses as they cope with a range of disruptions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are all welcome measures and are possible because of Singapore’s strong fiscal position, thanks to decades of prudent financial management by successive generations of leaders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my speech though, I wish to focus on one area that troubles me most – the breakdown of the international world order that provided a stable backdrop for Singapore’s success since Independence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For decades, an international rules-based order grounded in international law has underpinned global peace and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For small states like Singapore, this framework better ensured that sovereignty was respected, disputes are resolved peacefully and trade flowed freely.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It gives small states like Singapore a measure of protection in a world which may otherwise have been dominated by power politics.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the years, Singapore has consistently advocated for a rules-based multilateral system and respect for international law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We are witnessing heightened geopolitical rivalry, economic fragmentation and a growing willingness by some states to prioritise what they believe to be national interests over collective commitments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While international law remains indispensable, we must also be realistic and prepare for a world in which non-compliance is going to be more common and where major powers may not always abide by either the letter or the spirit of international commitments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the Middle East, the conflict triggered by Hamas’ attacks on Israel on and the subsequent war in Gaza have intensified regional instability and humanitarian crises and the findings of breaches of international law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In our own region, tensions in the South China Sea continue to test the strength of international maritime law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The most dramatic changes in the last two years have probably been the position of the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US plans to take Greenland put it on a collision course with its European allies and threatened to fracture the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), especially when it appeared that the US was considering the use of force to take Greenland in its earlier statements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Together, these statements suggest that while international law remains vital, compliance can no longer be assumed or taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For small countries like Singapore, it is especially important for us to stay vigilant and prepared to deal with emerging threats and challenges.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: During the Budget debate in 2022, I said that we need to remain committed to defence spending even during times of peace, and while there will be many demands for our spending and it will always be tempting to say we should cut defence spending in times of peace, that will be a mistake.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also said that we must continue to maintain and build good and deep relations as well as mutually beneficial economic and defence ties with as many countries as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this connection, I welcome the Government’s continued commitment to invest in Singapore’s defence, including physical warfare capabilities as well as cyber defence and counter-terrorism capabilities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A credible and technologically advanced defence force remains the bedrock of our sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Beyond its defence capabilities, however, Singapore has very sensibly also adopted the strategy of diversifying its foreign relationships and defence relationships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the security front, we maintain strong and longstanding defence ties with the US, including close training and operational cooperation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, we engage constructively with other nations, including China and ASEAN partners.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These agreements provide multiple avenues for growth and reduce over-dependence on any one market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They also signal Singapore’s continued commitment to open, rules-based trade despite global protectionist trends.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Going forward, we must continue to champion international law and multilateralism while widening and deepening our network of partnerships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, while we continue to advocate multilateralism, it is equally important to recognise that many international institutions were established in an era where great powers were more willing to cooperate consistently within established frameworks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Today, the legitimacy and effectiveness of these institutions are increasingly being challenged due to divergent national interests and competition.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When permanent members are in conflict or have opposing interests, collective action can be difficult to achieve.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For a small nation like Singapore, we must recognise that when large powers do not cooperate within multilateral fora, the system becomes weaker and the norms which such international institutions uphold become more vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This leads me to my second observation which is about minilateralism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the World Economic Forum puts it, minilateralism typically involves small groups of countries or organisations collaborating to solve shared problems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While multilateral institutions remain essential, and we must continue to support them, smaller groupings of like-minded states can move faster and more pragmatically when progress stalls at the global levels through smaller agreements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Such agreements help shape global norms and position Singapore as a trusted digital hub.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Going forward, Singapore can continue to champion issue-based coalitions in areas such as green and sustainable finance, carbon markets and emerging technologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Such coalitions complement and not replace the broader multilateral system.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, as a small nation, it is important that Singapore strengthen its capacity in emerging domains of competition.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Today, security is multi-dimensional and extends well beyond conventional military threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, cyberattacks can disrupt essential services including power generation and banking.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore must therefore invest decisively in these emerging domains.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Strengthening cyber defence capabilities, enhancing digital resilience across both public and private sectors, and building trusted AI governance frameworks which will be essential and which is envisioned by this Budget.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: By doing so, we not only protect ourselves but also enhance our relevance in the international arena.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fourth, Singapore is in a unique position to play a bridging role in the new world order.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In a world of intensifying major power rivalry, countries that can maintain credibility across divides become increasingly valuable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This balanced posture allows us to facilitate dialogue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our consistency and credibility are our strategic assets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore’s role is not to choose sides in power competition.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is to maintain open channels with all while remaining firmly grounded in principles of sovereignty, peaceful dispute resolution, open trade and international law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means we must speak clearly when rules are violated, but avoid rhetoric which will unnecessarily escalate tensions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We must continue to deepen ties broadly, so that no single relationship defines our position in international relations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: By combining principle with pragmatism, and openness with resilience, Singapore can continue to thrive, even in a more uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also spoke to a tech savvy SME entrepreneur who spent his breaks in between Chinese New Year house visits, building, orchestrating AI agents to automate many parts his back-office for his SME.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I met an accountant in her 50s, after watching a clip on the robotic wushu performance, turned to her family and asked, "What happens to my job?" And I met an investor who told me that correlation between Nasdaq and AI is now very close.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: He would notice a big drop in one segment of the Nasdaq stock market and that usually comes after Anthropic introduces a new part, a new module, a new feature in the systems.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, our people have sensed that AI has matured quickly and is now reshaping lives in ways that felt theoretical just a year ago.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Prime Minister Wong has decisively centered our Budget on AI, outlining a bold vision for Singapore in a changed, AI-charged world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I want to build on this vision by speaking on three areas where I believe we can move even faster: how the Government itself builds digital services with the world's leading AI firms helping us, how we can accelerate the IT service industry, and how we ensure our SME support reach more layers of our enterprise base.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: First, how can the Government build more digital services with the world's leading AI companies' support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, I believe that the Government e-services are still largely procured through traditional IT methods – where AI, if used at all, is bolted on rather than embedded from the outset.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: AI-centric development is fundamentally different: AI is integral to design, coding, testing and continuous improvement process.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Services are faster to build, cheaper to maintain and adaptive rather than ageing between upgrade cycles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I propose that this becomes the default methodology for all new Government services and to scale it as a whole-of-Government over time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These firms should not only help Singapore enterprises adopt AI; they should also be co-developing our AI-centric stacked deck itself, building together with the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is how we build a sovereign national AI system – something I spoke about in the last Budget debate – not from scratch at prohibitive cost, but through structured co-development with the world’s best, on our terms, anchored in our values.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When the Government is merely a customer, our leverage is limited.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When the Government is a sophisticated co-development partner – bringing deep domain knowledge expertise of public service delivery and regulatory complexity – we deepen their commitment to Singapore and build internal capability that stays here.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond our own services, Government should revive the spirit of the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) with an AI-centric lens – working together with Prime Minister Wong’s four AI Mission sectors to identify common problems solvable through AI across different sectors and building shared solutions together with the industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Next, how we accelerate the IT services industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Singapore's IT services industry – the firms that actually deliver technology projects across the public and private sectors – may not be adopting AI-centric development fast enough.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These firms are the delivery layers between AI strategy and real world outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If they do not transform, the strategy stays on paper.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our tech workers are ready – curious, hungry and well-educated.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The bottleneck could be structural inertia within the IT services firms, compounded by the complexity of making AI-centric development enterprise-grade.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Large companies have found it easier to continue with familiar methods while adding AI as a cosmetic layer.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, I propose a phased mandate: Government IT contracts should progressively require AI-centric development methods.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: New projects first, legacy contracts given longer runways and a clear three-to-five-year transition pathway.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is not without precedent – we mandated Building Information Modeling (BIM) adoption in the construction industry and we can transform that.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When the Singapore Government becomes the driver of demand, industry follows.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Alongside the mandate, the Government should also transfer its frameworks and playbooks to polytechnics, universities and IT service firms.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And over time, Singapore's AI-centric methodology will not just become a public sector asset but something that will drive industry capability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Third, our SME support can be more differentiated.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When it comes to AI, two groups are ready to move, and they need different support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The first group are SMEs led by founders with strong technology backgrounds like the SME entrepreneur I mentioned about – programming using AI agents over Chinese New Year.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For these founders, the barriers to scale have collapsed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They understand understand AI and can now grow at speeds previously requiring the capital and headcount of a much larger enterprise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yet our bespoke innovation grants have traditionally been reserved for larger companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And I urge the Government to open these grants to tech-capable SMEs – these are Singapore's next generation of high-tech growth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The second group are conventional SMEs that need help adopting AI in day-to-day operations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Here, Prime Minister Wong's expanded PSG is the right instrument.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But the approved vendor list today are very traditional tech companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Taken altogether, some will argue that the AI levels the playing field against Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In a narrow sense, they are right – a talented developer anywhere, armed with enough AI tools and call code credits, can generate entire applications overnight.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: On a pure cost, we were never going to win this race.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But this is the wrong race to run.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Economic Development Board (EDB) has long described Singapore's value proposition as Trust, Knowledge and Connectivity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: AI-centric development does not erode this advantage – it amplifies them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: On trust: in an AI-centric world, where AI agents transact and AI systems make decisions, trust becomes the most precious commodity in the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Businesses will site AI operations where they trust the legal framework and the Government behind them and Singapore has spent decades building exactly this trust.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: On knowledge: the tacit knowledge – the kind that cannot be Googled or prompted – lives in the relationships and expertise of the people based here.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: AI can accelerate the application of our knowledge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: On connectivity: we have at least seven distinct global hubs – aviation, shipping, regional headquarters, advanced manufacturing, biotech, chemicals, electronics, and finance – co-located on 700 square kilometres.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The collaboration density, between the hubs themselves and the world they connect to, is something no amount of digital connectivity can replicate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In an AI-centric economy, where the most valuable innovations emerge at the intersection of industries, this co-location is a profound and durable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If we move fast enough, if we adopt AI-centric development in Government, bring our IT services industry with us and equip many layers of our SME industry, AI gives us the chance to not just manage our constraints but re-invent our economy on foundations that took decades to build, and that no competitor can replicate overnight.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The advantages I have described – Trust, Knowledge and Connectivity – do not sustain themselves.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sometime ago, I had a chat with our Minister Josephine Teo who leads Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI), she describes our Public Service Media as Singapore's truth infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I would say that our Public Service Media are not just Singapore's truth infrastructure but also our trust infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Straits Times has a place in the hearts of most of our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Zaobao is already the most respected international Chinese-language outlet globally.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: CNA commands with credibility far beyond our shores and with strategic investment, The Business Times could become the Financial Times of Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because our media is a source of our trust, and is a key voice of our soft power.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My last point is about a home for every family.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A nation's ambition is not only credible if people feel secure in the most basic of things and I commend the Ministry of National Development (MND) for continuing to build housing quickly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There is one group that I would like to speak up for today, which is the sandwiched-class families with decent incomes who could comfortably service a mortgage but cannot secure loans from banks and Housing and Development Board (HDB).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Their incomes are too high for public rental, and Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) requires a waiting Build-To-Order (BTO).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Then, the rest of the world were dealing with COVID.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But our Budget not just helped us deal with COVID but also prepared Singapore to emerge stronger together from COVID.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The world, and even the major powers, are bogged down by geopolitical conflict, internal disputes and disarrays, and trade or even economic wars.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Globally, we are navigating tectonic shifts in security, trade and technology, while domestically our workforce is feeling the weight of disruption alongside continuing cost of living pressures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is attributed largely to the fund-loading of investments and a significant revenue surge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet for many Singaporeans and local small businesses, this success feels distant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (ASME) highlighted, we are witnessing a two-speed economy despite positive aggregate macro-economic data, local SMEs find themselves squeezed by a perfect storm of rising and operating costs and weaker domestic demand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Since wage growth is only sustainable when backed by productivity, when micro and small enterprises are stuck in a low productivity second speed, it becomes supremely challenging for them to offer the competitive salaries needed to combat the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, as we look toward a future shaped by rapid AI integration and automation, we must confront the risk of structural jobless growth where corporate profits and GDP continue to growth much faster than the labour market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must put our huge fiscal surpluses to use to support and empower the workers and sectors that find themselves stuck in this slow growth track.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is only by doing so that we can secure the necessary social licence for continued high growth strategies in elite sectors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When the average Singaporean sees tangible structural benefits from these outsized gains, rather than rising inequality, it fosters the public trust and political consensus required to maintain our open and competitive economic model.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The House should examine the Government's recurring pattern of overly conservative fiscal projections.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This $8.26 billion discrepancy is not an isolated incident.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is part of a trend where projected deficits regularly transform into healthy surpluses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the Government points to the volatility of tax revenue, this consistent underestimation raises fundamental questions of whether the Government is unnecessarily hoarding funds.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need more accurate forecasting that ensures our nation's abundance, benefits current generations as much as future generations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This fiscal abundance also raises questions about the Government's tax strategies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With surpluses of well over $1 billion in all but one of the last five years, totalling $22 billion, should we re-evaluate the necessity of the GST hike?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government said that the GST hike was meant to fund the increased healthcare spending in an ageing society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But the Ministry of Health's (MOH's) revised FY2025 Operating Expenditure was $305 million lower as estimated, mainly due to lower than projecting funding needs for public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government be revising its projections for future increases in healthcare expenditure?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: True prudence is not just about amassing vast fiscal buffers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is about balancing future security with the current needs of our people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unnecessary taxation drains liquidity from households upfront, creating a dependency on Government handouts, rather than fostering genuine financial independence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, it acts as a handbrake on economic growth by constraining household spending.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In 2025, vehicle quota premium collections were 31% overestimates, reaching $8.66 billion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Certificate of Entitlement (COE) was a primary driver of our massive surplus and the Government expects even more next year, projecting $9.42 billion in revenue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned that the Government may be reliant on high vehicle costs to anchor its fiscal position.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could create a perverse incentive to allow the COE to remain high and result inertia against necessary reforms to the COE system, which my hon friend Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, the MP for Sengkang had called for in his Adjournment Motion last September.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are other significant revenue spikes that I seek clarification from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Revenue from licences and permits has searched by $2.08 billion, a 29% increase from the original estimate to the revised FY2025 figure of $9.23 billion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to MOF's analysis of revenue and expenditure 2026, the transition to the new Singapore Public Sector Chart of Accounts makes year-on-year comparison for this item not meaningful due to changes in scope.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this accounting reclassification alone does not explain why the Government collected $2 billion more than it told the House that it would just a year ago.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister clarify what specific licences or permits drove this increase and whether this represents a permanent increase in a regulatory burden, borne by our households and businesses?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While reclassification of the FY2025 figures is promised for FY2027, was there some difficulty in providing it in this year so that Parliament could probably track spending changes for this debate?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Without a clear bridge between the old and new systems, there is a risk of losing oversight of expenditure growth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Turning to technology, our AI roadmap must look beyond white-collar co-pilots.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To ensure an inclusive social compact, we must deploy physical AI for blue-collar workers in manufacturing and logistics, for example.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could include tools like wearable haptic sensors that alert workers to ergonomic risks to prevent long-term injury or collaborative robots, to assist with heavy lifting on the factory floor.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, AI can be a powerful tool for blue-collar workers who may struggle with English Language constraints.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It can translate vernacular dictation into professional English documentation in real time, allowing workers to focus on their technical expertise rather than linguistic hurdles.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These tools enable productivity gains that lead to enhance wages and reduce physical strain for those on the front lines.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: AI should be an equaliser that elevates technical mastery, not a wish that separates our workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I propose that these should include corporate AI subscriptions to give workers access to corporate AI tools to improve their daily productivity while keeping company data secure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Giving every worker a digital assistant should be a baseline goal for our nation that aspires to be an AI leader.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This ensures that the benefits of the technology are shared by employee and employer alike.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Regarding our social safety net, a gap remains for the sandwiched generation, which falls just outside existing means testing thresholds.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need a more holistic means testing model that looks not just at gross income alone but disposable income after essential expenses are deducted.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, a household earning $9,000 with special needs children or elderly parents requiring chronic care, may be functionally less wealthy than a household earning $3,000 with no such burdens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, I urge a shift towards individual base assessments for our seniors to better protect their dignity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: No senior should ever be forced to plead with an estranged adult child for financial support simply because that child's income is bundled into the per capita household income calculation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When subsidies are tied to the disclosure of a child's salary, we leave vulnerable seniors at the mercy of strained family dynamics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our social safety net should be anchored more to a senior's individual income instead of their children's, to ensure they receive the care and support that they need.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the Government says this increase is mainly due to initiatives to enhance Singapore's economic competitiveness in an uncertain global environment, can the Minister shed more light on a specific milestone this money is expected to achieve?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There seems to be a disconnect between the Government's own risk assessment and its fiscal response.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Budget Statement identifies significant risks from an AI benefits reassessment and global trade tensions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the risk of job displacement and investment decline is as real as the Government acknowledges, our fiscal injection should be more robust and proactive, particularly when we are riding on a huge surplus from the previous year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should be building more buffers for our workers now rather than reacting after the displacement begins.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With the rise of in sophisticated cyberattacks and hostile information campaigns, it is essential to know the true allocation of security resources.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is a statement of our national values and priorities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We cannot be a nation that celebrates multibillion dollar surpluses while our middle-income families are squeezed, our seniors fear being a financial burden on their children and our workers worry about a digital future that feels out of reach.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us build a social compact that does not just manage growth but shares it fairly and transparently.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should measure our success not by the absolute size of our reserves, but by the security, dignity and peace of mind of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will speak about Singapore as a networked economy with trust as our new factor of production.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Economists have studied the classic factors of production, land, labour, capital and later adding entrepreneurship in the 1800s.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this uncertain fragmenting world and AI acceleration, I see a new factor of production – trust.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Trust enables flows – capital, data, talent, goods, decisions.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Trust is the reliability premium that allows counterparties to transact, coordinate and commit to actions at scale, even in the face of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For Singapore, as a small city-state, this is and should be our competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 1965, our population was a mere 1.9 million.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, as a first world nation, we have 3.7 million Singaporeans, 4.2 million if we include Permanent Residents.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Compare this to Tokyo, a city, 37 million people; Delhi, 36 million people; Shanghai, 21 million people; London, 10 million people; New York, eight million people – you get the picture.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even Kuala Lumpur and many of our Asian capitals/cities have a few times multiple, more people than Singapore.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Large countries within hinterlands can rely on internal markets, domestic, resources, national industrial stacks.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead, our hinterland must be how deeply we connect to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I see Singapore therefore as a networked economy, where trust becomes the connective tissue that allows a small node like Singapore to orchestrate value across a much larger space.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To be a successful networked economy in this globally fragmented and accelerating AI world, trust becomes our factor of production, our competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In finance, AI can position Singapore as the world's most trusted digital custodian enabling secure asset verification, counterparty validation and trusted trading ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In health, Singapore can be a trusted hub for clinical trials, diagnostics and genomic innovation.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In advanced manufacturing, by anchoring intellectual property with trust, Singapore can embed itself in high value global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, as a port, we cannot just compete by the number of boxes we move.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must use AI to pivot from moving boxes to become trusted coordinator, the operating system that optimises flows across ports, even across geopolitical boundaries.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When we are the trusted node in supply chains, essential good for Singaporeans continue to flow even during crises.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can create trust-centric jobs, coordinating systems, validating data, ensuring digital security.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In an AI driven world, Singaporeans can become that human layer of trust, providing empathy and compassion, on top of credibility and judgement which AI cannot.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Trust can be our new fact of production, our competitive advantage for a small city state, a network economy.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this way, Singapore exports trusted governance alongside technology.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Stewardship of such standards creates relevance and trust for others to deal with us Singapore.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the fragmenting world and AI acceleration, we can however, be that beacon of trust for the world as a networked economy.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When the world asks: "Who can we work with?", "Who can we rely on?", "Who can coordinate these critical systems for the world?", let the answer be Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my work, I have seen how capital relocates amidst volatility, how labour markets adjust when technology shifts and how nations either manage transition wisely or struggle when they do not.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My reaction to Budget 2026 is this: Singapore’s budget surplus reflects global volatility and our strategic credibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In a fractured world, capital flows toward stability, predictability and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is a vote of confidence for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At a time when many countries wrestle with debts and deficits, Singapore’s prudence is an asset.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It gives us room to act, credibility to lead and options in uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In a more dangerous world, fiscal strength is national defence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our buffers are not excesses, they are strategic insurance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They safeguard our sovereignty, resilience and freedom of action.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Chair of the Defence and Foreign Affairs GPC, I say this with conviction: fiscal resilience is strategic capability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It ensures we are not forced into decisions by constraints.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It preserves our strategic autonomy when circumstances demand it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I recognise that Government will, when necessary, need to raise revenue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But where new measures are introduced, they should be calibrated carefully and remain progressive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps there should be no additional effective burden on lower-income households and revenue adjustments should be designed with cost pressures firmly in mind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not to question earlier fiscal decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
