text: It is simply to say: where space exists, we should use it to cushion households and strengthen trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because trust in fiscal policy underpins trust in everything else.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And trust must also underpin our AI transition.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is structural, it is global and it is accelerating.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Recent analysis from technologists observing the frontier makes this clear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Model performance is not merely improving incrementally, it is compounding.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tasks that required research teams a year ago can now be done in weeks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tasks that required weeks can now be done in hours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What appears gradual suddenly crosses a threshold and becomes transformational.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: AI is no longer assisting humans at the edges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: AI is helping to build the next AI.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Engineers use AI to write code, debug systems, test approaches and accelerate research cycles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the recent AI coding revolution does not stop at engineers and programmers, because code is essentially logic and workflow.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And it is enterprise logic and workflow that is the fundamental basis of many knowledge jobs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This means that AI's ability to generate code and write software autonomously could eventually have greater implications on all knowledge workers, not just programmers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When improvements accelerate the next round of improvements, change does not move in a straight line.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Last week, I met a young Singaporean named Amir outside a tuition centre in Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In his hand was a neatly printed curriculum vitae (CV).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I asked whether he had hired a professional writer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He laughed and said, “No, I used an AI tool to help me.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It even suggested interview answers.” Then he paused. “But if AI can write my CV better than I can,” he said quietly, “what happens when it can do my job better than me?” He was not dramatic, he was also not angry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Stanford Prof Erik Brynjolfsson recently argued that the long-awaited AI productivity take-off may now be visible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Productivity rose about 2.7% in 2025, nearly double the previous decade’s pace.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First comes investment, then re-organisation, then, if we get it right, harvest.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some firms adapt faster, some sectors benefit earlier, others face displacement sooner.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And here is the elephant in the room.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The accountant whose reconciliation tasks are automated, the marketing manager whose drafting work is compressed into minutes, the operations executive whose reporting is replaced by dashboards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are parents, caregivers and Singaporeans with responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They want to remain useful, valued and respected in their work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Productivity can rise even as some workers experience displacement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Allow me to group my proposals into three themes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: AI Missions deserve praise, but alongside ambition, we need measurable labour outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, net new roles created, wage uplift achieved, time to redeployment, share of SMEs scaling AI beyond pilots.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If this transformation is national, its scorecard must be national and human.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It should include data readiness, genuine process redesign, measurable productivity gains and meaningful workforce upgrading.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if firms cannot demonstrate transformation beyond pilot projects within a defined period, support should be reviewed and if necessary, withdrawn.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Globally, the first wave is not mass layoffs but junior tasks disappearing: drafting, summarising, first-pass analysis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The future belongs to “AI conductors”, not merely “AI users”.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our juniors must learn to curate, steer and verify AI outputs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The competitive advantage is not pressing “generate.” It is about asking the right questions and judging the answers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we lose the first job pathway and if our juniors never get the chance to learn how to be "AI conductors", we lose the future workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For mid-career Singaporeans, the fear is not only unemployment, but stagnation and even decline.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If gains flow only to the margins and management, social cohesion erodes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Six months of premium AI tools must not become tokenism.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, build shared capability and trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will we provide shared credits, secure data environments and reference architectures so that they can compete responsibly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without shared capability, we risk an AI divide.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When AI affects hiring or evaluation, what is the audit framework?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And how do we remain trusted without slowing deployment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the AI Council’s explicit speed-with-safety model?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This should include: tiered risk categories, standardised evaluation, fast-track approvals for low-risk use.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They broke into mills and smashed the mechanical looms, the industrial weaving machines that automated the production of cloth, because they believed those machines would destroy their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These workers came to be known as the Luddites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They were craftsmen, fathers and providers who feared that mechanisation would render their skills obsolete.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The looms did not destroy prosperity, they transformed it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Industrialisation was painful and disruptive, but the societies that adapted built new industries, new skills and eventually a broader middle class.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The lesson is not that technological change is painless.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is that refusing to prepare does not preserve dignity, preparing does.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We may only have years, perhaps only months.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If AI disruption results in productive assets concentrated in a few hands while working people are excluded from opportunity, social strain follows.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Every major technological disruption has also created renewal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It means being prepared to recalibrate policy as the technology evolves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The PAP has never shied away from harsh truths.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will be honest about the challenges on the ground.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will be honest that some jobs will change.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will be honest that some roles will disappear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And we will be honest that the transition will not be easy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we will also be clear about this: we are here to walk with Singaporeans through the tough times.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When I saw him again, he had enrolled in a course.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He was no longer asking what AI could do for him.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He was asking what he could become. “The tool is not the point,” his instructor told him. “Learning how to think is the point.” “I realised,” Amir said, “that I needed to level up.” Mr Speaker, that is the future we must design.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Not a future where productivity rises but trust falls.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But a future where productivity funds mobility and automation finances upgrading.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we prepare honestly, govern wisely and act courageously, Singapore will not merely endure this wave of change.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we get this right, Singapore will not merely adopt AI.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And together, we will shape the future of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I would first like to congratulate the Prime Minister and his team on the forward looking and comprehensive Budget that speaks to the wide-ranging needs of our economy and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I will make some broad remarks on the Government's fiscal position and spending and use the rest of my speech to outline four priorities that I believe are critical for Singapore's future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Looking around the world today, a strong fiscal position is both rare and enviable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Fiscal strength allows for policy optionality and gives confidence that the Government has the resources to carry out its policy agenda.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As a public policy academic, I often speak to visiting delegations of public officials from other countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Many are eager to learn how Singapore has accumulated reserves and achieved such a healthy fiscal position, and they want to learn how their countries too can strengthen the public finances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The question then is how the Government can best deploy the fiscal resources at its disposal today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Should the Government set them aside for a rainy day by replenishing the reserves, earning financial returns in anticipation of future spending needs and exigencies, or should we invest in our earning capacity – in infrastructure capabilities and human capital?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Or should we strengthen social support dealing with the challenges we face here and now, which is so important for a sense of assurance and solidarity as a nation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is doing fairly well as a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As an optimist, I am inclined to see the glass is half full rather than half empty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: One could even say that for Singapore, the glass is more than half full.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: But even if the glass is, say, three quarters full, we cannot be complacent as the shortfall represents Singaporeans who are struggling or insecure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Gaps matter even in a nation that is doing well overall because social cohesion depends not on averages but on those at the margins.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: What we do to support fellow citizens could determine whether we remain a cohesive society or become one that is divided along socio-economic lines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I will touch on four areas I think need our attention and resources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: They form the acronym "FEAT" – "F" for future readiness, "E" for empowerment, "A" for assurance and "T" for togetherness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Assurance provides the confidence to navigate change and Togetherness sustains the trust that underpins our shared progress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This year's Budget focuses on frontier technologies, notably how Singapore can build a competitive, AI-enabled economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We are strengthening our security against new threats, expanding our infrastructure capacity ahead of time and building capabilities in areas such as nuclear energy, to give us more options.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In an uncertain world, adaptation matters more than prediction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to more details of these schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: How firms rework business processes will be critical, whether they use AI to augment or to replace human contribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: There is a need to support firms in building capabilities for human-centric job redesign.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Fundamentally, too, we will need to redesign jobs so that the jobs in demand are also the jobs that Singaporeans aspire to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I will elaborate on this at the MOM COS debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, preparing for the future is an individual responsibility as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We are not defined by our Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) score or "O" level grades, but by our willingness to learn throughout life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I took part in an SG60 commemorative book project entitled "Redefining Singapore".

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: One of the contributors to the book, Mr Mohammad Saleem, overcame a troubled youth to become the founder of a social enterprise that provides life coaching.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Drawing on his own life experiences, Mr Saleem contributed one of the best chapters of the book.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In both his writing and speaking, Mr Saleem stands out, even among the many eminent contributors to the book.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: His life story is a testament to the potential that is in each of us and how far we can go if we keep learning and improving ourselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The second priority I would like to highlight is to empower Singaporeans to pursue excellence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is where it is today because generations of Singaporeans gave of their best, pursuing excellence in what they did.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While we are more comfortable and affluent today, we cannot afford to lose this drive for excellence and, along with it, our society's dynamism and verve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Affluence does not mean we grow soft as a people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, we should think of our resources as an enabler, a springboard to greater achievement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I am not referring to excellence that is narrowly defined, nor am I asserting that the pursuit of excellence should be at the expense of physical or mental well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, our society ought to have a place for some who run faster and others who prefer a slower pace, recognising that people at different stages of life and career will have different priorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: But as a society, we need a critical mass of highly motivated people with the hunger and drive to succeed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This is not about hyper-competition but about setting high standards for ourselves, not being satisfied with the status quo but pushing the boundaries of possibility, often through collaboration with others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I know a teenager who constantly challenges his own limits, whether it is learning mathematics, programming, playing music or learning to juggle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Whenever he has mastered something, he was always on to the next target.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: His intrinsic motivation stems from curiosity, challenge and purpose, rather than extrinsic rewards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I hope this kind of spirit will be pervasive among our youths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We must encourage and empower Singaporeans to be the best each of us can be, whether in creative, sporting or academic pursuits, or in serving the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This includes significant investment in our national schools and preschools, as well as in lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Despite these efforts, we know the playing field is not level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Children from affluent families have access to private tuition and enrichment programmes spanning both academic and non-academic domains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The question is whether, as a society, we can provide even more resources and opportunities for children from lower-income or disadvantaged households.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The idea is not to fuel an education arms race, but to expand equitable access to programmes that are truly helpful in nurturing passion and potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to provide opportunities, not just during the schooling years, but also into working life and it is not just the Government's responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I know the chief executive officer of a private equity firm who, instead of only hiring top graduates from brand name universities, makes it a point to give opportunities to those from modest family backgrounds and less well-known institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: A number of those he has recruited and mentored have gone on to become successful investment professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Their success illustrates how opportunity, mentoring and the willingness to look beyond credentials can unlock potential that might otherwise remain untapped.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Empowerment enables social mobility and is vital for a fair society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: There is also tremendous benefit to society when more have the opportunity to fully realise their potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I will talk about strengthening assurance and social inclusion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is an expensive city, but it must never become an excluding one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The cost of living will always be high because land is scarce and incomes generally high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Prices are high because of supply and demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Many shops and eateries set prices according to what most Singaporeans can afford.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We must therefore ensure that those who are less well-off are not excluded from mainstream life in Singapore, for instance, by having to forgo social gatherings because they feel they cannot afford to pay for a meal or a shared activity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The aim must be for citizens to feel a greater sense of financial assurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This is necessary for our social compact, so that we can face challenges together with confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is also a pre-requisite for public support for Singapore to remain an open economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: There are many ways to strengthen assurance and support, but each comes with trade-offs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: If the Government holds down prices or rents, this may distort price signals and reduce market efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: If the Government mandates high wage floors, this may raise business costs and crimp employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Government could provide more direct support to the less well-off via social transfers, but this would incur fiscal costs and may affect incentives to work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This is not to suggest that we do nothing but rather to highlight that strengthening assurance inevitably involves trade-offs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Greater support may entail fiscal costs or modest efficiency losses but the society that provides confidence and dignity to its citizens is ultimately more resilient and cohesive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The first is to reframe or reposition CDC vouchers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans are, by now, very familiar with CDC vouchers, which we have received yearly since 2021.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: However, the vouchers also appear to some as mere band aid for the cost of living, something that is neither sustainable nor targeted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I see a useful role for vouchers and credits in our social support system, complementing structural or permanent transfers, such as the Workfare Income Supplement, Silver Support Scheme, the GST voucher, along with healthcare and housing subsidies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The advantage of vouchers is that they can be sized according to needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, more can be given when inflation is high and cost of living pressures are elevated, and when more fiscal resources are available, I believe that with a reframing, the role of the vouchers would be better appreciated by Singaporeans as a form of support that is anchored in the shared ownership of Singapore's success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Government can determine the size of the dividend it declares each year, depending on prevailing fiscal and economic conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The dividend should be universal and progressive, meaning that everyone receives something, while the less well-off receive more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: A social dividend would be a form of social support that compliments the structural transfers, is flexible in size and sends a clear message of solidarity and inclusion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This reframing would shift the narrative from short-term relief to shared participation and in national progress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has already adopted various forms of asset-based social policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: These include the CPF system to build up savings, the home ownership policy that has given most Singaporeans valuable housing equity and periodic CPF top-ups for those with less retirement savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Government could consider broadening the types of transfers to include income-generating assets, such as mutual funds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This could be designed so that recipients would not be allowed to sell these assets within a certain vesting period and can earn a stream of income from them over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Asset-based transfers can strengthen financial resilience and foster a shift in mindset, from short-term spending to long-term wealth building and stewardship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Provided they are carefully designed to manage market risk and complexity, such measures offer a complementary pathway to narrow wealth gaps and broaden participation in asset ownership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We could likewise track the percentage of households whose expenditure on food, utilities and other essential goods and services exceeds a certain proportion of their income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is particularly important that low-income Singaporeans have sufficient consumption choices, so that they can participate fully in society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is worth thinking about how this, too, can be tracked as an indicator of how inclusive our society is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This, I believe, will be the single most important determinants of Singapore's future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Togetherness is not merely a sentiment, but the culture and practice of respect, trust and shared responsibility within society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As a small nation at a time of geopolitical flux, we cannot afford to be divided along partisan lines, ideology or any other societal fault lines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Often, such division starts with disrespect and then progress to denigrating those whose views or practices are different from ours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: And very soon, people cannot work with one another on the basis of ideology, politics or worldview, and once the genie is out of the bottle, it is very hard to put it back in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: If Singapore gets mired in partisan battles or culture wars like what we observe in other countries, we could win our individual battles but lose the war.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Our fiercest fights would be with one another rather than against external threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Suppose in a hypothetical country, two-thirds of the population support a party or ideology and one-third support a rival, and suppose in the extreme, the two sides spend all the time and resources trying to negate the efforts of the other side.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The net strength of this hypothetical country would be two-thirds minus one-third, but if the country is united, then it is two-thirds plus one-third, or perhaps even more than the sum of its parts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: As Singaporeans, we must recognise and affirm that there is more that we have in common than what divides us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We must do everything we can to nurture a strong middle ground of citizens who are fair-minded and respectful towards one another, a middle ground that is not reflexive, but reflective in our approach to affairs in the public square.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Particularly at this time of severe geopolitical turbulence, Singaporeans must close ranks if we are to survive and prosper, and not be swept away by external tides.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: If we succeed in doing so, we will truly be an exceptional society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: And this, I believe, would be the greatest competitive advantage for Singapore in a world of deeply divided societies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is up to each of us, as Singaporeans, to exercise agency and influence to help mould our shared future.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this response, I will cover broadly on three issues.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The first is on the perceived support to parenthood; second, is on closing the opportunities gap; and third, it is a whole-of-Government approach in how we can tackle the first two issues that I have just mentioned.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, if we are serious about encouraging parenthood, we must reshape the lived experiences of parents or potential parents, which shapes perceptions of support given.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To be clear, Budget 2026 takes meaningful steps in the right direction, such as Child LifeSG Credits, raising of income thresholds for preschool subsidies and student care support, and others.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: All these follow comprehensive steps taken over the past few years to support parents and families, including significant enhancements to parental leave, the Large Families Scheme and many others.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But we have to be candid at where we now stand.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While we all hope that the Government's efforts over the past years would have improved our TFR, in my conversations with parents and also my residents, the current realities makes me doubtful whether this could significantly change in 2026.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My point here is this: we have done a lot to encourage Singaporeans to have children for the past decade.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But with the historical low of 0.97, it suggests to me that we may not have been effective in shifting the needle.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I propose the shift from doing "more" in an aggregate manner to doing "better".

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Allow me to propose some solutions regarding on how we can overcome such barriers and constraints, drawing from the conversations with young parents and also my resident.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I will cluster them into three "S" – first, spaces; second, stress; and third, support.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The first "S" pertains to space and housing.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore is land scarce and we have to use space efficiently.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Over time, HDB flats have become more compact and this is part of our reality today.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But if we are serious about encouraging parents to have children and supporting large families, we should make it easier for families planning to have children or more children to secure homes that are conducively sized for them.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: You see, if we want couples to start thinking about children early, the flats that they choose can influence their decision.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, such flats could include layouts with extra bedroom separate from the main living quarters that can accommodate domestic helpers and better soundproofing so that children can play, sleep or study without the entire household being disrupted.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If I were to push this idea slightly further, such flats could be priced similar to smaller-sized units through additional subsidies, but with clear conditions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I will be frank here, I do not think that we have really tried a "bigger home for bigger families" housing scheme that ties bigger flats and extra subsidies to having more children, so I think that the idea needs to be tested.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I think it is worth studying this idea.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At least, it addresses the concern of adequate space if a family is considering having more children and will certainly give them a good nudge in their decision-making before they get married.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A second idea is to give families more flexibility to upgrade their larger flats when a new child arrives and relax the existing rules on flat applications within MOP.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I am sure many of us, as MPs, have received such requests and what I am about to share is not uncommon.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Basically, some families already live in smaller HDB flats, and they find that space becomes too tight after having their second or third child.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In such a case, we should consider activating more flexible pathways for them to move to larger flats.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Of course, these details should be thoroughly considered and debated, but the broader point is this: we should be prepared to use policy design to signal that we are ready and willing to reduce the structural and financial hoops for families to jump if they want to secure bigger and more comfortable living spaces, if they want to raise more children.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The second "S" pertains to mobility and commuting stress.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We rightly pursue a car-lite vision, and as a member of the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) GPC, I support this as it certainly goes a long way in reducing our collective carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They navigate daily routines and logistics and arrangements.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For larger families, private mobility has economies of scale and can reduce stress.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On economies of scale, this is especially so when larger families have to send multiple children to childcare and school each day, and they would like to spare their household from waking up early just to catch public transport.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As a father to two, I know this reality myself, because every time I bring my children out, it is not just "bringing my children out", it is bringing out a stroller, a bag with diapers, milk, spare clothes, wet wipes, snacks and things that I would only realise what to bring after a spill, an accident, a tantrum or a sudden fever.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When you do this while navigating public transport, every transfer is a stress multiplier.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So against this backdrop, we should consider how we can support families with children to address these realities by providing commuting offsets, such as, another idea, private transport vouchers or even substantial family subsidies for large families for private vehicles.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: During my PAP Clementi market visit on Valentine's Day, a parent pulled me aside to raise a concern, which I have heard repeatedly from many parents – childcare leave.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If one person raises this issue, to me, it is a data point.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But when different parents raise the same issue independently, it is a signal.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is how it looks like in real life today, primary school children still fall sick and it is rarely a one-day occasion, and they still have medical appointments to go to, and there can be occasional school disruptions such as Home-Based Learning.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And for parents with two children or more, the odds of staying home at short notice is actually quite likely.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When leave runs out, that same parent told me, she has to take unpaid leave a few times.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our current support environment for parents, hence, may not feel supportive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It then raises a fair question whether the current structure remains fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The principle is this: we should keep childcare leave provisions under periodic review, answering the question whether they match the current work and family realities today.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Another aspect of support is accessibility to play.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We often say this: we do not want our children glued to their phones and I agree.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But in many new BTO estates, the alternatives are limited or not age-appropriate for older children.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I am glad that the Government's position has shifted from just simply stating constraints to saying that it is now being studied.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I still get occasional queries from parents of primary school-going children in Clementi Peaks and I cannot keep tell them that the Government is still studying, because they want to know a definite timeline.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, I urge relevant agencies to share the outcome and timeline of this study soon.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On this note, I also want to say that I welcome the expansion of the Dual-Use Scheme so that families can access school facilities conveniently.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But just as importantly, we should review pricing and access rules so that these spaces do not just become "available in theory" but out of reach in practice for lower-income households.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The release of MOF's Occasional Paper noted that incomes have risen and income inequality has moderated.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But I worry something that is not said explicitly: even if incomes rise, is the opportunity gap widening and is access to opportunities becoming harder?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because many opportunities today cost money, time and prior knowledge of their existence.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Families with more resources can buy enrichment, exposure and networks.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As we, as a country, continue to invest in growth and skills, we must keep our promise of social mobility alive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Specifically, I will address two "As" here – awareness of opportunities and access to opportunities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As we push into new growth areas and an AI-enabled economy, the first barrier, in my opinion, is not about capability; but it is about clarity.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In emerging industries, such as AI, quantum, advanced manufacturing and biomedical sciences, many people opt out early simply because they lack exposure.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They do not know what the work actually looks like, what the entry routes are, what are the pathways or what skills are really required there.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But those with stronger networks can ask someone, get an introduction and hear early about internships or externships.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And those without networks often find out late or, maybe, not at all.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Put simply: awareness is uneven and it can become a hidden advantage.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I will elaborate more on this during the COS debates.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The second "A" refers to access to opportunities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because today, such experiences come with a price tag.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Higher family incomes can pay, and families with stronger networks hear about opportunities earlier and get better guidance on what to try.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Before and since raising this idea, I have seen smaller-scale pilots illustrating how this can work, especially for children from lower-income households.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The principle is straightforward: access to discovery should not be a privilege but it should be part of how we keep social mobility alive and real.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond children and our growing years, allow me to segue into SkillsFuture too.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should also have this "try before you buy" a bigger part of our opportunity system.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That is why we should be open to bolder measures and widen genuine access at formative stages, especially throughout education, which I will expand a bit more on this in the COS debates.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The solution does not sit nicely in one agency, neither does the outcome rarely take the form of a voucher or a subsidy.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Taken in isolation, let me submit to everyone that many ideas that I just raised today run against the Ministry's baseline mandate.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I make this point because it links back to family and opportunities.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: My speech today is going to focus on three main areas.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The first area is a vibrant economy; followed by an active caring society; followed by the last topic, which is a resilient nation.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore transformed itself from the third world to the first world over the last 60 years, from a labour-intensive industry to a very much technology-intensive economy.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: What are the systems of governance that enabled us to do so?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Those are questions eagerly sought by participants of the Science, Technology and Innovation Policy class, while I was associate faculty at the Harvard Kennedy School.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Those answers probably will not be able or to solve our current economic situation going forward as we have entered into more advanced technology, more pioneering efforts and therefore, we probably have to switch our strategy, change our secret sauces or what is the new formula?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I was in conversation with Dr Paul Romer, who is the former World Bank chief economist and also the Nobel Laureate for Economics 2018.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Romer is well known for his endogenous growth theory, otherwise known as the new growth theory.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: That probably points a good direction for us.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The endogenous growth theory, conceptually, is very simple – matters over things.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Simply, they can be just factors of production – land, labour and capital.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The more you use the land, it suffers from the loss of diminishing returns.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, if we pursued these areas, how much land reclamation can we do, how many foreign labours can we import into this country – so there is always a limit, so that is matters.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Now things – matters and things are the same – but ideas are very different.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, ideas generally can be classified as intellectual properties (IPs).

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, patents, you came out with ideas, you filed a patent, what happens?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: You can reuse, reuse and reuse it again.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The more you use the patents, the more you generate production, the higher the productivity and therefore, it is not the law of diminishing returns.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It is actually the law of increasing returns.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: If we go along this formula, or this road, then, possibly, the GDP growth will be limitless or unlimited.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: This is actually a very far-sighted move, because we have to move ourselves from research to innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: With this amount of money that spans over the last 15 years, what have we achieved?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Well, it is not easy to measure because R&D is uncertain and of course, if you are doing biomedical applications, it could be 20 years or 30 years before you see any results.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: However, a simpler way to analyse this situation is to use the Global Innovation Index conducted by the World Intellectual Property Office.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We use it as a reference – Global Innovation Index ranking.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation input number one; innovation output number nine.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Are we, after 15 years or 20 years of R&D, still ranked number nine, which is not comparable with the amount of innovation input, or R&D dollars, we put into it.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, how do we measure the commercialisations of IPs?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: How many IPs have we generated based on the R&D dollars?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: That could be a factor for us to judge.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: A patent only has a 20-year lifetime and from the date of filing.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, if we file today, it does not mean we have the rights of it until that is awarded which is two years down the road, but the clock starts counting.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, we should quickly get it into the market or commercialise it.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: If after five years, that piece of patent is not commercialised, it is probably going to be obsolete very soon.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And if it is obsoleted, then what is the point of filing the patent in the first place because patent is really, really expensive.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, maybe we could consider that if, given a number of "X" years, if the patent is not filed or commercialised by our research institutes or universities, we might want to consider treating it as a public good and licence to any Singaporean companies or Singaporean individuals who want to use the patent for any other innovation purposes, free.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The National University of Singapore started technology commercialisation in the year 2000, when I was an adjunct faculty.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And in 2019, we started the Graduate Research Innovation Programme (GRIP).

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I designed the programme for the teaching part and I was a chief instructor.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that it has progressed to become the National GRIP.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I can observe that they are good firms, they have lots of support through the Singapore tech ecosystems.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, the seeding and angel funding are not an issue.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The issue then is how we bring them to commercialisation or early commercialisation, because there is a mismatch of expectations.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: When you move on from the seeding stage to pre-commercialisation or the pilot stage, you need more funding and the funding has to come from the venture capital market.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And the venture capitalists are looking at returns at maybe three years down the road and if there is no liquidity event, then they will just hold on.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And now, you have a mismatch: one is moving and needs money; one is waiting to see.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, it is a chicken and egg issue.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I think that the recent example might point us a way.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And the Minister of State Dinesh was there to witness, with the gong.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, we use this as a reference or the pilot point for us to say, "Hey, why not we create a special path for technology ventures?" Special listing rules for technology ventures that allow them, with criteria listed by the exchange, the sponsors and maybe a group of wise old men, meaning people who have done technology ventures before, to determine whether they are suitable for such acceleration programme, fast track, or we can call it, in Singapore style, through-train.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: On Catalist, this is something that it is possible for us to explore and make these companies anchor in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Because if they grow to a point that they are ready for IPO, what would they choose?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: No, likely overseas, where the market capitalisations or the valuation is much higher.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, this is something that we really have to grapple with and anchor them early in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I am proposing that we have an innovation within our Catalist for smaller market valuation companies.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I grew up not in a zinc roof house.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I lived and grew up in an attap roof house.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I think in our so-called categorisation of HDB, it would probably be a three-room for attap roof, and then zinc roof is a five-room.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We walked into our neighbour's house and slept on the floor – there is no couch – anytime we want.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: That is the kampong spirit of understanding and looking after each other.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We have talked so much about kampong spirit.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Did we really actually achieved the type of kampong spirit?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, block parties – you live on the 14th floor, I live on the third floor.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The closest people are the persons living here and there – your neighbours, your immediate neighbours, who can look after you if they really understand you.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I do not really have a solution for this because times are different.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe we should have, instead of block parties, potluck among the three neighbours together to understand each other, to know each other and to take care of each other and to actively look out for each other.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Not just care for each other but actively caring for each other.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I do not have a solution, but maybe a CDC voucher can help to let them have some potluck together among the three families, next to each other.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: One topic that I am personally involved in is fostering.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And we are very sad, very concerned in our fostering community over the Megan Khung case.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: My colleague here was the chair of the investigation committee.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But we think that there should be more plans, more awareness activities, more incentives to encourage more people to become foster parents.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I think I will explain later in the COS.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: It means that our population will halve in 30 years' time, that is what it means.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We know all the problems – we basically do not have enough space, marry late, have a career and all the kinds of issues.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I want to give a proposal: it is that for existing families who do not have kids, should we nudge them a little bit more?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe we should consider for the first-born, we have free childcare and infant care.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Because for the rest, we already have existing systems of subsidies and also the Baby Bonus.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But to nudge them on to having the first kid, when you have the first kid, then the joy of parenting and the confidence of bringing them up all comes into picture.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And when you have your first kid, then when you see them grow up, you will look at them and then say, "Oh, maybe we should have another one to keep him or her company." So, let us try out something that shifts the point of TFR a little bit – not to two, not to 1.5, but maybe bring it above one.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Literally, it means to think of dangers when you are dwelling in safety.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is a good reminder for us to always be mindful of future storms and adversities even when we are in peaceful and prosperous times.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I wanted to share this with the House because I think that it is a fitting framework for this year’s Budget.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It also encapsulates the thinking of the PAP Government very well.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: One of the hallmarks of the PAP Government is fiscal prudence, thinking far ahead, always with an eye to the challenges of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is this and good governance that got us to where we are today.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must not forget this discipline, for it is our strength and has enabled us to ride through many previous storms together.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: As the Prime Minister noted in his Budget opening, the old international order that enabled our current prosperity is fading away.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The global balance of power, trade patterns and economic structures are all shifting.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Geopolitical tensions, technological disruption and climate risks are no longer distant concerns, but challenges that directly affect Singapore.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We are maturing as an economy and aging as a society.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We need to prepare our people and economy for the disruptions ahead.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The demands on our Budget will only grow in the years to come.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: At the same time, our fiscal levers face real constraints.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We cannot raise taxes indiscriminately without imposing social and economic costs.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And our investment returns are subject to market cycles, global shocks and other uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: With the RIE 2030 Plan, Singapore commits significant resources to strengthen our capabilities in research and innovation frontiers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Over the years, we have invested heavily in research, development, building world-class universities, research institutes and labs, translational platforms, incubators and funding mechanisms.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These efforts have created an environment that nurtures and supports startups and anchor global companies here.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These investments have borne much fruit, creating jobs, strengthening our economy and positioning Singapore as a knowledge-based hub.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Today, Singapore is the second most competitive and the fifth most innovative economy globally.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Startups emerging from these ecosystems often attract global venture funding.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Yet Singapore’s sovereign stake in these successes is typically modest.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The primary goals of our R&D and innovation framework have been to spur economic activity, create high value jobs and anchor industries.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But direct fiscal returns, in the form of Government equity stakes, licensing of IP, or long-term sovereign income, while they exist, have always been a secondary objective and remain small.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Yet as public R&D spending grows, I wonder if we may be missing an opportunity to capture a more deliberate share of the upside?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Is there more direct value that we can capture?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: By taking a different approach, could we enhance public returns while continuing to nurture private sector dynamism?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Today, it is the world’s second most valuable semiconductor company with a valuation about three times the size of Singapore’s GDP.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This demonstrates that R&D efforts can create spin-offs that deliver substantial long-term sovereign value.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In contrast, I looked up two success stories listed in the RIE 2030 brochure: Advance Micro Foundries (AMF) and Mirxes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I discovered that we no longer have any shares in AMF, while in the case of Mirxes, Singapore's first biomedical unicorn, EDB International now holds a less than 2% stake after it was floated, ironically, on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is not about turning Singapore into a Government-run innovation economy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The private sector must remain the primary driver of innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Nor am I suggesting that the Government has been careless in deploying funds.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I understand that our vehicles, such as SG Growth Capital and SGInnovate, have a different mandates.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They operate primarily as catalyst investors, as opposed to being wholly focused on shareholder returns, like Temasek Holdings.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: What I am proposing is a tweaking of our approach.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: When taxpayer funds absorb the early-stage risks of spin-offs and startups from our RIE ecosystem, we can also ensure that we share more meaningfully in the direct upsides.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We want to retain a more tangible and meaningful share in the ventures that we help build.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This means evolving the roles of these Government vehicles from being purely catalyst investors, which seek an exit to move into the next big thing, to becoming strategic partners and long-term shareholders.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: However, we should have no illusions that this will produce quick returns.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The returns would only be substantial only if we can grow a few more unicorns.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But if we succeed, we will do more than just create high-value jobs or strengthen our global relevance.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We will generate enduring national value, create a new and sustainable revenue tap and provide long-term economic benefits for our future generations.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Occasional Paper on Income Growth, Inequality and Social Mobility Trends in Singapore, released not long ago by MOF, underscores both our achievements and our vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We continue to do well in most areas relative to other developed countries.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our social policies, public housing framework and so on have helped keep inequality in check and supported upward mobility.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But the paper also highlights pressure points that we must not ignore.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But meritocracy, if left alone, can create entrenched privilege and inequitable outcomes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our education system is the single greatest equaliser in our meritocratic society.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is here that meritocracy must be most staunchly defended, because it is here that privilege and divisions will strike first and, I think, strike the hardest.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must ensure that our educational pathways, especially at the starting points, remain fair and equitable.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We have built in different pathways to success into the system.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Over the years we have also introduced broader definitions of merit, to recognise diverse strengths and reduce the over-reliance on exam scores.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And we have many examples of successes of the system in this House.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are Members of this House who grew up in very unprivileged circumstances, studied hard, won scholarships and did very well for themselves.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And there are those who faltered at different stages of their educational journey, picked themselves up and came back fighting, succeeded in their goals.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These are classic underdog success stories of our meritocratic system, and we should be proud of all of them.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must look not only at individual success stories, but at broader trends.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: A few inspiring examples do not automatically mean that outcomes are as equitable for everyone.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Parents with higher disposable incomes are better positioned to invest in their children's development, whether through extra tuition and enrichment classes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Many fork out large sums for private lessons in sports, music and coding, all carefully curated to maximise their children's chances in the DSA exercise.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are now coaching academies tailored for entry to the Gifted Education Programme and aptitude tests of specific schools for maths, science and technology DSA.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I was surprised to discover that there are even coaches for DSA-oriented leadership development, entrepreneurship and portfolio preparation.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But we cannot ignore the unintended negative consequences of the DSA in its current form.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: A little while back, I posted a set of oral Parliamentary Questions, to see how DSA and affiliation admissions intersect and what it means for non-affiliated students who are unable to DSA in.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Some were balloted out despite meeting the even more stringent cut-off points for non-affiliated students.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Personally, I think that the arguments for DSA are sound and there are valid reasons for it to continue in some form.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: However, I certainly do not think it should continue in its current form and there are certainly things that we can change structurally to ensure a more equitable system.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is unfair for these students to find themselves crowded out from the race for a particular school even before they get to the starting line.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But what we can and must do is to ensure equal opportunity and equal pathways to everyone.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is the promise of equality as enshrined in our Pledge and the essence of our meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Singapore was built on this simple but powerful promise.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Meritocracy requires active maintenance in this imperfect world and we must be prepared to review, recalibrate and where necessary, restrain policies that bring about negative outcomes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is especially so in education, because this is where the trajectory of a life is first shaped.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Let us first acknowledge the board we are playing on.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Externally, the world economy is becoming more fragmented and less predictable.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Tariff shocks, supply chain re-routing and geopolitical alignment pressures are shortening planning processes and horizons for businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But execution at scale will determine whether this repositioning succeeds.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2026 elevates AI as a national priority to boost productivity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But enabling transformation for SMEs will be the real test.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: AI implementation is expensive – not just software, but data restructuring, cybersecurity, workforce redesign, up-skilling costs of workers and managerial capability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Big firms have both the talent and financial muscle to spread this fixed cost.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs often cannot – if transformation succeeds, gains are gradual; if it fails, losses are immediate.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Through the Champions of AI programme, expanded Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS) for AI expenditure and broader PSG support, Budget 2026 seeks to change the risk equation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The definition of "qualifying AI expenditure" must be unambiguous.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If not, SMEs will misjudge eligibility, misallocate resources and struggle to justify bundled AI costs embedded in broader systems.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Without precision, we risk entrenching a two-speed economy – where large firms execute full transformation while SMEs are left with isolated tools and superficial adoption.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In sectors, such as logistics, F&B, facilities management and manufacturing, robotics may deliver more immediate productivity gains than abstract AI tools.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The rapid deployment of advanced robotics and humanoid systems in China is already reshaping production economics.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Robotics requires high upfront capital and long payback periods, while labour remains the cheaper short-term substitute.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As long as that remains true, firms will default to hiring than automating.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we want AI and robotics to meaningfully raise productivity and preserve competitiveness, the investment signal must decisively shift behaviour at scale.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That suggests a different incentive logic – one that first reduces risk at the point of adoption, and then rewards firms that deliver measurable productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In practical terms, that could include accelerated capital allowances for robotics to improve early-stage cashflow, green-linked automation incentives where AI deployment also reduces energy intensity, and co-investment platforms or shared automation hubs to lower entry barriers for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government, therefore, consider layering outcome-linked incentives on top of entry support?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Without structured managerial uplift, AI support will concentrate in already capable firms and widen the competitive gap.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government consider working with the Singapore Business Federation (SBF), Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) and other trade associations to strengthen sector-specific management upgrading programmes tied directly to AI integration, job redesign and workforce planning?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we professionalise transformation management, adoption will become more even and less risky.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Recent increases in qualifying salary thresholds and adjustments to Local Qualifying Salary reflect a legitimate objective: strengthening the Singaporean core and reinforcing the social compact.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, in SBF's latest National Business Survey, 63% of firms continue to cite manpower costs as a top challenge.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: On the Employment Pass front, higher thresholds raise the cost of specialised expertise, particularly for multinational firms considering Singapore as a regional headquarters (HQ) or Centre of Excellence.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Combined with elevated rental and operating costs, this can influence marginal location decisions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We have already seen instances of HQ relocations with downstream job losses, and these signals warrant close attention.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: On the S Pass front, domestic sectors, such as F&B and retail operate on thin margins and face immediate pressure.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Qualifying salaries are intended to nudge productivity upgrading, but many firms in these sectors have already digitalised and streamlined operations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In sectors where productivity headroom is structurally limited, further cost escalation leaves little room to adjust.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Firms are effectively left with two options: raise prices, affecting consumers and cost of living, or compress operations, reducing service levels and employment scale.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That is the economic reality we must acknowledge.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, there are narratives suggesting future excess manpower in some service sectors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, on the ground, many businesses remain acutely short of workers for operational and frontline roles.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Backend productivity gains do not eliminate the need for human service at the front-end.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As such, where productivity headroom is limited and local supply gaps persist, would the Government consider a more granular, sector-calibrated approach, whether through refinement of the Non-Traditional Source Occupation List or conditional flexibility mechanisms tied to demonstrated upgrading efforts?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If adjustment is delayed until distress becomes acute, closures are sharper and workers more exposed.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Sector-level mapping can identify fragmented industries where consolidation strengthens resilience.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Structured advisory support for mergers and joint ventures, as proposed in SBF's Budget recommendations, can help SMEs scale non-organically before financial stress escalates.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Strategic consolidation can be treated as repositioning and not failure.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, worker transitions must remain swift and credible.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As structural cost pressures and technological change increase the frequency of adjustment, we should approach procedural changes carefully.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Retrenchment incidence remains below the long-term average and re-entry rates remain relatively strong.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Most employers comply with the existing five-day notification requirement.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In that context, before introducing additional procedural rigidity, such as mandatory advance retrenchment notification, we should ask whether shorter timelines would materially improve worker outcomes, or whether they may instead constrain firms during critical restructuring periods.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Most exhaust every option to stabilise operations before acting.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The more constructive question is how to enable early and more orderly adjustment.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Confidential early engagement channels could allow firms to signal emerging restructuring risks while recovery efforts are still ongoing, enabling agencies to prepare redeployment support without compromising commercial sensitivity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The objective should be responsible restructuring, preserving business viability while safeguarding workers through timely and effective support.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The extension of the Senior Employment Credit is welcome.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, wage offsets alone do not address the operational realities employers face.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Older workers often require role redesign, modular reskilling and workplace adjustments to remain productive over a longer career horizon.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs, in particular, face volatility in medical and insurance costs as their workforce ages.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If unmanaged, these uncertainties can become deterrents to hiring and retention.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I had previously suggested that senior and special needs employment be more directly linked to dependency ratio ceiling adjustments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It may also be timely to revisit whether such alignment can better incentivise inclusive workforce participation while maintaining overall labour discipline.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If Singapore is to move ahead of structural tightening, we cannot rely solely on cost efficiency alone.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That requires accelerating commercialisation of IP, particularly among SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We should therefore consider enhancing schemes that embed scientists and research talent directly within SMEs, not only as affordable project-based consultants, but through structured industry attachments that can shorten the path from lab to market.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, IP financing remains underdeveloped.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If Budget 2026 is a positioning Budget, then internationalisation is one of its most important instruments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
