text: For companies prepared to reposition and compete regionally or globally, these measures are helpful.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, emerging markets across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America offer growth, but they also carry higher political, regulatory and receivables risk.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While existing financing schemes provide access to capital, the binding constraint for many SMEs is working capital resilience in higher-risk markets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Many overseas projects are too large or complex for individual SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Procurement frameworks favour size, track record and integrated capability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we want our firms to compete meaningfully, we must move beyond supporting individual expansion towards structured collaboration.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It gives us the tools and sets the direction.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But forcing the move forward cannot be done by Government alone.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call the next Member, I have an announcement to make.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Sell the field, sell the land, just to eat the pomfret's nose.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Why would anyone liquidate their assets for a slice of seafood?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It was about the immeasurable value of a family reunited.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It was about the sacred act of ensuring that once a year, during the reunion dinner, the family table was abundant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: To look at a pomfret on the plate was to see sacrifices made manifest.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It was a constant, delicious reminder, that to provide for those you love, you must be willing to give up everything that we have.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: That same spirit sits on our dining tables, usually unnoticed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For those of us who grew up in the 1950s, 1960s, 1970s and 1980s, this bowl needs no introduction.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It is the chipped ceramic plate at the hawker centre, the bowl that held our grandmother's curry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For families and generations who seldom tasted meat, the printed rooster was more than a decoration.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The rooster crows and is first to rise.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: To see that image on the bowl was to be reminded that prosperity comes from hard work, from the rising with the sun, from the toiling while others sleep.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: First, it reminded us of the taste of a delicious meal and the labour needed to put meat on the table.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: But second and more importantly, it reminded us of home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: And the focus required to feed a family, meant that we understood, viscerally, that there were those who have even less.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Why did this design resonate so deeply in our region?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: You were holding "home." But let us be clear about the context of those meals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Back then, meals were simple, often eaten in haste.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Many of our forefathers were coolies and labourers, trishaw riders and factory workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: They were paid by the bag, by the piece, by the hour.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Lunchtime was downtime and downtime meant less money for the family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: In some traditions, the chopsticks and the spoon are seen as a complete set.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: They represented a life of fullness, of balance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: And that is why, in some funeral rituals, you only see chopsticks provided.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The spoon is absent because the completeness of life is gone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Despite this superstition, there was a harsher reality.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: To eat without a spoon was a sign of a hard life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It meant you were so poor, or so rushed, that you had to shovel food into your mouth with just a pair of chopsticks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Our Pioneers ate at roadside carts, standing up, backs against the wall, shovelling rice because the next lorry was waiting to be unloaded.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It was the pioneering spirit distilled into a meal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Every mouthful was a reminder, "This is why we do what we do.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This is why we sacrifice." I want you to wonder with me for a moment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: So, why did we not make them here?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: What we had was stoneware clay, rich in iron and silica.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: You could not make a delicate, translucent bowl out of it, but you could make something indestructible.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: You could make the dragon jars, People call it "Leng An”, “Giam Chai Ang” or “Geng” the massive ceramic water jars that sat in our bathrooms and kitchens before modern plumbing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Everyone in my generation remembers there was no instant heated water.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It was the cold showers, the plastic ladle, the heavy ceramic jar.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: If you were lucky, someone had boiled water and poured it into the jar to warm it up.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This leads us to the ground beneath our feet.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: If you have ever seen the earth turned over at a construction site in Jurong or at Redhill, you will notice it is not brown.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Singapore’s climate, as we know, high heat, heavy rainfall, is a chemical factory.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Over a millennia, rainwater filters through the ground, washing away soluble minerals, the soft stuff, like silica and magnesium.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: What gets left behind are the, hardier, less soluble minerals, iron and aluminium.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: When iron is exposed to oxygen, it rusts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: When that clay is fired at 1,200 degrees Celsius, the iron acts as a pigment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: With less oxygen, it turns grey or blue.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: With more oxygen, it turns toasty brown or deep red.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We did not have the fine clay, found elsewhere.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: And from that rugged earth, we forged an iron-willed, rugged people.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: As our Founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew famously said, we must have that iron.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: That iron is not just in our soil.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It is in our collective spirit, the character, the mettle, the verve in every Singaporean and in every Singaporean family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Through their lens, we see the joys, the struggles of each family, each diverse, different phases in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Each making the best out of the clay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Among them, three struck the deepest chord in me.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We all have a view of the perfect family dinner.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: For some, it is the TCS Channel 8 drama version.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Everyone gathered around a round table, laughing, passing dishes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: But for most of us, dinner is a time of reflection, of worry, of joy and of challenge.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The first story is of Amin Iskak and Azizah Binte Ahmad.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: After more than 50 years of marriage, they still sit side by side.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Age has slowed them down, but they are never alone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The second story is of Lee Changloong and his family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Many a times, dinner happens in the car, parked by the roadside, with takeaway containers balanced on their laps.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: He knows that time is not something to take for granted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Living with a condition that will gradually limit his mobility, one day he will lose his ability to move.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Every meal with family, is an extraordinary experience, one to be cherished.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: They are the Singapore Spirit, they are the iron which we forged and build together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: As the Malay saying goes, “Bukit sama didaki, lurah sama dituruni.” Hills we climb together, valleys we descend together. rain or shine, we must support these families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This spirit of sacrifice, of saving for the future, extends beyond the family table to the nation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It takes a lifetime to build a family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It takes effort, determination, risk and sacrifice to build a better life for tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It takes incredible forward planning and further sacrifice over generations, for our children to be secure. "前人种树，后人乘凉".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The hardships of one generation lead to the comforts of the next.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We are thankful for the past generations of what some might call "less-than-accurate fiscal marksmanship" for the prudence, the discipline, the refusal to spend everything we had.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: They are our pioneering spirit, forged by unique circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It is this trailblazing spirit that lets us stand tall.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: As we grow in success, as we grow in stature, we must always remember our roots.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: And in Malay, we say “Ikut resmi padi, makin berisi makin tunduk.” Like the padi stalk, the more fruitful we are, the more we bow our heads.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We bow our heads because we remember there are more who are less fortunate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: There are youth who need the guidance of the wise, and there are wise who need the renewed spirit of the youthful.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: May we embrace one another and give collectively.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We may be dusty, we may be earthly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Finance and Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: But in each of us, forged by fire, there is that iron-will in all of us.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Living well is not just about high income, big houses or rapid economic growth.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Living well is more about whether we have time and energy to be with families and whether we have space to explore and grow.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I would like to share three indicators for living well.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, time – a resource that money cannot buy.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the major focuses of this Budget is AI.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support Singapore in keeping pace with the times and embracing AI.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet while productivity has improved with the adoption of AI tools at work, workload has increased instead of decreased.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because the adoption of AI tools has accelerated the pace of work, expanded their scope of work and lengthened their working hours.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I cite this example, hoping that while we embrace AI, we also do not forget to face the potential risk that AI brings.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The risk is not merely that AI eliminates some jobs, but that it leads to job intensification, resulting in workplace burn-out.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore may find ourselves in this situation if we pursued AI adoption without relevant guardrails.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government and Singaporeans to consider not only how AI can help us improve productivity, but also think about how we can leverage emerging technology like AI to reclaim more time that we can spend with family and friends.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, presence – something that cannot be achieved even with time, but without energy.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A topic I often discuss with friends my age and young Tampines residents is that whether to have children.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The biggest consideration is rarely money, but whether we will be an exhausted parent who is physically present but emotionally absent.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We all hope to have sufficient time and energy to good parents who can provide our children with high quality companionship.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will allow more Singaporeans to have time and energy to be with family and friends.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, is space for exploration, which complements time and energy.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While AI can become a substitute for many things, it cannot replace personal experience and judgement.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather than spending more than a year preparing for written exams, we should focus more on cultivating children's empathy, curiosity, creativity and sense of purpose during the critical adolescent period.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is these difficult to measure qualities that will make young Singaporeans shine in the AI era.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do not advance, we will fall back.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must continue to develop and maintain our competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, at the same time, I hope that we do not forget that the basis of a prosperous nation is a people who live good lives.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lives where they have time to be with family.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lives where they have energy to grow their families and accompany their children as they grow.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lives where there is space for exploration so each generation can live better than the previous one.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I will share my observations and suggestions in English. : Speaker, I rise today to offer a complementary perspective as a young millennial Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many of us, the question we want an answer to is not whether Singapore is competitive.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is whether Singapore is still a place where we can live well.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wrote this speech in an attempt to answer one question that I believe is core for Singapore, as we chart our next phase: "What does it mean to live well in Singapore?" In his Budget speech, the Prime Minister spoke of growth, innovation and resilience.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are important, but a good life is not only built on GDP per capita or AI adoption rates.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is built on time – time for the people we love.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is built on presence – the ability to be there for our families and communities.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And it is built on space – space for Singaporeans to grow, to explore and to become themselves.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Budget 2026 already speaks extensively to Singapore's competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, today, I would like to speak about Singapore's liveability, because for my generation, these are not one and the same thing.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A significant portion of the Prime Minister's Budget speech was devoted to AI.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, AI will reshape how we work, how businesses compete and how public services are delivered.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support the ambition to harness AI as a strategic advantage, but I also want to acknowledge something that many Singaporeans feel but few are saying out loud – that AI fatigue is real.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the feeling that no matter how fast we learn, the ground is always shifting beneath us.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the worry that tools meant to make us more productive to make our lives easier are actually leaving us with more to do.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A recent Harvard Business Review article shared the findings from an ongoing study which tracks how generative AI changed work habits at a US-based technology company with more than 200 staff over eight months.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The researchers warned that what looks like higher productivity in the short run can mask silent workload creep and growing cognitive strains as employees juggle multiple AI-enabled work streams and tasks.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over time, it will become harder to differentiate between genuine productivity gains and unsustainable intensity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For employees, the cumulative effect is fatigue and burn-out.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This matters for Singapore, especially as we call on more Singaporeans to embrace AI at work.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The evidence suggests that the risk is not only job displacement, but also job intensification.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The risk is not that AI replaces us, though it will replace some jobs, but that it makes us run faster on the same treadmill.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: AI adoption without guardrails will not give Singaporeans their time back.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government and all Singaporeans to think about not just how AI can make us more productive, but also about how it can give us our time back.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore's average full-time working week stands at nearly 44 hours, not including unpaid overtime work.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is among the highest in a developed world.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sixty-one percent of Singaporean employees report feeling exhausted.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without deliberate policy choices, they tend to remain employer gains.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If AI can automate routine tasks, what comes next should not only be what additional tasks can be added to an employee's plate at work.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps it is that they leave the office on time most days to have dinner with their families and not only on quarterly "Eat With Your Family" day.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, the Prime Minister spoke of building a "we first" society – a society where we look out for each other, volunteer and contribute.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support this vision, but realising it requires something that money cannot buy – time.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A "we first" society needs people who have the time and energy to show up for each other – and I hope this will be one of the design goals of our national AI strategy and not an afterthought.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This brings me to presence, which requires both time and energy.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I want to share tidbits from conversations with friends, peers and young Tampines residents about growing our families, about having a child or having another one.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They begin with a pause, sometimes a sigh and then almost always a shared concern that we cannot be the parents that we want to be – present, engaged, patient, even after a long day at work – instead of giving in to screen time because we are exhausted and need a moment of peace.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 2021 Marriage and Parenthood Survey shows that over 90% of married Singaporeans want to have two or more children.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reality, however, is that over half of these married Singaporeans had only one or no children.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This gap between aspiration and reality is not a gap in desire.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Young Singaporeans today are not overwhelmed because we do not try hard enough.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are overwhelmed because we are encouraged to get married, to have children, to remain in the workforce, to upskill, to embrace AI, to volunteer and to care for our ageing parents so they can age in place.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet policies and workplace culture have not fully caught up.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Budget 2026 contains welcome measures for families, ranging from additional child Life SG credits, enhanced preschool subsidies and extended means-testing support.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These will help us to better support Singaporean families as they grow and age and hopefully, lead to higher fertility and stronger family outcomes.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And finally, Mr Speaker, I would like to speak about space.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have spoken about time and how the economy consumes it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have also spoken about presence and how families need it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now I want to talk about something that connects the two – whether our system leaves ample space for our people, especially our youths, to grow, explore and become themselves.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Budget speaks of the importance of strengthening AI literacy and ensuring that young Singaporeans develop rigorous foundations, so they use AI wisely and not as a shortcut.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree and would like to ask, what are rigorous foundations in a world where AI can generate code, analyse large datasets and even compose music?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, the competitive advantage is no longer what we know, but who we are – our capacity for empathy; for creativity that comes from lived experience and not pattern recognition; our ability to sit with uncertainty and not be consumed by anxiety; and our willingness to try something difficult, fail and try again.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome the long overdue comprehensive review of our education system.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If AI is going to change the nature of work, then surely it must also change what we value in education.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And changing what we value, requires changing how we measure.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a rational response to a system that sorts early and sorts sharply.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSLE, for all of its merits in maintaining a set of standards, should not be defining a child's sense of self-worth at an age where they should be discovering who they are and what they care about.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not calling for us to abandon the bell curve.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am calling for a rethink of how we use it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When access to opportunities is too tightly tied to early academic performance, those of us who take longer to find our footing may find some doors closing before we have even had a chance to knock.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This space in our education system should be complemented by space in our economy.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome the Budget's emphasis on lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lifelong learning for youths of today may also mean lifelong experimentation – the freedom and space to pursue different paths, combine different strengths and to build a working life that reflects who we are and not just what the market demands of us at the present.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of our youths are already doing this.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are building portfolio careers, combining roles, projects and pursuits that do not fit neatly into a single job title.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not a collection of side hustles.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a reimagining of work that values flexibility, autonomy and personal growth.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, I am for growth, I am for staying competitive, I am for the adoption of AI.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore must remain economically vibrant, strategically relevant and globally connected.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Budget 2026 is titled "Securing our Future in a Changed World".

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support this aspiration and I humbly suggest that securing our future is not only about securing our competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is about securing the conditions for a good life; a life of time for the people we love, a life where we can be present for our children, our parents and our communities; a life within our space in our schools, in our workplaces and in our neighbourhoods, for people to grow into who they are meant to become.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For six decades, we have built a culture that equates progress with movement.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has made many of us, including myself, feel guilty when we are still, because if we are not striving, then, surely, we must be falling behind.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps this explains why the Pace of Life project conducted by Prof Richard Wiseman found that we are some of the fastest pedestrians in the world.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Well, sometimes progress is indeed about moving forward, but sometimes, as I have learnt after leaving my first job at 31, progress is about floating, catching our breath, looking around, noticing things that we would have otherwise missed when we are rushing from point A to point B.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe Singaporeans are ready for a conversation about what we are willing to prioritise to build a Singapore that is both successful and sustainable.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government will be brave enough to measure what matters most; to trust Singaporeans with flexibility, with dignity and with a little more space to breathe and to be human.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.11 pm until 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The world around us is becoming more fragmented, more contested and less predictable.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: In this environment, resilience cannot exist only in our fiscal numbers or economic forecasts.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It must be felt on the ground, by our seniors, our hawkers and our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I will focus on these three pillars of grounded resilience.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore's ageing population is no longer something we talk about as a future issue.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: We should celebrate the fact that we are living longer.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Longer life expectancy reflects the strength of our healthcare system and our social policies.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But living longer must also mean living with security and with purpose.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If seniors feel uncertain or anxious about their future, that anxiety does not remain isolated.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It affects families and ultimately, it affects society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: As life expectancy rises, retirement itself is changing.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Many seniors today are healthy, experienced and still eager to contribute.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: So, the question we should ask ourselves is: are our systems ready for multi-stage careers?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: We could pilot structured second-career pathways in sectors where labour demand remains strong – healthcare support, community care, logistics coordination, SME administration – these pathways can combine modular training, job redesign and clear placement opportunities for workers aged 55 and above.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: While SkillsFuture is broad-based, some older workers may benefit from shorter, very practical modules directly tied to specific job roles.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: A clearly identified "Senior Skills Track" could lower psychological barriers and encourage more to step forward.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: We should also recognise that information today can feel fragmented.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Employment support, CPF matters, healthcare schemes and long-term care arrangements sits across different platforms.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: A more consolidated, senior-focused interface – even if it is simply a navigational layer – would go a long way in improving clarity and confidence.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, supporting seniors is not just about financial adequacy.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is about dignity, contribution and about sustaining inter-generational trust.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: And that trust strengthens us, especially in uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: When we talk about hawkers, we often speak of heritage and culture, and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But we must also remember: hawkers are small business owners operating on very tight margins.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, hawker centres are shared community spaces, places where Singaporeans from all walks of life gather.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: In a fragmented world, such shared spaces matter even more.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, rising rental pressures, volatile input costs and manpower constraints are placing real strain on many stallholders.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If costs continue to outpace revenues, the risk is not just about business closures.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: We risk weakening a layer of our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Publishing periodic rental sustainability indicators, even at an aggregate level, can reassure hawkers and the public that rental frameworks remain aligned with operating realities.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: On digitalisation, grants are available, but adoption is not just about funding.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Structured advisory support, perhaps expanded through hawker associations, can help stallholders with cost control, inventory management and digital payments, that will improve productivity without losing authenticity.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Pairing retiring hawkers with aspiring entrants through structured mentorship and phased handovers could preserve know-how while reducing entry risks for newcomers.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is about preserving everyday infrastructure that holds our communities together.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: They create jobs, anchor supply chains and generate domestic value.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But today, they face a dual challenge – geopolitical uncertainty and rapid technological change.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Budget 2026 strengthens financing schemes, internationalisation support and AI-related incentives.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: However, for many SMEs, the issue is no longer awareness.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Sector-specific AI playbooks, developed with trade associations, could provide practical, step-by-step roadmaps tailored to industries such as logistics, retail, professional services and F&B.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Shared advisory models within industry clusters could allow SMEs to access transformation expertise without bearing the full cost alone.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: We could also streamline grant processes through pre-approved solution bundles for common transformation projects that will reduce friction and speed up adoption.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: In some cases, SMEs within the same sector could even pool resources to invest in shared AI tools or digital infrastructure – that will achieve scale without overstretching their balance sheets.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If SMEs upgrade decisively, they strengthen both employment resilience and long-term competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But societal resilience determines whether that stability lasts.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If we strengthen participation for seniors, sustainability for hawkers and capability for SMEs, we build resilience that is both economic and social.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: In a changed and uncertain world, that layered strength will determine whether Singapore simply adapts or continues to lead.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This shows that rigorous debate in this House matters.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But Sir, the context has shifted – again.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Three years ago, the world was captivated by generative AI (GenAI).

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Agentic systems do not just predict or generate content.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They act with bounded autonomy and they improve through iteration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In other words, agents will not just assist work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are a small, open economy with no natural resources and limited land.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Productivity growth, therefore, must come from expanding capability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We cannot compete on scale or spend, but we compete on coordination, trust, governance and execution.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We may not build the largest frontier models or global AI platforms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we can build the most trusted agentic systems and applications – AI that is safe, accountable and designed for real industries.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With agentic AI, we can multiply cognitive capacity at national scale.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A leading bank in Singapore is already deploying Agentic AI to deliver what it calls "bionic" wealth management.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI Agents now conduct real time portfolio assessments, recommend personalised offerings and send tailored outreach material, all in seconds.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This frees the Relationship Manager to focus on judgement, relationships and strategy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is the opportunity: AI handling complexity at speed, while humans exercise wisdom.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, the question is not whether Singapore will use AI – we will.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The question is where the value will sit?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If the core systems are all designed elsewhere, the standards are all written elsewhere, we may use AI extensively, but see much of the value be captured elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We will optimise workflows, but not own the intellectual property.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We will upgrade processes, but remain dependent on other people's roadmaps.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our workers may use AI, but the highest value jobs will sit elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But if we build capability here, design systems here, govern standards here, then higher value work, higher productivity and higher wages will sit here.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Every Budget, we discuss vouchers, rebates and support packages.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They make a real difference to my Woodlands residents and to other Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They help families cope with this year's prices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But what determines whether families truly get ahead, in the years ahead, is not vouchers, but jobs and wages.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And this is about ensuring that our Singaporean families' incomes rise faster than prices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Small states do not get many opportunities to lead and to shape global frameworks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Leadership in the core systems that AI runs on; interoperability and audit standards; governance frameworks that are trusted internationally.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We should have open R&D agendas, cross sector labs and build cross border innovation models, partnering with global AI platforms, AI startups and talent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I would look to sectors where, one, we already have strong data infrastructure; two, trust and regulation matter; and three, coordination complexity is high and the value of intelligent coordination is high.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These sectors present opportunities to design, govern, deploy and export agentic AI solutions and governance frameworks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In finance, think autonomous compliance agents, real-time regulatory reporting and cross-border risk management.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Exportable "RegTech agents" that embed Singapore's regulatory philosophy – transparent, rules based, trusted – cementing our position as a global finance hub.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In healthcare, hospital workflow optimisation, preventive health monitoring, care-coordination agents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With one of the fastest-ageing populations in Asia, we can become a testbed for systems that reduce administrative burden on clinicians and support community nurses and caregivers and export these solutions to other ageing societies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In logistics and connectivity, orchestration agents that dynamically optimise supply chains, predict congestion or autonomous trade documentation agents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It will make the world's busiest port also the world's most intelligent port.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In urban systems and sustainability, our Smart Nation Infrastructure provides rich datasets.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI transformation, agentic or not, is costly and capital intensive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It requires compute, system integration, workflow redesign, cybersecurity, governance infrastructure and workforce re-training.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It will take years, not months, and it cannot run on annual budgeting cycles.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Champions of AI must not just be showcases that inspire.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They should publish playbooks, host cross-sector learning, mentor SMEs and bring along their supply chains and share implementation frameworks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because the true measure of a Champion is not how far ahead it moves but how many others it pulls forward.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I talk now about the organisational shift – from pyramid to diamond.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For over a century, organisations have been shaped like pyramids.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Few decision-makers at the top; a broad based of individual contributors, executing day to day operations; and layers of middle management, coordinating work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A narrower base, where AI agents handle routine work; a strong, skilled middle, responsible for supervising, designing and orchestrating of fleets of intelligent systems; and a strategic apex focused on judgement and direction.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not every sector will move at the same pace.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Construction or patient-facing healthcare roles will evolve more slowly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But in fields, like software development, marketing and customer service, the change will come sooner than you know it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, we must prepare Singaporeans for the middle of that diamond.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In a diamond-shaped organisation, the middle layer becomes more important, not less.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They must not only demonstrate AI literacy; they must master AI supervision and orchestration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They must be able to frame problems, direct AI agents, curate inputs, validate outputs, apply domain judgement and ethical reasoning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not humans versus AI; but humans with AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, entry-level jobs may narrow in sectors adopting the diamond-shaped organisation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must act early and create meaningful pathways into work for graduates and tertiary students.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we train our children to memorise, AI will outpace them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we train our children to question, to synthesise, to exercise judgement, AI will be their multiplier.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because in the age of agentic AI, the scarce resource is not information.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, we must modernise our human resources (HR) in career frameworks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In a diamond-shaped organisation, progression may no longer mean managing ever larger teams of people, but larger and more complex fleets of AI agents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Performance systems must recognise those who deploy AI effectively to increase output, accuracy and quality or to create new value.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we fail to modernise our institutional frameworks, we risk stagnation – not because Singaporeans cannot adapt, but because our institutions did not.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is a risk we must confront directly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But multipliers widen gaps unless access is equal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If higher-income households deploy AI to accelerate learning, entrepreneurship and career progression while lower-income households lack access, capability and confidence, inequality will compound.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI literacy cannot stop at universities, polytechnics, schools or corporate reskilling.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It must reach my most vulnerable Woodlands residents and across Singapore, who are already navigating multiple stressors in life.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must recognise the effort and responsibility our residents already show in working, learning and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The model includes case workers, customised action plans, milestone-based incentives and long-term engagement.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That architecture is actually what AI inclusion requires.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI literacy cannot be delivered as a one-off workshops.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Supported by AI coaches, we ensure every Singaporean has the skills to supervise AI; the tools to deploy AI; the confidence to question AI; and ultimately, equal access to opportunities in AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is the type of inclusion that ensures national multiplication, not division.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And if our AI strategy does not translate into higher wages and better opportunities for all Singaporeans, will we recalibrate our approach to ensure the value created by AI accrues meaningfully to Singaporean workers and families?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is a redesign of how value is created and how organisations function.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must build a nation that does not merely use AI but orchestrates it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But we must ensure our green transition is not sidelined by its energy demands.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Resilience requires addressing the inherent trade-offs of such growth.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Building on my previous Budget speeches, I will also be speaking on other pertinent aspects of green transition and healthcare issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, as we double down on this AI push with tax deductions and the new One North AI Park, we must not lose sight of the unseen costs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: During the Committee of Supply debate for the Prime Minister's Office last year, I raised a cut specifically on the staggering increase in energy and carbon use that comes with generative AI.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I cautioned then that an indiscriminate rush to integrate large-scale models for every minor task is a luxury our carbon-constrained nation cannot afford.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the Government has introduced the Green Data Centre Road Map, the current pace of AI adoption may risk outstripping our efficiency gains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are seeing a rebound effect, where more efficient hardware is being used as a rationale for allowing exponentially higher usage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is not enough to have green data centres if the AI models running within them are fundamentally wasteful.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must not be the target for the migration of inefficient workloads to regions with fewer software level environmental regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must also mandate transparency for the software that consumes energy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Just as importantly, I am concerned that recent move to allow more data centre construction will enable data centres to outcompete households and smaller businesses in Singapore in electricity purchases with the majority of our low carbon electricity import projects still in early development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Green electrons continue to be in short supply in Singapore, over the next few years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On one hand, households and small businesses may not benefit from the greening of the grid remaining exposed to the virality of the global gas market at a time of geopolitical unrest.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, Singapore's latest data centre requirements are relatively lax compared to other advanced states.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If data centre developers want to benefit from Singapore's strategic location, they should also play their part in supporting grid reliability and the development of further renewable electricity capacity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And while I do accept that the Government has taken steps to accelerate the expansion of renewable electricity availability in Singapore, setting up the Future Energy Fund and the Singapore Energy Interconnections, the roadmap still needs to be clearer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: True leadership in AI is not about the number of AI champions we can produce but about how sustainably we can grow this sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As I stated in my Prime Minister's Office cut last year, by being an early adopter of carbon-conscious AI regulations, Singapore can turn our resource constraints into a competitive advantage, exporting sustainable AI expertise to a world that is increasingly waking up to the ecological cause of the global AI race.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have consistently argued that Singapore's green transition must be more than a collection of ambitious targets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It must be transparent, inclusive and socially just process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am particularly heartened by his firm commitment that despite global trends, retreating from climate action is not an option for our own nation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Belem outcome was a pivotal moment, highlighting that that adaption is not just about engineering.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While our current strategy addresses coastal and heat resilience, I urge the Government to more explicitly integrate the Belem pillars of biodiversity and poverty and livelihoods into our national climate framework.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our current focus on infrastructure must be matched by a commitment to the social and ecological dimensions of the climate crisis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In Belem, the Mutirao Decision emphasised that climate action must be people-centred.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We need a plan that tracks not just the height of our sea walls, but the resilience of our homes against the urban heat island effect, including but not limited to challenges of rising cooling costs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This leads me to the urgent need to protect our biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As I argued in my Adjournment Motion last month, we must fundamentally rethink how we justify the trade-offs between development and the preservation of our existing green spaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must plan for the resilience of our homes against the urban heat island effect, including rising cooling costs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This requires us to value existing green forested sites as strategic green belts, even if they are not original primary forests and have been subject to previous development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This requires a more transparent approach to land use that recognises the inherent climate value of our natural ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is strategically superior to preserve existing green belts for heat mitigation, such as the Serangoon River Forest, than to rely on artificial parks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I call on Ministry of National Development (MND) to institutionalise mandatory functional assessment for all forested sites before any developments to protect these vital assets and will elaborate on this at the COS.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We need clarity on whether the current owners' lease includes mandatory decarbonisation milestones to prevent Bukom from becoming a carbon haven where emissions are simply offloaded to new entities rather than reduced.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beyond infrastructure, we must also address the human costs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, we must apply this same rigour to land transport.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Industry observers have said that this is likely to dampen industry demand for non-electric vehicles (non-EVs), as this will increase the depreciation of non-EV cars while EVs are unlikely to be affected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Prior to the recent PARF announcement, the resale cliff has been a growing risk.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As of 1 January 2026, the Early Adoption Incentive rebate cap has dropped to $7,500 and used EVs are taking longer to sell than internal combustion engine cars, resulting in the decline of EVs' resale value.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I urge the Government to study consumer concerns about EV battery longevity and replacement costs and consider how to strengthen consumer confidence in this area.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While electric cars have increased despite having their own issues, motorcycle adoption remains stuck at a mere 0.2%.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the Ministry consider upfront purchase incentive for motorcycles to bridge this gap?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A transition is only green if it does not leave our workers or our residents in the raid.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our people need a transition that is fair, funded and fundamentally just.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I spoke about the overlooked issue of dental care in our healthcare system in my Budget debate speech last year and I welcomed the announcement during the Ministry of Health's (MOH's) COS debate for higher dental subsidies and flexi-Medisave use for patients aged 60 and above for root canal treatments and permanent crowns at Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) clinics and public healthcare institutions last year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But I still hope more can be done.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A recent longitudinal study by the Centre for Ageing, Research and Education at Duke-NUS Medical School revealed that nearly one-third of our seniors have not seen a dentist in over five years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Assoc Prof Rahul Malhotra noted, many visit only when they have a problem but missing the window for prevention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Poor oral health, such as untreated tooth decay, gum disease, ill-fitting dentures or tooth loss, has important consequences.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Dr Eugene Tang, President of Singapore Dental Association opined in a recent letter to The Straits Times that it can affect chewing ability and nutrition, leading to unintended weight loss, reduce muscle strength and increased frailty.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: According to NHG Health, the proportion at-risk of malnutrition among hospital patients aged 65 and above rose from three in 10 in 2022 to four in 10 in 2024.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Preventive care is the heart of healthy ageing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yet, dental care remains excluded from our national preventive scheme – Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For the third time in this House, I call for dental care to be integrated into Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must treat oral health as a basic pillar of well-being, not an optional extra.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Healthier SG connects us to a family doctor clinic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They will help manage our chronic diseases and monitors our health habits and carries out preventive care that can help us stay healthy and active.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The same is needed for preventive care for good oral health.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And to better care for our seniors, we must also prioritise improving affordability and accessibility of preventive care for oral health.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Affordability of dental care remains an issue for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, patients referred to tertiary institutions, like the National Dental Centre for complicated procedures, often due to pre-existing frailty, find themselves ineligible for the same Pioneer Generation CHAS subsidies they will receive at the polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My hon friend, Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Member, Kenneth Leong's recent Parliamentary Question, asked about extending subsidies for complex denture cases that had to be referred to a tertiary institution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A letter to The Straits Times' Forum Page by Mr Stephen Tan described a similar situation where his 83-year-old mother's teeth extraction had to be done at the National Dental Centre satellite clinic at Changi General Hospital due to fear of complications.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While intended to curb over consumption and rightly so, this shift, combined with rising premiums may drive many to abandon private healthcare, potentially overwhelming our public search capacity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For many seniors with pre-existing conditions, retaining an IP is not a luxury.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yet, many find it frustrating that their hard-earned MediSave savings are locked once they hit the basic healthcare sum.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At age 65, any excess is moved by \default to the Retirement Account.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This will allow them to withdraw funds specifically for IP premiums.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By helping Singaporeans maintain their private insurance, we moderate the demand on our public system, ensuring national healthcare delivery remains sustainable for all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, the Budget proposes to accelerate the development of AI, establish a national AI Council and launch multiple industry AI programmes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, I already raised during the Committee of Supply debate for the Prime Minister's Office last year that the energy consumption and carbon emission of generative AI are growing very rapidly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can we talk about green transition on one hand whilst underestimating the urgency of this programme on the other?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We cannot become a destination for high energy workload transfers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should require large AI companies to disclose energy data to protect the interests of the national grid and taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Whilst promoting digital transformation, we must also care for seniors with lower digital capabilities to ensure that they are not left behind in this wave of AI development. : Mr Deputy Speaker, let me round up my speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We cannot achieve our 2040 and 2050 targets with a slow-charged mindset that ignores the practical realities of our people, whether we are discussing the carbon footprints of AI, the hurdles of EV adoption or the fundamental right to affordable dental care, the common thread is clear.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A transition is only green if it is also just.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Notwithstanding my concerns and clarifications, I support the Budget.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: I support this Budget and its emphasis on strengthening opportunities, supporting families and enabling Singaporeans at different life stages to progress with confidence.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: My remarks today are, therefore, offered in the spirit of constructive support.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: As we consider the spirit of a “we first” society, it may be useful to examine not only what support is provided but how policy initiatives shape the capacity of Singaporeans to participate meaningfully in shared institutions, such as schools, workplaces and community networks across the life course.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Research in human development suggests that positive long-term outcomes are influenced not only by access to programmes, but by the extent to which individuals remain embedded in common social institutions through key transitions in life, such as entry into post-secondary education and employment.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: From this perspective, I would like to offer four questions that may serve as a lens for considering how initiatives within this Budget strengthen Singapore’s social foundations over time.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: First, does the initiative enable participation in common social life or does it primarily deliver services within specialised settings?

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: While specialised supports are often necessary for competence-building and protection, their long-term effectiveness depends on whether they ultimately scaffold participation in everyday life.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: The question, therefore, is not whether specialised supports are needed, but how they connect individuals back into common settings over time.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Second, do our institutional arrangements connect people across life domains or do they channel them into separate tracks?

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Life course research suggests that systems which bridge education, employment, healthcare and family life are more often able to sustain continuity in developmental pathways.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: In contrast, fragmented or categorised service structures may inadvertently introduce discontinuities that may constrain participation or mobility across transitions.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Many policies provide valuable programmes, but the coordination of care, the navigation of services and the sustaining of participation are often undertaken by families or professionals.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: An approach that places disproportionate reliance on a single individual increases the likelihood of cumulative strain and, over time, heightens the risk of stress and burn-out.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Correspondingly, it is important to consider whether those involved are adequately supported.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Evidence from co-production and community development suggests that outcomes are strengthened when families and communities are engaged, not only as recipients of services but as partners in institutional design and delivery, thereby supporting sustained engagement and reducing risks of disengagement over time.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Taken together, these questions invite us to consider how policy investments can influence participation trajectories over life stages and particularly at transition points.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: For many families, one of the most significant transitions occurs when their child exits the formal education system at about 18 years of age.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: This transition often entails a loss of structured routines, peer networks and community participation, while families navigate a new landscape of adult services.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: As the capacity of DACs expands, it may be helpful to consider how transition pathways connect individuals across education, employment and community life.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Anchoring transition supports within community-based employment partnerships, shared-use facilities or neighbourhood organisations can help ensure that the specialised supports continue to scaffold participation in everyday institutional life over time.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, developmental vulnerability is often closely intertwined with family stressors, such as housing instability or caregiver fatigue.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, we may wish to consider how our resourcing for programmes in early childhood connects families across domains of daily life.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Strengthening linkages between preschools and services that support families may enable caregivers, not only to access programmes, but to sustain the support of their child or children's development within the home and community environments in which the children spend most of their time.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: From a developmental perspective, youth transitions are not only about access to opportunity but about participation in the institutions and communities they will inherit.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Platforms, such as Youth Panels, may therefore be understood not only as consultative mechanisms but as opportunities for co-production that can strengthen engagement, persistence and alignment between institutions and the developmental needs of young persons.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: And for these reasons, I support the Budget.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If our goal is not just to get through the next year, but to thrive for the long term, what should an ideal Budget prioritise?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But not productivity in the narrow sense of GDP or output.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: True productivity is about enabling people to realise their full potential – our young, our mid-career workers, our seniors who continue to contribute and our persons with disabilities who deserve full opportunity to do so.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We rely entirely on our people – their skills, resilience, values and unity.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If we want to stay competitive and cohesive, we must invest in enabling every Singaporean to reach their potential.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Productivity is not about squeezing more from people.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Even in a more uncertain world, we are fortunate to discuss this from a position of fiscal strength.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: With surpluses last year and this year, we have the capacity to invest prudently and strategically in our people.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In every Budget, there are two responsibilities: to provide support and to invest.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Support reduces inequality and ensures no one is left behind.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Investment unlocks potential, because if people cannot reach their potential, the economy cannot either.
