speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They have clear aspirations: good jobs, affordable housing, meaningful careers, stable paths to marriage and family and lives with purpose.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At my Meet-the-People Sessions, housing concerns often surface.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Decisions about flats are tied to life decisions – marriage, career stability and family planning.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This was also reflected in the PAP Policy Forum’s Pre-Budget Survey.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Many also flagged family-raising as a major worry.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When cost pressures weigh heavily, aspirations become cautious.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This shows that the issue is not simply job creation but whether jobs enable growth.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: For long-term productivity, young people must see credible and coordinated pathways ahead.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This means continued investment in strong school-to-work transitions, better skills-job matching, predictable housing supply, mid-career mobility support, and accessible lifelong learning frameworks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When aspirations are supported by stable pathways in jobs, housing and skills, people can plan confidently.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And when they plan confidently, they commit to families, careers and to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But our youth are not just beneficiaries of policy, they want to contribute.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When they feel trusted and supported, they step forward.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Supporting aspirations is just part of the equation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We are raising a generation that is capable but also under pressure.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They face academic competition, social comparison fueled by technology, economic uncertainties and rapid AI-driven change.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Access to courses is not the same as confidence, training enrolment is not the same as career stability.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As we embrace artificial intelligence, we must also not neglect another "AI" – actual intelligence.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Our people must know how to use it, but also how to question it.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We must nurture judgment, empathy, critical thinking and moral reasoning.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In my maiden speech, I spoke about the paradoxes of technology: tools that can connect can also isolate; convenience can erode capability.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If we let machines think for us without strengthening our own thinking, we risk weakening the qualities that make us adaptable and innovative.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: In my classrooms, I see bright young students already worried about burnout before their careers begin.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They are asking whether they can keep up without losing themselves.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If productivity depends on human capacity, resilience must be part of our economic strategy.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We must invest in school-based mental health support, workplace mental wellness frameworks, community sports and physical activity, curriculum that builds emotional regulation and bounce-back ability, soft skills that help navigate setbacks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: These measures matter for students, mid-career workers adapting to change and seniors staying engaged.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A burnt-out population cannot be a productive one.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Resilience is not a side issue; it is the foundation of sustainable growth.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Managing pressure is not only about coping, it is also about shaping social norms.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If success is defined narrowly by grades, pay or title, we risk creating pressure and weakening cohesion.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Success is knowing your work – whether in business, arts, sports or service – matters to your community.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Our identity as Singaporeans must embrace the diversity of talent through culture and arts, sports and teamwork, academic and technical excellence, entrepreneurship and service.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When young people see that there are many legitimate ways to contribute, they feel seen; and when they feel seen, they step forward.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This is why continued investment in youth engagement, culture, arts, sports and community initiatives matter.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They build belonging, shape identity and strengthen a "we first" mindset.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When people feel included, they contribute with confidence.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And when they feel part of something larger, they act differently.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I have seen this spirit of agency in Tampines.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: After residents raised concerns about near-misses, I brought these to him and a group of advocates.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: He stepped forward, organised others and worked constructively with the authorities.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Singapore has no natural resources; our greatest resource is our people.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When young people have stable jobs and affordable housing, they can plan their lives with peace of mind and start families and careers.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When middle-aged workers receive support during transitions, they can continue to contribute their experience and skills.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When seniors feel respected and needed, they can remain active and continue participating in society.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If we invest only in machines, we may grow output.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But if we invest in people, we grow a nation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When people feel supported in their aspirations, equipped to manage pressure and confident that success is defined fairly, they do not disengage.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They carry forward the values that built Singapore.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is about ensuring the next generation is resilient, capable, inclusive and united.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is in our people across every generation, especially those who will carry Singapore forward.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Because when our people realise their potential, Singapore realises hers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Many of us find it hard to picture what the world will look like in the years to come.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: There is the geopolitics, a world that feels less stable, less predictable and less governed by rules that we can rely on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And then there is AI, which, in some ways, feels even more unsettling because it is not happening out there in some distant theatre, it is happening all around us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In the classrooms that our children will enter, in the industries that Singapore has spent decades building.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: My husband and I wanted to protect our two children from online content.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They are still very young, so we decided to try and stop giving them screentime sometime last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I told them that Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said "Screentime is bad." They looked a little bit confused, and it was tough for us for two weeks, but since then, they hardly ask for screens anymore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But I know that this artificial safety will not last.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They will have friends or classmates who will tell them about the fun and exciting AI content online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They may learn about the companion AI tools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: They will need to differentiate between content generated by humans versus AI and they may ask: "What is the point of striving to learn and becoming good at something if AI can do it so much faster?" All of this can feel very frightening whether we have kids or not.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: My fellow colleagues may share some of them during the Committee of Supply debates, but there is no new list of programmes that you will hear from me.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Instead, I wanted to try to address three hard questions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: What is really changing, what will not change and what must we do together?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, when young Singaporeans tell me that they worry that what they are learning today in school will be obsolete by the time they graduate, I do not brush that aside.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Many are already encountering this as they start to apply for jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And when workers in their 40s and 50s tell me they have spent twenty years building expertise in a domain but now worry that AI is helping junior colleagues close that gap much faster.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I do not tell them that their concern is misplaced because all of their anxieties are rational.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But what matters more is what we do with it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I asked AI to give me an analogy of itself.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It suggested the following with very nice elaborations for each suggestion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Bicycle, electricity, calculator, turbo engine, all of these sound very useful.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Then I asked it, give me the scary analogies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: AI suggested fire, pandoras box, trojan horse, puppet master, among others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The range of answers in itself is telling, because that is exactly the question we have not yet settled as a society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: What is our relationship with AI and who gets to decide?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We know that AI can give us significant economic edge and amplifies the abilities of our people, but we have to carefully define our relationship with AI as individuals and as a society and we can only do so if we first get to know AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We need to first understand what it is, what it is capable of.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We must understand the motivations of the people behind it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We must understand the risks and the invisible dangers that it can come with, and understand how vulnerable you can be to it, even if you think you are the most educated person in the room.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: A world where everything is changing feels unsettling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But there are some things that will not change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: What will not change, is the value of genuine relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Relationships that build trust and deep human connection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In my dialogues with young Singaporeans, many can see clearly how AI makes their lives more convenient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But when I ask them, "What you do with the time freed up?", they pause.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Some will murmur, "Sleep", some say, "League of Legends", and a few say they will spend more time with their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The things that make a life feel worth living – being known and loved by a real human, building something and celebrating achievements with other people, showing up for people when it is hard – AI cannot replicate these.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And the more automated our world becomes, the more these human connections and capacities will define what differentiates us from the machines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: What will also not change is the need for human accountability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And accountability means developing AI governance frameworks that are robust and ethical.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It means being more transparent with citizens about how AI is being used in Government services and allowing them to still connect with human Public Service officers, if they need to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: AI can process, but it cannot be held responsible on its own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: AI can generate lots of options, but it cannot own the consequences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will still need humans: for ethics; for creativity and imagination; and for the ability to look someone else in the eye and say, "I take responsibility for this." So, what do we do?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our education system has consistently produced people who can learn and relearn, not just people who know things.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We have a population that takes education seriously, that invests in their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Our people are discerning and curious about the latest technologies available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Mid-career workers are reskilling, not just because they are told to, but because the system makes it practical and financially accessible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will build on this and guide Singaporeans towards the capabilities and qualities that AI cannot replicate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In Singapore, we have a labour union that is aware of the impact of AI on workers and already putting together plans to make sure that we are ready for the workforce disruptions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: So, we are starting from a good position.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But we need more people to learn about AI and learn how to use AI, and not just observe to see which way things settle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Moving, building and doing, does not mean rushing or speeding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It means getting started and moving at a pace most suitable for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And whether you are an employer, a worker, a student, a teacher or a parent, the mission is to turn your anxiety into action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: For our businesses, especially our SMEs, who form the backbone of our economy, you do not need to have all the answers before you begin.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We heard in our Economic Strategy Review committee consultations that many SMEs feel they cannot afford to be guinea pigs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The hackathons and collaborations between students, SMEs and business leaders over the past year were not just photo opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In those sessions, our SMEs got access to low-cost AI prototyping.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The students gained domain experience and learnt about real problems that businesses deal with on a daily basis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Business leaders spotted talent they then went on to hire.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We will systematise this, to ensure that more SMEs and students benefit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But we must also make sure that our SMEs, most of whom are genuine and often already tight on resources, we must make sure they do not get turned away too early by onerous and cumbersome paperwork.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: These are all ideas that our Economic Strategy Review Committee 2 on Technology and Innovation will continue to work on in the months ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And we are encouraged that the Prime Minister had mention many of our recommendations in his Budget Speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: For our young people, economic resilience begins long before workforce entry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It begins in how children and students learn to think.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: As a parent, I am often tempted to help my children find the answers instantly, when they begin to struggle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Sometimes, we see this as our way of protecting and teaching our children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But when answers become instant, the more deliberate we must be in protecting the struggle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Because it is in the struggle of making mistakes, trying again, finally breaking through – that real learning happens and confidence grows.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: We want more young Singaporeans to learn about AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Not just learn how to use it, but learn about it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Not just to do their homework in routine and repetitive ways, but to create new value for themselves and others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And to actively decide when not to use AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: A student asked me recently, whether I use AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I said yes, often, especially for research, summarising articles or preparing speeches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But recently, I tried to build my first web app.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It is called "Family Fun Time", and it is designed to give me one activity a night to do with my kids.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The activity must be dinosaur-themed; take less than 15 minutes; and should not require any equipment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Over time, based on my rating for every activity, it will give me customised suggestions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Yesterday's activity was about dinosaurs' feelings and letting the kids suggest what to do when their favourite dinosaurs are scared, hungry, lonely, happy or angry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Unfortunately, I only get to try it with them tonight, because I had to work on this speech last night.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: The real fun and the real learning does not come from the app or from AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: It comes from the minutes we share as a family, the conversations and laughter, and correcting each other's silly responses to our dinosaur's feelings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: I did not know it was now so easy to build an app, until I had tried it myself.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Only in doing, trying and experimenting, will we find out the value of AI and shape our own relationship with it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: And only in doing, trying and experimenting, will we find out the real value of ourselves as humans and understand what AI cannot and should not replace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In the years ahead, as AI continues to evolve, we will need to review what education means for our children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: How do we teach our children about AI, in particular its limits, biases and blind spots?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: How do we balance the weightage of our education to emphasise character and social development?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Beyond content recall, what higher order thinking do we want to equip our children with?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: How do we help them understand the value of problem definition and design?

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: In closing, let me be direct about what I believe.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: AI is here and its possibilities are endless.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: This matters, because it means AI can improve the lives of our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: But this journey, no doubt, will cause much disruption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information, and Education (Ms Jasmin Lau)
text: Because we feel the fears, because we feel the anxieties, we must find a way forward that keeps our people together.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These perspectives are understandable, particularly when many needs remain pressing.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, I would suggest that the surplus can also be seen in another light.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When the world is becoming more contested, when supply chains fracture and the guardrails that once managed international disputes and tensions are eroding, it is better to discover we have more than expected than to discover that we have too little.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In uncertain times, a surplus is not a mistake; it is a buffer.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Hence, for those who disagree – we were perhaps not looking at the same target; as our bullseye will never be pure numerical accuracy, but rather, overall fiscal and social resilience.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But I think what we all agree on is that a surplus should not sit idle.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It must be deployed deliberately to improve the lives of our people today and to fortify Singapore against the uncertainties of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With that, Sir, allow me to frame my speech around three "S": first, supporting the "Sandwich Generation"; second, securing a sustainable future; and standing with every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The majority of these parents also believed that their children and grandchildren would continue to be caught in this "sandwich generation" trap.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These working caregivers are already stretched and require more support.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For example, the Large Families Scheme focuses its enhanced support on the third child and beyond.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While these schemes are valuable, we should also be mindful that the pressures of raising a family do not increase in neat steps, as the first two children already place significant demands on household resources.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As such, we should consider stepping up our support even for smaller families especially for middle-income families who do not qualify for the highest tiers of assistance, but who feel the squeeze most acutely.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As the Prime Minister has rightly acknowledged, we must help our seniors age with dignity, security and peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We should remember that caregiving is not only about subsidies and CPF top-ups, important as they may be.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is also about setting aside time and nurturing a supportive ecosystem of care.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A perfect example of this would be the work done by the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC).

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In just under a year of serving my Pasir Ris-Changi residents, I have had many great experiences with partnering them in solving some of my elderly residents' challenges with healthcare and daily living, which always brings much relief to their family members.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many families have had complex cases resolved, from navigating care placement to assessing subsidies.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We should continue strengthening AIC and find ways to make their good work even better.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In this regard, eldercare leave also deserves further study.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Just as we recognise childcare responsibilities, we must acknowledge that accompanying an elderly parent to a specialist appointment or arranging post-hospital care, is not discretionary – for many, it is duty.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On the childcare front, I will speak more extensively during the Committee of Supply debates.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But I wish to express concern, especially with regard to the cost of outpatient paediatric care.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Even for relatively routine visits, expenses do add up quickly for families with young children.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There may be room to review fee benchmarks or expand support frameworks.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Last but not least, support can also come in ways that seem unrelated at first glance – such as transport.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When we enhance bus frequencies, add more bus services, extend Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines and build sheltered walkways, we are not just improving infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ten minutes saved on a commute is 10 minutes with a child before bedtime or 10 minutes more to check in on an elderly parent.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For the sandwiched generation, time is the scarcest resource and they will need all the support they can get.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is tempting – especially amid global backsliding – to slow down.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But climate risks will not slow down for us.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Rising sea levels will not pause while we debate in this Chamber.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The investments we make today may not be fully appreciated now, but decades from today, our children will understand why we made them.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This reflects realism – balancing competitiveness with climate responsibility.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But beyond pricing, perhaps more can be done.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Instead of viewing it merely as tax, we can perhaps more explicitly ringfence or mandate that a meaningful portion be reinvested by companies into low-carbon technologies, energy efficiency and innovation, and not have all these funds be centrally managed.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This ensures the price mechanism translates directly into transformation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This will also help boost survival rates of energy intensive sectors which are also critical to our economy and yet reduce the carbon emission intensity of their operations.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But it is also time we pivot to examine the broader ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These include examining whether our grid connection timelines are fast enough, whether we have skilled manpower in solar engineering and maintenance and how we progress our transition into a green workforce.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Regional power imports are also critical and more government-to-government arrangements and government-to-business arrangements may be necessary.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Government must ensure that imports are sustainable, reliable and defendable.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And for this reason, the Government must not leave long-term energy security to the whims of market forces.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I also welcome diversification of our energy mix in geothermal, hydrogen systems and even advanced nuclear technology.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But public acceptance for these will be key.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Public education must begin early and be transparent.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Yet this transformation cannot be driven by market forces alone.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These foundational elements are essential to give investors and operators the confidence to commit to long-term energy infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Given the significant development risks and long gestation periods associated with such infrastructure projects, the Government could also work closely with industry from the outset to address potential barriers and mitigate critical risks before they become insurmountable obstacles.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When the stability of our economy and the daily lives of our citizens depend on the future of our energy system, we cannot rely solely on commercial market dynamics.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To secure a sustainable future is no simple feat.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We will need to work on aligning policy, workforce, infrastructure, businesses and public trust.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A coordinated national effort is not optional – it is imperative.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There are residents in areas with limited bus services, such as parts of Flora estate and Upper Changi – the last residential estate in the north-eastern part of the country.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Connectivity shapes opportunity and so, we should continue refining route design to better serve such pockets.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There are families with special needs children who face a cliff at age 18, when school-based structures fall away.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As our population greys, there are seniors asking for safer pedestrian paths and more pedestrian-only zones.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There are the SMEs that employ 70% of our workforce yet struggle even as we push ahead with AI adoption and digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Individually small, collectively, they form the backbone of our economy.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: (In Mandarin):   Similarly, the residents and businesses on Pulau Ubin pay electricity bills that are far higher than ordinary household users on the mainland.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They may be few in number, but they are Singaporeans just like us and their problems equally deserve our attention and concern. : Each group may not represent a majority.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is my hope that in this Budget and beyond, we will commit to supporting the sandwich generation – those holding up both the past and the future; securing a sustainable future – for ourselves and our children; standing with every Singaporean – especially those whose voices are softer.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And that is what this Budget must ultimately build.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is reshaping industries, redefining work and influencing the resilience of nations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore must move decisively, but we must also move wisely.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: When SSAs become AI-enabled, the most vulnerable of us benefit.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Ambition is necessary, but it is execution that determines whether progress is shared.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: That, is AI adoption without regret, bringing everyone along.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And you just made it with 10 seconds; do not cut it so fine next time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In moments like this, what matters most is whether our people feel they can keep moving forward to find good jobs, support their families and plan confidently for the future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Budget 2026 refreshes our economic strategy with ambition and discipline.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We cannot compete on size, but we can lead in trust, excellence and speed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are a regional leader in enabling green transition, with Southeast Asia’s first carbon tax and a national hydrogen strategy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In AI governance and digital trust, frameworks, like the AI Verify and our Digital Economy Agreements, place us as a global reference point.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Budget strengthens this foundation by encouraging high value segments of global value chains, sustaining long term R&D through RIE2030 and supporting growth capital.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These moves ensure that Singapore remains relevant in a volatile world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But strategies must translate into outcomes, especially for SMEs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many may still struggle to navigate schemes or put together a growth plan.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A “human in the loop” advisory model for SMEs scaling overseas or entering deep tech could complement GoBusiness, helping firms access support quickly and confidently.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On AI, acceleration must go hand in hand with clear governance, integration support, change management help and strong cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will speak more on enterprise AI readiness during the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Economic ambition only matters when it translates into better jobs and livelihood for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Budget’s National AI Missions, the National AI Council and the Champions of AI programme signal Singapore’s commitment to being a trusted global hub for AI.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But to ensure workers benefit from this transformation, we must align AI missions with workforce pathways, scale employer led training and apprenticeships, expand modular, employer recognised micro credentials that enable quicker redeployment, and strengthen HR capabilities so enterprises can manage workforce transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will speak more about the critical role of HR in accelerating enterprise transformation during the MOM Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For our mid‑career and senior workers, the measures in the Budget will help workers through the disruption and changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With rapid shifts in the job market, many of my residents have expressed anxiety about finding new employment after their short-term employment contracts end or following retrenchment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Tripartite partners and Enterprise Singapore have stressed the importance of faster, dignified support when workers are displaced.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we can still do more to shorten unemployment transitions further by providing earlier notifications to placement hubs; sector specific placement packs with skills mapping, bridging courses and job fairs; as well as streamlined access to training and employment support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will dive deeper into the topic of career health and employability of matured PMEs in the MOM Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must ensure that our refreshed economic strategy is matched by a workforce that is resilient, ready and able to seize the opportunities ahead, and this matters whether they are just starting out or making a mid-career transition.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For the sandwiched class, the question is: can my family cope?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will my children and parents be cared for?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These will definitely ease cost pressures temporarily, but gaps remain for families who are asset rich but cash poor, especially with the rising caregiving costs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Care needs are rising and so is the emotional and financial load on mid career caregivers who must work, upskill and care for both young and the elderly in their families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While real progress has been made in building up our care ecosystem – and I must stress this, there has been a lot of progress in our care ecosystem – but families still experience the system as fragmented.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And we should consider piloting integrated family support hubs that coordinate childcare, eldercare, respite services and employment assistance, providing a one stop touchpoint for families for case management, streamlining subsidy applications and help in navigating complex systems.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is a time load and a well-being load.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Employers have a role to play as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Incentives for caregiving friendly workplace policies, such as caregiving leave, flexible hours and phased return-to-work schemes, would encourage more companies to adopt practices that keep caregivers employed and productive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Expanding daycare and short notice respite capacity will give caregivers the breathing space they need to work, train, rest or respond to emergencies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Budget 2026 charts the right course with focused investments, responsible AI adoption, a responsive skills system and deeper support for families.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Before I begin my speech in Mandarin, I would like to express my sincere appreciation to several groups and platforms that provided valuable opportunities for me, and our MOF and MTI GPCs Members, led by Chairman Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Vice Chairman Mr Edward Chia, together with Mr Shawn Loh, Ms Tin Pei Ling, Ms Denise Phua, Mr Victor Lye and Mr Ng Shi Xuan and myself to better understand ground sentiment ahead of the announcements of the FY2026 Budget by Prime Minister and Finance Minister, Mr Lawrence Wong, and during this ongoing Budget debate since this morning and for the next few days.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One, our very own GPC resource panel comprise almost 20 to 30 businessmen running their own business.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Four, the Institution of Singapore Chartered Accountants Roundtable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Seven, the Society of Modern Management of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We had candid discussions on cost pressures, manpower constraints, digital transformation, skills upgrading and strengthening Singapore's competitiveness in an increasingly uncertain global environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Such open and constructive dialogues are critical in ensuring that our policy remain grounded, responsive and forward looking.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The insights and feedback shared have been invaluable in shaping our perspectives as we consider measures that support businesses, uplift workers and position Singapore for sustainable and inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, this year's Budget was not formulated in a stable environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, the global economy has been unstable, relations between countries remain complex, supply chain is restructuring and technological advancement is reshaping many industries.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For an open economy like Singapore, these developments are realities we face everyday.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As the old saying goes, "prepare ahead for a rainy day." When the environment is uncertain, it is even more important to secure our foundations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In an uncertain world, Singapore's most important assets are not its size, but our capability and our credibility.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The focus of this Budget is not only to provide immediate support but also to ensure that we preserve national stability, capabilities and long-term sustainability amidst changes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, the dual pressures on businesses, survival and upgrading.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Yesterday morning, I had a discussion with them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They did not talk about macroeconomic figures but very concrete realities.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some SME owners have told me that the pressure of doing business today does not come from a single direction but from multiple fronts at once and they feel overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On one hand, they must control operating costs and safeguard cash flow.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On the other hand, they must invest in system upgrades and capability building or risk gradually losing competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One SME owner describes it as "repairing the road while running".

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They often ask, interest rates are so elevated, should they invest now?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If employees go for training, who will do the work?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With the market conditions still unclear, if they switch systems or adopt AI and the results are unsatisfactory, what then?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What if the staff do not know how to use, and work becomes slower?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These concerns do not reflect an unwillingness to upgrade.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Rather, there have been many businesses that cannot afford the cost of trial and error.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But the important thing is that businesses must have the confidence to take the first step.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If policies are clear and consistent, businesses will be willing to upgrade with peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: During the New Year, many people use AI to make New Year's greetings and short videos, and people find it very interesting.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Society's acceptance of new technology has also clearly increased.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, when businesses seriously consider adopting AI solutions, the situation becomes more complex.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: There are now many AI service providers in the market, but the price can be very high.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some businesses worry that there may be a case of using AI for the sake of using AI.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: AI development is a long-term trend and will not see immediate effect.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The key is whether technology can truly help companies' daily operation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Businesses are most concerned about whether AI can reduce repetitive administrative processes, improve customer response efficiency, optimise inventory and data management and enhance training effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For SMEs, the true value of technology is not for display but in actual integration.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, in promoting AI adoption, I think there are three things that we have to focus on.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, ensure that subsidy structures encourage capability building rather than simply stimulating procurement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Enterprise upgrading is not the result of a single policy but of an entire system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Investment direction, enterprise capability building, skills transformation, financing support and the institutional environment are different gears within it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If one gear turns too quickly while others cannot move in sync, then friction arises.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, if industries upgrade rapidly but local enterprises are unprepared, opportunities cannot be translated into value.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If technological adoption advances quickly but workforce skills do not keep pace, productivity may suffer.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If policy support exists but the process is too complicated, deterring companies from applying, then the tools will fail to achieve their purpose.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Thus, the key lies not in the strength of individual policies, but in the depth of coordination and the pace of implementation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Only when the system operates smoothly can upgrading be steady and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Fourthly, I want to talk about fiscal space and long-term responsibility.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Although we have surplus now, but we cannot just look at one year.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Supporting enterprise upgrading and safeguarding social stability also requires resources.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We have to provide for today, as well as tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As a saying goes, "Store grain against famine".

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is not conservatism, it is preserving choices for the future.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In today's international environment, overseas expansion presents both opportunity and risk.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Different regulations, market volatility and geopolitical factors can influence our businesses.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A stable diplomatic network provides businesses with predictability and trust.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Links with Europe and other major economies create diversified market opportunities for our enterprises.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When our local enterprises create jobs and provide professional services abroad, they also strengthen Singapore's reputation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our fiscal policy must balance present needs and future responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Diplomacy must safeguard stability and space. "Steady steps carry us far." So long as we maintain a long-term perspective and continuously refine implementation, Singapore will remain stable and competitive in a complex environment. : Mr Speaker, artificial intelligence presents real opportunities, but adoption must remain disciplined, transparent and grounded in productivity gains rather than short-term momentum or inflated solution pricing.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The focus should be on measurable business value, clear evaluation and tiered support so that SMEs can adopt effectively without excessive burden.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, I have received feedback from several SME owners.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Interestingly, when he was later invited to serve as a judge for the AI for All Hackathon organised by Manus AI in collaboration with the Nanyang Technological University, he took the opportunity to present the same problem statements to participant students.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To his surprise, the students were able to propose multiple variable solutions that address about 70% of his business needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This experience demonstrated not only the capability of our students but also the untapped potential for cost-effective and collaborative approaches on AI adoption.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Perhaps, there is scope to support structural collaboration platforms where students can work on real-world business challenges as part of their coursework or innovation programmes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Such partnerships could lower adoption costs for SMEs, provide practical learning opportunities for students and accelerate AI diffusion across our economics in a more inclusive and sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Perhaps this could be a meaningful starting point for both SMEs and students.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: SMEs would not need to shoulder the full burden of high AI implementation costs upfront while students would gain valuable exposure to real-world business challenges even before graduation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Such collaborations would allow students to apply their knowledge in practical settings, sharpen their problem-solving skills and better understand industry needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, SMEs could benefit from fresh perspectives, innovative ideas and prototype solutions that can be further refined and skilled.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This creates a win-win ecosystem, one that supports enterprise transformation while strengthening workforce readiness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: After all, most students will one day become an employee or a worker, and we know every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: NTUC's strong networks with companies and workers and their AI strategy could help bridge SMEs with Institutions of Higher Learning, ensuring that training, innovation and job readiness efforts are better aligned with industry transformation needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Stable external networks create opportunity space for our enterprises to expand overseas and create value.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With steady direction and disciplined implementation, Singapore will remain resilient and competitive in an uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar): Mr Speaker, notwithstanding the speaking time budget of 20 minutes, I endeavour to utilise less time and, therefore, run a speaking time budget surplus.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I begin, I declare my interest as Group Managing Director of Commonwealth Capital Group.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are a Singapore global enterprise operating a conglomerate of businesses.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Like all other companies, our business decisions are influenced by the Government's strategies and its policies.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: My views today are shaped by the numerous interactions I have had during this Budget season.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: My colleague, Mr Lee Hong Chuang, spoke about this in quite a lot of detail.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The GPC for Finance, led by Mr Saktiandi Supaat, engaged widely, far more than in previous terms.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are grateful for the time taken by more than 1,000 PAP activists to participate in the PAP Policy Forum's surveys and focus group discussions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The business community, including the Singapore Business Federation and other trade associations, also shared their perspectives with us.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We even had a resource panel of experts across industries that provided more insights.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I particularly enjoyed the candid conversations on the Budget with our residents from Jalan Besar and Whampoa, during house visits and through policy dialogue.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But it is not the largest in recent years.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The fact that we have a surplus is not surprising.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But what is surprising is how large the surplus is and why it is so.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A pleasant surprise was the surge in business profitability, leading to a windfall budget surplus from corporate taxes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A rule of thumb that fiscal planners used to have is that corporate income tax would be around 3% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That is a significant sum, around $10 billion more.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am sure that MOF is already updating this planning assumption for future years.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is a reflection of an increase in the "Singapore premium", the premium of stability and security that Singapore offers in a more unpredictable and dangerous world, a premium from trust, to borrow Mr Victor Lye's words.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is a direct result of past Budgets, which invested in economic infrastructure as well as long-term security infrastructure, from national defence to cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In the past, then-Deputy Prime Minister Tharman used to say that economic policy is part of social policy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Well, in this changed world, it is increasingly clear that security policy is part of economic policy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Our defence spending is consistently around 3% of GDP, more than many North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) countries and more than South Korea.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But credit should be given to all Singaporeans who supported a Government that spent a consistently large sum on defence during peacetime.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A short-termist and insecure Government would have taken a more popular approach to redirect security spending to more direct social benefits.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That said, fiscal planning will enter a period of higher uncertainty next year as the impact of the domestic top-up tax and other Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS)-related measures kick in.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Once the domestic top-up tax commences next year, we should probably see a short-term bump in revenues.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But how long this lasts will be incredibly uncertain, as these measures will impair our competitiveness over time.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To that end, I take a different view from Mr Gerald Giam on being less conservative with fiscal projections.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As it gets harder to predict revenues, it is better to find ourselves in a budget surplus position than struggling to reduce budget deficits, which many other countries are facing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: With the large surplus this year and potentially over the next few years, we should then ask ourselves: how should we use this extra money to improve the lives of Singaporeans and address long-term problems before they become more intractable?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A good way to think of our problems that remain unsolved is to consider what Singapore would look like, if Government policies stayed the same and if current trends continued.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In the next five years, there will be fewer Singaporeans feeling the direct benefit of economic growth.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In the next 10 years, there will be fewer Singaporeans feeling that they are part of one cohesive society, if wealth inequality continues to worsen.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And in the next 20 years, there will simply be fewer Singaporeans, if we do not address our declining birth rates.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Today, many Singaporeans already feel that the headline economic numbers do not gel with their lived experiences.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I see this in Jalan Besar and Whampoa, especially amongst our seniors who have retired many years ago.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And increasingly, with our younger residents who are looking for jobs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As well as those who are retrenched, some of whom are under 40.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, by all measures of the hard data, Singapore has done really well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But the question is: do you feel that your standard of living has improved by 5% compared to the year before?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do businesses feel that they have done 5% better?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: These economic figures seem theoretical, and the trickle-down effect that we had hoped for, has for some indeed, been just a trickle.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The likely reason is that the direct benefits of economic growth are captured by a decreasing proportion of Singaporeans who are earning higher wages in sectors that are globally competitive.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For the growing number of retirees who do not earn salaries, economic growth may only mean higher prices.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For workers who are used to working in the same company for a long time, economic growth may only mean a greater sense of job risk amidst technological disruptions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: To make matters more complicated for this generation, wealth inequality will also be an issue.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A modest level of wealth inequality is not in itself a bad thing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is the meritocratic approach that has made Singapore successful and uplifted generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: However, there are concerns that birth circumstances are increasingly determining life outcomes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is of course natural for parents to want the best for their children, and to spend time, money and effort to give their children advantages in an increasingly competitive world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But this parental help must not be determinative.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: All Singaporeans must continue to be able to aspire to success and to a better life, regardless of the situation they were born into.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I see a need to systematically lean against the natural tendency in any economy for wealth inequality to become entrenched across generations – so that Singapore remains home for all, hope for all.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are not too late to address this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And finally, beyond our current generation, our falling birth rates are the existential crisis that we will face.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, how should we use this extra money to address these problems?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We can do better to uplift Singaporeans today and assure them that any unexpected fiscal surpluses will be shared with all.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Our Government policies should embody the value of taking care of our most elderly such as the oldest five percent of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We should assure Singaporeans that when Singapore does well, all Singaporeans will benefit.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This can be achieved through a longer-term commitment from the Government on a surplus sharing mechanism.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Or if there are concerns that CDC vouchers may increase inflation, we could do so through universal CPF top-ups or other rebates for Government services such as transport and utilities.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is similar to the social dividend mentioned by Prof Terence Ho.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And to provide more assurance, some of our temporary support measures can be made more permanent, or at least longer-term.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: After all, as Milton Friedman famously said, “Nothing is more permanent than a temporary government programme”.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Second, companies should be the conduit to provide a greater sense of assurance to workers, amidst greater disruption.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: No amount of Government hand-outs is as good as giving a leg-up through jobs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Companies are the platforms and partners for the Government to achieve its policy goals.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Support given to employers to do so should be greater and for longer.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Progressive Wage Credit Scheme and other short-term support measures are but band-aids for companies, many of whom have been taking the hit year after year after year with escalating manpower costs, in part driven by Government policy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And in the words of another famous person, Taylor Swift: "band-aids don’t fix bullet holes".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We should now give Singaporean workers the confidence that the Government has their back and anyone who is earnestly looking for a job for a while will be strongly supported by the Government through a more ambitious jobseeker place-then-train programme.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For example, the Government could give all employers time-limited salary support to hire any jobseeker who has been actively looking for a job for at least six months, regardless of age.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Third, we should decisively address our existential issue of low birth rates.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Parenthood is a deeply personal decision and the joys of bringing up children can never be quantified in dollar terms.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But that should not mean that the Government stops trying to remove economic barriers to having children.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This remains part of the enabling environment that Ms Eileen Chong and Mr David Hoe mentioned.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I believe that we can promise Singaporeans that the basic costs of child raising should never be a barrier to having children.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The LifeSG credits for families are a small move in the right direction, but with the fiscal resources at our disposal, we can do more.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is conceptually no different to how we provide all Singaporeans with basic education today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I urge the Government to think of childcare and preschool as a public good.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Second, LifeSG credits can be systematically given to all parents with children up to 16 years old and should be sized to cover more of the basic out-of-pocket costs of child raising.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Although my own four children have outgrown their toddler phase, parents in our Whampoa community often remind me about the costs of milk powder, diapers and doctor visits.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Surely the Government can do better than that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That is not to say that the Government’s tax policy should be constrained.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Taxes are not only for raising revenues, but for reflecting our values and for signalling what is important for society.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But that is another speech for another day.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Two, spending wisely and decisively to improve the inclusive Singapore that we know and that we love, and that all of us in this House fight for.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This means doing right by our seniors, our families and our workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And keeping the Singapore dream alive, not just for this generation but for future generations to come.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Giam, you have a clarification to ask?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I think I heard him say that he takes a different view about my approach to conservative estimates and suggested that it is better to have a surplus than a deficit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Is he suggesting that I was asking for Singapore to run budget deficits?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I have no disagreement with that, as long as it is put to good use.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: What I was focusing more on was our budget marksmanship.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I think overly conservative budgeting is actually inaccurate budgeting and something we should avoid.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: But I think we agree that if it is above 2%, he agrees with my suggestion that we can redistribute that to all Singaporeans, so thank you.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In my speech, I want to focus on two areas: our efforts to support Singaporean workers and businesses in embracing and thriving in an AI-enabled economy; and our efforts to support Singaporeans to build not just careers, but also families, to be able to care for their families so that Singapore is Made For Families.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many of these roles are knowledge-intensive and involve analysis, coordination and decision-making – areas where AI is increasingly being deployed to augment how work is done.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: AI is already reshaping white-collar jobs, with greater emphasis being placed on judgement, adaptability and higher-order skills.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This means that a significant proportion of our workforce will be impacted by AI in the form of job redesign, changing skill requirements and evolving career pathways.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I hope we can look into the following three areas as we try to stay ahead of the AI curve.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, on youth and the alignment between AI education and enterprise AI adoption.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In the recent AI Festival Asia 2026, and a pre-Budget dialogue organised by young PAP, the youths have called for greater alignment between AI education and enterprise AI adoption.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Singapore has made strong investments in AI education and skills development.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, the pace of AI adoption across enterprises, especially SMEs, remains uneven.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: SMEs may find it harder to attract and retain young talent if they are unable to offer comparable opportunities.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If this gap persists, young Singaporeans entering the workforce may gravitate towards firms that can offer AI-enabled roles, many of which are better-resourced global companies.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We would not want this to create a structural pull of talent away from local enterprises over time.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I hope that we can look into aligning career pathways across how we train our youths for the AI economy and how our enterprises adopt AI, so that working in Singapore remains competitive and accessible across firms of different sizes.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, mid-career workers, particularly PMETs and professionals, face a different set of challenges.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: AI will reshape professions by changing how work is performed, how roles are defined and how value is created.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The core value of lawyers and accountants lies in judgement, contextual understanding and accountability.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These capabilities underpin trust in these professions and remain central even as AI tools are introduced and implemented.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In a more fragmented global environment, where partnerships are increasingly strategic and selective, the ability of Singaporean lawyers and accountants to build trust, navigate cultural contexts and sustain relationships remains critical.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is especially given the nature of these professions, which are cross-jurisdictional in many respects, and which must account for different regulatory regimes and cultural practices and norms in different countries.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These are inherently human skills which cannot be replaced by AI.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But AI can assist lawyers and accountants in their tasks.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I hope that we direct the assistance to help lawyers and accountants to work more efficiently and improve their overall work output, so that they can focus on honing the core skills of the profession.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: That said, we must recognise and be cognisant of the fact that mid-career lawyers and accountants are not AI-natives.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They did not grow up with AI and using AI effectively may not come naturally to them.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We must, therefore, be cautious about the impact of AI on our mid-career professionals.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When we consider job redesigns, we should ensure that the redesigned jobs are suitable and allow the professional to maximise their strengths and value.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As roles evolve, we also need to guide transitions in a way that preserves the professional standards and identity.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In adopting and implementing AI, we must not lose sight of the core functions of the professions.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And when we consider AI training and reskilling, we need to approach this in a way which is accessible and which works for these mid-career professionals.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I suggest that we do not stop at encouraging firms to take up AI technology and for employees to train themselves on AI technology.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
