text: Firms and employees will adopt this at different speeds, and will vary in how they perceive the necessity, the convenience and the reliability of AI implementation and training.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There needs to be thought at a sector level on how to redesign jobs, so the industry can be uplifted together.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, a not insignificant group also warrants attention: accountants and lawyers embedded within enterprises – that is, in-house accountants and legal counsel.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These in-house professionals are central to governance, compliance and strategic decision-making within companies.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Their ability to work effectively with AI will directly influence how enterprises adopt AI across functions.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is, therefore, important that AI training, tools and support frameworks extend to such in-house professionals.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Supporting this group will strengthen enterprise capabilities more broadly and enable the profession to better capture the opportunities presented by AI.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, in supporting our local SMEs in their adoption of AI, we may need to reassess the current method of support.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Without the deep pockets and resources of larger firms, how can micro- and small SMEs also ride on the train of transformation?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: AI adoption for micro- and small SMEs at scales and speeds comfortable for them, will give them the confidence needed for sustainable and more permanent adoption of AI.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our task is to ensure that education, workforce transitions and enterprise adoption move in step, so that opportunities are more broadly shared and our economy remains cohesive and competitive.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But at the core, our economy is about families – every job supports a home.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I support the Government's investment in Singapore families.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I have previously spoken about what I called the "Singapore Puzzle" – Singapore's challenge lies in figuring out how we might remain competitive in a fast-changing world, while staying anchored to the values, our communities and the aspirations of our people.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is reflected in whether Singaporeans feel able to build their careers while, at the same time, starting and/or supporting their families.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For many, these aspirations are clear: a meaningful job, a stable family life and a confidence that effort will lead to progress.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One area that warrants closer attention is how workplaces support Singaporeans in managing family responsibilities alongside work.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These needs arise across different life stages: parents raising young children; working adults caring for ageing parents; and families navigating periods where additional time and flexibility are needed.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These are part of everyday life for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many continue to navigate tensions between career demands and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Alongside these structural measures, day-to-day workplace HR practices are also critical.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How managers respond when an employee announces pregnancy, how performance is assessed for employees returning from maternity or paternity leave and how urgent caregiving needs are handled – these are practical decisions that determine whether employees can remain engaged at work.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When these situations are handled well, employees are more likely to remain in their roles, continue progressing in their careers and contribute consistently over time.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When they are not, the outcome may be that employers lose talent, with employees leaving and exiting the workforce or disengaging at key stages of their careers to fulfill caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Young Singaporeans who otherwise desire to start their own families may also be discouraged from doing so in fear that their careers will suffer.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These are operational and human considerations that sit alongside policy.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How they are addressed will shape whether workplace support translates into sustained participation, stronger teams and continued productivity.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They seek to build meaningful careers, achieve stability and have the confidence to plan for their future.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, sustaining these outcomes requires a careful balancing of choices.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Economic growth, workforce strength and social cohesion are shaped by how we participate in the economy, how responsibilities are shared and how we respond to changing demographic realities.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As a society, we must continue to make adjustments, whether in the way we organise work, support families or remain open and connected to the world.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These adjustments require collective understanding and shared responsibility.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many are already stepping forward, building their careers, supporting their families and contributing in different ways.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As expectations evolve, so, too, will the ways in which individuals, employers and the Government respond.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our young people will graduate into a workforce where AI is embedded across industries and everyday tasks – from the workplaces they will enter, to the problems they will solve, the challenges they will face and the opportunities that they will seize.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For them, AI will not be optional; it will be the new normal.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will certainly have an impact on the older workers too.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This context, AI is not merely a technological shift; it will define the economic and social landscape of the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as the Prime Minister said in his Budget speech, and I quote: "AI is a powerful tool; but it is still a tool." Tools do not determine outcomes – people do.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The question before us is not whether AI will transform our economy, but whether Singaporeans are equipped to harness it confidently, responsibly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, used well, AI can amplify human capability and creativity; used uncritically, it can weaken judgement and erode independent thinking.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our responsibility is to ensure that Singaporeans, especially our youths, are equipped not only to access AI, but to understand it, question it and use it responsibly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such efforts must begin early in schools where habits are formed and competencies are developed and I will speak more on education and AI during the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, I would like to focus on a more foundational, more fundamental enabler with regard to the whole issue of AI – ensuring that every student has equitable access to the digital hardware and competencies required before they can even begin to start understanding AI and how to meaningfully leverage it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Without reliable access to personal computing devices, for example, students cannot build foundational skills or experiment with digital tools in ways that will allow them to engage meaningfully with AI later.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Students who lack access to devices risk falling behind in learning, developing fewer self-directed learning habits and having reduced confidence in tackling technology-based tasks.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But conversely, equitable access to devices provides every student with the ability to explore, learn and innovate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Introduced progressively from 2020 and fully implemented by the end of 2021, these devices were integrated with the national e-learning platform, the Student Learning Space and was supported by financial assistance schemes to ensure that no student – no secondary school student – was left behind.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, as Singapore increasingly positions itself as an AI-ready nation, this principle remains essential.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wish to repeat my call to explore providing similar opportunities for our younger learners.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Extending PLDs to primary school students would equip them with the tools to access digital content, develop computational skills and build confidence in navigating technology from an early age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the meantime, Sir, let me reiterate again how providing PLDs to primary school students would bring multiple benefits.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By ensuring that every child has access to a common device, we prevent unequal access to technology and strengthen social mobility.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: No student would be disadvantaged by relying on shared or outdated devices, reinforcing meritocracy in a digital age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Early exposure to personal devices also allows schools to guide students in responsible use, cyber wellness and structured engagement with digital platforms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Habits formed in primary school are enduring and introducing these practices early can set the stage for lifelong literacy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The ownership of a PLD encourages students to take greater responsibility for their own learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It fosters curiosity, self-directed exploration and the confidence to engage with online educational resources.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With AI increasingly embedded in learning platforms, these early habits will prepare students to adapt and thrive as technology becomes a key part of their education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Aligning this initiative with the objectives of Budget 2026, providing standardised PLDs to primary students is not merely an educational reform.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a strategic investment in Singapore's future human capital.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It strengthens the foundation for a digitally fluent, AI-ready workforce that will support our nation's long-term competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The framework for secondary school PLDs, including procurement and financial assistance mechanisms, provides a blueprint for extending this policy to primary students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A phased rollout, like the approach used for secondary schools, would allow careful implementation and adjustment, ensuring that all primary school students can benefit from this opportunity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In short, Mr Speaker, MOE has done it before.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They had done it very well – the secondary school students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I see no reason why we cannot extend this scheme further upstream to our primary school learners.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: True resilience begins in our classrooms, long before students enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Equipping them therefore with the tools – the hardware tools – and competencies to navigate technology confidently nurtures a generation capable of leveraging AI responsibly and creatively, rather than simply using it passively.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By taking this step, we are not only strengthening the foundation for AI literacy but also preparing our youth for an AI-driven future.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, for many, this feels less like a triumph but more like a collective sigh of relief.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Amidst such uncertainty, Singaporeans often feel torn between the safety of the conventional route and the risk of forging their own path.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, in this age of disruption, we cannot afford to choose one over the other.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Success today requires a marriage of intentional strategy and individual passion.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How can we support every Singaporean to not just survive the waves but navigate them with purpose?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Our young graduates have always been viewed as a highly employable group, due to their ability to perform quickly as they learn on-the-job.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, the ground is shifting as companies hire for highest productivity at lower cost, experience becomes the differentiator from day one.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: While most students complete internships, many find that these stints lack the technical depth or clear conversion pathways needed to secure a full-time role in a competitive market.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How can the Ministry of Manpower and the Ministry of Trade and Industry actively create and recreate job opportunities in response to these shifts?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Supporting start-ups to hire local graduates would also enable these workers to take ownership while providing start-ups with the much-needed pairs of hands, while aligning with the strategic focus on supporting high-growth companies.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Also on jobs, our construction sector continues to face significant cost and manpower pressures.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Policies must be carefully calibrated to support both workforce transformation and business sustainability.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This will help firms manage workforce costs responsibly, while continuing to support fair wages.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I will speak more on this during the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Given the prevalence of GenAI, teaching our students to fluently converse with these models has become a non-negotiable for the future.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, students risk letting ChatGPT fill in the blanks for them at the expense of their own development and losing critical thinking.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How do we create an environment where students are innovators and creators of AI and use GenAI as a tool and not a crutch?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I suggest we look to current initiatives tackling general technology use for inspiration.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, the National University of Singapore college held its first "Touch Grass Week", named after an online term for disconnecting from technology and stepping into the outside world.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: During that one week, students used pen and paper or went 24 hours screen-free without using technology to complete their assignments.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, students should be required to submit initial drafts or brainstorms on pen and paper for peer, teacher review, which encourages them to think critically before using GenAI as a sounding board or editor.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Let our young be innovators, be creators, not users, of AI.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Harnessing AI to facilitate students' education looks different at every stage.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In pre-tertiary education, AI's best use case might be critiquing a PSLE composition; in tertiary education, it might be supporting a literature review; in internships, it might be turning an admin task from a day's work to an hour's work through automation.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: While MOE has already provided parents and students with general resources on GenAI and EdTech, students would also benefit from a guideline on specific GenAI use cases across educational levels and subjects.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Our youth are and have always rose to the challenges of this generation.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: We need to provide platforms, define pathways and envision possibilities in partnership with them, giving them room to become our future changemakers.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Third, navigating back to the workforce for returning parents, many of whom are our senior youths.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Whether due to personal circumstances or a desire to focus on their children's early years, some parents choose to take a break from work.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: When these parents return, they face an uphill battle to re-integrate themselves back into the workforce, especially if they have taken a long break due to multiple children or even waiting to help their children prepare for the PSLE.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: They re-enter a workplace with new tools and skills needed, their networks having moved on and a short runway to prove themselves again.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This could be daunting enough to put them off returning altogether and we lose out to their valuable experience and productivity.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As we push forward with our plans to build leadership in growth sectors, falling behind for these parents is even more likely.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: To make the best choice between time for their children and the ability to return to their careers.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Trade-offs will exist, but it will be a waste if parents feel the door is closed once they slow down for a few years.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Having a dedicated set of courses targeted at returning parents, with course requirements and schedules built around those with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This includes encouraging employers to offer flexible hours, part-time professional roles and phased return-to-work options, so parents can rebuild their careers while meeting caregiving roles.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: When we enable parents to return with confidence and dignity, we not only strengthen families – we also retain valuable skills, experience and talent in our workforce.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Our seniors are not only a group that needs support, but have also become an important pillar of the workforce.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The life experience and seasoned wisdom that our seniors have are difficult for AI to replicate.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: They are the most reliable defence against the AI hallucinations.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Young employees may rely on models' output, but our seniors who have lived through decades of trials possess the intuition to spot errors and this is their unique advantage.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Japanese refer to the marginalised senior employees as Madogiwa-zoku.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But I see it as a more positive vision.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: These senior professionals can sit by the window and provide guidance and mentorship to the younger generation.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, as Singapore stands at the edge of these historic inflection points, from the AI disruption to the transition into a super-aged society, we must remember, above all, our people are here to stay.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: And it is only in a place that feels like home, which offers both the stability of purpose and the promise of progress, that we bring out the best in our people.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: When Singaporeans feel they have found their place, they will, in return, bring the best of themselves to shape the future of this country.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As an MP for Holland-Bukit Timah GRC in Zhenghua division, I speak on behalf of my residents.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over recent months, many have approached me during my Meet-the-People Sessions and community engagements to share their concerns.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Young families in Zhenghua are not only raising children.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The so-called "sandwiched generation" is feeling pressure from both ends.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this Budget provides important support measures, I would like to highlight one area where residents have experienced unintended consequences – the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In effect, families sometimes feel unintentionally discouraged from living together.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Supporting seniors ultimately strengthens young families by easing intergenerational pressures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Workers want to stay relevant but must also maintain income stability for their families.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, businesses want to transform but struggle to find skilled manpower.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers, especially SMEs, continue to face significant cost pressures, particularly manpower costs and, for businesses located in dense areas, rising rents.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recent announcements, such as increases in S Pass qualifying salary and Local Qualifying Salary, while aligned with broader workforce objectives, have direct cost implications for SMEs that rely on foreign workers to complement their local workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, such cost increases do not remain isolated at the firm level.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many manpower-intensive services, such as cleaning, stewarding, security and facilities management, operate as outsourced functions supporting larger enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As labour costs rise, these service providers inevitably pass through higher costs, leading to increased operating expenses across the value chain.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Larger enterprises may therefore face higher facilities management or operational costs even when they are not directly affected by manpower policy adjustments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The impact is systemic and felt across the broader business environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many SME employers recognise the need to transform, leverage AI to improve productivity and seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, some feel that they are currently treading water, needing to keep their heads above water before they are in a position to fully pursue transformation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SMEs employ seven out of 10 workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Supporting SMEs is therefore not only about helping individual firms.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I welcome the merger of SSG and WSG.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Career Conversion Programme (CCP) has been an effective bridge.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For the man on the street, this means a worker can switch into a new role while still receiving a fair wage to pay bills and support their family.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers are supported through wage subsidies while the worker undergoes training and is still building productivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given that the MOM's budget has increased this year, there is an opportunity to further strengthen such schemes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As technological disruption accelerates, the duration and flexibility of CCP support may warrant review.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Digital and AI-related roles often require longer adaptation periods.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I suggest reviewing overall budget allocation, support duration flexibility and awareness among employers, particularly SMEs, many of whom may not fully understand the available support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am heartened that the Government has introduced the Champions of AI programmme and tax deductions on AI expenditures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, many SMEs need support not just in funding but in literacy and practical adoption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There needs to be faster diffusion of relevant AI tools, clear use cases that SMEs can realistically implement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SME Centres play a pivotal role in building awareness and guiding adoption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, may I ask the Prime Minister what expanded role SME Centres will play in accelerating AI adoption?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How are advisors being upskilled to guide businesses effectively?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Healthcare represents both a social imperative and an economic opportunity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Historically, healthcare systems have focused on treating illness after it occurs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, advances in AI, genomics and precision diagnostics allow us to shift upstream, toward prevention, early detection and health optimisation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is uniquely positioned to lead this transition.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We already possess a strategic advantage in high-quality longitudinal population health data, supported by trusted governance frameworks and secure platforms such as TRUST.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, our multi-ethnic population provides nuanced genomic and health insights across diverse Asian ancestries, creating datasets that are both scientifically rich and regionally relevant.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This differentiates Singapore from Western-centric datasets and positions us to develop preventive health innovations tailored for Asia.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a platform would move beyond research into regulatory-grade validation, positioning Singapore as a trusted global hub for testing, certification and scaling preventive health technologies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These efforts demonstrate how precision medicine can shift healthcare toward earlier intervention.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, earlier fertility screening and intervention could help individuals make informed decisions sooner, potentially improving fertility outcomes and contributing positively to our total fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Population-level data and AI analytics will be foundational to this shift.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With advances in AI, we can analyse complex health data more quickly and affordably, significantly expanding diagnostic capability.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To fully harness this potential, we must also strengthen diagnostic infrastructure, increasing access to testing facilities, genomic screening and AI-assisted diagnostics.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond healthcare delivery, preventive and precision medicine present a new economic frontier.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By aligning public investment, private capital with scientific innovation, we can scale new enterprises while improving societal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The global wellness and preventive health economy is expanding rapidly.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather than viewing wellness as a lifestyle sector, Singapore can develop exportable intellectual property and scalable health optimisation solutions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach creates new business opportunities, generates good jobs for Singaporeans and positions Singapore as a global hub for healthspan optimisation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For seniors, we must ensure support schemes reflect individual realities and preserve family unity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For young families, we must ease caregiving pressures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For workers and employers, we must provide practical pathways that enable confident transformation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By investing in preventive and precision healthcare powered by AI and strengthened through blended capital, we can build an economy that improves lives while creating new job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With thoughtful refinements and bold execution, we can ensure that the next phase of our development benefits every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, it is not a failure of marksmanship.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is a testament to fiscal discipline, strong revenue performance and a resilient economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Some argue that every dollar of surplus should be locked away in reserves.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But prudence must serve people and solve their current problems.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Even if we were to place the entire $15.1 billion into the reserves, it would still not fully offset the roughly $40 billion drawn during COVID-19 to protect jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We built our economy by drawing on past reserves during the pandemic and that was the right decision.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Now, with a surplus early in the term, we have both the responsibility and the opportunity to calibrate wisely.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Hence, I have the following suggestions: First, invest in AI.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Artificial Intelligence will reshape industries and the speed will be faster than many workers can adapt.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We should provide heavy subsidy to AI and digital training for Singaporeans earning below the median wage or blue CHAS card holders to avoid the digital divide from becoming an income divide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If we do not uplift them now, the digital divide will become an income divide.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For students, I recommend that the Government provide free or heavily subsidised access to paid AI tools for all students from upper primary to university levels.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This would enable students to learn AI knowledge more deeply and systematically.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: More importantly, narrow the gap between low-income and high-income families in accessing these expensive paid AI tools, thereby creating a level playing field.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Such investment is not merely expenditure, but economic defence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, improve ageing estates that is more than 30 years old.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Residents need practical improvements: covered linkways, water leakage solutions, wheelchair-friendly access, safer walkways and better first- and last-mile connectivity.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I suggest that we significantly enhance funding for Community Improvement Projects Committee, the Neighbourhood Renewal Programme and Estate Upgrading Programme under the Ministry of National Development as well as first and last mile infrastructure scheme under LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These are not luxuries, they are dignity-enhancing investments for seniors and families.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many families have benefitted from the CDC vouchers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This will help to offset the effect of higher cost-of-living after the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as the GST increases.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Prime Minister Wong announced that the Government will continue to distribute $500 CDC vouchers to Singaporean households in January 2026.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The distribution of CDC vouchers not only help households deal with daily cost increases but also support heartland businesses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There is feedback that the public are concerned with the issue of fairness.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Currently, a single household and household with 8 members will get the same amount of CDC vouchers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Although it embodies the universal principle, families with more members will have higher daily expenses in food, transport and childcare.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This will more accurately reflect the needs of families, especially for middle and low-income families.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, this measure will continue to promote local consumption and support neighbourhood business development.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Through such arrangements, we affirm a simple yet important principle, where the nation achieves development success, the people of Singapore must tangibly feel these results in their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Fourthly, we should thoroughly resolve the issue of residents being unable to access lifts on the same floor.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Currently, approximately 100 HDB blocks still do not have direct lift access to every floor due to high costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many residents were still mobile and valued privacy when they purchased their flats over 30 years ago.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As they age and have mobility issues, they still need to climb stairs daily to access lifts, which is very arduous.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I hope the Government will address this issue seriously and even if the costs are higher, we should still consider building additional lifts so that all HDB blocks can have lift access on the same floor.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The civilisation of a society is reflected in how we treat our elderly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Fifth, better care for persons with special needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Over the past decade, we have made significant progress in strengthening our special education system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With the Ministry of Education's continued investment, many students with special needs are able to receive structured support, life skills education and vocational training before the age of 18.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These efforts have brought hope and dignity to many families.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, when these young people graduate and are unable to find or maintain employment, many quietly disappear from the system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They remain at home, gradually becoming isolated from society.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Overtime, their social skills decline, their confidence weakens and their life goals gradually become unclear.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Behind them are their caregivers, often aging parents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And these parents bear increasingly heavy emotional, physical and financial burdens.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I witnessed this firsthand when working with family of Purple Heart in Nanyang.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is a grassroots organisation that supports persons with special needs and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Their love is unwavering, but their resources are increasingly strained.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For those who cannot work and require long term sheltered care, day activity centres or structured support, the challenges are even more severe.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The value of a society lies not in how it treats the strong, but in how it supports the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Let us also spend purposefully to enhance resilience, support vulnerable groups and build a more inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Only in this way can the surplus truly benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We are living in a disrupted age, marked by greater geopolitical and economic fragmentation and uncertainty; technological disruption; and a rapidly ageing population.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) and younger workers were the most concerned about the impact of technological disruption on their job security.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This Budget is, therefore, critical to lay a strong foundation for this disrupted age.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The choices we make today will shape the course of our future and the lives of our workers and families.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC and the Labour Movement will study your suggestions carefully.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Yet, as President Tharman recently reminded us at Davos, in a changing world, we must do more to strengthen trust internally.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And that is done by acting pre-emptively to address people's hopes and fears.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This is why the Labour Movement is calling on the Government to re-double efforts on three fronts.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, strengthen support for workers who are vulnerable to disruption at the individual level.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And third, strengthen the Labour Movement's ability to protect and uplift our PMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I will outline these calls in my speech today.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: My fellow labour MPs will build on them in their speeches across different worker segments.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: They ask good practical questions: what core skills must they build up so that they can keep up with AI?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: How can they use AI to become more productive in their specific job roles and industries?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And how can they keep pace with rapid AI developments to future-proof their careers?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Singapore, indeed, has built a comprehensive skills and training ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: There are more than 1,600 AI courses listed on the SkillsFuture course catalogue.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: These range from basic to highly specialised courses, costing anywhere from a few hundred dollars to a few thousand dollars after funding.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But for the average worker, it is not easy to know which course or pathway that will genuinely help them to become AI‑ready.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: At the same time, many businesses recognise the value of AI but struggle to translate that recognition into clear, implementable strategies that will deliver productivity gains and a competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: That is why I support the establishment of the National AI Council to be chaired by Prime Minister Wong.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I look forward to a comprehensive and cogent national AI strategy, one that will chart clear implementation roadmaps for industries and provide practical guidance so that every Singaporean can benefit in the AI era.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The Labour Movement calls on the Government to ensure that every worker, regardless of their background, experience or current skill level, will know practically how to equip themselves to be AI-ready.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Every worker will have the support they need to access AI-related training, including those who have used up their SkillsFuture Credits or wish to take up more specialised courses that cost more.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And, Mr Speaker, the Labour Movement will play our part too.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC has launched "AI-Ready SG", a one-stop platform that will help train and upskill workers to be AI-ready; support firms in business transformation and job redesign, towards better jobs with better wages and work prospects; and improve, also, job-matching so workers can access better job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This will encourage our members to experiment and adopt AI more confidently.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: For workers who may not know where to begin, NTUC LearningHub will roll out AI training pathways tailored to different skill levels, job roles and sectors; and also, a career mentorship programme for PMEs to receive guidance from certified and experienced mentors.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) will strengthen job matching with AI-augmented career coaching and offer personalised guidance and placement support for workers navigating career transitions.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our NTUC Company Training Committees (CTCs) will assist employers to embark on practical AI transformation by identifying the best business case for AI adoption through the AI Transformation Blueprints and Sectoral AI transformation playbooks developed together with industry partners, connecting them also with relevant training so that their workers can adopt AI more effectively and quicker.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And of course, accessing CTC Grant funding to fuel these efforts.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In sum, AI-Ready SG aims to harness AI to fuel business growth in ways that translate into good jobs with better wages and better work prospects for our workers – win-win outcome.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: These objectives are aligned with the national-level efforts, such as the National AI Council and the AI Missions in key sectors.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We call on the Government and employers to partner the Labour Movement in our efforts through AI-Ready SG, so NTUC can do our part to support our businesses and workers to be AI‑ready.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Even as we prepare every worker to be AI-ready, some will still face disruption at the individual level.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: To be clear, I think we are in a relatively strong position overall today.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our economy performed well last year and overall employment remains healthy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Around nine in 10 graduates secured employment within six months of graduation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Nonetheless, there emerging headwinds and signs of strain that we should pay attention to and should not ignore.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Around 900 respondents in NTUC's survey were caregivers and close to one in two of them considered leaving their job at least once a month due to the stress from caregiving.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must therefore strengthen support for our workers so that they navigate transitions confidently and where needed, bounce back stronger.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, we must continue to support our young graduates to secure good job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Tripartite partners must be ready to step in building on existing measures, like the GRaduate Industry Traineeships (GRIT) Programme.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, we must do more to support our PMEs who face retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As more PMEs may experience churn, it is timely for the Government to review this income threshold, so that the JSS can provide baseline assurance to our middle-income PMEs during retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And third, we must refresh our Caregiver Support Action Plan to help our caregivers remain at work, return to work when ready and safeguard their financial resilience and retirement adequacy during periods of career disruption.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And this brings me to my final point – strengthening the Labour Movement's ability to protect and uplift our PMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Tripartism has been the bedrock of our success.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: With strong tripartite partnership undergirded by a representative Labour Movement, we have been able to weather many storms, including COVID-19, and emerge even stronger.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In this disrupted age, we need to reinforce the ability of our Labour Movement to stand alongside our workers, especially our PMEs as they navigate transitions.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, let us move towards advance retrenchment notifications.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In the last few years, there have been a few high-profile retrenchments which made the news.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Many times, these incidents could have been avoided if companies worked with the union involved and if NTUC were informed and notified earlier.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Advance retrenchment notifications support our ability to work together with companies to provide timely and tangible support of our affected workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Before retrenchment, and not five days after retrenchment, when many of the workers may have already left the company and are no longer contactable.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In fact, in many major economies, like the United States (US), the European Union (EU), Switzerland, Australia, Japan and China, these countries already have some form of laws or policies requiring advance retrenchment notifications.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The intent of the Labour Movement is not to constrain companies' flexibilities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It is to put out tripartism to work, in upholding responsible retrenchment and delivering more coordinated support for workers, including PMEs amid this disrupted age.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, let us strengthen the ability of our unions to represent more PMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We all know that our workforce is becoming increasingly PME-centric.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Over the years, the Labour Movement has been innovating to improve our relevance to PMEs, including by rolling out programmes that PMEs want, such as mentorship, and we will do more.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I urge the Government, together with tripartite partners, to continue working with the Labour Movement to support and enable our PMEs in the AI-disrupted era for win-win outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: AI is advancing quickly and the population is ageing.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: A top concern among many workers is whether they can keep their jobs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: According to NTUC's survey conducted last year, about 40% of white-collar workers were worried that they might lose their jobs beyond the next six months.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Many are asking: "Will AI replace my job?" Many workers are also struggling to manage both work and family responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We can address these challenges in three areas.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, help every worker turn AI into an advantage.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Just as we learned to use computers and smartphones in the past – we need to clearly guide workers on what to learn and how to learn it so that AI becomes a helper, not a competitor.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, review the income ceiling of the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As of September last year, about 60% of applicants were rejected, with one reason being that they exceeded the income ceiling.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In 2025, the median income for PMETs was about $7,600.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: NTUC proposes linking the income ceiling to the PMET median income so that more jobseekers can receive timely support during their transition.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: One possible approach is to update the Caregiver Support Action Plan to help them remain in the workforce while caring for their families, maintaining stable incomes and continue building up their retirement savings.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the past week, many have moved between reunion, Ramadan and reflection – with meals shared around the table.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some tables are full, while others have empty seats.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Elders with their time-honoured recipes, children pulled up close with baby chairs and extra seats pulled out at the last minute.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Budget 2026 is delivered at this festive and reflective moment, set against a backdrop of profound structural change.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The global order is fracturing, job augmentations facilitated by technology are accelerating and economic competition is intensifying.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But there is another transformation, which is equally consequential that we must confront.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An ageing society is not simply about older persons.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It reshapes childhood, work, caregiving, retirement and community life for everyone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we prepare late and view ageing as a burden, we will have to manage decline.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But if we prepare early, perhaps we can design longevity with meaning through our years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, I will speak about how we must respond across the life course, so that every Singaporean continues to have a place at our national table.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means fewer classmates, siblings, workers and caregivers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2024, 29,237 new Dragon babies were born – one of whom was our son Mizan.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every child is not just precious, but pivotal in securing Singapore's place in the world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When couples consider parenthood, they are not just calculating financial costs across their children's lifetime; they are assessing confidence – be it in childcare access, sufficient housing, quality of life, our climate, the way the world is going in what the stakes are like to raise a child.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Before we were fortunate to have Mizan in our sixth year of marriage, my husband and I would often talk about the kind of parents that we hope to be, the kind of Singapore that he might grow up in.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Budget 2026 includes financial measures, such as Child LifeSG Credits and Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers, and for some parents, this means a few months of milk powder covered, which is much appreciated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the past two years, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong highlighted the Government's support for a Singapore Made For Families.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One substantial policy shift has been the expansion of paternity and additional 10 weeks of shared parental leave during that precious first few months.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond monetary support, these are the kind of changes that help to make family "feel" possible in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must build on this momentum, through changing mindsets about shared responsibilities and consider adjusting childcare leave proportionately to the number of children a couple has; enhancing flexible working arrangements which are crucial for many modern, dual-income households; normalising career pauses and supporting re-entry for both men and women; improving opportunities for access to housing with more space or that are nearer other family members for support.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is the invisible infrastructure of fertility – when parents trust the system, there is less anxiety about parenthood and there may be a greater willingness to give it a go.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As every child is precious, we must also make sure that every child is safe.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Preschool and student care oversight needs to be strengthened, so parents have peace of mind when leaving their children for the day.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our systems must also hold the most vulnerable of children with care and competence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether under child protection, in residential care homes or in the juvenile justice system, we must strengthen safeguarding standards and empower officers working with these children, through adequate resourcing and coordinated support across agencies to intervene and tackle the root of the issue.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The system must fight for them, not fail them, as these children are part of our national family too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Budget 2026 strengthens workforce support, such as the expansion of AI training under the TechSkills Accelerator.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But disruption is already here – long-term unemployment of those under 30 is higher than pre-pandemic norms and mid-career transitions are lengthening.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For youths, I hope to see more structured, meaningful internships for learning, not as proving ground, to become the norm.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, some stack internships out of pressure, not purpose.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Students from lower-income families sometimes feel torn about pursuing an internship they are passionate about versus the opportunity to work for their households.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And when some graduates turn to internships instead of full-time roles, we must ask how else we can support the school-to-work transition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Organisations like The Astronaut's Collective, Access Singapore and Halogen run programmes that help facilitate exposure to career opportunities for, among others, disadvantaged students to broaden their horizons to the possibilities they may not even know of.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that such important work can further be scaled.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Work-study pathways should be integrated into curriculum, not peripheral as just stand-alone programmes and industry co-development of curricula should deepen.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a potential hundred-year life, this may translate to multiple careers across our lifetime.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Conversion programmes should be strengthened with concrete employment outcomes, so that these transitions feel like renewal, not regression.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is clear that our Government takes an active stance on ensuring that: one, there are high quality jobs for Singaporeans; and two, that Singaporeans are well equipped with the skills to take on these jobs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Among young people, marriage plans are increasingly being postponed because they need to prioritise building their careers and financial stability to cope with challenging living costs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For young couples who fall into the “sandwich generation”, pressure and time constraints lead to decisions to have one or two children, something that requires significant consideration.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, we need to rebuild the “kampong” for our families and strengthen support networks.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether these are families transitioning from rental flats to their own flats, single mothers or fathers raising children or caregivers who sacrifice their careers to care for elderly parents, all Singaporeans need to feel that support is always available, and systems are easily accessible for them to get help.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some families in our community still depend on a single source of income.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This makes them more vulnerable to economic uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When their source of income is affected, they worry whether their daily needs can be met.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whatever choices families make in childcare arrangements, women who take career breaks should always feel that the door remains open for them to return to work and fulfil their aspirations if they choose to do so.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I applaud initiatives, such as MARA Mentoring by MENDAKI and the SkillsFuture Job Seeker Support Scheme by WSG.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While many rely on foreign domestic workers or care services for the day to day, caregiving does not end at the door.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sons and daughters from the sandwiched generation continue to carry the quiet responsibilities with love – the emotional vigilance, decision-making, unexpected hospital appointments and the guilt of not being able to be there.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we should also encourage structured parental care leave frameworks and employers who go the extra mile to support employees.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And finally, we must keep an eye out for particularly vulnerable double ageing segments, such as the persons with disabilities and caregiver dyad.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An ageing society with changing family structures requires caregiving language and norms to evolve – we cannot keep stressing family systems until they break.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That represents valuable wisdom and experience which should be tapped on.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Ang Mo Kio, 40% of our residents are over 60 years old.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their life stories and gentle resilience, inspire me deeply.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While efforts, such as the Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) 2.0 and the Silver Upgrading Programme make ageing in place more possible, we must continue to design empowering upgrades and inclusive spaces so they feel confident to participate in community life instead of taking a deficit-based approach to thinking about what they cannot do.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And in the midst of all the upgrading and construction to do so, we must also be mindful in the process, how even changes in pedestrian walkways, lack of lifts or escalators at overhead bridges, can result in our seniors being fearful of leaving their house to do their favourite market run and end up staying isolated home alone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that over time, public spaces and Active Ageing Centres can evolve into intergenerational hubs, where grandparenting sessions are a norm, seniors mentor youths and take on micro-work opportunities, even as some recover in community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It may be slightly jarring going between lohei and terawih in this period, but this is also, what it is, as the beauty of a multi-religious and multiracial society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Budget challenges us to do the same at a national level.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is the first Budget of our super-aged phase.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must think structurally, not incrementally and across life stages from childhood confidence, to workforce resilience, to ageing with purpose as one congruent Singapore story.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we design intentionally and strengthen the compact between generations, then longevity will not feel lonely and will not weaken Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And whether one comes home to a large reunion, bringing the next generation along, or a small gathering, or a community who becomes family – every generation of Singaporeans should know, that they always have a place at our national table.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our national coffers are fuller than ever, yet the structural burdens on the average Singaporean household remain stubbornly heavy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There are many recurring themes and issues that continue to be not just relevant but also increasingly pressing for Singapore and Singaporeans, and I sincerely hope that the Prime Minister and Minister for Finance can seriously consider my suggestions for the current term.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is not an isolated incident and as I highlighted in my Budget 2025 speech, higher-than-expected surpluses have been a consistent feature of our public finances since at least 2021, often following initial estimates of deficits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This persistent issue of fiscal marksmanship raises fundamental questions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is the Government consistently taking more from the economy than it truly needs?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And what are the implications of this for our private sector?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When a government persistently runs a budget surplus, it is effectively withdrawing liquidity from the economy and reducing the net savings of households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Persistent government surpluses are, by definition, private sector deficits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the Government may argue that these surpluses are necessary for long-term planning and unforeseen contingencies, the sheer magnitude and regularity of these upward revisions suggest a systemic issue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And let us also not forget that Singapore's way of accounting differs from international norms, such as that of the International Monetary Fund.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Including these receipts would reveal a much larger fiscal surplus, reinforcing the argument that the Government is extracting more resources from the economy than is necessary at the time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the face of these record surpluses, the Government's primary response remains a reliance on one-off handouts and ad hoc vouchers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have argued previously, we need better structural levers that automatically adjust to reflect the economic realities Singaporeans face, instead of uncertain one-off handouts that may or may not be renewed each year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The personal income tax brackets in Singapore have not been updated for over 24 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Since 2001, nominal wages and the cost of living have risen significantly, leading to "bracket creep," where taxpayers are pushed into higher marginal tax brackets, even if their real purchasing power has stagnated.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Earned Income Relief is another example of a structural feature that is long overdue for adjustment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The relief for workers under 55 years old has remained at S$1,000 for many, many years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And worse still, the personal income tax rebates from the last two years were discontinued in Budget 2026.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke at length about AI in his Budget speech, where AI is recognised as a critical driver of economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is incongruous that personal expenditure on AI-related tools and education does not receive the same tax relief consideration as corporate AI investments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we are serious about fostering a future-ready workforce, we must incentivise individual upskilling and adoption of new technologies through our tax policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I shared last year, it would be wise for us to introduce a broad-based "Skills Investment Relief", allowing individuals to claim a capped deduction for out-of-pocket training expenses.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would be an expansion of the existing Course Fees Relief, which only provides relief for specific approved academic, professional or vocational qualification.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, for businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs), the current system of fluctuating corporate income tax rebates, varying from 20% to 50% over the last decade, lacks the certainty and predictability needed for a long-term planning.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ironically, in the face of the Base Erosion Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0, the concessionary corporate income tax rates for approved global trading companies of as low as 5% on income from qualifying transactions in qualifying commodities, was extended from 2016 to 2031.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should embed the same level, if not higher level of stability into our personal and corporate income tax regime, moving away from discretionary rebates towards a more transparent and consistent framework that truly supports our Singaporean base.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Next, let me touch on two issues, which I believe were missing from the strategic focus of Budget 2026.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first of which is the issue of wealth inequality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in my Budget speech last year, I believe the deepest divisions in our society today are not based on race, language or religion, but based on socio-economic status which is closely tied to wealth inequality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we do not take a concerted effort to address this issue head on, as we have done with race and religion, these divisions will only deepen.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Unsurprisingly, to the extent that wealth at the top of the distribution is under-reported, measured wealth inequality is likely to be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the paper notes broad-based improvements in income mobility, it is also highlighting a "gradual moderation" in social mobility as our economy matures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Property is already a preferred means by the Government to tax wealth, such as via progressive property taxes and stamp duties.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Bringing back the NAV tax would serve as an effective complement to our system of taxing wealth, ensuring that those who benefit most from our economic growth contribute proportionally to our collective well-being.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As with the estate duty pre-2008, exemption thresholds can be set such that only those who are truly wealthy will be affected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, the exemption threshold for dwelling houses was set at S$9 million from 1996 to 2008 and an updated threshold adjusted for inflation can be determined as with other asset classes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development's (OECD) 2021 report titled "Inheritance Taxation in OECD Countries", states that, and I quote, "an inheritance tax, particularly one that targets relatively high levels of wealth transfers, can be an important tool to enhance equality of opportunity and reduce wealth concentration.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The case for inheritance taxes might be strongest where the effective taxation of personal capital income and wealth tends to be low".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we all know, there is no capital gains nor dividend taxes in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The challenge with taxing wealth via property tax, stamp duty and motor vehicle-related taxes is that the middle-income and upper-middle-income groups end up suffering too.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Consider the recent changes to the Preferential Additional Registration Fee (PARF) rebates in Budget 2026, which saw a 45-percentage point cut and a cap reduction.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I had welcomed the Government's move in 2023 to further adjust the Additional Registration Fee (ARF) and cap the PARF rebates at $60,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This time round however, while ostensibly aimed at luxury cars, the impact of the PARF changes is felt across the spectrum.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But even an entry level Suzuki Swift, which is one of the cheapest cars in Singapore at a so-called mere $152,000, we will see its PARF rebate slash from $6,600 to $660, resulting in an increase to its annual depreciation to about $15,000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This demonstrates how policies intended to target the affluent can also impact the middle-income segment while the truly wealthy, like those who rent high-end properties, remain largely unaffected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure our tax policies are truly progressive and do not inadvertently burden the middle class.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should therefore also study wealth tax issues in other nations, such as Norway and Switzerland, where they are present.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government might point to Norway as a cautionary tale, claiming that the increase in the rate of wealth taxes had resulted in an exodus of wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ironically, many of the wealthy turn to Switzerland, which has a wealth tax, instead of other jurisdictions without the wealth tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Swiss model which, with its "forfait fiscal" or lump sum taxation based on lifestyle expenditure or multiple of living expenses, offers an interesting alternative to traditional wealth taxes based solely on asset valuation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This approach could be explored to ensure that those who benefit most from Singapore's security and conducive environment contribute their fair share even if their declared income or assets are difficult to fully ascertain.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some may argue against wealth taxes, citing fears of capital flights.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, Singapore's unique value proposition, similar to Switzerland, remains a powerful draw for global talent and capital.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many wealthy individuals would still prefer to reside and operate here, especially in the context of what Prime Minister Wong said about the weakening of the multilateral system, where countries everywhere have less confidence that common rules will protect their interests.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we can establish an AI Council to provide strategic direction and to drive Singapore's AI agenda, where is the equivalent council or dedicated high level focus to act with clarity and resolve on our existential demographic challenge?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The truth we must confront is whether the Government is genuinely committed to structural solutions for our fertility crisis, or whether it is increasingly leaning on immigration as an easier way out.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the recent Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) Singapore Perspectives 2026 conference, Acting Minister Jeffrey Siow described our TFR of 0.97 as abysmal, but simultaneously argued that we need to do more integration so that we can do more immigration.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I also believe that the Government must do more to nurture fertile environment for parents to grow their families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of taking the path of least resistance, we must be bold and innovative in our approach to raising our TFR.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wish to draw attention to Hungary's aggressive pro-nationalist policies, which offer a case study in comprehensive, albeit sometimes controversial interventions, where its TFR rose meaningfully from around 1.2 in 2011 to 1.6 in 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While some may point out that Hungary's TFR declined to 1.39 in 2024, arguably macro economic factors may also have a significant role to play.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are we willing to be this bold in our approach and exempt mothers from personal income taxes?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For sure, money is not the be all and end all when it comes to having children, but according to a 2024 Nanyang Technological University survey of 230 young Singaporeans, financial considerations were raised by 70% of respondents as a reason why they do not wish to have children.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
