text: This reason was also mentioned by the majority of married respondents to 2021's Marriage and Parenthood Survey as the biggest hurdle that prevents them from having children.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, given that parenthood is a massive undertaking that lasts decades, I believe that more can be done across the spectrum.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As of the 2020 census, 53% of married couples were dual income.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While not all dual income couples have children, those who have often need to balance their parenting and work duties.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, I have previously suggested that the Government implement the statutory right to request for flexible work arrangements as well as increase statutory childcare leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the caregiving burden is often unequally shared as the odds are usually stacked against the mother's favour.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Recent Nobel Prize winning economist Claudia Golden observed that this motherhood penalty usually arises from mothers halting their careers right after childbirth and as their child gets older, they would turn to jobs that offer greater flexibility, but lesser pay.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, our policy should aim to recalibrate this imbalance, such as via tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if the Government does not wish to take the Hungarian approach, the least we can do is not make mothers pay more taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And I have shared on many occasions in this House, I hope the Government would revert back to the previous iteration of the Working Mother's Child Relief (WMCR), which is applicable only to mothers with children born before 2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there could be a small group of lower-income working mothers who would benefit from this change, the majority of would be working mothers will be worse off with the change in methodology.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For lower-income working mothers, a tax rebate can be given, and even if the tax rebates granted exceeds the tax payable, tax credits can be paid out in cash to ensure the reliefs are not lost.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, single mothers are not eligible for the WMCR, and even if we cannot raise their children on their behalf, the least we can do is to ensure that our tax policies do not discriminate against them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The bottom line is that structural issues to our low TFR such as work life balance, societal expectations and the high cost of raising children must be comprehensively addressed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must learn from international experiences and our own experiences to further tailor our policies to our unique context, ensuring that we create an environment where Singaporeans truly feel supported and confident in starting and raising families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, my speech today focuses on four areas requiring urgent attention in the 2026 Budget.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government's continuous over-collection of taxes compels us to question the necessity of raising tax rates and their impact on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This pattern of "annual over-collection" has become the norm rather than an exception.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking back at 2022, the Government predicted that the comprehensive GST increase would generate approximately $3.5 billion in additional revenue annually.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This includes adjusting personal income tax brackets according to inflation and updating various tax reliefs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We cannot allow the middle class, who are "rooted here and cannot flee" to bear a disproportionate burden due to fears that "the ultra-wealthy might withdraw their capital and leave", making them casualties of the wealth divide.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government may argue that these measures are too risky or that we must maintain a conservative approach.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I ask: what constitutes the greater risk?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But more importantly, it must be a Budget that reassures Singaporeans workers who are anxious about their place in a changing economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Foreign investments are creating much fewer jobs than before.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Economic growth is not always translating into worker confidence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They worry about whether the next disruption will be theirs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My first "U" worker group is the unemployed, specifically the involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To be candid, last year we saw many retrenchments and many "bad retrenchments" as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Employers who did not abide by the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment (TAMEM) made headlines.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Each time, NTUC and their unions stepped in, fought for members and workers including securing payouts, and escalated the issue to the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Drivers of retrenchments like business restructuring and uncertainties will persist this year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC and unions stand ready to support impacted workers, including PMEs who may not be covered under collective agreements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I ask the Government to give NTUC and the unions more time, strength and information to do so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Currently, employers with at least 10 employees are required to notify MOM within five working days after notifying employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government can consider all MRNs to be made prior to retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, there should be stronger penalties for employers who do not comply with this requirement and not just a slap on the wrist.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: According to NTUC’s most recent Survey on Economic Sentiments, about 40% of almost 1,000 workers expressed concerns about losing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I therefore opine that more can be done to support the broad middle of involuntarily unemployed workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By easing financial pressures, JSS helps workers avoid rushing into poor job matches that lead to underemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Time-related underemployment, such as when an individual who has the capacity to work a full-time position works part-time, is measured by MOM and widely studied.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, non-time-related underemployment, such as when a highly qualified, skilled or experienced expert holds a junior-level position, is more difficult to determine.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is why NTUC has collaborated with the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) to study this issue since 2023.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Voluntary underemployment, where workers opt to work fewer hours or in a less demanding role to pursue better work-life balance, personal interests, or a less stressful career, can represent diverse aspirations and values.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is the involuntary underemployed group that warrants our attention.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These are workers who stay in contract or gig work because they cannot secure a full-time position.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are also over-qualified workers who seek to move up the career but are stuck in junior level positions and pay.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over time, underemployed workers can become trapped in a vicious cycle of low-paid and insecure work, limiting opportunities for upward mobility.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Women and caregivers, in particular, are at a higher risk of underemployment and consequently, unequal pay, as they take more time out of the workforce and seek flexible work arrangements to balance caregiving commitments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I therefore submit that the Government broaden its definition of underemployment and collaborate closely with our tripartite partners to monitor this issue and maximise the productivity and earning potential of every worker, especially after NTUC and SUTD's underemployment study findings are released in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Fixed Term Contract (FTC) workers are one group acutely vulnerable to job insecurity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government can encourage employers to emplace FTC workers into permanent roles after two cycles of contract renewals, and regard successive contracts renewed within two months of the previous contract as continuous service, instead of the current one-month window stipulated in the Tripartite Advisory on the Employment of Term Contract Employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Another group vulnerable to involuntary underemployment that has been concerning of late is young workers and fresh graduates.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While this is in part due to the younger generation's propensity to explore diverse and flexible career paths, many also face external challenges like the shrinking of entry-level roles accelerated by AI and increasing saturation of diploma and degree-holders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Earlier this month, NTUC hosted a dialogue with students at the Singapore Management University on the subject.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Students spoke frankly about sending out dozens, even hundreds, of job applications without even a single reply.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Even "internship-stacking" may not be deemed as sufficient as employers increasingly preferred to hire applicants with at least minimum one to two years of full-time work experience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Early career professionals impacted by retrenchments are also met with stiff competition as "job-hugging" or resignation rates hit a historic 20-year low.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Labour market transitions can eliminate existing opportunities but also yield new ones, such as new sectors and more flexible or meaningful forms of work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For example, Singapore is constantly ranked as one of the most AI-exposed countries in the world, but also one of the most AI-ready.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Young people will need to know how to reach these new opportunities and our institutions must be equipped to support them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To avoid skills-jobs mismatches or youths getting stuck in gig, contract or part-time work after long and unfruitful job searches, a more concerted effort must be made to invest in human capital and skills, broaden the range of good jobs with good prospects and growing local companies and startups, many of which are aligned with recommendations outlined by the Economic Strategic Review.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government can consider launching an extended and higher-value iteration of GRIT in high-growth and high-demand sectors with opportunities ranging from one to two years and with monthly traineeship allowances on-par with starting salaries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Host organisations must convert trainees into permanent full-time employees unless a valid reason and supporting evidence are submitted.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government can also set aside more resources to groom early-career professionals by sending them for overseas work postings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is opportune as the Market Readiness Assistance grant and a host of other schemes are enhanced to support local companies to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is a global problem in the age of automation and AI but in Singapore, we cannot accept an economic model where growth advances while workers are left behind.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Structured career pathways and raised wages should continue to be encouraged in traditionally undervalued fields with unmet demand like the skilled trades, education and care services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My third "U" worker group is the under-represented, referring to local PMEs who make up about almost half of the workforce and disproportionately impacted by economic restructuring and technological disruptions, but who may lack representation and protection benefits.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government can also consider reviewing the Industrial Relations Act, which stipulates that PMEs cannot be represented by unions if they are in senior management and executives with duties involving hiring, firing or confidential information that present a conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I suggest there be greater clarity about exclusions, other than what is provided in the Tripartite Guidelines, as there are employers and human resource (HR) professionals who are still riding on this exclusion, to disallow unions to extend their scope of representation, especially for purposes of collective bargaining.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Currently rank-and-file unions can represent eligible executives on a limited individual basis for specific industrial matters including retrenchment benefits, dismissal, breach of individual contract, victimisation and re-employment disputes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I ask that the Government broaden this scope to also include grievance handling.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For over a decade, I have advocated for a compendium of measures to level the playing field and strengthen the Singaporean Core for our local PMEs, including legislation against errant employers who discriminate against Singaporeans, a foreign-PME dependency ratio, stricter Employment Pass (EP) application conditions and many others.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Yet, local PMEs, especially those who work in multinational corporations (MNCs), tell me that they still sometimes feel under-represented in numbers and rank at their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We can say time and again that it is not a zero-sum game, but when MNCs retrench equally knowledgeable, skilled and experienced local PMEs to retain cheaper foreign manpower, or when local PMEs are disproportionately underrepresented in senior and leadership positions and paid less, it can feel like this.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To be clear, foreign PMEs remain essential to complement Singapore's workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They fill critical skill and labour gaps, bring global expertise and networks and help keep companies growing rather than relocating.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many are friends and neighbours in our communities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But Government also needs to watch for parity of Singaporeans who do the same work and are paid similarly, and work alongside some these of S Pass and EP holders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I will also continue to call on the Government to monitor, previously coined as the "triple weak" companies and sectors and encourage them to improve their workforce profiles by removing preferential tax or not awarding public sector contracts for recalcitrant companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government can also consider awarding bonus points under the Complementarity Assessment Framework (COMPASS), based on the proportion of Singaporeans in management positions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My fourth "U" worker group is the "untrained".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Unlike other countries, where unions often must lobby for uneven training and upskilling opportunities, Singapore continuously doles out funding and promotes continuing education and training (CET) as a national priority.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, we enjoy a wide range of courses and schemes like SkillsFuture Credits to improve accessibility.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, there remains a minority of workers who have not accessed these resources we can work to reach.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A next step is to enhance Career Conversion Programmes (CCP) to cover even more sectors and increase offerings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the transition to an AI-driven economy approaches, NTUC has launched its AI-ready Singapore initiative to strengthen workers' long-term employability through learning and applying AI skills to daily work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Notwithstanding, a tripartite standard on ethical and non-discriminatory use of AI in recruitment, performance, promotion and termination can boost the AI-readiness of Singapore's workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Government can also encourage employers to partner unions to start upskilling and/or redeploying impacted staff early on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Together, we will move AI-literacy to AI-fluency for every worker, every department, every company and every industry, so that no worker is left behind.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My fifth and final "U" worker group is the underserved, referring to persons with disabilities and ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I contend that Diversity, Equity and Inclusion in workplaces should not be a compliance obligation but treated as workforce infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This means equipping managers and HR with the skills to productively operate a team with different needs, entrenching flexible work arrangements as a norm and avoiding cliff effects in policy support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As persons with disabilities and ex-offenders are more likely to be concentrated in lower wage and lower-skilled jobs and sectors that have higher rates of unemployment and/or underemployment, a more concerted effort can also be made to prevent reproducing inequalities for these two groups.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is why this Budget must work for the "5 U's": the unemployed, the underemployed, the under-represented, the untrained and the underserved.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In a time of transition, we will only succeed if "U" and "Me" move forward in Unity.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Singh, you have a clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The intention to pursue this point was made by NTUC before the Budget debate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is so important to come home to a space where one can feel safe and rested.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Housing and Development Board (HDB) projects are the pride of our nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This money gives us the ability to plan for and secure our future with greater certainty.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I will like to start with an appeal to the Government to invest more expeditiously in the rejuvenation of our older HDB estates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to ensure that our maintenance and replacement works can continue to uphold the standard and quality of our HDB housing.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some may suffer from more issues than others.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When one has to deal with unexpected and recurring problems, such as water ingress, mould and spalling concrete, our homes can become sources of stress and anxiety instead.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Take for example my residents at Henderson Crescent estate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Life at home can be stressful because they constantly have to watch out for leakages and check their ceilings and walls.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They worry about the effect the persistent mould have on their health, especially the children and the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The repairs also put a strain on their finances, especially for the elderly and families with lower incomes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important to rejuvenate problematic HDB blocks so that they remain good homes for our people and remain attractive enough for prospective buyers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If that cannot be done, I would like to call upon the Government, on behalf of my residents, such as our residents from Henderson Crescent, to grant their request for Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If there are no plans for SERS, can the Ministry review the criteria for Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS) on a case-by-case basis, depending on the particular condition of the blocks?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is not a request to help residents enjoy a windfall, but a request for every Singaporean to go home to a pleasant and liveable environment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, homes become a source of distress because of disamenities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most Singaporeans live in a compact environment, in close proximity with our neighbours.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, being part of a “we first” society, it is important to be considerate and be aware of our actions and behaviours on our neighbours and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This next issue that I would like to raise is almost ad nauseam – the disamenities suffered by my residents of Skyville at Dawson.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, some of the problems continue to persist and it is a reality that my residents continue to face, day in and day out.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many years have passed and I hope that time has allowed the Ministry of National Development (MND) to observe thoroughly the problems and possibly have a fresh perspective on possible solutions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Residents of Skyville at Dawson continue to suffer disturbances and nuisance caused by inconsiderate visitors to the roof and sky gardens at their HDB blocks, especially during the weekends, eve of festive seasons and public holidays.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Excessive noise disturbances, smoking and drinking, urinating at staircase landings, litter and rubbish, obscene activities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These problems have not abated, even with the concerted efforts of our grassroots volunteers, the HDB, Town Council, the National Environment Agency (NEA) and the police, disamenities still persist.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I appeal to MND once again, to reconsider my previous suggestions: install gantries for registration, install more closed circuit televisions (CCTVs) to monitor visitors and their activities, limit the number of visitors and require payment of a small fee to support the operations and cleaning of the sky gardens.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Again, this is because every resident deserves to go home to a pleasant living environment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that requests, if taken onboard, do take time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I myself first raised this in Parliament back in 2016, nearly 10 years ago, and my fellow PAP MPs had also continued to raise this request over the years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: You can imagine our great relief and joy that it has been taken up by the Government and is finally coming to fruition.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Still on the topic of housing, I would like to talk a little about property taxes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the lead-up to the Budget Statement, some of my residents have shared their concerns that property taxes may rise again, even though they are relieved by the one-off property tax rebate for 2026 for owner-occupied homes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Singapore has enjoyed a healthy Budget surplus with property taxes as one of the contributors, perhaps more can be done to calibrate this carefully or to consider longer-term support for owner-occupied properties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is especially needed by private estate residents who are elderly and no longer working but are living in their own homes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will also help our seniors age well and age in-place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other than homes, Singaporeans are very much concerned about jobs and the impact of AI on them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am very heartened by the Prime Minister's commitment that no Singaporean would be left behind in our push for AI and in this spirit, I salute our NTUC stepping up to this call in rolling out the AI-Ready SG initiative.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are also sectoral AI playbooks for workers and businesses in the sectors that face the most disruption from AI.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What the NTUC is offering is very much needed, but we need to ensure that it reaches the workers who need it.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there ways we can ensure that access to these AI resources is as easy and seamless as possible?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our seniors also do not wish to be left behind.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, AI training and tools have already been made widely available, but the real fear of disruption from AI tells us that what our people need most, is the support and career guidance to journey together with them as they navigate these changes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should also support the redesign of workflows and job scopes to enable greater productivity, while helping to alleviate the labour shortage in some of these industries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singaporeans worry about jobs and AI's impact.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am reassured by the Prime Minister's commitment that no one will be left behind in our push for AI.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge the Government to deploy them to ensure a conducive living environment for all Singaporeans and to transform Singapore into the most AI-enabled nation in the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But what truly matters is not our fiscal marksmanship year to year, but rather, our fiscal marksmanship for the long term, our fiscal marksmanship 10 years down the road, in 2030 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This is basically two full percentage points of GDP higher than the spending of around 17.5% of GDP 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In FY2025, we are spending 17.9% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, our fundamental challenge, the fundamental mission when it comes to fiscal marksmanship is really about raising revenues structurally to around 19.5% of GDP by 2030 to meet our spending needs in the long term.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It is fiscal marksmanship not year-to-year, but over many years, on the revenue side, to make sure we cover our needs many years out.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The key question however is, looking at the revenue mix in Budget 2026, can the mix be sustained?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Can it become a reliable blueprint for our fiscal security in subsequent Budgets?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: That is the key question for our fiscal marksmanship for the long term.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And to answer this question, I will focus on GST, corporate income tax and asset-related taxes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And unless consumption contracts suddenly, we can expect GST revenues as a percentage of GDP to continue at this level.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In other words, raising GST has been essential in helping us achieve fiscal marksmanship for the long term.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The real failure in fiscal marksmanship would have been if we dropped the ball, or lost the gumption to raise GST to secure our long-term fiscal future – because it was too difficult.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Budget 2026 estimates corporate income tax revenues to come in at 4.5% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It has gone up to 4% of GDP in FY2023 and FY2024, and then gone up further to 4.5% in FY2025.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Coming out of the COVID-19 years, who could have seen this sharp uptick coming?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But the key question going forward is: can we confidently assume that this will continue?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: How much of it is a secular increase in corporate profitability?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I think we should be conservative and we should also be sanguine about the revenue upside of BEPS Pillars 1 and 2 combined.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Indeed, a real failure of long-term fiscal marksmanship will be if we bet on something as new and uncertain as BEPS for our long-term fiscal future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, taken together, we can probably revise our long-term assumption for corporate income tax revenues upwards to 4% of GDP, not 4.5% as in Budget 2026, but 4%.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: That in turn means a difference of 0.5 percentage point of GDP.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, where do we raise another 0.5% of GDP, reliably, structurally, from other revenue sources?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Which brings me to the third point, asset-related taxes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: To my mind, we need to look at taxing assets more, much more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In this regard, I agree very much with hon Member Mr Shawn Loh.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Property taxes are estimated at 0.9% of GDP in Budget 2026.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Actually, property tax collections went down to 0.6% in FY2020 and has gradually come back up to 0.9%.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In short, for me, the real story coming out of Budget 2026 in terms of long-term fiscal marksmanship is that we can and should raise asset-related taxes quite a bit more, to meet our long-term future spending needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: First, while we can say that the Government may be over-collecting in certain areas, for example, in asset-related revenues which have been revised upwards by $4.5 billion in FY2025, and this is not so much by design, but due to cyclical factors, we absolutely cannot say that the Government has been over-collecting in GST.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In GST, by design, the Government is absolutely not over-collecting.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Because by design, the GST increase has effectively not started yet for most families and will effectively start only in 2028, five years after the increase in headline rate.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: By design, the GST increase for families below median income will effectively start only in 2033, 10 years after the headline increase.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And by design, there is effectively zero GST increase, permanently, for families in the bottom 30% by income.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Because alongside GST collection, we have also a system of GST offsets – the GST Voucher Scheme and Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: GST in itself is regressive, but our GST system of taxation combined with offsets is net-net highly progressive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The only people paying effectively more GST now are the most well-off Singaporeans, expatriates and tourists.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, we cannot say that because of the recent surpluses, the Government has been over-collecting GST in the past few years and not even for the next few years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But beyond GST, it is simply not very meaningful to draw conclusions and pass judgement on over-collections based on fiscal surpluses year-to-year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: What is meaningful to look at is whether a term of Government balances its collections against spending, over its entire term in office.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: A year of surplus can well be followed by crisis, and a budget surplus can swing very quickly into a deficit to overcome crisis the next year.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We have swung from surplus to crisis, many times, in the past decades.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And in FY2020, we swung to the greatest fiscal deficit any PAP Government has seen, ever.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It feels like a bad dream now, but this was just a few years back.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We do not quite talk about that in this debate.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Or look at the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) – the deficit for FY2003 was 1% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In other instances, the crisis was not pandemic, but economic.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And economic crises have usually been preceded by very good years – an exuberant economy, strong growth, larger-than-expected fiscal surpluses.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But precisely because of over-exuberance, markets eventually corrected and we swung from surplus to crisis overnight.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: A fiscal surplus of 2.8% of GDP on the back of 7.9% growth in 2006.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Growth disappeared completely in 2008 and so did our fiscal surplus.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Looking at FY2025 and this year with AI investments on an absolute tear and boosting the economy, can we say with certainty that this time will be different?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Or might a sharp pullback in AI investments, coupled with a secular slump in external demand due to even sharper tariff uncertainties, not be a real risk?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Precisely when we get a larger-than-expected fiscal surplus because of stronger-than-expected growth, I think we should be quietly worried.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Not about short-term fiscal marksmanship but about the risks of economic and fiscal correction that are being signalled.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And when a crisis does hit, we should not expect the Government to turn to the President, turn to our Past Reserves, in the first instance, to fight the crisis.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Each term of Government should be looking, in the first instance, at using its own fiscal resources, within its term in Government to fight crises and protect Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: That is why surpluses in some years within each term of Government is important.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Surpluses within a term of Government are a design feature, not a bug, in the PAP system of Government.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And these surpluses protect current generations of Singaporeans against shocks.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Rather than benefit future generations, they benefit the current generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And sometimes, the actual surpluses do turn out larger than expected.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But there will be times when they turn out smaller than expected too.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: It is normal to get a surprise, either on the upside or on the downside.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In fact, the surpluses for FY2025 and FY2026 are not unusually large at all in GDP terms.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Mr Shawn Loh made the same point yesterday.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Going back to FY2007, our fiscal surplus was 2.8% of GDP, I mentioned that.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Although it was just $7.7 billion in dollar terms.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But in dollar terms, the surpluses of $15.1 billion and $8.6 billion can create a sticker shock.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But we should be clear that this is not so much an indication of over-collection by the Government as it is simply a reflection of how much our GDP base has grown in nominal dollar terms over the last 26 years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The final point I will make, over the last 26 years, since FY2000, we have had surpluses in only 11 years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Over the last 26 years, we have had surpluses in only 11 years, including FY2024 and FY2025.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Our Budgets were essentially balanced in another 11 years, and we ran deficits in four.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, the bottom line really is: budget surpluses are actually not so common in our fiscal history.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Large surpluses in GDP terms, even less so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We have been largely balanced over each past term of Government, and it is really not very meaningful to pass judgement on fiscal marksmanship on a year-to-year basis.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: When we do have fiscal surpluses, we should count our blessings.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Across the OECD countries, the average fiscal position in 2023 is a deficit of 4.6% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We are in a special position to have surpluses.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, let us not talk of surpluses as if they are a failure in planning or something to be frowned upon.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Let us not give surpluses a bad name.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But it does beg the question, what should we do with the surpluses?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And I will make just one suggestion today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I say, let us plough back part of the surpluses.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This will cost the Government probably $1.5 billion – well within what our surpluses can afford.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, I thought to conclude this speech with a pantun.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And in the spirit of this Budget, and in line with the zeitgeist, I asked generative AI (GenAI) for help.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I prompted for a pantun about balance amid abundance, using a fruit tree as a metaphor.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And in one second, literally, GenAI gave me this, "Rimbun dahan pohon bermutu, buah manis lebat di dahan; harta melimpah syukur bersatu, sudi berkongsi tanda iman." Mr Zhulkarnain is smiling.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Translated loosely into, "Lush are the branches of a quality tree, sweet fruits hang heavy and thick.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: When wealth overflows, let it be joined with gratitude; to share willingly is a sign of faith." And then AI asked me if I would like another version, with a more specific fruit metaphor, like the durian tree.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, you refine the output?" So, in another one second, GenAI gave me this, "Pohon rimbun emas citranya, gugur sebiji di celah dahan; ambil sekadar perlu sahaja, selebihnya rezeki alam tuhan." Or "The lush tree has a golden aura; a single fruit falls between the branches.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, in conclusion, Mr Speaker, Sir, "Pohon rimbun emas citranya, buah manis lebat di dahan; ambil sekadar perlu sahaja, selebihnya rezeki alam tuhan." (In English): The lush tree has a golden aura; sweet fruits hang heavy and thick.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Take only what is needed, leave the rest as sustenance for God's nature.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Giam, you have a clarification to ask?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I recall him saying that, effectively, long-term fiscal marksmanship is what matters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is he saying that the year-to-year fiscal marksmanship does not matter?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And does he agree that there is an opportunity cost to inaccurate year-to-year fiscal marksmanship?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I will just reiterate two points that I have made in my speech.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: First, I think it is more meaningful to look at how a term of government balances its collection against spending over its entire term in government.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Second, if we look at the statistics, Table 3.1(b) of the statistical annex to the analysis of revenue and expenditure for Budget 2026, the figures are all there.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I referred to that; the Member can refer to that.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The point is, large surpluses are not that common in our history at all, over the last 26 years; and to zoom in on those large surpluses in GDP terms and draw conclusions about overcollection, I think, is an overstatement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Mr Xie mentioned that we could plan for corporate income tax contributing up to 4% of GDP and he also proposed more asset related taxes, including higher property taxes and making stamp duty more progressive by introducing a new tier for residential properties above $5 million.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does he agree then, that if all these new taxes and duties are included, there will be less need in the future for increasing regressive taxes like the GST to balance the Budget and meet our future expenditure needs?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can I ask him what is the basis for that statement and does he know the percentage of people who do not pay any net GST because of GST vouchers?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am not talking about net GST increases but just the net GST in total.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: So, the real question is, how do we get there, from 17.5% 10 years ago?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And so, the point is, we do need a whole mix of revenue strategies to raise revenues structurally to meet our long-term spending needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And this Government, the PAP Government, has been taking steps well ahead of time and having the courage to do that so that a future government can have the wherewithal to meet our future needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: So, that is the response to the first question.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: On the second question, it was about GST progressivity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: On that, I think it has been mentioned many times in this House and outside, I think Prime Minister put up a chart two years ago during the round-up speech, on the net GST rate, net of transfers, that Singaporean households at different income deciles will be paying because of our system of collection and offsets.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: So, I would encourage the Member to refer to that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am wondering if the Member would accept that the constitutional requirement that governments run balanced budgets over their full term necessitates that a balanced budget would occur at the end of this five-year term even when there may be surpluses, simply by transferring any additional surpluses to reserves to ensure that the constraint is respected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second question: I ask if the Member will not accept that, even if a surplus need not be detrimental under all conditions, which is unobjectionable on its face, it nevertheless imposes a disproportionate cost on our households when they are already struggling with high prices and cost of living.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: My basic response to both clarifications is yes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I accept that surpluses can be transferred into Past Reserves at the end of a term of government.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: But surpluses within a term of government serves two purposes: first, it buffers Singapore and Singaporeans against shocks and crises within the term of government, and then at the end of the term of government, if we pass through that term without crisis and we have accumulated surpluses, then that could be transferred out, or that could be transferred into Past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: That is our system of government, and it is, I think, the envy of many countries around the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: It is something that is precious that we should really cherish; something that we should really cherish.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans have seen much progress in the material aspects of their lives, yet some continue to face significant economic changes from blue collar workers, whose wages like PMETs, far more than in comparable countries, to young graduates who struggle to land first jobs due to offshoring and tightened MNC passes, and employees who care for loved ones.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During the opening of Parliament, I spoke about the importance of us together and the role I hope to see us take as we move forward beyond early nationhood.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must make Singapore a healthier society to live in, rather than simply a wealthier one.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In previous Budgets, I called for moving beyond GDP as our measure of success through dashboards of social development indicators of our social and sustainability goals to ensuring that we also measure our resources beyond economic data, which can take the form of how we quantify our resilience and societal well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Today, I will focus on what I see as three pillars of a healthier Singapore society: first, measuring our demographics; second, ensuring well-being in the time of the smartphone; third, supporting environmental well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are issues that underlie our day-to-day feelings of being in crowded trains and roads, as well as the happiness and flourishing of our children in a time of change.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They are the lived reality of our fellow residents on this island, for whom the optimisation of their humanity will mean little if it cannot lead to a healthier society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: You just need to take the North East Line during peak hours and experience the feeling of being packed like sardines on the train.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When squeezed between other passengers, it is easy to imagine that our Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines and indeed, our entire public transport system, was designed to serve a population far smaller than the living reality we see today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Under such circumstances, it is not difficult to understand why many Singaporeans ask: "Are we on the verge of crossing our population limit?" A crowded train versus an unbearable train is not just about the number of passengers but whether passengers believe the train has a timetable and operational plan.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What are the population plans for various towns nationwide and what are the measures to mitigate the impact of population changes?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Large-scale population changes are not merely abstract data, macroeconomic effects or word games.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They also have concrete impacts on ordinary people's lives. : On any weekday on the North East Line, the question about Singapore's population limits answers itself.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And it is only human for people to ask, are we on the verge of crossing our population and demographic limits?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government has said many times that we do not have a population target.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet when we say that we will "be significantly below 6.9 million by 2030", it fails to assuage concerns that residents have about what they can expect their daily lives would be like in five, 10, or even more years from now.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The instinct to avoid having conversations about our population limits may backfire.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is a visible uncertainty that may cause anxiety and actively dampen positive emotions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is thus fair for Singaporeans to ask for greater clarity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The difference between a crowded train and an intolerable one is not just the number of passengers in it, but whether the passengers believe that the train they are on has a timetable and a plan.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During January's Singapore Perspectives Conference, there was much talk about how immigration will keep our economy dynamic amid persistently record low TFR.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must learn from the mistakes of our past and be clear eyed about the question of infrastructure sufficiency.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Research on perceived control in high density environments finds that stress responses are less affected by the actual density of the environment, but more on whether people believe that the crowding itself is being managed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: By releasing granular projections, the Government has an opportunity to show our efforts to tackle crowding.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This matters deeply to how we, as residents of Singapore, experience our daily lives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will provide a clear picture of whether our region's infrastructure is or will be sufficient for comfort and also help us advocate more meaningfully about urban related well-being issues, such as access to nature and blue spaces.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And what care has always required, whether within families, between bosses and workers, and across communities, is presence, trust and reciprocity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is not merely a resource to be allocated, but a relationship to be sustained.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet our response is often to optimise, to identify the gap, design a handy scheme and roll out a niftily named subsidy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps this works for transactional problems, but care is not transactional.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When policy treats it as though it were, we risk ending up with technically correct solutions that quietly missed the point.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We close every quantifiable gap in our care support initiatives but still may widen what I would call a humanity gap, and this gap shows up in the distance between what our schemes try to provide and what the actual hole is that we humans feel.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It shows up in the daughter whose disabled parents receive the Home Caregiving Grant but still feels completely alone.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It shows up in the parent who receives new LifeSG credits but still feels really burnt out, trying to keep up with class WhatsApp chats and Parent Gateway notifications.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It shows up in the employer who checks the flexible work arrangements box but judges the employee for using it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Efficient policies may have unintended consequences on society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I cite this to draw attention to how a society can respond to a policy because people are more complex than we can simulate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: None of this takes away from the progress made on our caregiver support.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The enhancement of parental leave last year was a meaningful step to recognise that caregiving is shared.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But we still have work to do for an economy that supports employees who also do unpaid care work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government must foster workplaces where workers do not feel like taking this leave would limit their careers or made them feel like difficult workers with scheduling problems.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must see workers as whole persons with obligations that extend beyond work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that many Singaporeans turn to hired living help to run our households and families, we must be responsible for their welfare, not just because treating them better will pragmatically improve their ability to perform their jobs, but because it is the right thing to do.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What are the other options available to us, particularly when in the long run, workers from our rapidly development region may not be willing to leave their own loved ones behind to do care work in Singapore?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: By understanding this humanity behind the choices that we make in care work, we can open ourselves up to responding more creatively to the demographic challenges.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I spoke earlier of the Beijing Vehicle Lottery System as an example of how policies that are highly effective on one problem could be inadvertently shaping decisions, like whether one should have children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The lesson from this is that we should be less fixated on pure optimisation and be more willing to accommodate the quarts of society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, when Sengkang MP Assoc Prof Jamus Lim called for a more needs-based Certificate of Entitlement (COE) system for parents with multiple young children with care needs and with care needs, it drew criticism for being subjective, divisive and benefiting too few.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Surely, there is room to take into account lived experiences, as those of us with multiple young children and loved ones with care needs will attest to.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, it appears that some Government policies already take similar concerns into account, such as HDB's free parking scheme on Sundays and public holidays, which aims to promote social integration and stronger family ties.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This Budget takes place in the context of widening scrutiny of social media platforms, online games, digital tools like AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of us have raised concerns on digital safety.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, despite passing legislation that deal with discrete harms, we must also have interventions on the harms caused by the digital environments themselves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we may not be interested in and can admirably resist all the myriad offerings big tech has for us, this does not mean that big tech ceases to be interested or invested in us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And the dangers of digital harms extend beyond our youths.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A recent article in The Economist warned that older people too are seeing increases in smartphone addiction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Scientific evidence has emerged and tells us that children's brains and, in particular, are not developed enough to handle these digital environments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As social psychologist Jonathan Haid argues, unsupervised in person, that is, offline play, has seen a huge decline, replaced by near limitless virtual social interaction.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while the jury is out and there is criticism of Haid's argument that digital childhood is the overwhelming cause for the youth mental illness epidemic, other jurisdictions are already proposing social media bands for children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I will raise this issue in more detail in my Ministry of Digital Development and Information's (MDDI's) Committee of Supply (COS) cut, I believe this development has to be studied with public participation and visibility through Select Committee hearings like we did with fake news.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This Budget has seen the Government announced wide- ranging support.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, while many Singaporean see it as a way to replace mundane tasks, others worry about GenAI that risks taking away our culture and yes, work and what it means to be human, and not because AI is seen to be better than a human hand, coming up with pantuns in a second, but because it is cheaper, faster and often ruled by models and scripts that we have no access to and thus, have no say in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many also worry about the impact of AI on our society's valuation of human creativity and consciousness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Forty-three percent of respondents to a Millennials Insights Survey from last year were concerned that the extensive use of AI in their daily lives might result in a loss of human touch.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government has a clear responsibility in technology regulation, financial backing and its own adoption of such tools.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And I raise two suggestions of how to mediate the societal impact of AI.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What seems to be absent are the input of social scientists and psychologists; also, representatives from Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), given AI shaping of the arts and influence on culture, as well as Ministry of Education (MOE), as AI rapidly changes the way that students learn and develop or not.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as we harness AI for industrial transformation and economic progress, we should take a leave from the UK's AI Council, which sat from 2019 to 2023.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That Council included members from industry, public sector and academia, and focused on diverse areas from developing public confidence in AI to developing frameworks to deploy safe, fair, legal and ethical data sharing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For our own AI Council, ensuring formalised input from Ministries dealing with diverse groups also means that the conversation will also include the important factors of what our shared humanity means in the true spirit of us together.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, our education system must be constantly incorporate the latest findings on the impact that AI has on learning.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will be even more marked in the developing child's brain, characterised by higher neuroplasticity and its still undeveloped prefrontal cortex.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The skills degradation argument was also cited in the safe and responsible use of AI in classrooms manual recently introduced in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which includes provisions for GenAI use only in settings where direct teacher oversight is available.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is commendable that we have set an ambitious goal of ensuring that all households are within a 10-minute walk from a park by 2030.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But as a small city-state with an ever-growing population and few places to go, we should also be extending this goal to ensure greater access to blue spaces, such as seas and lakes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Aside from widely accepted benefits of being in contact with nature in the form of greenery, numerous studies have also found that living near blue spaces positively influence mental restoration among adults and is something which we should work on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must increase the quality of engagement with nature conservation groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While such groups are now sometimes consulted ahead of development work, feedback is that this engagement can sometimes feel like a one-way information process, rather than a deep consultation or even a negotiation where concessions are made.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, as we move on in our society's continued evolution, we have to be more willing to relook our previous reflexes, which cite costs or economic reasons as trade-offs that we cannot accept, when the alternative is a deterioration in the health of our society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we must confront not just fiscal costs, but also human costs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They are the costs borne by the caregiver with no one to relieve her, the costs for the child plagued by intrusive thoughts and heart palpitations, because the digital world does not switch off, the costs borne by the resident who helplessly watches as the last wild space in their neighbourhood disappears.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are real costs, but they simply do not appear on any balance sheet nor measure of GDP.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Wealth without health is a house that is not a home.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The choices that we make are ultimately a clear indication of what we as a society value – and I believe that we are ready to make them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Is $155 billion a lot to spend for a country of our size?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Compared to OECD countries, Singapore sits around the mid-pack, 24th out of 41 entries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The highest per capita spenders are Luxembourg, about US$69,000; Norway, about US$65,000; and Denmark, about US$40,000.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The global top rankings are mainly small countries and very well-resourced ones, with relatively high tax rates.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: So, when I say this is a generous Budget, I say it with the confidence of these benchmarks.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: At the same time, there is some disconnect with the feelings on the ground.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The ordinary man in the street will see the big numbers, including those set aside for AI and technology, but feel that very little of the money is actually trickling down to them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is like a rich towkay who spends a lot of money to buy the best equipment and house them in gleaming big factories, but his employees do not feel that their bonuses are getting bigger or that their training is helping them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Instead, they feel like life is squeezing them dry, their commute getting longer, their food prices increasing and their lives a little more precarious.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Here, there are two groups of Singaporeans in the young seniors demographics, the well-prepared and well-resourced, mainly the upper- and upper middle-income group, and those who are struggling and worrying about making ends meet.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: To be honest, this second group appears to be increasing in numbers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Whether warranted or not, many of us are worried.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: My concern is that these mega shifts have caused or will cause more to slip into the lower middle-income group.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Once there, they may be unable to rise above this employment black hole on their own.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I argue that we need to fundamentally review our strategy to keep our workforce relevant.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Otherwise, we may end up with deeper structural unemployment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There is a growing number of a generation of displaced and frustrated young seniors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They become unemployable in their 50s and 60s, giving rise to deep discontent.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In the marketplace, companies are unable to grow or even to stay above water, due to unfilled job roles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Also, longer life expectancy means that we have to make our retirement funds last longer.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: So, it will be a two-step reinforcing cycle.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: First, shorter economic cycles especially with AI, means higher chance of displacement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With more Ordinary Account locked up in property, our Central Provident Fund (CPF) Retirement Account is no longer sufficient for retirement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: So, it is understandable that sometimes, even with $155 billion spent, there could still be pockets of discontent and despair among those who feel the money is not reaching them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: How can we break this cycle of discontent and bring in hope and optimism?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There are three things we can work on: skills, health and money.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In Singapore, people are our only asset and every worker matters.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Businesses and employees must be responsive to changes in market trends and new job demands.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: IHLs and Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) must also be more aware of job market requirements and are nimble to offer short courses and skills certification.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: No number of Japanese pastry lessons or scented candle classes will get us where we need to be to compete against a world which is AI-enabled and technology-powered.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We need discipline and expertise, not just “busy work” in retraining.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We need to offer the courses back in IHLs and ITEs with market-recognised certification.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Progressive Wage Model can be more aggressive with higher salaries for frontline or high-touch jobs so that Singaporeans will be keen to join them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: To do this and still keep ourselves cost-competitive, we need to look at productivity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In this we can look at the use of AI and robotics especially for the “dull, dangerous and dirty” jobs and upskill our young seniors to operate and supervise the robots.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: For example, we have seen how senior cashiers in supermarkets, are now helping with self-checkouts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The self-checkout kiosks are reducing the need for manpower and offering each person a platform to increase their productivity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Government, businesses and people must work closely together to help this group of young seniors stay employable and prepare them well for retirement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In fact, the "back to school every 10 years" should start from 30 years old and be a Government co-funded programme as an investment in our people.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: From where we stand, going back to school at 30 years old when we have left school barely six or seven years ago seems extravagant.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But this is the pace of new knowledge creation nowadays.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We no longer can count on our initial degrees bearing us through our careers without supplements.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Continuous education is a way of life, no matter our professions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This leads me to my second point about mental and physical health.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This sounds like a philosophical question so let me ask it in a more practical way.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Is the Singaporean Dream about building a million-dollar nest egg and retiring early?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Do we start our working life with the aim that it will be a short one and our life thereafter be a life of ease, comfort and plenty?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The chance of a life of ease without labour may be true for the very few lucky enough to be born into wealth or marry into one, or with a magic touch at the races.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But for the majority of us, life is a journey of work, meaning and growth, with most of our average 85 years of life spent accumulating judgement, skill and knowledge.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But work, like life, is a long marathon and not a sprint to get rich quickly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many who think about retiring young and may sacrifice their health with long and intense work hours in their 20s, 30s and 40s, only to find they end up with poor health in their 50s and 60s and are unable to live, let alone retire well.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: One often does not factor in the economic and psychological cost of poor health and often poor health is less a matter of genetic endowment or bad luck, than it is an accumulation of bad decisions relating to diet, lifestyle and sleep.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Health is wealth may sound empty until one ends up on the wrong end of the hospital bed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: So, in relation to work, I would suggest for us to think of healthy work as the key policy goal.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The rules for healthy working life are quite simple – have enough sleep, make friends and observe some simple health guidelines relating to diet and exercise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Second, consider going back to school every 10 years, which is also a sabbatical from work.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Last and most importantly, view working as a way of staying relevant, engage with community rather than retiring early.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: And to me, this is truly a life well-lived.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Quite aside from dry policy issues of planning, providing and financing, there are personal decisions and convictions about meaning and connections.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is part of health and a good life.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As a national conversation, we should include these important considerations in our planning and policies about working life.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many low- and lower-middle income groups cannot even meet the minimum retirement sum and yet we know that it has to keep increasing so as to keep pace with inflation and longer life spans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many in these groups also do not have savings and may have to downgrade their flats or opt for Lease Buybacks.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Over the years, I have assisted numerous residents in their 50s and 60s who struggled to repay their monthly housing instalments due to ill health or job losses or both in some cases.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Eventually, many of them had to reluctantly downgrade into smaller two-room Flexi flats.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: One example is Mr N, who suffered from a chronic heart condition which rendered him unemployable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: He and his wife do not have sufficient CPF funds to pay off their two-room Flexi Build-To-Order (BTO).

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: After many rounds of appeals, they finally received special approval to use their limited funds in the Retirement Account for their BTO.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But they had to pledge their flat to CPF Board because the funds in their Retirement Account were below the Basic Retirement Sum.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: While they now have a roof over their heads, they still worry constantly about their ability to cope with rising living and medical expenses for their retirement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is a fact, a pressure point, for young seniors who are beginning to see the importance of their CPF in their retirement journey.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This may be considered for such a long-term investment horizon and the large funds quantum.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Giving better returns will help reduce the calls for increased employer contributions to CPF, which risks making our workforce less competitive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: First, those who are ready and financially capable, compared to the increasing number of those who are struggling to make ends meet.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I am also concerned that more and more people are falling into the lower middle-income bracket and facing structural unemployment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The first is, I think, the more radical.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We need for Singaporeans to think of a meaningful working life as a fit companion for their adult life and not just a stage before the bliss of retirement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We need for all of us to consider work differently, to see it as a long running endeavour and one that is important and meaningful in itself, rather than something we have to do in order to make enough money for retirement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With this mindset change, we have two important implications.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: First, we need to continually get better at work, and to become not just relevant but skilled and accomplished at our jobs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We should be confident in our abilities that we are better than and are more than machines, that we can stay ahead and abreast of new technologies, and we can continually master new skills.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We must think of health as a key asset in our lives, not just our properties and other economic assets.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If there is one thing that money cannot buy, it is good health.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is a better asset not just of national healthcare financing, but of personal quality of life.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, in the face of rapid technological transformation, particularly in the age of AI, we need to conduct a fundamental review of our overall workforce strategy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Courage because this will require hard mettle and tough choices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The tide of discontent is borne out of uncertainty and fear about the changes that await us.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Against this, we have a strong track record of collective action, strong policy-making and a united, cohesive framework between the private and public sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Our country is small enough and nimble enough to find a living even in a turbulent world economy.
