speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In a Budget, workers look forward to two things most: assurance today and confidence for tomorrow, especially in an age shaped by rapid technological shifts, demographic change and workplace transformation.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Their aspiration is simple and shared: stable jobs, sustainable wage growth and dignified progression over longer working lives.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: And they want to know that even as industries transform, they will not be left behind.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened by the many of the hon Members' speeches who shared similar concerns that our workers must be at the heart of this transformation.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2026 gives assurance to households while laying long-term foundations for a more resilient workforce and brighter economy.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: On the ground, workers, especially PMEs, tell us candidly that they want to keep up.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Workflows are being digitalised, re-designed and more AI-enabled.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: So, many workers do the responsible thing, they try to upgrade, learn new tools, adapt to new work.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: However, challenges remain – fear of failure, insufficient time to upskill or reskill and not knowing what to upskill or reskill for sometimes, and at times, there is no change after all that upskilling and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I urge the Government to encourage companies, small and big, to partner the NTUC and the unions to leverage on the CTCs to prepare for the future of work and to grow both the organisation and its workers as part of the transformation journey.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The earlier we prepare, the better the chances of workers being upskilled and to be more efficiently deployed.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2026 also takes a decisive structural step.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This will tighten the link between training and jobs, offering more seamless career guidance, upskilling, job matching and transitions for workers and integrated support for employers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This move recognises the faster cadence of technology and job transitions, and the need for a single "Jobs-Skills" backbone.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The merger builds on a decade of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This signals a workforce investing in its relevance and wanting to stay relevant for the future.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We therefore should make the merger count for outcomes: track and publish conversion metrics, such as time to placement; wage growth post training; and employer adoption; co-design more CTC-like Jobs-Skills pathways, so training is planned with job redesign and hiring from the start; extend mid-career training support in ways that do not penalise caregivers or SMEs with lean staffing.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They have seen colleagues retrenched after restructuring, roles outsourced, functions automated.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In these moments, unions step in to ensure fair process, negotiate fair benefits and facilitate placement support through the e2i.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Early notification to unions is not a procedural nicety; it is the difference between proactive help and reactive damage control.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They give unions advanced notice of upcoming retrenchment exercises, sometimes even months ahead.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We should institutionalise advance retrenchment notifications across all firms, including for PMEs, so that affected workers can be rendered meaningful assistance early and with dignity.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Another structural concern is the year-to-year contracts where is there ongoing work, but a whole lot of ongoing uncertainty and insecurity.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The continued prevalence of fixed term contracts, especially annual renewals, put pressure on workers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For them, renewal uncertainty makes long-term planning and upskilling harder, which puts them at risk of falling behind.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This issue is felt acutely by mature workers who already face longer job searches.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Their reality should push us beyond administratively convenient renewals, towards clearer pathways to permanency where work is ongoing.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The Public Service is one of our largest employers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Public sector data show nearly 24% of officers are 50 and above.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We should be more transparent about contract tenure patterns, renewal outcomes and pathways to permanency where roles persist, so officers can contribute with confidence and plan for retirement with clarity.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: I urge for regular employer reviews of fixed term contracting, particularly for workers and for the Public Service to publish more granular indicators on a contract-to-permanent pathways, where functions continue beyond a cycle.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: PMEs today operate at sustained high intensity, long hours for some, but more often, it is the constant connectivity, with limited mental space to recover.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Officially, average weekly hours for employed residents have moderated to about 41 to 43 hours, and MOM has encouraged flexibility through the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests, but the intensity outside formal hours matter too.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Rest is not about doing less, it is about sustaining efforts and well-being.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Without sustainable norms, even the best upskilling will under deliver.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to encourage employers to set organisational norms around after-hours responsiveness, escalation rules and protected focus time.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: I also call on the Government to monitor hours and intensity indicators and spotlight firms that redesign work to raise productivity and protect recovery.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This broadens pathways for workers who can take modest market risk across a long horizon.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: These measures matter, because not all workers reach retirement with the same trajectory.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Some face mid-career retrenchment, illnesses or years on rolling contracts that depress CPF accumulation.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We should continue targeted CPF support for workers with disrupted careers, tracking cohorts with extended unemployment or caregiving breaks and calibrating top-ups to close adequacy gaps over time.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: They are motivated by purpose, health and some as much as by income.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: But access to career guidance training remains uneven.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Many who tap on these opportunities find them helpful, yet others have shared that they feel disadvantaged or overlooked in being considered for them.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We already see credible models in healthcare, age inclusive job redesign and assistive tech to help older staff to keep contributing productively, with unions partnering management and tapping on the CTC support to scale solutions.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This is precisely the kind of redesign we need to mainstream.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We should embed career guidance as a default in mid-career pathways under the new jobs-skills agency and to scale union employer pilots that pair job redesign with structured upskilling for older teams, across sectors.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs often tell us their challenge is not only funding, but time and manpower to release staff for training.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: The Public Service can catalyse norms through transparent dashboards on contract renewal patterns and clearer pathways from fixed term contracts to permanent posts when work is ongoing.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: That signal will ripple to the wider labour market.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: What Budget 2026 means for families today and for our future workforce is that there were expectations on the ground for more support, given the surplus and there are many uncertainties still looming.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: These measures cushion near-term pressures while structural changes mature but, ultimately, confidence comes when a worker sees three things clearly: "If I learn, there is a job at the end"; "If my role changes, there is fair process and early help"; and "If I work longer, the work is sustainable and my retirement is secure".

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Our task is to translate policy into predictable pathways at the firm and at the worker level through initiatives like the CTCs, the new jobs-skills agency and tripartite norms that protect both adaptability and well-being.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Workers are not stopgaps; they are partners in transformation and productivity.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: When we invest in their skills, support them responsibly through change and give them time and space to adapt, workers repay that trust with commitment and employers benefit from a qualified workforce that will boost productivity and bring about growth.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: But direction must become delivery, and delivery depends on all of us.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Let us Government, employers, unions and every worker, move decisively together, build new jobs and skills backbone so every Singaporean can see a pathway forward.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Let us redesign work so that transformation uplifts and not exhausts.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Let us strengthen fairness and security, from early retrenchment notifications to clearer contract to permanency pathways.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: And let us ensure retirement adequacy, especially for those whose careers have been disrupted.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: With that, notwithstanding my thoughts, I support Budget 2026.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: But of course, I had to ask AI, what are the new "5Cs".

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: According to Gemini, it is Choice, Convenience, Contentment, CPF, as well as Care or Community.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: From the OG 5Cs in 1990s to the post-pandemic 2020s, tangible goals have seemingly morphed and evolved into intangible ideals.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: So, how do we keep the Singapore Dream, as the hon Member had earlier mentioned, alive and kicking?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The strong closing to the financial year should motivate the Government to invest more where it matters most – our people, our businesses and our economy.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The question we must keep in mind: how can and what should Budget 2026 do to trampoline Singaporeans towards this Dream?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: On the cost of living, I appreciate that this year's Budget is for the long game, long term, long run – intentional commitments to levelling up how we harness AI as a strategic advantage, supporting our local companies to manage business costs and build a regional and global footprint, as well as strengthening our enterprise ecosystem to support public listings and to develop the equity market.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: My Fengshan families, both living in landed homes and HDB rental flats, have different lifestyles but share the same concerns on rising costs.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Yesterday, my neighbour in this House, the hon Member Shawn Loh, of Jalan Besar Group Representation Constituency (GRC), proposed surplus sharing if Budget surplus exceed 2% of the GDP.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I hear of similar aspirations from the ground even as many appreciated Singapore's fiscal prudence.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A decline in inflation from 5% to 2% does not reverse cumulative increases over the past few years.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It means prices are rising slowly from an already increased base.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Households experience this most acutely in everyday expenses – groceries, meals and utilities.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In response to a Parliamentary question I filed earlier this month on the impact of the Assurance Package, the hon Member Finance Senior Minister of State Jeffrey Siow said combining structural measures and additional one-off support allows to provide for more responsive and targeted support, while remaining fiscally prudent.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: And that in the longer term, the most sustainable way to help Singaporeans cope with cost pressures is through broad-based wage growth that outpaces inflation.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: This reminds me of the Chinese saying, "授人以鱼, 不如授人以渔", similar to the English saying: "Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day; teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime." While I am aligned with the wisdom behind the design and appreciate the new Cost-of-Living Special Payment, perhaps future iterations can have a tiered structure for a range of income with larger payouts concentrated at the lower spectrum of the income range.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For example, the bottom 10% of the range could potentially receive a higher payout than the next 20% income group.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Such a structure would redistribute more direct fiscal support to Singaporeans that experience intense cost pressures the most.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The additional $500 in CDC vouchers remain on course to fulfil its mission of supporting Singaporean households with daily expenses, as well as support heartland merchants and hawkers.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Since January 2023, 50% of any tranche of vouchers could be used at participating supermarkets, a welcomed move by Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: That said, there are opportunities to refine the scheme to enhance its impact.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Greater flexibility on how and where they can be used may increase its value to households and support more local businesses.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For example, in private residential estates or new neighbourhoods where a market or food centre are a few precincts or zones away, allowing the CDC vouchers to be used at locally owned enterprises in privately-owned buildings or malls, will expand help for families.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Alternatively, aligned with my earlier suggestion for Cost-of-Living Special Payment, the CDC vouchers could take on a similar tiered approach.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Plus, distributing CDC vouchers on a per person versus a household basis, may more accurately tackle the cost-of-living pressures in multi-generational, multi-family households.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The future is young and everything begins at home.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I welcome the move to support families, especially in the early years of a child's development.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Upstream efforts to keep preschool and student care affordable are the right steps towards a thriving Singapore society.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: While making preschool and student care more affordable is the right move, we must also guard against unintended consequences, such as driving up costs in the long term or placing undue strain on teachers and resources.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Maintaining the quality of education and care while expanding access is key to sustaining these initiatives over time.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Alongside the timely assistance, how will the Government ensure that increased subsidies not lead to upward pressure on preschool and aftercare fees over time?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Would the Government also be studying to what extent childcare affordability remains a barrier to workforce participation among mothers, particularly in lower- to middle-income households?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A critical consideration on these efforts include developing the expertise and professionals who form our care economy.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I call on the Government to be intentional in expanding the capacity of the sector – partnering social service agencies and community-based partnerships is key.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I carry the hopes of Singaporeans who have personally shared with me the lived realities of caring for a special child.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A dedicated Fengshan father once shared, how a simple bus or MRT ride can be a complex mission.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: He is a uniformed officer, protecting our shores.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I urge the task force to expand the support and relief for families and caregivers to alleviate the added pressures across several domains, including transport, therapy and medical assistive devices, among others.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I stand guided by the Prime Minister that it is a shared responsibility for all of us.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Speaker, Sir, each family is different with unique circumstances.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We cannot choose the family we are born in to, but the system should equip families to shape the future they aspire to have.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The recent Occasional Paper on Income Growth, Inequality and Mobility Trends in Singapore revealed that while Singapore has done relatively well in sustaining social mobility compared to other advanced economies, our social mobility has shown signs of gradual moderation as Singapore's economy continue to mature and develop.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It is in all our interest to ensure that as many Singaporean children have a fair go.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Speaker, Sir, I spoke on cost of living and caring for families before my final "C", that is, Core, I will speak in Malay, please, Sir. :   Mr Speaker, Budget 2026, like previous Budgets, underlines the importance of preparing for a rainy day.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The additional investments and funds channeled are meant to build and strengthen, so that future generations can create opportunities – for progress, income and success.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Regardless of whether they live in HDB flats or terrace houses, among other things, the price of daily meals, the expenses incurred when raising their children and caring for ageing parents often linger in their minds.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The assistance measures announced in the Budget will enable our people to continue being self-reliant and progress.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: However, the Budget must also help strengthen the resilience and competitiveness of the community now, as I mentioned earlier in English.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Additionally, Singapore also needs to enhance support that is localised and centred on the community as well as the organisations that offer it.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For example, the Malay/Muslim organisations and Indian/Muslim organisations that offer services to seniors, support families in need, obtain jobs as well as skills upgrading.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Essentially, Singapore must facilitate and diversify support networks comprehensively in the neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I will elaborate further, Mr Speaker, during the COS debate on the Malay and Muslim community affairs later.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: As someone who cares deeply about our community's well-being, progress and sustainability, I also wish to underline the importance of opening up more opportunities for our youths to compete and fly the Singapore flag high.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The Singapore we build must be secure, where every individual feels that they have opportunities to succeed and contribute to the nation.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We need to collectively improve the quality of life for our people across all areas – strengthening financial assistance, generating opportunities, offering support and building hope for the future.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I will summarise this section by going back to basics, the "ABCs". "A" for AI access, ethics and governance.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Much has been said about AI – from AI fatigue to how it must a friend and never made a foe.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: AI is also fast becoming a core tool of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: To level the playing field and access, AI intervention has to come upstream.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: By starting in schools, we can mitigate widening the AI divide, where only some will thrive in an AI-driven future.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Enhancing AI literacy across all Institutions of Higher Learning is a good start, but earlier is better.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Emphasising strong foundations will help students to learn how to use AI in a responsible manner and not as a shortcut.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: But we must note, the needs of a senior at 55, 65, 75, 85 and 95 is vastly different.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Providing more investment options for CPF members also offers seniors the opportunity to grow assets, enabling them to age without worry.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It is crucial to ensure initiatives aimed at enabling our seniors to age well are practical in improving seniors' financial security and quality of life.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singapore's young have a strong sense of purpose and social justice and aspires for their employer to be on the right side, play a part in building a community of good and drive social impact.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: This is an aspiration many young talents carry.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: By better understanding our young talents, their world view on meaningful work and their desire to be multifaceted, I am hopeful of a generation of Singaporeans who is committed to building a better future for the next one in time to come.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I intend to touch more on supporting our youths during the MCCY COS debate.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Budget 2026 demonstrates a thoughtful and prudent approach to building a forward-looking Singapore with a keen eye on current affairs.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: While Singapore is less than 750 square kilometres, the region and the world is a shared space and we must protect ours.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I plan to elaborate more during the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Defence's COS debates.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singaporeans across generations and backgrounds must have the feels for the Budget, so every Singaporean can feel secure and optimistic about what lies ahead.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: All being said, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Budget.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is my first Budget debate in this new term of Government and my first Budget debate in my second term in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In writing this speech, I spent time reflecting on the work we had done in our previous term and the legislative moves we had made which will have long-term impact to our Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They changed daily lives, both at work and at home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: With a healthy fiscal position, we now have the opportunity not only to cushion immediate pressures, but to build thoughtfully and boldly for the decade ahead.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Today, I will speak on three areas: inclusive workplaces for women in every season of their lives; a kinder workplace for persons with disabilities; responsible preparation for AI transformation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Because women do not experience work in a linear fashion.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We experience work in seasons: the season for early ambition, the season for caregiving, the season of returning, the season of mid-life change.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When we speak of inclusive workplaces for women, it cannot mean just guidelines.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And policies must move so that new safe progressive cultures can take root.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We see this clearly in flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But because they fear being seen as less committed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And this gap is especially felt in the season of caregiving.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Women returning to work tell us that flexibility is top-most in their consideration to stay or return to the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But what worries them more is whether in asking for FWAs, they would be “marked” by their organisations, and even if they managed to get their FWAs approved, whether their bosses and teammates will genuinely support them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Because the lived reality is that even with FWAs, caregiving does not go away.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Ms N, a resident I met, knew about the guidelines.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: She wanted to ask for flexibility because her childcare does not operate on weekends and closes at 7.00 pm sharp daily.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In her small company, she feared being labelled as the one who inconvenienced everyone and she feared being replaced in her job, by a boss who does not understand her needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must recognise that workplace flexibility alone cannot solve caregiving strain.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must also speak about women in mid-life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Perimenopause brings fatigue and physical changes that are rarely discussed at work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Yet progressive employers are showing that this conversation can be normalised.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I was encouraged to learn from our Education Services Union Leader, Sister Brenda, that her organisation openly engages employees on how to better support women through menopause.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These may seem like small changes, but they signal respect.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Indeed, small tweaks like more comfortable uniforms can make all the difference as women go through the different seasons in their lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is what cultural maturity looks like in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Similarly, breastfeeding mothers tell us that workplace lactation rooms may exist, but culture matters more.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If lactation rooms become storerooms or moms feel rushed, the message is clear: support is conditional.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: A kinder workplace for persons with disabilities and their caregivers means removing barriers, not lowering standards.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Like all Singaporeans, our persons with disabilities and their caregivers have career aspirations and dreams.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But limited caregiving resources and rigid employment structures – fixed hours, inflexible expectations, lack of assistive tools – unintentionally exclude them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: My Punggol resident, B, who has hearing impairment, struggled to secure a host company for his ITE Work-Study Diploma and he and his family suspect that it was due to his impairment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As with many of our youths, B is a bright-eyed, curious and hardworking young man.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: His family is supportive, and understandably worried about his future.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: With a secured place in the ITE Work-Study Diploma, they will be more assured of his future independence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I have since reached out to several employer contacts as well as SG Enable for assistance but stories like this remind us that talents do exist, but access is uneven.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must strengthen upstream support in placement and upskilling even in our schools.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I support initiatives such as the SG Enable Enabling Mark, which recognises disability-inclusive employers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But the Enabling Mark must go beyond just being an award.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must also strengthen the Singapore Opportunity Index as a national signal that inclusive hiring is part of business growth strategy and not charity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This will not only improve job matching but also make inclusion visible and measurable.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   AI will affect our nation's future development, but this transformation must be responsible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: New technology should make people's lives and livelihoods better and brighter, not bring anxiety.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The impact of autonomous driving technology on the bus industry is a concrete example.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: To this end, the National Transport Workers Union (NTWU) has already begun training on electric buses and autonomous driving with public bus operators.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The tripartite partners have also started discussions to understand the impact of autonomous driving on bus captains and maintenance personnel as well as future career development and renumeration arrangements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But when engaging with bus captains, I saw one thing more clearly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: One captain told me that driving only accounts for 20% of her work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The remaining 80% involves serving passengers, assisting elderly and mobility-impaired individuals and handling emergency situations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This reminds us that when discussing this transformation, we cannot only look at the surface aspect of driving; you must truly understand what that job entails in real life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: There are now also proposals for new positions, such as remote drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Upon further study, we discovered that these positions require skills like data analysis, which current captains may not immediately be able to handle.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Then, based on real circumstances, design training and transformation pathways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Technology can advance but transformation must be planned and have safeguards. : Mr Speaker, today I have spoken about three priorities: inclusive workplaces for women in every season, a kinder workplace and responsible transformation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Inclusive workplaces for women mean moving policies for workplace culture shifts to take root.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: A kinder workplace means barriers must be redesigned away.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They require courage to change policies, faith to shift cultures, commitment to redesign systems and discipline to transform responsibly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If we are serious about building a Singapore that is not only competitive, but fair, kind and humane, then these must be the collective Singaporean ambitions that we have.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The Budget speaks not only to today's pressures, the costs of living, which is the immediate anxieties of our constituents, but also to tomorrow's transitions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Over the years, I have had the privilege of working closely for youths and young workers in my various roles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Their hopes, their aspirations and their quiet concerns have always stayed through to my heart.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Today, our young Singaporeans are entering the workforce at the moment of profound historical inflection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: AI is shaping the very definition of a job or a good job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Economic restructuring is creating pockets of uncertainty, and the traditional pathway from school to work, once a relatively straight, well-lit expressway, might no longer be so straightforward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: If we look at the macro data, the picture is indeed reassuring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In Singapore, education, employment outcomes for youths remain strong.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: But, Sir, numbers alone might not always tell the full story.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We hear on the ground worries for the pathways into the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We hear of concerns over entry level opportunities and career progression.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Their reservations about whether hard work would still translate into advancement in a fast moving economy shaped by technological changes, cost pressures and global volatility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: As a case in point, this year's Lunar New Year conversations took on a different texture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: There were the Nanobanana-generated Lunar New Year family portraits and video greetings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We joked about how AI could never replace the traditional "lohei", the human spirit of tossing to prosperity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: But there were also conversations that were far more serious.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We talked about the impact of AI on work, especially on entry level jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: I heard concerned parents speak about how much harder it was for the children to get jobs after school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: I heard of some young Singaporeans admit quietly, often with a sense of frustration about sending out hundreds of job applications before they got an interview and I heard the other side too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: I heard bosses steering about how they could deploy AI faster in their companies to overcome the manpower crunch.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: I heard supervisors wondering how to get how they could get their juniors to compliment and supervise AI in the daily work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Everyone is trying to grapple with how AI should work for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They are hungry, but yet, many are not fully confident they are equipped for this new job market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They asked: would there be enough entry level jobs for me?

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: When these youths enter the workforce, they do face competition and a narrowing of good entry level jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They asked: will the skills that I have acquired be relevant, especially in this age of AI?

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Their concern is also sharpened by technological change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: For them, AI is not just a tool, it is an immediate disruptor that is already reshaping some entry level jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: What they are worried about is the focus of my speech today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is a critical structural challenge facing our workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is a challenge that might threaten to change the social compact for an entire generation of Singaporeans in the years to come.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In the past, a fresh graduate enter the workforce and learn by doing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The junior coder does code maintenance, fixes some minor bugs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We have all done it before in our careers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Today, GenAI performs or could perform many of these routine cognitive task in seconds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: What once took a week now takes an hour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: What once required many juniors to do, require a somewhat a more senior person armed with some AI tools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: But let us be clear, AI does not spell the end of work as we know them today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In fact, many might still be boosted by AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Research from a 2023/2024 National Bureau of Economic Research, studying 5,000 customer support agents found that AI assistance significantly boosted productivity, especially for less experienced workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In some cases, a two-month old employee perform like someone with six months of experience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This means the learning curve has been shortened.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The AI did not replace the entry level worker, buy it empowered them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It allowed them to punch above their weight almost immediately.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It may be what economists called a rebound effect too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: If AI allows us to build software faster, we may build more software; if it lowers the cost of service delivery, demand may expand.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Even if AI raises overall productivity, it can still shrink traditional entry level roles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Entry level workers have historically been hired not because they were immediately productive, but because firms invested in their future productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Companies paid a premium today to build capability tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: If AI can perform the training task, the learning task faster and cheaper, the short-term economic incentive to hire juniors weakens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In the long term, it can hollow out the pipeline of middle-level Singaporean talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Compounding this, our higher cost structure and manpower tightness in Singapore have prompted some companies to site teams of knowledge, entry level workers in the region; while retaining the quality control and supervisory roles here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This is understandable as companies seek to control cost while retaining quality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In isolation, this is not a bad situation for Singapore as we retain higher value work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Powerful algorithms, a thin layer of senior experts and too few local managers and specialists in between.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This will not just be an economic problem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Our youths are looking at this landscape and asking, if the AI can do the junior entry level work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The crux is not whether the job exists, but whether the human can adopt and adapt to AI in his or her work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: As Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng had shared earlier and Senior Minister of State Desmond Tan in his early public speeches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This is different from earlier decades when industrial growth naturally produced many manufacturing jobs and clear entry points.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: But this is natural and to be expected as the global economic structure changes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: According to economist Dani Rodrik, the future of jobs will rely largely in services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Last year, job creation in Singapore was driven mainly by investment in services, particularly in financial, health and social services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: However, as globalisation has made outsourcing of services increasingly pervasive, this is also the sector where it is increasingly difficult to keep entry level roles in the same numbers and scope.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, the question is not how do we stop the AI disruption?

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The questions are: how do we keep the entry pathways open while we transform; how do we prepare for this possible new future of entry level work?

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is probably gone in some industries or going through overtime in others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We should not try to preserve the routine work in the age of AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We must fundamentally redefine what it means to be entry level in the Singaporean economy of the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In the past, workers value was production – write this memo, draft this code, compile this report.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: In the future, entry level workers value must be increasingly supervision, integration and judgement: audit the AI's output for truth and bias, integrate system securely and provide context, empathy and machines that machines cannot replicate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: This is a higher value role, but it is also a harder role because it assumes a level of maturity and skill early in one's career.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: And here is why we need a new industrial policy for entry level jobs to prepare for the new frontier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Singapore has never been passive in the face of structural change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: When we industrialised, we did not wait for jobs to appear.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: When low wage stagnation threatens dignity, we implemented the Progressive Wage Model to redesign jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We have similar conviction for the AI era as expounded by many of our Members today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We can put in place a policy framework ahead of the potential change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Allow me now to outline a possible three-pronged approach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We often admire the apprenticeship systems of Germany and Switzerland.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They expand into banking, insurance and advance services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The state and industry partner are to standardise training, so that apprentices contribute proactively from the start.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Why should we not adopt this approach to our economy on a larger scale?

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We can incentivise some to convert traditional execution roles into structured apprenticeships with core elements of AI oversight or AI integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: For example, if a law firm hires a graduate to audit AI-generated contracts or just draft from scratch, that firm may face an initial efficiency gap.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Over time, we can also formalise AI's oversight as a recognised skill within industry frameworks, portable, certified and valued across employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is an investment in the next generation of Singaporean middle managers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We will also need to identify queen bees industry leaders to lead such transformation in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Denmark offers a promising initiative to its National AI Skills Pact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: It is committed to strengthen AI capabilities among one million citizens by 2028, positioning itself as a leading human-centred AI nation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The approach is deliberate – joint flagship projects, employer led commitment and coordinated capability building across sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We can think about this as an investment for future generation of middle managers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Second, equip our students for semi senior entry responsibilities from day one of their working lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We must accept that routine tasks might no longer be guaranteed training grounds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Prompt Engineering could be a thing of the past now, but output verification, ethical evaluation and knowing when human judgement must override machine recommendations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: As machines take on routine tasks, uniquely human capabilities become more valuable – communication, partnership, leadership and ethical reasoning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Initiatives, such as NTUC's Youth Excel programme, one of the few programmes out there and youth-led policy platforms are important, because they do more than train for employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: They signal to young Singaporeans that they are not passive recipients of change, but participants in shaping it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: I look at our latest cohort of NTUC Starter Awards participants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The winning team presented on the idea of cross sector internships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: One of the core team members and a student at Temasek Polytechnic, Valerie, shared that the experience showed her how youth-led insights can meaningfully contribute to broader policy discussions and hopefully, industry changes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Our young people have the ideas; we need to give them the platform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: A diploma holder entering the workforce at, say, 21 years old, may find within a few years that additional credentials are necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Reskilling is hardest when there are bills to pay.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Structured pathways that combine employment and training reduce risk and increase participation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: Each time our economy evolved, we did not retreat.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We responded with policy creativity and tripartite partnership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The question before us is not whether AI will transform work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The question is whether transformation strengthens or weakens the Singaporean promise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: The broken rung is a structural shift, but it need not be a structural failure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We risk discouraging our youths and weakening our social compact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: But if we act now to recreate the entry level job, we can turn this disruption into opportunity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We can build a workforce where every entry level worker is an architect of their own future, supported by technology, rather than by being replaced by it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: We ensure that the Singaporean promise remains unbroken for the next generation – that if you work hard and master your craft, there is a ladder for you to climb.

speaker: The Minister of State for Defence (Mr Desmond Choo)
text: And NTUC will do its utmost to support our workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the chair at 2.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 2.29 pm until 2.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: What they are watching this debate for is something different, whether the design behind those promises is sound enough to actually deliver, whether the support will reach the families who needed it and whether it will do so in time and with the certainty required to make the most consequential decisions of their lives.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: That is the lens through which I wish to examine the family support measures before this Chamber today.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Stepping in the right direction, enclosing the distance are two different things.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The question is whether the way these schemes are built, who gets what, when they get it, how much and whether families can count on it, is working as well as it should.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For a family trying to meet ends meet every month, these details are not small things.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It is the difference between support that reaches them and support that is promised but falls short in practice.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I will raise three specific points on that gap.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, on equity across childhood, the missing equivalent for older children.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I want to test that aspiration against a structural feature of Budget 2026 that I do not think has received sufficient attention.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These Credits are flexible, usable at a wider range of physical and online merchants for groceries, pharmacy items, transport and daily household expenses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: There is no corresponding credit, no top-up and no new flexible support for household costs that continue to accumulate as children grow older.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The $500 in flexible relief is available for the 12-year-old.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For the same child, one year later, there is nothing new in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I want to be careful about what I am and am not saying.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I am not suggesting that older children receive no support from the Government at all.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Edusave contributions continue annually and families with children in secondary school can draw on those funds for approved educational expenses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: But Edusave funds are ringfenced for educational uses – school fees, enrichment programmes and approved school-related expenses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They cannot be used for transport, groceries, utilities or the broader household cost of living pressures that do not disappear once a child moves beyond primary school.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Childhood LifeSG Credits address precisely those costs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Their absence in Budget 2026 for families with older children is a gap worth examining.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I anticipate the Government may say that the Childhood LifeSG Credits is designed for the early childhood stage, where developmental evidence supports concentrated investment and that the Edusave system addresses older children's education needs adequately.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I accept that developmental argument, but the question I am raising is not about developmental priority.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A family with a secondary school-going child faces transport costs, utility bills and grocery expenses that are undiminished by the age of their child.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Budget 2026 provides flexible relief for one cohort of families.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I invite the Ministry to clarify whether it was a conscious decision to limit flexible support to children aged 12 and below, leaving families with older children without an equivalent, or whether this gap has simply not been revisited as family expenses have evolved.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: If it is the former, I will appreciate clarity on the rationale.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: If the latter, I urge the Ministry to review whether some form of flexible household support for older children should be introduced in future budgets.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, on scale, ComLink+ coverage ceiling must be named and addressed.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: ComLink+ represent a serious and thoughtful attempt to tackle inter-generational disadvantage in a more structured way.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The family coach model of proactive outreach, co-created action plans and multi-agency coordination represents a meaningful shift from passive assistance to an active empowerment.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I have no concern with the model but with the scale.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I am not comparing ComLink+ 10,000 families to the total public rental housing population.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I am asking about families in public rental housing with children who meet the programme's own eligibility criteria, specifically households with at least one child under the age of 21 and assessed as requiring sustained support.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Budget 2026 enhances the progress packages for families already in this programme – high quarterly payouts, better milestone incentives and more flexible disbursements.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These are meaningful improvements, but only for families who already have a family coach.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They do not reach families who are eligible but not yet served.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that scaling and intensive coaching relationship cannot be done overnight.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Training effective family coaches takes time and the Ministry is right not to compromise quality over speed.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: But that argument, while valid, does not explain the absence of any stated coverage target in Budget 2026.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I am therefore asking the Minister three things.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Second, to state the Government's coverage target, expressed as a proportion of eligible families and the year by which it intends to achieve it.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: And third, to confirm what investment in coach recruitment and training is included in this Budget to move toward that target.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These are not an unreasonable ask for our flagship empowerment programme entering its third year.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The stakes of this coverage gap extend beyond the families themselves.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: ComLink+ design is premised on early intervention, reaching families before their difficulties compound, before school attendance deteriorates and before debt accumulates beyond manageability.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Every year, a family is eligible, but unserved, is a year in which the programme's own preventative logic is not applied.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Enhancing payouts for those already inside the programme is valuable but it does not recover the ground lost while eligible families wait.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A coverage target will allow the Government to hold itself accountable to the programme's objectives.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, on implementation, closing the gap between announcement and delivery.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I also note that the reduction in fee caps for both anchor operator and partner operator preschools, which took effect in January 2026, already provides some interim relief to middle-income families.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: But even accounting for that, a family earning $13,500 a month above today's subsidy ceiling and below the incoming one is still paying more than they should be for another nine months.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The principle of their entitlement to support has been conceded by this Budget.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A household with two young children that spends $1,200 to $1,800 monthly on childcare fees would have to continue paying this amount for nine more months.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I will ask the Minister whether a transitional budget measure, targeted specifically at families between the old and new thresholds could be introduced for the interim period.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The January 2027 date is also worth pressing on.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's financial year begins on 1 April 2026, and many budget measures take effect on that date, and this is not a new subsidy category being built from scratch.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: MOE and the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) already have the means-testing infrastructure, the disbursement systems and operator reimbursement processes in place.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: So, what specifically requires this expansion to wait until January 2027 rather than taking effect at the start of the financial year in April 2026?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: If this is a deliberate policy decision rather than one driven by operational constraints, we must recognise that the families who were promised this relief will continue to bear a significant financial burden for an additional nine months.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: A bridging measure will also be welcome; it is not unusual.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: When GST went up, the Government did not simply announce the increase and leave the lower-income households to absorb the gap until the next Budget.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Offset packages were timed deliberately to cushion the transition.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: CDC vouchers have been deployed at short notices because cost of living pressures do not wait for administrative calendars.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: That same instinct, targeted, time-limited, with a clear end-date once the new thresholds kick in is exactly what I am asking for here.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The instrument already exists, it has been used before and it can be applied here again.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, the gap in Budget 2026 for families with children above 12 years old.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These credits are flexible and can be used for various household needs, such as groceries, transport and medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: However, there is no equivalent flexible support allocated in Budget 2026 for families with children beyond the level of primary school.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The cost of living for a household does not decrease as children grow older.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I hope the Government can look into this matter in future Budgets.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This programme is a serious effort that has looked at methods to address inter-generational inequality issues in a more organised and systematic manner.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Budget 2026 increases the support package for families that are already in this programme but does not state any targets or plans to increase the number and the training of coaches.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Third, the time gap between announcement and implementation of preschool subsidies.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: I ask that the relevant Ministry to consider whether interim transitional measures, such as those previously implemented through GST offset packages and CDC vouchers, can be introduced for families in this group. : Mr Deputy Speaker, I want to close not with demography but with equity, because that is ultimately what each of these three points is about.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The same conditions, cost uncertainty and the gap between announcement and delivery are shaping whether the next generation of families forms at all.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: They are signals that the conditions for forming a family do not yet feel sufficiently stable or attainable to many.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore company, which covers business, local and international, employment and employability, Singapore family and the Singapore dream.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has achieved significant success through strong and clean leadership.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Pragmatic long-term economic policies, a pro-business environment and substantial investment in human capital.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Internally, we are dealing with an ageing society, low birth rates and high cost of living.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Externally, geopolitical tensions, a multipolar world and a shift from rule-based to a power-based order that are influencing our landscape.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore company reflects the good work of the Government of Singapore, managing Singapore like a well-run engine.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The recent Budget announced by our Prime Minister is a positive step in supporting businesses and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Yet in this transformed environment, we must act differently and decisively.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Trade remains the life blood of Singapore's economy, making it essential for the Government to support companies in maintaining strength and pursuing global growth.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial for the Government to provide support to businesses at all levels, whether they are startups, SMEs or MNCs based in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We ought to build resilience, be adaptable and constantly innovate to stay competitive and be relevant.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget 2026 shows that the Government does listen to the ground.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This initiative serves as an immediate short-term support to alleviate operational costs.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to these, there are various forms of support by the Government, such as increased funding for grants, loans and international growth, which are highly crucial.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these businesses have successfully transitioned to formal companies.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Malik Hassan, whose parents started their business selling nasi lemak, I think some of you may know, from a stall at Adam Food Centre.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Malik, who is also the president of the SMCCI, has expanded to now having 40 branches across Singapore and has evolved to provide a variety of food and beverages.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: On a personal experience, Deputy Speaker, my mother ran a home-based business selling rojak initially at our kampong house and then moved to our three-room HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, I helped make the rojak to be sold to our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Today, our engineering company has offices in seven countries – Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Uzbekistan, with our headquarters in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: My mother's entrepreneurship spirit has rubbed onto her son that has allowed his company to grow regionally.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This can also be achieved by having entrepreneurship as non-examination subjects introduced at the primary, secondary and high institutions.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Such subjects will enhance their creative and innovative minds.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We should be a country of creators and innovators that develop new businesses, thereby increasing the economic status of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Other forms of programmes, like Partner for Business Growth, were performed.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: When guided effectively, economic growth driven by these companies benefits not only the business owners, but also the employees they hire.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: As a small nation, our greatest asset lies in our ability to forge a powerful coalition of companies, Government bodies and trade associations and chambers working collaboratively to support one another.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I would like to touch on support for international growth.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The enhanced Grant and Market Readiness Assistance are welcome initiatives that can significantly benefit our companies.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial for our business to expand beyond our shores and establish presence in various regions, including the Association of Southeast Asia Nations (ASEAN), Africa, Middle East, Latin America and many others.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This initiative enables companies to explore the best opportunities in their target countries.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry for Foreign Affairs to look at having our passport be visa free in as many countries as possible.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We are already in good position, but there are still countries we need to apply visa and these are countries we need to ensure visa free to ease travelling and business operation.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to the grant, it is essential that trade associations and chambers, and the Enterprise Singapore, which has an international network, aid our local companies.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I am pleased to note that the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) has established an office in Dubai.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The ecosystem will empower Singapore companies to set up their operation overseas in the most effective manner possible and be very successful.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The support provided by the Government through initiatives like SkillsFuture has been very encouraging.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: New industries such as space technology, advanced manufacturing, utilisation, data centres and renewable energy are emerging, offering a wide range of employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: As with every sector, AI will play a significant role in enhancing productivity within these fields.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans are navigating the transition from sunset industries to these new sectors and the ability to learn quickly is essential, especially as AI becomes integrated into these industries.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, the support from both the Government and employers is invaluable.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Training and transition to these new industries to be made easily accessible.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: A strong foundation for any worker lies in the attitude and many Singaporeans exemplify qualities such as intelligence, hard work and honesty.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: By enhancing their skills with AI competency, they can become valuable assets to companies.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I often think of the Government as the greatest family of all.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Just as a parent ensures each child gets the specific support they need, our Budget must reflect that same targeted compassion.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: On providing support for Singapore families, we must also move towards a more sophisticated, data-driven model of support.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This dream is a promise that every citizen, whether their passion lies in the arts, sports, business owner or the boardroom, can become the best version of themselves.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: But the dream is about more than just economics.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: We must ask ourselves: are Singaporeans proud of the country they were born in?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Will they sacrifice for their children's children's future so that they may live with dignity?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The answer will be yes, if we continue to provide that this Government is a caring, responsible partner in their success.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: By strengthening our economy, companies, global outreach, respected career for our workforce and refining our family support, we ensure that the Singapore Dream remains a living reality for all.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It positions Singapore to seize opportunities in the age of AI, strengthen our engines of growth, and build a resilient and skilled workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the lead-up to this Budget, MOF released an Occasional Paper on Income Growth, Inequality and Social Mobility.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Over the past decade, income growth has been broad-based.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement is heartened because these outcomes affirm the impact of the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unlike a blunt, across-the-board wage floor, PWM is sector-specific, covers over 40 job roles and links wages to skills and productivity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It recognises operational realities while creating structured progression pathways for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Had we not adopted PWM, we may well have followed the global pattern, where median wage growth consistently outpaces that of the lowest-paid workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I therefore thank the Government and employers for working with the Labour Movement to make PWM work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But Mr Deputy Speaker, we must not be complacent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Recent MOM data shows that median wages are beginning to outpace those at the 20th percentile.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If this trend persists, the gap will widen again.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Singapore also remains some distance from the OECD benchmark, where wages at the 20th percentile are around two-thirds of the median.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
