text: As our economy matures and pivots towards AI-driven growth, tripartite partners must exercise leadership.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Growth must not pull away from those at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To uphold a “we first” society, we must ensure that every Singaporean progresses, regardless of where they start.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement reaffirms our commitment to work closely with the Government and the employers to ensure that the fruits of growth are shared fairly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must maintain momentum in PWM through our tripartite institutions, especially the National Wages Council’s Progressive Wage Guidelines.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One key recommendation was that firms employing foreign workers pay at least the Local Qualifying Salary to all their local workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A Local Qualifying Salary of $1,800 corresponds roughly to the 10th percentile wage in nominal terms in 2023 – some three years ago.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If the Local Qualifying Salary lags too far behind actual wage distributions, adjustments will become reactive and steep.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I therefore urge the Government to consider three actions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, publish the latest nominal gross monthly wage, excluding employer CPF, of the bottom 10th percentile of resident full-time workers, so that the Local Qualifying Salary adjustments are benchmarked transparently.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, clarify what proportion of workers at or below the 10th percentile will be covered when the Local Qualifying Salary rises to $1,800.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must ensure that the policy meaningfully reaches those it is intended to protect.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Third, move towards a more regular review mechanism or an advance schedule of increases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A predictable glide path will give businesses certainty while preventing the Local Qualifying Salary from falling behind wage realities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we believe in sustained wage uplift, we must institutionalise it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It helps businesses adapt to higher wages as they transform and improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, for PWM sectors where baseline wages have already crossed $3,000, and/or wage increases are below $200, support may taper off too quickly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I therefore urge the Government to review the PWCS parameters to include all sectors and occupations under PWM and the Occupational Progressive Wages.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Where industries are undergoing longer-term transformation, co-funding support should be calibrated to match their transformation timelines.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we expect employers to sustain higher wages, we must align our fiscal support with operational realities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond the Local Qualifying Salary and PWCS, we must strengthen PWM itself.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The PWM Bonus functions very much like an Annual Wage Supplement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It provides workers with an additional payment to cope with cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, it applies only to cleaning, lift and escalator, waste management, and landscaping sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There is no principled reason to confine it to just these sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, we must address leave entitlements in outsourced service sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many workers in these sectors see their leave reset when service contracts change hands.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a calibrated enhancement focused only on sectors where the contracts' churn structurally limits leave progression.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: By setting a higher baseline within PWM, we strengthen retention, recognise accumulated service and improve workforce stability while allowing service providers and service buyers to price this transparently into contracts in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Third, we should expand PWM to more sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Where sectors are ready, we should move decisively.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As with other PWM sectors, we will make sure to bring onboard a good representation of industry players, including service buyers, to make sure ground realities are adequately addressed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Prime Minister spoke about strengthening lifelong learning through SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: SkillsFuture has embedded a culture of continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But in its next phase, we must address a structural weakness.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, there are around 500 training providers offering 9,500 courses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The rush to utilise expiring credits revealed a real challenge: choice paralysis – too many options, too little guidance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We already see how AI works in everyday life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When we shop on e-commerce platforms, products are not shown to us randomly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Algorithms study our past searches, purchases, and preferences, and recommend items we are most likely to need.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If AI can do this for shopping, surely, we can harness it for something far more important – our workers’ careers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Each worker should receive tailored training recommendations aligned to their experience, their career trajectory, aspirations, and life stage.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we are serious about AI, let us use AI to empower every worker, not just those who are already digitally fluent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will next move on to address cost of living pressures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Budget 2026 provides important cost of living support measures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement will also continue to do our part.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our NTUC Survey on Economic Sentiments shows that wages keeping up with cost of living remains the top concern across all age groups and income brackets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A Consumers Association of Singapore poll of over 360 Price Kaki users found that nearly 60% of respondents felt that grocery expenses increased the most in the past year, and 82% said the Cost-of-Living Special Payment and the CDC vouchers would help their households the most.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Through FairPrice Group, we benchmark more than 500 key value items and offer over 3,500 house brand products to stretch household budgets without compromising quality.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond daily essentials, we stepped in when families face deeper difficulties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These programmes support school-going children, assist families facing sudden income loss and provide relief during periods of hardship.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This year, NTUC has cast a wider net by increasing the income eligibility of our Care Assistance Programmes to $4,300, aligned to the 20th percentile of gross household income in 2024.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We will also strengthen support for single caregivers as well as families with younger children with special needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In 2025, its community programmes delivered close to $12 million in support to over 1.2 million beneficiaries, including more than $1.6 million in fresh groceries and hot meals delivered through "A Full Plate", Singapore's largest food donation drive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But beyond support measures, the most sustainable answer to cost of living pressures remains wage growth.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And that brings us back to PWM, the Local Qualifying Salary and tripartite resolve.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Hussin is a cleaner and the sole breadwinner for his family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: He has three children, aged 23, 20 and 11.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Every day, Mr Hussin wakes before dawn to head to work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: His job is physically demanding and often unseen, but he carries it out with quiet dignity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For nearly 20 years as a union member, he has done his part – working hard, providing for his family – and believing that if he persevered, things would improve.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Through NTUC's Care Assistance Programmes, he received support for his children's school expenses and essential daily needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For Mr Hussin, structured wage progression under PWM is not just a statistic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: His story is not unique and that is precisely the point.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When tripartism works, we translate policy into possibility for families like his.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, let us ensure that as Singapore rises in the age of AI, we rise together, leaving no worker behind and carrying every family forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: We are operating in a world that is more fragmented, less predictable, in a world where small missteps now carry larger consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we delay reform, the competitive gap widens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we neglect skills, the deficit compounds and if fractures emerge within society, they may take years, even generations, to repair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: For small states, there is less room for error.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Survival depends on foresight, adaptability and unity of purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to frame my remarks to Budget 2026 around two themes: capability and cohesion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2026 rightly accelerates Singapore's push in AI and other strategic capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The support for business transformation through enhanced enterprise schemes and AI adoption incentives is timely and necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But transformation is not merely about investing in new technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It is also about redesigning processes: how work is done, who does it, with what tools and to what effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It is people who interpret signals, exercise judgement and bear responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: While technology may drive new processes, it is people in the organisation determine the pace of change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If work flows evolve but mindsets do not, progress stalls and competitors move ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: So, just as we supercharge our AI strategy to enable firms to adapt, we must ensure that we are preparing people to adapt at the same pace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we want transformation to be fast, we must also prepare people to be adaptable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And that is why support for SkillsFuture and adult learning is critical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, firms will still adapt but they will do so by sourcing talent elsewhere and Singaporeans will risk being left behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: So, just as we reskill adult workers in the short term, we must also invest in the longer-term development of our youths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: When information is instantly accessible and machines can generate high-quality work at scale, speed and recall no longer set individuals apart.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Preparing our young for this future requires more than updating content.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If technology can elevate baseline cognitive performance, then assessing students solely on the outputs they produce becomes less meaningful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And in a world where information is abundant, the current focus on high-pressure exams built around memorisation risk misallocating our efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The competencies that will be valuable lies elsewhere – in discernment, collaboration, ethical judgement and the ability to navigate complexity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Twenty-first century competencies must sit at the heart of our educational goals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: We should bring the same intensity and focus to nurturing these capabilities as we have historically devoted to excelling in examinations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But I am not advocating that we all run out to purchase 10-year series for creativity or adaptability; please do not do that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: For a country whose only natural resource is human capital, this is not academic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And in an age of AI, serving that purpose requires more than incremental adjustments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Not only in what universities teach, but how they teach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Not only in how they conduct research, but how that research connects to evolving societal and industry needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Primarily the young at the start of their careers or also adults returning mid-career to reskill and adapt?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Must programmes remain anchored to a traditional four-year model following junior college or polytechnic pathways, or can the duration, pacing and credentialing become more modular and flexible?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: How should funding models evolve when knowledge cycles shorten and industries transform more rapidly?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If universities are to remain relevant in an AI-led world, they must be prepared to rethink purpose, restructure and rethink how they deliver content not just in terms of their pedagogy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But transformation does not occur in a vacuum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: For universities, those incentives are heavily influenced by global rankings, many of which are operated by privately owned, commercial organisations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: These metrics shape how institutions allocate resources and define success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Universities must guard against allowing external metrics to redefine their mission.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If reforms that strengthen teaching quality or societal alignment risk affecting ranking position, institutions may hesitate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: To be fair, existing rankings attempt to incorporate elements of impact and engagement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But they remain heavily weighted toward research output, citation counts and reputation surveys.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Such a framework would not replace existing rankings, but rebalance incentives toward learning outcomes, meaningful societal impact and long-term capability building.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If metrics shape incentives, then shaping metrics is part of our national strategy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And doing so would empower our universities to pursue necessary reforms without being constrained by narrow indicators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: My second point, Deputy Speaker, is on cohesion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: As work and learning become more personalised and technologically augmented, shared spaces of belonging become more important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: And the sport and the arts play a central role here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: They are where resilience is demonstrated, imagination expressed and identity projected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But it is only half of the equation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we invest in facilities without strengthening the practitioners who animate them, we dilute the return on national investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Ensuring that support for practitioners grows in step with capital investment is not imprudent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond public spending, we should also consider how to mobilise more private capital into this ecosystem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In uncertain times, cohesion becomes even more critical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It is an investment in the vibrance and resilience of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In my remarks, I have outlined how we can build capability – by reforming education for an AI-led world and aligning university incentives with societal needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I have spoken about strengthening cohesion by investing in the people who front our sporting and cultural life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we act decisively in both, we can ride the next wave rather than be overwhelmed by it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, some may claim that AI is overhyped and we are in an AI-bubble.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But the cost of being caught off-guard far exceeds the cost of being over-prepared.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: It now requires equal resolve, in both capability and cohesion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we do so, this period of uncertainty can become one of renewal – not because the world has become easier to navigate, but because we have become stronger as one united people.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And in previous debates, I have spoken up on mental health, education and lifelong learning and in support of educators and our healthcare workers, causes that remain close to my heart.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Stepping into this new role has made something clearer to me, it all converges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And so today, I wish to focus on how we can better support workers through transitions in the age of AI.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the past months, through my engagements at NTUC, I have observed that transitions are not "one-size-fits-all".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For young people entering the workforce, the transition is from education to employment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many wonder whether the skills that they are learning today will still be relevant to them in the future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are thinking about more than just their first job.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are thinking about independence, stability and of course, building a future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They need clearer exposure to industry realities, earlier signals of growth sectors, stronger alignment between education and employment, and of course, meaningful mentorship.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This would ease some of the burdens on our mid-career workers and help them juggle work, upskilling and caregiving more effectively.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many have spent a large part of their lives working and take a great pride in their jobs, careers and the knowledge they have built.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are living longer and healthier lives, and would like more options to continue contributing, such as flexible work arrangements and part-time and even community-based work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For them, it is not just about the job redesign, but also ageism and social stigma, and presumptions that they are less productive and slower to adapt.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our seniors want to feel accepted and valued in the workplace after a lifetime of contributing to Singapore's economic development.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They have undergone many rounds of technological change and they believe they can adapt and acquire AI skills.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It can paralyse decision-making and in such moments, clarity and coordinated support matter greatly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These groups face different friction points, but whether young or senior, mid-career or displaced, their concerns converge around three pillars: clarity, early and trusted engagement, and confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At last year's debate, I spoke about workers' uncertainty regarding the returns from upskilling.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It begins to address the fragmentation that I raised previously.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I met a mid-career worker who completed multiple courses over three years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet, she asked whether she had upgraded in the right direction.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Clarity must mean that workers understand what skills are in demand, which sectors are growing, what roles can they realistically move into and what progression looks like over time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is particularly important in the age of AI, where change is faster and signals be very much blurred.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For our young people, clarity must begin even before they graduate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this is why early career exposure and structured mentorship matters.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Through platforms such as NTUC Youth, young members receive career guidance and industry exposure to help them navigate this first transition with greater confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Clarity must also translate into action at the company level.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Transformation is ultimately about process redesign, tool redesign and of course, job redesign.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I therefore call on more businesses to take a worker-centred perspective when implementing transformation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When workers see how their roles are redesigned, rather than removed, clarity becomes tangible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Clarity turns the transition from something feared into something navigable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: No worker should have to navigate transitions alone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, I was involved in a retrenchment exercise.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It gave me a deeper appreciation of how important early engagement is.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Not just a concept, but as a lived, practical mechanism of support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Alternative employment options could be identified in advance to minimise the period of uncertainty for the worker.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In contrast, when information flows to the union too late, workers feel blindsided.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The difference between being informed before and after an announcement can be profound.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This experience reinforced something I have spoken about in previous debates.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are built on trust, regular dialogue and mutual respect, long before disruption occurs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As transitions accelerate in the age of AI, restructuring may become more frequent across many sectors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The strength of our system will depend not only on economic agility, but on relational trust.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To strengthen this commitment, we should review and reinforce norms around early engagement and consultation where feasible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It means earlier dialogue, greater transparency, shared responsibility in transition planning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our approach need not replicate theirs, but we can continue strengthening norms that encourage responsible employer conduct and early partnership.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Because trust cannot be built at the point of retrenchment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This confidence comes from two sources: external assurance of clear pathways from education and training from work, and internal resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What I have observed is that this anxiety often stems not from the resistance to change, but from uncertainty about identity and value.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Is there still space for me in this economy?" And these are deeply human questions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In one conversation, a senior professional shared that his greatest fear was not unemployment, but irrelevance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As digital systems were introduced, he worried whether the expertise would still be recognised.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In another case, a displaced worker delayed updating his resume for weeks, not because he lacked ability, but because he felt uncertain about how to position himself in a vastly changed market.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Transitions, therefore, are not merely about skills transfer.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we strengthen workforce systems, we should also be intentionally ensuring that our students and workers have the confidence to navigate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this means that as we design transition support frameworks, whether for youths entering the workforce, mid-career switchers or displaced workers, structured activation and confidence-building components should sit alongside upgrading and job matching.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Career guidance should not only provide listings of available roles, it should help workers reframe their value.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Transition programmes should not only provide technical certification.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They should help individuals rebuild momentum and self-belief.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we deliberately embed confidence-building into transition support, we strengthen not only our individual workers but also the resilience of our workforce as a whole.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Resilience determines whether change feels like an opportunity or a threat that gives individuals the confidence to take decisive steps to embrace the future of work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Allow me now to focus on the role of Focus Area 4 (FA4) under the MENDAKI, MUIS, MESRA initiative (M3), covering Employment and Employability.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: FA4 will ensure that the Malay/Muslim community is prepared and competitive in a changing economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In this month of Ramadan and with Hari Raya approaching, I know many residents in my constituency are running home-based businesses selling cookies, clothing and various products online.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They can use AI tools to design more attractive posters and product images, write more effective marketing captions, automatically reply to customer queries and even manage bookings and financial records more systematically.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This technology is not just for large companies.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also for small businesses who want to grow.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: AI is also not merely relevant in business.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a father, I myself have seen how this technology can be used responsibly in learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My child, who has dyslexia like me, sat for the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) last year.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We all know PSLE questions can sometimes be quite "interesting".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By using AI tools in the appropriate learning mode, called “study and learn”, it does not provide answers directly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead, it provides step-by-step guidance, helping to understand ways of thinking and approaches to solving questions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This makes it a support tool, not a substitute for effort.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I was able to sit with him and go through those questions with more confidence, seemingly turning into a "pro dad" for a moment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That experience showed me that if used correctly, AI can build confidence and strengthen learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we can utilise AI wisely in education and small businesses, then we should also be bold enough to do the same in employment and skills upgrading.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I will provide further details in the upcoming COS debate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about how we choose to use it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Even if we quibble about details, the statistics speak for themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yet, this success while not undeserved, belay an important reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it is highly uncertain if we will continue to do so, especially in an AI age where traditional educational advantages are being rapidly upended by the advance of this technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As Prime Minister Wong stated in his Budget address, our response to AI cannot be one of fear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This year's Budget exhibits an explicit tilt toward helping our nation confront the challenges of AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And having spoken on the importance of AI in my Budget response two years back, I agree wholeheartedly with this stance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it would be foolish to be blind to the immense transformative potential of AI to not just disrupt, but also completely overturn the competitive advantages of the Singapore model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We need change, not because our educational system is failing to deliver today, but because it is not adapted to deliver tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is the hardest type of change, requiring foresight, wisdom and courage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, "If it ain't broke, why fix it?" Let us first acknowledge how far our system has come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Public mass education began in earnest a decade before Independence, following the establishment of our MOE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: MOE's goal at the time was to reconcile the diverse approaches to education, given our multiracial population and to orient schooling toward the goals of nation building and workforce preparedness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Indeed, if you ask economists what they think was the most important factor underlying our nation's move from third world to first, many will likely point to our educational system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We must not take this success for granted, however, because the global educational landscape is rapidly changing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Emerging research already points to how AI compresses the skills gap by raising the productivity of inexperienced and lesser trained workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is the case even for college-educated professionals engaged in cognitive tasks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While this may fail to translate at the aggregate level, AI is nevertheless rapidly fulfilling its promise to vastly improve the efficiency of individuals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This was the thrust of my speech to the Budget Statement two years ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In the interim, AI has advanced at a breathtaking pace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Tasks that may have eluded AI, save for some determined and curated prompting, are now routinely answered with speed and accuracy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In the courses I teach at university, I struggle with how to best obtain separation between students based on submitted assignments alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The undeniable conclusion is that our traditional model of climbing the ladder of human capital development to become competent, reliable and trustworthy executers and operators is no longer likely to be the distinguishing factor for our workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The AI revolution will upend the way we approach education at all levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This was never tenable in so far as large classrooms affect not just the ability of our kids to receive sufficient teacher attention and absorb lessons, but also the ability of our teachers to adequately manage their pupils without excess stress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It has become even less acceptable today in an AI age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Furthermore, while educational technology may confer some benefits, notably in language acquisition and problem solving, these are frequently offset by drawbacks, such as reduced attention spans, diminished memory and weakened critical thinking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The saving grace for such applications is that if they are applied in a thoughtful and deliberate manner, which occurs when edtech is treated as a compliment rather than a substitute for the teacher.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This, in turn, calls for a better ratio of teachers to students in the classroom.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am also keenly aware that at the early ages, it is absolutely crucial that kids build a solid foundation for all that is to follow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This will set them up, not just to succeed in their subsequent academic endeavours but also in all sorts of life outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is, therefore, crucial that we do not allow our youngest learners to be left behind in their formal educational journey, reliant on supplementary tuition and parents turn teachers to make up for shortfalls in understanding that they would ideally have received directly from teachers in the classroom.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Much of what primary school students learn may seem like a boring reprise of known concepts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But these ideas are new, at least to the kids that are being exposed to them for the first time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And if these kids do not grasp the basic premises that they are being taught, do not get excited about acquiring new knowledge and resort to memorising and in lieu of true understanding, we set them up to be incurious individuals, ill-prepared in an AI-centric world, where the ability to absorb and regurgitate information will no longer be sufficient to set a student apart.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather, children need to be excited about their educational journey and approach school in a holistic way, as a place not just to be fed dry academic mater material, but a safe space to ask all sorts of questions, to challenge prevailing wisdom and assumptions and to have fun, picking up pursuits that are as varied as art and music and sport and of course, if they are so inclined, languages, along with Math and Science.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Major high stakes examinations long, a mainstay of gauging student understanding and evaluating student performance, will be less relevant in an AI age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This requires us pardon, pardon the pun, to re-evaluate how we evaluate our kids, especially in secondary school.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We need a mindset shift away from testing as a signal of competence and a means of streaming students to a way to check progress and identify if any particular student may have inadvertently fallen behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This need to change mindset is not lost on our educators or learners themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: MOE officials at the highest levels have acknowledged that examinations are the be all and end all, and students that embrace freedom from an examination-oriented curriculum often come to see that studying can be even a joyful and meaningful affair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Continual assessment has been a long-standing component of our educational system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It certainly was since I was in school, which was a long time ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But our weightings reveal lip service paid to the notion of continual.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Indeed, the continued presence of a relatively high stakes year-end examinations can leave students and parents feeling unprepared that they do not have a mid-term gauge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Anecdotal evidence even suggests that students and parents are making up for this change by simply having tuition centres administer mock mid-terms in lieu.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I, along with others on both sides of the aisle of this House, have repeatedly called for a reconsideration of these examination milestones, to grant more students the chance to pursue through-train education if they so choose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In an AI age, opportunities for late bloomers to catch up will be more abundant, which also means that such flexibility becomes even more important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The fact is, until the incentives for performing well in exams are truly changed, it is hard to expect anyone to relinquish the single-minded focus on exams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There is substantial evidence that genuine continual assessment is even far better in bringing about learning and understanding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Nor should we fear that this approach, which admittedly is commonplace across East Asia, need undermine ultimate student performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Systems like those in Estonia and Finland, as well as the US states of New Hampshire and Vermont have relied on formative assessment and continuous feedback for years and have produced a steady stream of excellent students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: To be clear, this call to shift attention away from exams and toward continual assessment decidedly does not mean a relaxation of standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather, it calls for the sort of steady engagement that can keep standards consistently high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This change emphasis is also better aligned with fixing one of the principal challenges that educators face in the modern AI-enabled classroom – students who simply cannot sustain enough attention and interest to complete basic tasks expected of educated individuals, like reading an entire book cover to cover, to grasp what they have read accurately, to write with accuracy and originality, and to internalise mathematical skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I will pause here to declare that I am, indeed, a college professor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Until now, university education has had a two-fold aim: to impart the workforce with modern, value-added skills via high quality teaching; and to infuse our economy with the latest cutting edge innovation and technology through research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What does it mean to transmit knowledge to undergraduates when such knowledge can be easily accessed and repurposed at the touch of a button, is rapidly devalued within years of graduation and can usually obtained at a fudge of the cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What does it mean when answers to assignments usually arrive after extensive reflection, discussion and struggle, may be obtained within minutes with a simple prompt?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There are already inklings of the tsunami of change that is about to come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Indeed, I believe that it will not be foundational models, which has captured so much of the public imagination and excitement with their clever answers to questions and seemingly human interactions, but rather agent-based ones that will be at the forefront of this disruption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Cognitive jobs are all the more vulnerable to replacement by such tools, which produce faster, are often more accurate and increasingly are higher quality output than humans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The best models are even able to do so with minimal guidance and instruction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The superior capabilities of AI are not limited to intellectually intensive activities either, like research or analysis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: AI can perform better in just about any profession where intellect, brains and ingenuity is deployed – from vacation planning to financial planning, from video game design to building design, from data analysis to legal analysis, and from diagnosing bugs in software to diagnosing cancers in humans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The aspirational careers of Asian societies – doctors, lawyers, engineers, bankers – are now all potentially replaceable by AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Moreover, we must not be lulled into a false sense of security by our nation's current unemployment rate, which has yet to capture the potential displacements of jobs that could result when AI and robotics become more entrenched in the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The future is much better inferred from the unemployment rate of new workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Reports of fresh graduates struggling to secure employment are also piling up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What this means is then that the skills we teach in lecture halls and labs need to evolve away from rote learning and solving known problems to leveraging what makes humans unique.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Soft skills like empathy, networking, judgement, creativity and vision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The way to separate weaker students from stronger ones is frequently no longer what they submit in written assignments – something Singaporean undergraduates often excel at – but by their inquisitiveness, their willingness to question prevailing wisdom, their ability to think outside the proverbial box and their strength at bringing others together on a common task.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In last year's COS, I suggested that we move forward with granting entry based on satisfying absolute entry criteria.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is now even more urgent given how relative academic performance will be ever less relevant to university success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Reform must also percolate to more advanced levels of tertiary education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is natural to ask, what is left of research when even at the PhD level, only a tiny, talented minority may still credibly lay claim to intellectual superiority and methodological sophistication?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But the reality is that scholarship is not borne out of funding alone, as important as it is, and especially in an AI age where differences in the capacity to produce research are likely to collapse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Instead, what is relevant is the sophistication of the questions that we ask and the way that we approach problem solving.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For this, we must still appeal to what is inescapably human.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Our most groundbreaking innovations have always relied on humans affording their imaginations the absolute freedom to follow wherever the ideas lead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This occurs best in open, liberal, democratic societies, which offer the best conditions for the accumulation of productive human capital and the generation of world class scientific output.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: These conditions then contribute to productivity and in the long run, economic performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Our autonomous universities must stop chasing global rankings for their own sake, but instead focus on the genuine nature of academic enterprise, a point that Member Kenneth Goh, a fellow academic, has just made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In doing so, I am certain, nevertheless, that recognition and reward will find their way to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yet, this AI moment also offers tantalising opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Teachers can tap on AI generated resources to offer education that is more interesting and more customised, a luxury that would have taken previously hours of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Those who are blessed with superior hand-eye coordination, or are more innately social, or exude practical intelligence, or possess a tinker's mentality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Let us allow diversity to be the core strength of our educational system in this AI age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I think it is one that provides critical stability in the midst of uncertainty and chaos.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And with this stability, it helps us to propel forward to pursue progress for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Last September, I spoke about the two forces shaping Singapore's future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: AI number 1 is "artificial intelligence", which generates information at lightning speed, changing the way we work and we live.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: AI number 2 is ageing individuals, experienced workers who bring their wisdom, their judgement and their perspective to the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Today, I would like to build on these two AIs and on this idea.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Singapore's success will depend not only on how quickly we find answers, but whether we ask the right questions about our future economy, our workforce and our jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We support strengthening CPF contributions for senior workers and to progressively raise the ceiling to protect retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We backed the Workplace Fairness Act to reinforce protection against workplace discrimination, and we have consistently pushed for job redesign, lifelong learning and stronger mid-career transition support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: More seniors today are financially prepared for retirement and more are choosing to remain economically active.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is a structural challenge that will affect our economic resilience in the long term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, many seniors still face barriers in staying meaningfully employed, such as hiring filters or reduced benefits at re-employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I am sure Members here would have also heard of anecdotal experiences among our residents who face challenges in the job search.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Third, many seniors worry about keeping up with technological advances and its impact on job security specifically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While many are willing to learn, they face constraints of lower familiarity with new technologies and also heavier caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Employers have also cited difficulties such as mismatched salary expectations, skills gaps and concerns about higher wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While these are not straightforward, and also difficult issues to deal with, but I remain optimistic that Singapore can navigate these challenges through our deep tripartite cooperation, and also, especially in this time of AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The first priority is to enable seniors to remain employable with choice, flexibility and inclusion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many seniors want to continue working beyond their retirement age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But this is not about expecting seniors to simply stay in the workforce longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is about giving seniors the choice and flexibility to continue contributing meaningfully, building on their strengths, their experience and their skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Tripartite Workgroup (TWG) for senior employment, which I co-chair, is exploring ways to expand and broaden these options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through the Alliance for Action on Empowering Multi-Stage Careers for Mature Workers (AfA-EMW), companies have piloted promising models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One example is Mandai Rainforest Resort’s hobby- or interest-based job roles, and also recruitment prototypes, where seniors are hired based on their hobbies and interests, with roles redesigned to build on these strengths and these passions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through this approach, Mandai gave Mr Richard, a 60-year-old nature enthusiast, the opportunity to serve as a Welcome Ambassador in a role aligned with his love for nature.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With support from his colleagues and employer, Richard now takes pride in bringing his guests around the resort to experience the natural surroundings he cares deeply about.
Some employers have also created structured pathways that allow seniors to transition gradually into retirement while continuing to contribute meaningfully.
These initiatives show that when employers redesign jobs thoughtfully and provide structured pathways, they can unlock the full potential of our senior workers.
Senior workers must also be able to contribute with dignity and without fear of discrimination.

This need was actually reflected in the experience of Mr Sunil, a senior jobseeker who shared in a forum letter last week about how NTUC’s Career Festival gave him more than job advice – it restored confidence and reassurance at a critical stage of his job search when he walked into the Career Festival.
His experience reminds us that beyond advice, senior jobseekers benefit from personalised guidance and support as they navigate career transitions.
We should therefore continue to encourage our employers to support and to invest more in training and job redesign for mature workers and also to facilitate multi-generational workplaces.
I am pleased to share that the first three playbooks have been launched and I encourage employers to work closely with us to tap on these resources in their transformation journey.
Our CTCs, including our growing network of queen bees also play a critical role in business and workforce transformation.
They bring employers and workers together to co-create upskilling and job redesign plans that directly benefit their business and also upskill our workers.
I met senior enrolled nurse, Lilian Teng, who is 69 years young.
She shared how the system eliminated frequent manual labour, reduced physical strain and allowed her to focus on higher-value clinical work.
Importantly, her younger colleagues helped her adapt and gain confidence to handle the new technology, while Lilian contributed and shared her clinical experience with the younger colleagues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This Budget strikes a balanced approach to meet the pressing needs of today, while preparing us for the challenges of tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This is also timely as we enter a new phase of Singapore’s economic journey where the global economy is increasingly fractured and uncertain.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Where technologies, are advancing at unprecedented speeds, reshaping how companies operate, and how we live and work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Many of our forefathers built successful businesses and contributed to nation building, including Pioneers such as Lim Nee Soon, Seah Eu Chin, P Govindasamy Pillai, Syed Omar Aljunied and Edwin Tessensohn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Perhaps one of the most iconic pioneer entrepreneurs was Tan Tock Seng.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: His story started when he arrived in Singapore in 1819 as a vegetable seller to a successful shop owner in Boat Quay in 1827 and to a thriving businessman.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Through his many businesses that spanned real estate, agriculture and of course healthcare, he provided thousands of jobs to Singaporeans, then and even now.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Like our Pioneers, our generation has also our avant-garde entrepreneurs who have succeeded and have been able to entrench themselves here and beyond Singapore’s shores.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This company was founded by three National University of Singapore (NUS) graduates, who were inspired by their exposure to Silicon Valley through the NUS Overseas Colleges programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Carousell began with a simple idea: to make the selling of pre-owned items as easy as taking a photograph.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: What started as a mobile-first classified ads app had since grown into a leading online marketplace and omnichannel re-commerce business operating across Southeast Asia, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and serving tens of millions of users across the region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: I am very glad that Mr Marcus Tan, one of the founders of Carousell, and others like him are part of the Entrepreneurship Committee.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: They, together with venture capitalists and business leaders have added tremendous value to the committee.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Just like our early days, today's entrepreneurs have spurred innovation, created jobs and established themselves internationally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Our startup ecosystem benefits from a pro-business environment which includes our established companies, our talent pool, dedicated startup spaces such as the LaunchPad at One-North and supportive Government policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Many founders of startups have proudly shared with me on how the Singapore brand had helped them forge partnerships and to break into new markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: However, we cannot stand still and rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We need to continue to strengthen our startup ecosystem, to maintain our attractiveness to startups, talent and capital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This is because of intensifying competition from startup hubs in Asia, the Middle East and even further afield.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Venture capital remains tight, particularly outside of the US.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Over the last few months, Minister of State Alvin and I have spoken to more than 300 stakeholders including startup founders, business leaders, venture capitalists and our youths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This was to understand their concerns and to propose strategies to help them and future generations of entrepreneurs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We would like to thank each and every one of you for your feedback and for your support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This was only possible with the strong support of our committee members and ecosystem partners such as the Action Community for Entrepreneurship (ACE), SBF, Singapore Fintech Association and the National Youth Council.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: And third, we will facilitate investors to exit and recycle their capital and expertise into new ventures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Several years back when my son was then five years old, he told me of a "paper clip" challenge, which apparently, he chanced upon on YouTube.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Starting from a paperclip, he was required to barter trade upwards until he reached a valuable item.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: After a couple of weeks, he presented a beautiful pen to me and tried to sell it to me for $20.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: What started off as a humble paper clip, after multiple trades, had been traded upwards towards a pen.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: I am sure my story is not unique and there are many budding young entrepreneurs with very interesting ideas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: However, when I ask successful founders whether they would support their children in pursuing entrepreneurship, some of them were reluctant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: They know well the risks of failure and how difficult the journey was.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It is therefore important to double our efforts to sustain and grow our entrepreneurship spirit in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: And we should start from a younger age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Initiatives such as the Applied Learning Programmes in schools and the Direct School Admission for Entrepreneurship are a good start.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: These programmes allow students to gain practical skills such as critical thinking and the resilience needed to succeed in today’s fast-paced business world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: And on that note, I fully agree with Mr Azhar Othman who had indicated earlier the need to start entrepreneurship in schools at an earlier age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We should also encourage Industry-led programmes, like the "My First $1,000" programme spearheaded by one of our committee members Mr Willson Cuaca from East Ventures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This allows our youths to road-test their ideas and experience the ups and downs of entrepreneurship.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Some may fail, but the lessons learnt would surely stay with them for life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Registrations are still open, but they will be closing quite soon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Ultimately, we must view setbacks as a stepping stone towards eventual success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Every successful entrepreneur will tell you that their path was filled with obstacles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: They will also mention that they would not have succeeded, if it was not for the lessons learnt from overcoming these challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The key is to learn quickly from setbacks and bounce back stronger.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We can also support our entrepreneurs in more tangible ways and encourage entrepreneurship across all ages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Entrepreneurship communities and startup spaces, like LaunchPad, allow people to collaborate, learn from each other and develop their ideas in a supportive environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This can be open to interested persons of all ages, including our mid-careerists and our seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: These communities, alongside mentorship from experienced entrepreneurs, create a strong ecosystem of support that gives budding entrepreneurs the confidence to take that first step.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: While new technology, products and services are disrupting traditional industries, it is also not uncommon to see startups with the right product or idea to achieve phenomenal success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: It is therefore exciting to work in a startup and perhaps, even more exciting to start one.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: And so, I would like to call on our aspiring entrepreneurs to believe in yourselves and to boldly take that first step.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Second, let me touch on those who have taken the leap of faith, achieved some success and are ready to scale globally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: To do so, they may need specialised talent, a range of financing options and access to new markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: They may need to raise funds for research and development, infrastructure, hiring and sales.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: But many start-ups speak of difficulties to access fundraising options at the growth and pre-Initial Public Offering stages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Further, the expansion in scope to cover early growth-stage companies, will help our startups raise the funding they would need to then scale.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: In addition, the new Growth Capital Workgroup, led by Minister Chee Hong Tat, will look into measures to support the financing needs of companies across various growth stages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: We will share the feedback obtained through our engagements with the Workgroup and to support in their efforts as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: As Singapore is a small market, our startups must think global from day one to succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: But we know this could be challenging for some, especially if they do not have a strong track record or if they are unfamiliar with the new markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The Budget measures to support Singapore companies as they venture abroad, such as the enhanced Global Innovation Alliance and the Market Readiness Assistance grants, will therefore be very useful.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: By strengthening the ecosystem's access to financing options and support for entering new markets, we hope to create an environment where good ideas can flourish and companies, including our SMEs, can grow and compete.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Thirdly, let me speak about facilitating exits to support capital recycling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Many successful founders want the opportunity to exit and to reinvest their time, talent and capital into new ventures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Thus, if we want a sustainable and dynamic ecosystem, we must ensure that capital is available for promising companies to exit at fair valuations and for the early investors to recycle their capital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: This will be especially important as more startups mature and want to seek capital for their growth plans through public markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: The committee also welcomes the $1.5 billion top-up to the Financial Sector Development Fund, to expand the Monetary Authority of Singapore's Equity Market Development Programme, which aims to develop our fund management industry and increase investor participation in Singapore equities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: I look forward to seeing the positive impact of these efforts in boosting listings on the Singapore Exchange.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Unsurprisingly, he was able to convince me to buy the $20 pen and he cashed out the venture, therefore, with tremendous bragging rights.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: He then recycled this princely sum into his next venture, of buying several other nicknacks and started the process all over again.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: If I recall correctly, most of it went to chocolates, which were quite quickly gobbled up by him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: There would be setbacks and they would have to navigate along uncharted waters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, and Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash)
text: Those who are able to adapt early, move decisively and invest ahead of the curve, will succeed.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, I speak in defence of our seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many carry with them daily realities and pressures very quietly.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I will highlight four areas that require our attention: nutrition vulnerability; rising cost pressures; digital anxiety; and the fast evolving threat of scams.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In a food-secure city like ours, it is worrying that we are seeing signs of rising malnutrition among seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This shows the issue is not marginal but persistent.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Doctors at the National University Hospital also highlight that malnutrition is closely linked to falls and poorer recovery.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many do not see food as part of healthcare.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When eating becomes painful, tiring and lonely, nutrition suffers, not from ignorance, but from circumstance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some stop walking to hawker centres and rely instead on biscuits and instant noodles.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Others shift to softer but less nutritious foods because of untreated oral health issues or chewing difficulties.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over time, protein intake drops, strength declines and frailty rises.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we are serious about healthy ageing, nutrition policy must address access and the daily realities of how our seniors eat.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My first proposal is a national movement, which I will refer to, for now, as Strong Seniors SG, with a simple goal: helping seniors stay strong through better nutrition, especially adequate protein intake.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Affordable foods, such as eggs, tofu, beans and simple fish dishes are already part of everyday meals.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yet nutrition gaps among seniors often arise not from the lack of food, but from practical barriers; difficulty chewing, fatigue from cooking, eating alone, or uncertainty about what foods truly support strength.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Strong Seniors SG would therefore focus on making protein intake easier, more familiar and part of the daily routines.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This can be advanced through three practical pathways: where seniors eat; how seniors eat; and what seniors eat.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can partner hawkers, food courts and Active Ageing Centres to make protein-rich meals more visible and accessible.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Stalls to highlight affordable protein options or label balanced set meals, including softer choices for those with chewing difficulties.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the healthier option is easier to spot, it becomes easier to choose.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Seniors eat more and eat better when they eat together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some Active Ageing Centres already run communal meals and we can build on this.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the UK, general practitioners (GPs) go beyond medication by recommending communal dining and social activities as preventive care.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can adopt the same approach in Singapore, with GPs and polyclinics referring seniors to community meal initiatives that provide both nutrition and social connection.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Countries like Japan and South Korea are investing in senior-friendly food innovation, including texture-adapted, high-protein meals.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: South Korea goes further by setting a national senior-friendly food standard, with clear nutrition and texture benchmarks.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Certified foods are labelled by texture levels allowing seniors to buy ready-to-eat meals from supermarkets.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Singapore, Health Promotion Board's Nutri-Grade has shown how clear labels can guide healthier choices.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could we build on this success with a similar approach for senior-friendly foods, signalling both nutritional value and eating comfort?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our food innovation ecosystem can support this through grants, pilots and partnerships with industry and community providers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because when seniors maintain their health, they maintain their independence, confidence and dignity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The second area that requires attention is rising cost pressures.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Cost pressures for seniors are often less visible.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One overlooked area is oral health, which directly affects nutrition and overall health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many seniors assume tooth loss is simply part of ageing.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some quietly share, "I don't go to the dentist because I cannot afford it".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
