text: With subsidies, full dentures can cost between $500 and $800 and require multiple visits.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such a measure would strengthen preventive care, while giving us a clearer national picture of our seniors' oral health needs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While Agency for Integrated Care's Medical Escort and Transport subsidies help some, many mildly frail seniors fall outside eligibility.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They may be able to walk, but could be unsafe in crowded transport.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Taxi fares of $20 to $40 per trip quickly adds up.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: About one-third of seniors live alone or with another senior; which means managing healthcare, from appointments to follow-ups, can be stressful, costly and physically demanding.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To ease this burden, I propose two practical steps.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Among seniors-only households, smartphone ownership is near 90%, but access does not equate confidence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A simple SMS that says: "Reply 1", "Click this link" can be confusing.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A hospital appointment message can trigger days of worry, especially when it is to reschedule.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Seniors often leave the hospital with a printed appointment slip they rely on.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When an SMS later arrives with a new date, certainty disappears.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those who depend on escorts or family to arrange transport, this anxiety is compounded.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Then, there is what I call the "two-minute OTP race".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For a senior, it means searching for their glasses, unlocking their phone, switching screens and trying to read an English message within a time limit.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For our seniors, it can feel like emotional roller-coaster.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Digitalisation must therefore include human fallbacks and senior-friendly design.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I suggest to: include a direct phone line to a real person in automated messages; keep government apps simple, with clear mother-tongue options; offer guided "safe update" sessions so seniors can navigate their devices confidently.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And for seniors with mobility challenges, I urge MOH and our healthcare institutions to proactively assess transport needs when appointments are rescheduled.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When seniors feel unsure on the digital front, some withdraw, others avoid transactions and many feel embarrassed to ask for help.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As one resident shared, "英语不会, 电脑不懂"; or "I do not know English, nor am I IT-savvy." When seniors feel unsafe in the digital space, these consequences are not only stressful; they can be dangerous.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this brings me to my fourth point: scams.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From financial loss to trauma, scams affect people of all ages.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But for our seniors, the consequences can be life-altering.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Seniors may be fewer in number, but they often suffer the highest losses and the deepest emotional turmoil.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For someone in their 70s and 80s, money represents years of effort and strength they can no longer earn back.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The loss therefore cuts far deeper than the dollar value.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is shame and fear of being scolded.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some suffer sleeplessness, anxiety and a loss of confidence in their own judgement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One senior in his 80s shared with me that after recognising the scam tactics and refusing a second request for money, he feared retaliation and stopped going out alone.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some scam tactics are advancing quickly, with AI-enabled deepfakes far harder to detect.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I suggest three areas where our response to victim support can be strengthened.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Automatic referral pathways to ensure victims are quickly linked to counselling, guidance and family support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Banks and agencies can adopt protocols, including private consultations, multilingual guidance and staff trained to respond with empathy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I would like to say a few heartfelt words to our senior residents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you have been deceived, please do not blame yourself too much.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Scam tactics are becoming increasingly sophisticated nowadays and anyone could have a momentary lapse.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is important is not to put yourself down because of one experience.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Be more self-forgiving and carry on living courageously.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to the Singapore Police Force’s data, scam cases in 2024 reached a new high.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Among these, senior citizens suffered the most losses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is even more heartbreaking is that many seniors dare not speak up after being scammed because they feel ashamed and are afraid of being blamed.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a result, they experience long-term anxiety, difficulty sleeping and even begin to doubt their own judgement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Facing such situations, I would like to offer some advice to all our seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, do not be afraid but remain vigilant.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: You can agree on a simple "code word" with your family beforehand.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This way, when you receive calls or video calls, you can confirm whether the other party is indeed your family member.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They can even imitate the look and voice.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One lady received a video call from her "husband".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The caller said his phone was lost and needed her to transfer money immediately.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The person on screen looked like her husband and the voice was identical too.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But in fact, her real husband was at home at the time.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, all seniors must remember – for any call asking for money, you must pause and confirm the caller’s identity first.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, if you suspect or have already encountered a scam, please immediately notify your family or bank.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The earlier you seek help, the greater the chance of reducing losses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to a 2021 Ministry of Home Affairs survey, 45% of victims have been scammed again.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, learning is the most important line of defense.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because scam tactics constantly evolve, only by learning together and reminding each other can we better protect ourselves.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When parents encounter scams, they often blame themselves and are more frightened than we imagine.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Please give them more understanding, comfort and support and help them emerge from the shadow. : Mr Speaker, across many cultures, how a society treats its seniors reflects its moral strength.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: She has six chronic conditions, the kind of complexity that team-based care was built for.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Every quarter, despite a worsening gait, she makes her way to my polyclinic with a plastic bag of medications.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Down the corridor, a nurse with years of clinical experience and an advanced practice qualification waits for Mdm Tan as scheduled.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: So, Mdm Tan expresses politely that she would like to only see the doctor instead.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The doctor's queue grows and the nurse waits for her next patient.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I am questioning whether the system gave patients enough reason to choose differently.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Trained professionals underutilised while doctors run behind, and patients like Mdm Tan wait longer as their healthcare and social needs compound.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: What I saw in that corridor is not a clinical gap.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It runs quietly through the domains this Budget touches.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget rightly bets on AI as an engine of growth.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But the longer serving engine is our people.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The test is whether they are better off.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We measure what the system produces – wait times, enrolment rates, disbursements with extraordinary precision – but we do not yet assess whether the system changed the outcome for the person it was built to serve.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review spans four themes and dozens of indicators across domains, across every domain of national life.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It does not capture whether a person's health, housing, employment and social connection are collectively improving.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That is the gap, not an effort in integration.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: No one sees the whole person, the very thing a family physician is trained to do.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If there is a place where the whole person view should begin, it is Healthier SG.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The most significant shift from episodic treatment to sustained health management in primary care this country has undertaken.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: My question is, what else it can carry?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond Active Ageing Centres and sports programmes, social prescribing pathways remain narrow.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The culinary class at my community club, five minutes from my clinic, is not linked; neither is the e-sports interest group for seniors near my home.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Because no one has built the bridge and that bridge is key for heartfelt social connection.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If we already have the infrastructure and we do, the question is not whether social prescribing works, is why the connections remain incomplete.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The gap between what we measure and what matters does not stop at the clinic door.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: A couple sits at their dining table after their toddler has gone to bed.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The laptop is open, the childcare fees, mortgage, career plans, caregiving help.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: They are doing the sums on a second child.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I have met such couples a few times along their healthcare journey at their six weeks postnatal checks through their children's milestones and their own health reasons and concerns.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: On separate occasions, the fathers come in for something routine and ask, almost as an afterthought, whether it is normal to feel this overwhelmed.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: These are the conversations that never reach a policy paper, and they are the conversations that shape whether a family grows.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Thirty weeks of parental leave, once fully in effect this April, is among the most generous in the region.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This couple's question is not just about money.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It is whether their workplaces will make room for the life they want to build, whether a supervisor will raise an eyebrow, whether a promotion will be quietly deferred, whether flexibility is a policy on paper or a practice in the room.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: They do not decide against the second child.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: And that decision acquired, private and unmeasured one, is exactly what across domain well-being framework would catch.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The gap between a parental leave policy that looks generous on paper and a workplace culture that quietly penalises those who use it.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a gap any single policy can close.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: No single Ministry sees both sides of that equation, which is precisely why no single Ministry has closed it.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Each of them – Mdm Tan, the nurse, the couple – was counted.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: A well-being framework would have seen Mdm Tan not as six diagnoses, but as a person whose trust the system had not yet earned.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It would have given the nurse something the current system does not, proof that her care made a difference.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: And it would have seen the couple not as two incomes, but as a family doing calculations on hope.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Not because it adds new programmes, because it asks a question the current architecture does not: across domains, is this person's life improving?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: What matters is not just the policies we announce, but the outcomes they deliver in people's lives.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That standard is the right one and I am asking this House how we intend to measure ourselves against it.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I believe we can, because no country has yet done what Singapore is positioned to do – link individual level administrative data across domains, organise it through a well-being framework and run it as routine Government infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Nordics built rich individual level datasets but channelled them primarily through academic research.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The OECD adopted well-being frameworks at the supra-national level but could not bridge sovereign data silos.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Wales passed the Well-being of Future Generations Act but lacked the digital infrastructure to wire it to individual lives.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We have the data infrastructure, the governance density and, with the Public Sector Governance Act strengthened last month, the legal authority for cross agency data sharing with appropriate safeguards.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: To be clear, I am not proposing open access to individual records.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I am proposing linked analysis governed by the same rigour of the Public Sector Governance Act and the protections of the Personal Data Protection Act, so that outcomes across domains can be assessed without compromising the privacy this House rightly guards.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Social prescribing gets data to prove what works.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Team-based care gets validated by outcomes, not throughput, whether the workplaces truly support the families they depend on becomes a question we can finally answer.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If linked data show that a housing intervention reduced downstream healthcare costs for the same cohort, that is not a well-being insight.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It is the difference between allocating by tradition and allocating by proof.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This House asks every Ministry to justify its spending.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The question is whether we have yet given them the tools to do so across the domains, and that tool must carry weight.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If the data show that a cohort's well-being is declining across domains, this House should expect that finding to inform the next budget cycle, not the next study.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Measurement earns its place only when it is tied to decisions.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That is real progress and it is the closest model we have to what I am describing.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But ComLink+ is programme-specific and population limited – lower-income families with children living primarily in public rental housing.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The elderly enrolled in Healthier SG with complex chronic care demands is not covered.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The middle-income couple weighing a second child is not covered.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The question is not whether we can do this for some families in need.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The question is whether we are ready to build this as routine Government infrastructure across populations, across the life course.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Cross-domain measurement cannot live within a single Ministry, not because any Ministry has fallen short, but because the architecture was never designed for it.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Not a new dashboard, not another satisfaction survey.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: A single report that tells us whether our elderly are living better and whether our young families are getting the support they need.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: One cohort at each end of the life course, one proof of concept.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If the linked analysis through the well-being framework works for these two, there is no reason it cannot extend to the sandwiched generation caught between them and, in time, across life's course.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If the infrastructure to do this already exists and I believe it does, then what remains is a decision on timeline.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I would welcome the Minister's indication on when this might begin.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The timeline itself signals how seriously we take the integration this Budget promises.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If there are barriers I have not accounted for, I would welcome that candour too, because understanding what stands in the way is in itself progress.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware that what I am proposing is not as modest as it may sound.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Cross-domain measurement means the Ministry's outcomes become partly shaped by another Ministry's performance.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That is a significant shift in how we govern.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I am not asking it for it to be easy.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It is not a call to change direction.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It is a call to see clearly whether our economic progress is reaching our people.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Prime Minister asked us to strengthen our social bonds and build a Singapore that belongs to all of us.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I am asking how we will know if we have.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The couple is still pondering at the dining table.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But if this well-being framework exists a year from now, Mdm Tan walks into that clinic and an important arm of a complex chronic care is addressed by the nurse who already knows her by name and social background.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This is what it means to see people clearly.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Prime Minister began his Budget speech by describing the profoundly volatile, fragmented and contested world we live in.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The moment I wake up, my phone pings with negative news.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In various parts of our world, we have armed conflict and wars.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On top of that, we have trade wars and, increasingly, we are fighting tech wars, over AI, chips, data and digital dominance.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: AI and digital activities have also displaced healthy social connection and mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our young people are experiencing what The Straits Times is calling a "contagion of despair".

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many are also anxious about AI displacing their jobs.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And as technology and the rest of the world advance at breakneck speed, some are left behind.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We used to feel much more secure in our economic connections with other nations and our social connections with other people, but that has changed now.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, apart from the threat of global instability, isolation is an equally pressing threat for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite the challenges that we face, I am glad to hear in the Prime Minister's speech a glimmer of hope.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The various strategies and support systems highlighted will take Singapore forward as one people.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not an isolated Singapore from the rest of the world.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But a connected Singapore, a shared Singapore, a Singapore that is for all of us.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To do that, we need to turn from isolation to connection.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is great temptation to give in to the dog-eat-dog mentality, in a world where it seems like we are playing a zero-sum game.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If you have more, it means I have less; and we start to compete against one another.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But imagine if we and our neighbours could work together and uplift one another, sharing our resources, each of us contributing our strengths to create shared prosperity and more economic opportunities within the ASEAN region.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To achieve this, we need to first empower Singapore workers by helping them to be economically connected to the region.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Global trade is fragmenting, with tariffs and the "weaponisation" of trade impacting ASEAN supply chains and raising uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Tangible Government support is critical for Singapore companies seeking to venture abroad and helps Singapore stay economically relevant to the region.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are encouraging success stories, such as that of Happy Fish, an indoor swimming school which now has 10 branches in Singapore and 11 in Malaysia, with its first Jakarta branch opening this quarter.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They plan to open more branches in Malaysia and Jakarta and expand into Vietnam, Thailand and Japan, with support from Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such stories inspire confidence in the Singapore brand.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore enterprises or global companies which have headquarters in Singapore often require Singaporean workers who are prepared to venture abroad to take up regional or global leadership roles.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet many Singaporean workers are reluctant to venture overseas.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But companies are looking for workers with global or regional experience to take on leadership roles or who are prepared to venture into the region to support growth initiatives.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, I wish to speak on the economic isolation of a group of people who have sacrificially taken time out for a noble cause.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are among the most capable people I have met.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During their time out, these people have honed a range of valuable skills.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They have experience in strategic planning, financial oversight, conflict resolution, multiple stakeholder management, event planning and execution and healthcare coordination.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They have to manage competing priorities, optimise limited resources and lead with resilience under pressure.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These super power workers I am referring to are stay-at-home parents.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a crucial piece in the overall national effort to support Singaporeans to feel confident in starting families.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It supports the long-term objective of arresting Singapore's local population decline and creates a pathway back for parents to be productive members of our economy.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, as we strategise for Singapore to surge ahead and ride the AI wave to advance our economy, let us not forget that there are groups of people who may be left behind.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These individuals are often unable to maintain long-term employment and not many employers are willing to give them even a chance.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While this social enterprise is determined to help such workers, they are struggling to do more because of rising cost pressures and increasing Local Qualifying Salary thresholds.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the push towards productivity, it is important that the most vulnerable are not inadvertently made worse off or further excluded from employment opportunities.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond economic isolation, we must also address social isolation.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last year, I had the privilege of addressing a group of young people in the Rotaract Club of Raffles City at their 25th installation ceremony.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I shared about how we were seeing quiet quitters.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are young people in China lying flat, or "躺平"; in Japan, we see hikikomori, directly translated, it means "pulling inward and being confined".

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Research by IPS has found a direct statistical link between high screen time and greater loneliness.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, the young people of the Rotaract Club defied these trends.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They painted rental flats, ran community projects with homes for the disabled, homes for the children, and even launched cross-border collaborations across ASEAN, including launching the inaugural Rotaract ASEAN Young Leaders' Exchange to foster cultural understanding and youth dialogue across Southeast Asia.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I saw how confident and how purposeful they are.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I also asked myself: how might we empower more young people to be changemakers?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How might we connect with young people who feel so disconnected from real life that they have retreated into their digital worlds?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With an increasing reliance on AI, how might we help people build strong social skills, strong communication skills and competencies to navigate cross-cultural environments with sensitivity, respect and moral courage, qualities that AI will never be able to replicate?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In an AI-saturated world, with everyone upping the game on AI to improve productivity, for Singaporeans to remain competitive, we need to have more than just AI and that must mean more social-emotional and cultural intelligence.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For youths who want to do more and who are not content to be mere spectators, but want to build our nation together, I see immense potential in the Budget announcement of a $50 million SG Partnerships Fund, so we can support more ground-up community initiatives.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But turning to those who are struggling, I wonder if we can recruit and train befrienders and mentors trained in psychological first aid so we can form a first line of defence for our young people.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my community, I have seen mothers and volunteers form support networks on their own, from playground groups to a group of young widows who call themselves Hope Herd and who ensure no one journeys alone.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what about our youths who may be struggling on their own?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While we have Centre of Excellence for Youth Mental Health (CHAT), which provides mental health assessments at *SCAPE and CREST-Youth to do outreach, we lack intermediate spaces in the heartlands.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Traditional spaces like our void decks have "No Football" signs put up and malls require spending.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Without free, unstructured spaces to congregate, our youths have nowhere to go.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it any wonder they are retreating into their digital worlds?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Overseas, youth-friendly spaces that combine drop-in socialising with mental health support have shown real results.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also compelling evidence for the arts as a driver of health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would therefore like to explore the power of the arts in promoting mental well-being and social connection among our young.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is an opportunity to scale up the work that arts practitioners are already doing.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some are using theatre to address bullying and build empathy in schools.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I propose that MOE increase partnerships with them to build socio-emotional competencies, complementing what teachers and counsellors already do.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Further, participating in arts programmes also reaps significant socio-emotional benefits.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This provides access to the arts to every child, strengthens family ties and involves parents in the artistic development of their children.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most of all, doing so also benefits their overall health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also have to combat the isolation of those with special needs.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One particularly heartbreaking instance of social isolation that I came across was during the Walk of a Lifetime, organised by Saint Andrew's Autism Centre.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Punggol Regional Library and the National Gallery have far more beautiful and well-equipped rooms for those with special needs.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But wherever we can, let us provide more of such spaces across our country.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us break down the barriers that have kept those with special needs apart from us.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After work, Ain finds time to serve her neighbours.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She attends wakes, visits those who have been hospitalised and organises activities with fellow volunteers and even accompanies single mothers to my Meet-the-People Sessions to advocate for them.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a Singaporean who refuses to let others fall into isolation.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She demonstrates empathy, shows kindness and pulls her community together.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ain is an ordinary woman doing something truly extraordinary.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I think the way Ain lives, the way she is a role model for her child as she presses on with hope and love, is a wonderful, powerful way to take Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With a small and mature domestic market, Singapore companies seeking sustained growth must look beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: External markets are essential, not only for revenue expansions but also for diversification and resilience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Encouraging and supporting enterprises to internationalise has long been a cornerstone of Singapore's economic strategic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Successive economic reviews and budgets have consistently emphasised overseas expansions as one of the key growth drivers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the years, many Singapore companies have ventured abroad, both regionally and globally.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And one market where our companies have internationalised particularly successively is China.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Today, iconic brands, such as Raffles City, Breadtalk, Charles and Keith, Jumbo Seafood, TWG Tea and others, operate extensively in China.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: China is also one of Singapore's top markets, particularly for electronics, machinery and related equipment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Why has Singapore companies been successful in China?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It has been reviewed and upgraded periodically to remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are also the key flagship government-to-government projects that further anchors relationship, including the Singapore-Suzhou Industrial Park, Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City, China-Singapore (Chongqing) initiatives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And there are also regular high-level engagements, such as the annual Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation meetings and the various Provincial Ministerial platforms that continually review and expand areas of cooperations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Indeed, many meaningful commercial opportunities have emerged from these engagements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the most recent Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation meeting, Singapore's role as the major offshore renminbi clearing centre is further enhanced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The bilateral relationship between Singapore and China was often described in official communication as "all round, high-quality, future-oriented partnership". "全方位、高质量、 前瞻性、 伙伴关系".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It sounds a mouthful, but it reflects the shared commitment and willingness to continually explore new areas of cooperation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And this special relationship has provided is supportive environment for Singapore companies operating in China.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore's bilingual and bicultural strengths provide a natural edge, the ability to communicate effectively and understand cultural nuances, build trust and facilitates businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, Singapore is regarded in China as a trusted and well-governed business partner known for strong institutions and strong governance standards.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our companies internationalised into China during a period of market liberalisation and rapid economic reform.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: China then was both growth hungry and capital hungry and Singapore businesses were well-positioned to ride on that wave for expansion.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, in Chinese, this alignment may be described as "天时地利人和"; that is, favourable timing, geographical proximity and strong relationship.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The question is: can this success be replicated elsewhere?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Well, we must strive to replicate this success in other markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is neither prudent nor sustainable to rely excessively on a single external market for growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And there have been pockets of success in other markets like India, Vietnam, Malaysia and Indonesia, although these have not reached the scale achieved in China.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government can help identify and signal markets with strong long-term potential, particularly those where Singapore enjoys strong bilateral ties.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And beyond China, the Government has encouraged expansion into India, Vietnam, Indonesia and more recently, emerging markets in Latin America and Africa.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The establishment of new embassies support this diversification strategy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have also signed digital economy agreements, green economy agreements, as well as the investments agreements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I suggest that government-to-government engagement be extended further to regulator-to-regulator platforms.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Such dialogues could help align regulatory frameworks to reduce market entry barriers and facilitate licensing approvals in regulated industries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And this will be helpful to significantly ease market assessors for our companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Next, trade associations and chambers, such as SBF, the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises, the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry, play a critical role in supporting SMEs overseas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It makes sense for Singapore companies to internationalise collectively where feasible.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Sharing market intelligence, pooling resources, learning from each other can shorten the learning curves and reduce costly missteps.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Larger Singapore firms with established overseas network can act as queen bees, anchoring smaller companies with their ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have seen that in retail malls, industrial parks and integrated developments, but led by major Singapore players.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Banks, healthcare groups, investment holding companies could seemingly play a catalytic role.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, the Market Readiness Assistance scheme could be further enhanced to provide higher support for consortium-based applications and recognition could be given to firms that play anchor roles overseas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As in previous Budgets, Budget 2026 continued to provide a whole set of support measures, including supporting building leadership in key clusters, strengthening our enterprise ecosystem productivity enhancements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Companies also require sound financials, strong balance sheets and access to growth capital when they internationalise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These initiatives will strengthen enterprise financing and support risk-sharing investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Increasingly, countries expect quick brokerage on trade and investments, and a balanced trade relationship.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Supporting companies to invest abroad while maintaining a strong core in Singapore, helps to mitigate such risk and enhances our overall economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What contributed to the $15.1 billion dollar surpluses for FY2025?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Similar to last Budget, there is a $5 billion capitalisation of the nationally significant infrastructure, which in essence is a non-cash item and will need to be depreciated over the lifespan of the infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Not to mention, there is also the interest cost because this involved borrowing which needs to be serviced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second component comes from the significant increase in the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) – a hefty $3.4 billion from FY2024.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Being investment returns, it can of course be subjected to the vagaries of the markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And the third component, the remaining $6.7 billion of the $15.1 billion surplus, comes from the increase in tax revenue, primarily the corporate income tax.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, there is also the personal income tax, GST and vehicle premiums.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And of course, the other taxes like personal income tax, GST and vehicle-related revenue also increased.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: According to MOF's 2023 Occasional Paper, Government expenditure is projected to reach 19% to 20% of GDP between FY2026 and FY2030, and may exceed 20% by 2030.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Meanwhile, the total revenue including NIRC is approaching 20% of GDP in FY2025.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given that corporate income tax revenue is expected to remain elevated, I would like to seek clarification from the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance whether we are likely to see continued high surpluses for the remainder of this five-year term or should we expect greater volatility going forward?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the two previous Budgets, the Government provided additional subsidies of $250 million and $200 million respectively.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This continued calibrated support would help households manage cost of living pressures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are already observing higher tender prices on the ground from, for example, cleaning contractors, because they have to price in the higher wages for their low-wage workers, and that is putting pressure on the Service and Conservancy Charges as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, greater transitional support would ease these adjustments for businesses to pay low-wage workers better salaries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, I will hope that the Government can also provide enhanced grants for the upkeep of ageing estates, including problems that we face frequently for older towns – repairs for water seepages and structural deteriorations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I also hope that the Government can provide higher subsidies for flats that are still without lift access.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is something like 100 blocks of flats that are still without lift access and I hope the Ministry of National Development can look at that as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And thirdly, to have expanded grants for barrier-free accessibility improvements – something that is much needed in older estates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As I have outlined earlier, while the increase in GST has added to our revenue, the bulk of the surplus comes from increase in corporate income tax, as well as the capitalisation item and the increase in NIRC.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, it is worth reminding Members again that in our unique construct, a substantial portion of our GST revenue, approximately 60% is borne by higher-income earners or foreigners, foreign visitors who are here, whether to attend a convention or to attend Formula One.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are the ones who pay the main bulk, the 60%.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And the remaining 40%, which is contributed by the broader base of the lower- to middle-income households, is mitigated through the permanent GST Voucher Scheme and related offsets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While we operate in an increasingly complex and uncertain global environment, I am confident that the renewed leadership team possesses both the resolve and capability to navigate what lies ahead.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to speak on how we can do better to support Singaporeans and families with children.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is well below the replacement rate of 2.1.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the one hand, it means we must do much more to support parenthood.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But to me, a low TFR means that each child born to or adopted by a Singaporean, is precious.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not just to their parents but to all of us as a society.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And our policies and structures must reflect the full weight of society's support, regardless of the circumstances of their parents.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the Government has done much to support each child, I would like to highlight four groups of children that we can do much more for today.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our policies across the Government systematically disadvantage this group of children today right from birth, as it penalises their unmarried parents who look after them.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are not eligible for schemes like the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are not eligible for Working Mother’s Child Relief, even if the unmarried mother has to work doubly hard to bring up her child.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Neither are they eligible for the Qualifying Child Relief.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I do not believe that any Singaporean that will wake up one day and decide to have a child without getting married, just because we change our policy stance and allow them to be benefit from all the above benefits as provided to married parents.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even married parents are not incentivised to do so, as evidenced by the low TFR.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If given a choice, I believe that not a single one of us in this House or in this country will want to be an unmarried parent.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Behind every child born to an unmarried parent is a story of tears, agony, confusion, uncertainty, but overcome by only a burning desire to bring up the child.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have met a couple of residents who are single and unmarried.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They have burnt the candle at both ends because they tell me they want their child to grow up feeling like they are the same, like any other child in school.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Have our policies inadvertently tipped the balance against them?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is not how a society where each child is precious should be or can be.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is time to stop the policy differentiation between married and unmarried parents who take care of their children.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is not an abandonment or de-prioritisation of the family nucleus.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is not an encouragement of people to have children out of wedlock.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this is not going to lead to a sudden spike in the number of children born out of wedlock.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All it is is a reflection of a society that cares for each child and that does its best to alleviate the challenging circumstances they face at birth and give them a better chance in life.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, they will have to pay several hundred dollars more each month if they would like to place their children on these programmes.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Moreover, there will be some of us that think, since the mother is not working, well, she can care for the child, no need to place in childcare or student care.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He came across many students from complex, disadvantaged family backgrounds who would have benefited from the structured environment after school, but who were deprived from doing so because their families decided they could not afford it.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In some cases, the parents had many children.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In other cases, they had a child with special needs amid siblings.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, the mother had to stay at home to take care of the children, but as you can understand, she could not take care of each of them adequately well.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There were also other mothers he encountered who were absent.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are not working but nor are they taking care of the child.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Deputy Director and his team were determined not to let the working mother criterion hold back these children from the most disadvantaged backgrounds from accessing structured after school care.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From the ground up, they worked hard with school educators and the Ministry of Social and Family Development, and devised a protocol where the school educators would identify the children from the most disadvantaged backgrounds, facilitate their registration in the school-based Student Care Centre, highly subsidised.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This meant much more work for the school educators, but they all supported the initiative, and dedicated their time and energy to identifying and engaging these students because they knew that having a structured after school environment could be so helpful for these children.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, the Deputy Director has grown a little older, has some white hair, stands here in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But he still has the same dream and the same fire burning in him.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should support all our children to have affordable childcare and after school care, regardless of whether their mother is employed.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are many more children beyond those currently identified in the schools that will benefit from this.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And our school educators and teachers will also save time from having to make the case for each of these children.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, Mr Speaker, my plea to the Government is, "Come on, let's get this done".

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should also extend free frequency modulation systems for all children in preschools, just as we do today for those in primary schools.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not something that every parent or any parent or child would wish upon themselves.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And therefore, as a society, we should give them our fullest support in their developmental years, because each child is special and precious.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many have invested significant amounts of time and energy, including going for in-vitro fertilisation to have children of their own.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Adopting a child is not a decision that any couple takes lightly.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is no backing out, just like the rest of us who have children of our own.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I spoke to a resident recently, who also happens to be a childhood friend of mine.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She and her husband came to my Meet-the-People Sessions and shared with me their adoption journey.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, they had to attend a pre-adoption briefing and a disclosure briefing and then obtain a favourable adoption suitability assessment (ASA).

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The ASA took several months, whereby they had to undergo, and they had to complete copious documentation, identify several referees and go through multiple intrusive interviews.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But they, however, understood the need for this, because we do want to ensure that parents who adopt are ready and equipped to do so.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After they cleared the ASA, they signed up to be on the waiting list of an accredited agency, so that they could identify a child for adoption and this was a very long waiting list, so there are many among us who would like to adopt a child as well.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After matching with the identified child, they had to apply for a Dependent's Pass for the child to be able to come to Singapore, because they need the child to be in Singapore for them to apply to the Court for the adoption order.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But the Court process takes several more months as well, because as part of the review, the Judge requires a report from the Guardian-in-Adoption, who is an officer appointed by the Ministry of Social and Family Development, and she interviewed them again, made home visits, similar questions as the ASA.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And it was only after she had completed her report, then could the couple request for a final hearing for the Judge to issue the adoption order.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After receiving the adoption order, they then need to apply to the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority, finally, to get citizenship for their son.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their son had been in Singapore for close to a year and, at that point, were they able to apply for citizenship.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During the entire period, when their child, their son, was in Singapore, they had to pay foreigner fees for all the medicals associated with him, because he was not a Singapore Citizen, at least not yet.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They shared with me that they felt like second-class parents.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But to top it all off, they wanted to adopt a second child so that their first child has a sibling.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the Ministry of Social and Family Development has informed them that they are strongly encouraged to start the process at least nine months from the date of their first child's adoption order, so that they can bond adequately with the first child.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And thereafter, they need to go through the entire process again – registering for a new ASA, going for all the interviews and putting up all the documentation.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their first child has already been with them for close to a year.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, on the one hand, we want them to bond longer with the child, but on the other hand, the leave period is shorter.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are Singaporeans who have put in great resolve to care for the child just as their own.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To me, a strong family nucleus means testing, these remain critical, but equally important is that we take care of each and every child, regardless of their parents' circumstances.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us not let the heartbreak or the regrets of one generation affect the chances of success of the next.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I was very heartened when Minister Desmond Lee announced that the Government and MOE are reviewing high stakes exams, especially the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the last Parliament Sitting, I asked MOE for a detailed breakdown by grade across several national exams – what proportions scored what grade – for the PSLE and the "O" level.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That is obviously not what I asked for, because I asked for a detailed breakdown of each grade.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But let me explain why I asked for this.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But if we ask any general 15-year-old in Singapore, I believe a very small percentage will tell us that they are top performers in any of these subjects.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because their lived experience going through the exam system in Singapore has told them that they are not top performers.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Again, MOE did not release the data, but I believe that way less than 40% of each cohort, PSLE or "O" levels, will have received the top or top two grades for Math, for example.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this is because, while our grades for both the exams are no longer assigned on a bell curve base, they are now based on the objective scores of the students – the philosophy behind how the exams are set has not changed.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is set to be able to segregate the children by ability very finely.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, you have X% of very challenging questions, Y% of challenging questions, so in and of itself, the exam will be able to differentiate the students and by that, affect their grades, thereby school selection – which is the key cause of the education arms race.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I do not think that this needs to be or should be the case.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am not against challenging our students or against facilitating the best or most inclined of them to achieve greater skill and accomplishment.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is just that I disagree that our national exams should serve this purpose.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is the role of national competitions – Math Olympiads, Science Olympiads, English Olympiads – to reward and recognise excellence.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And once students clear the threshold of competency, they should get the top grade, without any further finer segregation.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: Now I need to be like a robot.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: We are only seeing the tip of the iceberg.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: If our students are able to put in effort and they can achieve top grades with decent effort, I believe it will build up their confidence.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: It will build up their interest and motivation of the subject, and they will acquire good competency, which forms the solid foundation and springboard for them to leverage the potential of AI.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: I believe that the suggestions I have made in my speech will further strengthen us as a society and give all of our children a better chance to succeed in life.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Technology is advancing at a pace few governments and even fewer companies can confidently predict.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Budget 2026 is delivered in a changed world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Prime Minister Wong has described it as the first step towards securing Singapore's future in this new environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our MDDI GPC, across this term and the last, has consistently championed six themes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Together with fellow PAP MPs, including Ms Tin Pei Ling, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Alex Yam and Ms Hany Soh, we filed a Motion with 13 Calls to Action in the last term.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I am encouraged that many of these themes that we have championed for are reflected in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But alignment must translate into decisive execution and measurable outcomes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our response must rest on three pillars: competitiveness, inclusive growth and digital for good.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we get this right, we will not only remain competitive and relevant in a global market, we will also remain united as a society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When I speak to workers, business owners, young graduates and mid-career professionals, I hear both excitement and anxiety.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Anxiety because many are unsure where they stand in this race.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In just the past six months, we see how the global AI race has accelerated at pace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the Global AI Summit, it was evident that we are entering the era of frontier and foundation models powered by massive compute scaling and multimodal capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is embedded in enterprises, in public services and national infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The shift towards Agentic AI and AI-native enterprises signals structural transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In China, AI is embedded across platforms serving hundreds of millions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In the US, AI copilots are integrated into productivity tools used globally.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In India, AI is woven into telecom and digital services at the national scale.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Next-generation chips are being ordered in unprecedented volumes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Hyperscalers are investing billions in AI data centres.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Sovereign funds in the Middle East are investing heavily.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The European Union is securing its own compute capacity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Chips, data centres and energy are now strategic infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: AI is embedded in manufacturing lines, in logistics networks, in defence systems and in energy grids.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is about industrial competitiveness and national capability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: AI safety, alignment, model evaluation and red teaming are central to credible deployment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Advantage will not come from models alone, but from diffusion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The winners will be able to align compute, capability, governance, talent and industry integration into one coherent strategy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But we can compete on precision, on trust, on regulatory credibility and deep sectoral integration.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But if we move too slowly, routine work will be automated elsewhere, and higher value functions may migrate, and our workers will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The world is moving at scale and our responses must be fast, deliberate, workforce-centred and outcome-driven.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To achieve this, we must address key questions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we build both deep AI specialists and broad AI literacy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we redesign jobs so AI augments rather than replaces?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we drive real end-to-end business value with AI?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What is our strategy on compute capacity, compute sovereignty and resilience?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we power AI growth with sustainable energy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How will the National AI Council evolve NAIS 2.0 and orchestrate our ecosystem across Ministries, AI missions, Centres of Excellence, talent development, investment, deployment, removing friction across Ministries and deployment across Government and industry?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My fellow PAP MPs and I in the MDDI GPC will elaborate further at the COS.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: National ambition must translate into scalable enterprise capability and better jobs on the ground.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We already have digital grants, pre-approved AI tools and Chief Technology Officer (CTO)-as-a-Service.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But SME owners tell me candidly, "I know AI is important, but I am managing cashflow.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I am not sure my data is ready.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I cannot experiment without clear returns." Behind each SME owner is a workforce wondering how AI will affect their roles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Most SMEs face three constraints: the cost of talent, the lack of validated use cases and integration challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If AI adoption is concentrated among large enterprises, the productivity and wage gap will widen.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must move from advisory support to shared capability infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I welcome Minister of State Jasmin Lau's emphasis on lower-risk, structured experimentation and shifting funding towards implementation and workflow redesign.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These validated solutions reduce blind experimentation and lower development costs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By crowd-sharing capabilities and lowering adoption costs, we can create a faster "IKEA moment" – a term Minister Josephine Teo used to describe the point when enterprises move beyond experimentation to fully integrating technology into their operations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we treat AI infrastructure like physical infrastructure, shared and accessible, SMEs can compete by agility, not size.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: AI must be a multiplier for the many, not a privilege for the few.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: AI is not a specialised skill that is only relevant to engineers or programmers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: AI cuts across all sectors; from manufacturing, logistics, finance and education to small and medium enterprises.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The question is not whether we work in the technology sector or not.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The question is how AI will change the way we work.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we are not prepared, we will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But if we are prepared, AI can become a tool that empowers us.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We need to encourage more of our workers, whether young or mid-career, to upgrade their digital skills and understand the basics of AI usage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Not everyone needs to become an AI expert.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But everyone needs to know how to use AI to increase their productivity and job value.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is the key to building strong and sustainable wage growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The same applies to businesses within our community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We should not just become passive consumers of technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must see how AI can help businesses grow.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For example, using chatbots for customer service, data analytics to understand sales patterns, automation for inventory management and more targeted digital marketing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Last week in Pasir Ris, for the first time we held a large Ramadan Bazaar.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I noticed several stalls were already using signboards generated by AI.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This shows that our small businesses have already begun taking the first steps.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We should encourage the use of AI like this, not just for design but also for stock management, online promotion and business expansion, and many other areas.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must view AI not as a threat, but as an opportunity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we are bold enough to change and are prepared to upskill, our community will not only remain relevant but can play a leading role in the new economy. : Mr Speaker, in English and to my second point on inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A recent MOF report on income growth, inequality and social mobility shows meaningful progress.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But as disruption accelerates, the risk is not just income inequality.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Senior Employment Credit and CPF Transition Offset support retention.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Job Redesign Grant helps firms redesign roles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But more importantly, we must expand structured pathways for seniors into roles, such as trainers, mentors, safety supervisors and quality leads, where experience is a strategic advantage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This will widen meaningful employment opportunities for senior PMETs who, today, still struggle to find roles aligned with their expertise.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In an ageing society, enabling seniors to remain productive, respected and fairly paid is not just manpower policy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I look forward to hearing more on how we can further strengthen senior employment at the COS debates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While headline statistics remain stable, many graduates share a different lived experience.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Entry-level tasks, such as market research, coding and reporting, are increasingly automated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Fellow PAP MPs Mr Henry Kwek and Ms Denise Phua shared this as the "broken ladder" scenario.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At a recent Chinese New Year conversation in Pasir Ris, some of the residents were managers, told me that they can now complete such tasks with AI tools themselves, reducing the need to hire and train fresh graduates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What are the outcomes and how can we scale it up faster?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must also strengthen our internships to be more structured and industry-embedded so that students graduate business-ready, not just AI-literate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is something that I have spoken on in my earlier speeches.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I look forward to hearing more on encouraging seniors and fresh graduate employment in the COS debates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we get this right, we strengthen mobility across generations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As we advance technologically, we must invest in technology for social good with equal urgency.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, we must ensure children from lower-income families are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must expand AI literacy, exposure to automation and robotics, and industry mentorship.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In Pasir Ris-Changi, our M3 organisation runs RoboWars and hackathons to expose students, including those from lower-income families, to digital skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We should scale such efforts nationally so that every child has a fair start in this digital economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: AI-enabled fall detection, smart home sensors, remote health monitoring and telemedicine can allow seniors to age safely at home.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When designed well, these tools ease the burden on sandwiched-generation families juggling work and caregiving.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Remote work tools, assistive AIs and job sharing can expand meaningful employment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A high-trust digital society requires strong safeguards and responsible governance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We face geopolitical uncertainty, technological disruption and social change all at once.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must sharpen competitiveness, ensure growth remains inclusive and harness technology for good.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we align ambition with action and innovation with trust, we will not merely respond to disruption.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We will shape it and secure a resilient, united and forward-looking Singapore for generations to come.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: What struck me about this Budget is not just the package of measures, but the signal it sends.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In a more uncertain, fractured world, it reassures all Singaporeans that we can remain steady, confident and united, it reassures Singaporeans that we are always here to take care of each other.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This Budget carries a clear "we first" direction, reminding us that progress is not just about growth in figures, but about shared responsibilities, stronger bonds and a social compact that is real in everyday life.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In that spirit, whilst I will touch briefly on ComLink+, measures affecting small and medium enterprises (SMEs), I will focus my main remarks on the revised Preferential Additional Registration Fee (PARF) policies and the issues of transitional fairness.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
