text: But I want to raise the practical issues on transitional risk.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Moving from public rental housing into a new home is not that simple.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For some of these families, there is a degree of vulnerability as they encounter moving – there are renovation costs, furniture costs, new travel routines, childcare, school logistics and sometimes, a change in a workplace too.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Some of these families may not yet be stable to absorb a sharp drop in social and financial support if they are immediately treated as having "graduated" out of ComLink+.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is only human nature that if families fear that by buying a home triggers an immediate loss of support, they may delay taking up the step of home purchase that the policy is trying to encourage.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If we want families genuinely to take the difficult step from rental to ownership, or from assistance to self-reliance, we should make the transition predictable and safe.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I hope the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) can share how support is tapered when these families transition out of ComLink+ and whether their family coaches can help with a transition plan, so they do not fall into gaps between schemes at their most vulnerable and most fragile moments of the transition.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, the Budget also introduces policies that affect a large majority of SMEs.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In doing so, the Government typically engage trade associations and chambers to gather feedback of on-the-ground perspectives.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: However, not all SMEs is required to be part of these bodies.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Even the Singapore Business Federation (SBF), as the apex business chamber, only has compulsory membership for companies above the $0.5 million paid-up or authorised capital threshold.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This means a substantial segment of the micro-SMEs may not be in the room when these policy feedback are being gathered, even though they are the ones who are most sensitive to cost and compliance changes.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I therefore urge the Government to consider opening feedback channels you hear from these small and micro-SMEs, via channels, such as the SME Centres, so that in all fairness, the policy does not get shaped mainly by the larger companies.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Since the announcement, I have received ground feedback from residents and people who are concerned about the sudden implementation and the financial hit they may have to take, through no fault of their own.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Policy can and do change all the time.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: One of my Geylang Serai resident shared with me that before Budget Day, he committed to a vehicle purchase and paid a deposit based on the prevailing PARF rules.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: However, after the announcement, the dealer's position was that the deal will proceed, and if the buyer cancelled, this deposit would be forfeited because the dealer did no wrong and any dispute should be taken to the authorities.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In reality, for many committed buyers, there is no meaningful option to renegotiate the pricing or cancel their purchase without losing substantial deposits.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These buyers bear the downside of an immediate policy shift.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The next COE cycle started after Budget was announced and before this House got to debate the policy change.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: When the PARF rebate framework changed with such a short runway, the assumptions that buyers and sellers made at the point of contract no longer stands, yet buyers remain locked in because they cannot back out of the contract without any penalty.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I, therefore, have six questions I hope the Ministry for Transport (MOT) can consider.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, why was there no interim measures for buyers who had already committed and paid deposits before Budget Day, and would the revised PARF framework have started in a later COE cycle or with a longer lead time, so that the buyers have time to react and consider their decision to buy?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, in deciding on an immediate start date, did the Government consider industry practices, such as non-refundable deposits, and was it anticipated that some buyers would face the dilemma of either proceeding at a loss or forfeiting their deposits if they cancel their car purchase?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For example, mandating a short grace period, a cancellation-without-penalty window or other measures to prevent immediate hardship to this group?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If so, can the Government clarify whether our infrastructure is ready?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Otherwise, it creates a perception that when Government provides support, there are conditions and waiting period.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, in closing remarks, Mr Speaker, I support the Budget's "we first" direction.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: However, I urge the Government to view the issues that I have raised through the lens of transition and in fairness, whether it is social, economical or business in nature.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had reached a recognised life stage when society deemed it fit to accord me a public travel concession.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also made me reflect more about the demographic group I just entered and what this next phase of life should be about.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), healthy ageing is defined as the process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables well-being in older age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It moves beyond a disease-focused model, aiming to maximise a person's capability to be and do what they value, whether in terms of mobility, relationships or societal contribution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our own Ministerial Committee on Ageing has adopted a similar approach.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In its 2023 Action Plan for Successful Ageing, it is stated that, and I quote, "Ageing is not only about illness and frailty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also provides opportunities for longer years of active engagement, good health and contribution to society." Sir, I have spoken about ageism in this House in the past.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead of seeing a grey-haired individual as weak and helpless, we should as far as possible see how that person's ability and potential can be unlocked.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, various taxpayer-funded schemes have been put in place to uplift seniors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Senior Singaporeans have also been included in the SkillsFuture programme, making lifelong learning affordable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our public buses are now fully wheelchair-friendly, with bus stops mostly barrier-free, encouraging disabled seniors to go out and stay connected.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet, at the same time, amidst this relentless pace of change, we must ensure that we do not leave our seniors behind; many of whom are struggling to keep up with a world vastly different from the one they used to know.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, I would like to highlight three areas that seem to me to be recurring issues facing seniors: first, the push towards digitalisation; second, the withdrawal of face-to-face services; and third, the Government's means testing policies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The relentless pace of digitalisation is epitomised by the use of Singpass.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To transact with all Government departments, Singpass is the default mode.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singpass has overall been a great enabler that eases authentication and transactions across many sectors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For some seniors, however, it is bewildering and disempowering.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Seniors who never had a smartphone have to purchase one in order to download the Singpass app and utilise its functions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even so, many are unable to operate the app as it is simply alien to what they are used to.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They find it difficult to open the app to quickly scan QR codes or to toggle between the app short message service (SMS) functions and websites in order to key in one-time passwords, all within a short time limit.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Seniors with close relatives or friends can get help for digital transactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, this still engenders a feeling of dependency and helplessness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Then, there are seniors without children or close relatives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These vulnerable seniors may end up trusting the wrong people or may decide not to transact with the Government at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many seniors, especially the older ones, did not have the opportunities for schooling, unlike later cohorts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Education levels tell us something about comfort with technology, as using technology usually requires higher level language skills, often in English.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, I am aware that the Silver Generation Office is doing health-related outreach to isolated seniors at their homes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How far are they trained and able to assist such seniors in digital transactions?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now move on to the related point of the withdrawal of face-to-face or over-the-counter services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One huge change is in banking, with banks driving their customers to digital banking apps and the reduction in physical bank branches.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For Government services, this has been happening as well, with face-to-face services being reduced for one reason or another.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, we have been told that due to manpower constraints in the Home Team, Neighbourhood Police Posts and some neighbourhood Police centres no longer have manned counters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although the closure of this office was due to the site being sold for development, the lack of a replacement physical branch has upset and worried residents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the Department of Statistics, as at June last year, the Hougang planning area is one of those which has a high concentration of residents over the age of 65.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this, Sir, please let me continue in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Residents told me that they now must travel to the more distant Sengkang Branch to do their business, which is very inconvenient.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Here, I would like to ask HDB, before deciding to close the Hougang branch, was there sufficient assessment of the impact on Hougang residents?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Hougang area has many old flats and senior residents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does the Government believe that after the branch closure, residents simply have to adapt to digital services?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If it were in newer areas with younger residents where physical branches were closed, I might be able to understand.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But in a community like Hougang where senior residents are the majority, is such an arrangement appropriate? : Sir, back to English.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Residents of the area have been asking what is next on the Government's agenda for the removal of face-to-face services?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They worry that the Hougang Neighbourhood Police Centre is next.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Budget speech, Prime Minister Wong emphasised that families were the bedrock of society and the first line of support for every individual.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is useful to examine whether some Government policies might inadvertently discourage family support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Take, for instance, the means testing criteria for Government subsidies and schemes, the Silver Support Scheme and healthcare subsidies for long-term care and outpatient treatment under the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) are prime examples of policies affecting seniors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These schemes have eligibility criteria, such as per capita household income (PCHI).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The same would apply to a single aunt or uncle with very limited resources, but living with a family of working adults.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This surely cannot be the message the Government wishes to send.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I agree with the principle of means testing, as our resources are finite.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, some refinement of our means testing criteria is due.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I must give credit to the Traffic Police and the Land Transport Authority (LTA) for something meaningful they have just implemented to help senior drivers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For years up to now, drivers aged 65 or older have had to undergo medical examinations for renewal of their licences – for the general driving licence issued by the Police, once in three years; for the vocational licence issued by LTA, it is annually.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Senior drivers have come to the Meet-the-People Sessions, expressing confusion over these two requirements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is similar to the way medical examination reports on migrant domestic workers are being submitted to the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) by clinics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With collaboration across agencies and with Singaporeans, we can forge a kinder, more conducive environment for all generations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the Head of Advocacy for the People's Action Party (PAP) Women's Wing's Seasons of Life, I am heartened by the Budget's emphasis on supporting Singaporeans through every stage of their journey – from youth to parenthood and into the golden years.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Drawing from my engagements with residents in our Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC and various community partners and stakeholders, I wish to raise recommendations that build on this foundation, ensuring no one is left behind as we navigate life's seasons together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the Deputy Chairperson of the Education Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC), my colleagues and I remain unwaveringly committed to ensuring access to education at all life stages.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I fully agree with the Prime Minister that learning must extend beyond theory and translate into hands-on applications that empower individuals to thrive.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: An example which I wish to share with this House is the YMCA's Vocational and Soft Skills Programme (VASSP), an initiative I have proudly supported for the past few years which aims to equip out-of-school youths and youths-at-risk with job competency and specific vocational skills.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I regularly attend their dialogue sessions, where I share my personal story: starting as a student in the Normal (Academic) stream, facing doubts about my future, yet finding the confidence to pursue a law degree and becoming who I am today.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This programme is a vital effort to uplift youths who may feel disillusioned about their future due to influences like misguided peers or challenging family backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such initiatives should not only be encouraged but normalised, aligning with the Prime Minister's vision in his Budget speech: that every Singaporean, regardless of where they start in life, should have a fair chance to pursue their aspirations and realise their full potential.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As our nation ramps up efforts in artificial intelligence (AI) education and encourages lifelong learning, we must ensure that the right infrastructure is in place to support every keen learner.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have previously suggested in this House that we consider establishing another Institute of Technical Education (ITE) in the North.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This new ITE could also serve as a dedicated campus for lifelong learning, collaborating closely with the nearby Republic Polytechnic and collaborate closely with the adjacent JTC industrial areas.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such a facility would democratise access to practical, skills-based education, bridging gaps and fostering a culture of continuous growth.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Turning to marriage and parenthood, I applaud the Budget's recognition that families are the bedrock of society and the first line of support for every individual.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Building on this geological metaphor, Budget 2026 should enhance support for family starting and building, much like the stratification of bedrock that provides enduring stability.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Prospective parents face unique concerns and challenges; there is no silver bullet to improve our ever-low total fertility rate (TFR) overnight.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The decision to marry and have children is deeply personal.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The key question is: what are the "right conditions" that would help couples feel confident and ready to start a family?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through my engagements with fellow Singaporeans, in particular my Woodgrove residents and Fertility Support Singapore (FSS), I have been motivated to continue to spotlight support for assisted conception procedures.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As Minister Indranee Rajah noted in her speech at FSS' "Fertility and Inclusion in the Workplace" forum, and I quote, "There are couples who wish to have children but have difficulties conceiving.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For these couples who clearly wish to start families but face daunting hurdles, we can and must do more.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Beyond conception, the journey after birth, subsumed under SG Made For Families, also influences decisions to start families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Concerns include accessible and affordable housing as well as mitigating career impacts for parents raising children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is regrettable that not every need can be met as each family's circumstances are unique.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That said, this House will strive to ensure that every Singaporean family is cared for.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A common appeal from my Woodgrove residents is for housing that allows them to build true homes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Obstacles that my residents face include successfully balloting for a HDB flat, upgrading to a larger flat to accommodate their growing family, which for buyers of resale flats means needing to fork out at times significant cash to meet the cash-over-valuation component.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many do not wish to burden their children, and seek to remain active and healthy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Grassroots organisations and Active Ageing Centres play complementary roles in this, supporting seniors with face-to-face interactions, helping them to embrace digitalisation, organising regular engagements to foster community bonds while keeping our seniors’ minds sharp and prevent physical frailty.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At this juncture, I wish to declare that I am a practising lawyer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As part of our PAP Senior Group initiatives, Woodgrove Branch has organised three sessions of pro bono LPA certification sessions last year serving our seniors in need.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am immensely grateful to our group of dedicated volunteers and lawyers, who have given many of my Woodgrove residents a peace of mind and more importantly, assisted them in completing their legacy plans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC, we have more pro bono LPA certification sessions in the pipeline, which we hope our residents will sign up for and attend when the dates are announced.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Building on the momentum, I intend to speak during the Ministry of Law’s Committee of Supply (COS) to propose ways to enhance access and protection to encourage legacy planning.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By supporting Singaporeans through youth, parenthood and seniority, we build a resilient nation where every season of life is one of opportunity and dignity.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He asks us to harness it as a strategic advantage.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The question I want to put to this House today is: a strategic advantage for whom?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The answer will determine whether Budget 2026 fulﬁls its promise; that growth must translate into good jobs and rising incomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can we own the technology rather than just renting it?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can we protect the worker who is being asked to adapt in this new age?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And how can we ensure that the gains are shared with the people who helped create them?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If our industrial strategy remains focused on fast adoption, we are agreeing to a permanent, compounding transfer of value to foreign technology companies.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every API call we make, every subscription, every enterprise licence, is rent paid to a landlord in Silicon Valley or perhaps China.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore has never just accepted that kind of relationship with any industry.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We move up the value chain, extracting value at the source.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not just use semiconductors; we manufacture them.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And our ambition for AI should be no different.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to stake out our own defendable positions and capture the value that comes with them.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The question is therefore where, speciﬁcally, we have a right to win.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I think that the answer starts with understanding Singapore’s constraints.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We lack the land, the power grid and the capital to train trillion-parameter frontier models.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we faced constraints in other industries, we did not try to outspend our larger competitors.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, we identiﬁed niches where our speciﬁc combination of capabilities gave us an advantage and we built from there.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore has produced SEA-LION and MERaLION, large language models built on open-weights foundations, ﬁne-tuned for Southeast Asian language context and our cultural context.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We identiﬁed a gap in our region and we ﬁlled it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The rest of the world is running into the same energy wall that we face when deploying.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The United States (US) is planning new nuclear plants, speciﬁcally to power AI data centres.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Dennis Tan, earlier highlighted in this House the outsize environmental impact of an indiscriminate rush to embrace large-scale models for every minor task, a dilemma that every nation is grappling with.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The result is what practitioners call “Edge AI” – intelligence that runs on the device itself, rather than routing data to a distant server.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister announced four national AI Missions in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I want to look at two of them through the lens of Edge AI.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In advanced manufacturing, the robots on a factory ﬂoor cannot depend on a cloud connection.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A production line that hesitates because of network latency or halts because of an outage is a competitive liability.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The AI running that factory needs to operate locally and be resilient to disruption.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In connectivity, the autonomous systems that manage our containers at our ports make thousands of routing decisions every second.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our ports handle a large proportion of the world’s transshipment volume.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These decisions cannot wait for a round trip to a data centre.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the rest of the world scrambles to solve their energy and latency constraints, the software that makes AI run efﬁciently on local hardware will command a signiﬁcant premium.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are already being pushed to solve this problem.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should be solving it deliberately and with an eye on selling the solution.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not a deep technical expert and I am not offering a comprehensive blueprint today.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I am suggesting is a way to think about where Singapore has a right to win, and Edge AI is one possible answer to that question, among many others.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same logic points towards explainable AI – building tools that make the reasoning that AI models make transparent enough for regulated industries to deploy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Finance and healthcare, the two other sectors that are the focus of our AI Missions, are just these industries that operate under obligations to explain automated decisions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore's regulatory institutions and our reputation for the rule of law may give us a genuine advantage in the space as well.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are just ideas, and there will be other niches that neither side of this House has yet identiﬁed.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My more speciﬁc ask concerns the national AI Missions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I ask that each Mission consider Edge deployment capability as a key design criterion, whether an efﬁcient, low-latency, sovereign Edge model is appropriate for the use case.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And more broadly, I ask that the Government establish a formal process for identifying Singapore’s AI export niches, applying the same constraint-aware logic that produced SEA-LION and MERaLION, across our strategic industries.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A systemic search for where Singapore has a right to win and a commitment to back those niches with capital.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The goal is to ensure that in years to come, Singapore is a genuine owner of commercial AI capability that we can export to the world.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not just a well-compensated tenant but a landlord of our own.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But owning the technology is only the ﬁrst part of the answer.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second is protecting the people being asked to adapt to it, including those the market has already started to leave behind.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But averages can be dangerous and they can mask a speciﬁc problem that I think deserves more attention.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not have such granular data for Singapore but that alone is part of the problem.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is what I call the broken bottom rung of the ladder.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, I want to be clear that what is at stake here is not just in economic terms but in human terms as well.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the place where you discover what you are capable of.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Where someone more senior takes a chance on you, teaches you something you could not have learned any other way and passes on a standard of craft or judgement that you will carry for the rest of your career.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that rung is gone, not because graduates are less capable, but simply because it is now cheaper to automate the tasks that used to justify hiring them, we do not have an unemployment problem; we have a rupture in how knowledge and expertise pass from one generation to the next.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The experienced professionals of 2046 are the junior hires of today.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do not hire them today, we will not have any in 20 years.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After my Parliamentary colleague, Eileen Chong, and I put out a call for feedback some months ago, we heard from many young Singaporeans who are living this.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Graduates who applied for over 100 roles; who took unpaid internships, hoping it would lead somewhere; who are talented, willing and being told by the market there is simply no place for them yet.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are simply asking for a chance to start.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The broken rung is the most visible symptom, but the disruption does not stop at entry-level workers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mid-career workers face a parallel challenge – skills that took years to build being absorbed by AI faster than retraining programmes can respond.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the broken rung is happening here, we need to see it in our numbers before we can respond to it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's 400% Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS) tax deduction for AI expenditure is a powerful lever as well.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public money for AI adoption should come with a commitment to developing the workers who will work alongside it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's announcement of six months of free premium AI tool access for workers taking selected courses is also a welcome step.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: AI is not a course you complete, it is daily practice, much like using spreadsheet programme is.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A worker who builds that habit over six months and then has the access removed is being set up to fall again.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) has called for SkillsFuture Credit to cover AI tool subscription on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I renew that call today – for young workers starting out and for those mid-career workers who need to stay current as well as for our senior workers looking to embrace new technology.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme currently targets workers aged 40 and above, but the disruption is hitting many earlier.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans in their mid to late 30s, the Millennial cohort, whose careers were built on skills that AI is now absorbing are facing displacement before they even qualify for mid-career support.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That brings me to the third and final question.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: AI is not just changing how we work.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is changing what we owe each other.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The assumptions baked into our social contract about risk, about reward, about the relationship between capital and labour were written for a different economy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Budget 2026 is an opportunity for us to update this.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The WP has called for a redundancy insurance across multiple Parliaments.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I argue for it myself in my maiden speech.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will not repeat the following argument today.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I want to offer a different frame for it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Redundancy insurance is the engine of the economic agility that this Budget demands.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A worker with six months of financial breathing room can say yes to retraining.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can take the risk of moving sectors.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can be the bold, adaptable Singaporean that the Government is asking them to be.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Paralysis is exactly what we cannot afford in an economy that is undergoing structural transformation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government is rightly optimistic about AI's potential, but responsible governance requires managing all our outcomes, including the downside.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Redundancy insurance is a suitable hedge; and I urge the Government to act on it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The EIS deduction condition I proposed earlier on maintaining graduate and entry level pipelines as a condition for tax deductions addresses new workers entering the workforce, but there is a parallel question about existing workers.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What happens to the person already in the job when AI arrives?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, the tax system is largely neutral on the question.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A firm can deploy AI to augment its workforce or to replace it and incentives are often available either way.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without a nudge, the default logic of capital is to substitute labour.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us make the fiscal system reflect that.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Which brings me finally to the distribution question.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Global evidence consistently shows that productivity gains from AI do not automatically translate into wage growth.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government is investing taxpayer resources and regulatory sandboxes in four national AI Missions: advanced manufacturing, connectivity, finance and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The strategic advantage of AI must be felt in the wages of our workers, not just in the earnings reports of the companies deploying the technology.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are not obstacles to Singapore's AI ambitions, they are the conditions that make these ambitions worth pursuing.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In mathematics, we assume that one plus one equals two.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But even something as simple as one plus one only works when the foundations are sound.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many Singaporeans ask, "Can healthcare be more affordable?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why does it feel more expensive?" These are valid concerns.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But when we look beneath the surface – at ageing, chronic disease, medical inflation, workforce pressures and rising expectations – we see that healthcare is not a simple sum.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As more Singaporeans live into their eighties and beyond, demand will continue to rise.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This $20 billion is not just a number.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Behind it are countless hours of system design, workforce planning, infrastructure development and careful budgeting by our policy-makers, healthcare leaders and civil service.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It represents: subsidies that keep care accessible; investment in hospitals and community facilities; expansion of long-term care; and training and retaining of healthcare professionals.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Healthcare is a system that must be carefully balanced.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And like any equation, the outcome depends on how responsibly each part is managed.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Affordability therefore cannot mean only what an individual pays today.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It must also mean what the nation can sustain tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If costs are not shared responsibly, they do not disappear.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are simply borne elsewhere – by taxpayers and future generations.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is the elderly resident sitting quietly outside a specialist clinic.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is the working adult taking leave to accompany a parent.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is the anxiety of waiting for clarity.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Tengah, residents share these concerns with me.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are asking for reassurance that care will be timely, accessible and sustainable.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Rising waiting times do not happen in isolation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans are living longer, chronic conditions are more prevalent and mental health needs are growing.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Medical advances also mean we can treat far more conditions than before.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Demand is rising partly because we are doing more and doing it better.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Waiting time is the visible symptom of rising demand in a more capable system.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It continues to invest in hospital capacity and manpower.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It expands community hospitals, step-down care and long-term care capacity.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Capacity is necessary, but sustainability also depends on managing demand appropriately and delivering care in the right setting.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hospitals are best focused on acute and complex care.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Stable chronic conditions, prevention and recovery are often better supported closer to home, through our general practitioners (GPs), community teams and integrated networks.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is about delivering care more appropriately so that access remains protected over time.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we manage demand wisely today, we protect access tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This reflects a simple reality: long-term sustainability depends not only on how we treat illness, but on how early we prevent it.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They diagnose, manage complexity and intervene when risk is high.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But health is shaped less by crisis and more by consistency.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In rehabilitation work, I often see how small, sustained interventions change trajectories.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What appears to be a simple back strain may reflect years of cumulative weakness and poor movement habits.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With early strengthening and education, recurrent injury and future specialist visits can be avoided.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Maintaining strength and balance before a fall leads to hospitalisation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These interventions are quiet but they determine whether someone remains independent at 75 and beyond.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For many families, that independence determines whether caregiving remains manageable.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The most affordable hospital bed is the one we never need to use.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Embedding prevention early through thoughtful design in our residential estates and active ageing programmes allows us to shape healthier habits before chronic strain accumulates.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Extending healthspan alongside lifespan reduces pressure on families, hospitals and public finances.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is about sustaining independence, protecting dignity and preserving the system for the next generation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This reflects an important evolution in how we organise care.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hospitals are built for acute and complex conditions.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Doctors stabilise patients after stroke, surgery or serious illness.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But long-term outcomes are determined by what happens after discharge.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When rehabilitation is timely and coordinated, patients regain function earlier, caregiver strain reduces and hospital capacity is preserved for those who need it most.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When recovery is delayed or fragmented, avoidable readmissions return pressure to acute services.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Strengthening community rehabilitation and home-based recovery therefore improves both patient outcomes and system efficiency.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is not an additional layer of care.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These refinements do not compete with acute medicine.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, in my constituency of Tengah, as a young and growing estate, planning neighbourhoods that are ageing-friendly and rehabilitation-supportive from the start will reduce avoidable strain as our residents grow older.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nurses sustain care across wards and communities under rising demand.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we want better access and shorter waits, we must strengthen not only capacity, but coherence.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When responsibilities are organised clearly around training and competency, duplication reduces, bottlenecks ease and patients move more smoothly through the system.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Sustainability is not only about infrastructure and funding.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is about work design, career pathways and workforce well-being.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: No healthcare system succeeds if any part of the team is persistently overstretched.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To our healthcare workers, your work is demanding and it matters deeply.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A sustainable system must also be one that sustains you.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When the workforce is supported, patients benefit and when we steward both carefully, healthcare remains strong for generations to come.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin): Mr Speaker, healthcare has never been simply a matter of "how much money is spent." It concerns the peace of mind of families, the dignity of our seniors and whether our system can endure over time.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many Singaporeans ask, "How much will I have to pay this time?" This is a very real and reasonable question.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But we must also honestly ask another question: "If individuals bear none of the cost, who will ultimately shoulder it?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will it be taxpayers, the next generation, or society as a whole?" Healthcare costs do not disappear; they must be borne by someone.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is precisely one of the most difficult aspects of healthcare policy.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, we must ensure that the system remains sustainable.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Healthcare is not simply a matter of adding or subtracting costs; it is a responsibility shared by society as a whole.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As long as we strengthen the foundations, Singapore's healthcare system can go further and remain stable. : Mr Speaker, to conclude, in mathematics, one plus one equals two only when the foundations are sound.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are the result of careful choices, shared responsibility and long-term stewardship.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Stewardship is not about choosing between care and cost.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is about protecting both – with balance and foresight.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because in healthcare, one plus one does not automatically equal two.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It equals two only when we build it carefully – together.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In his Budget speech, the Prime Minister identified that the spirit of our people is our greatest strength.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: He also said that Singaporeans must be active participants rather than mere spectators in our nation-building effort.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If the Government is sincere about the spirit of our people being our greatest strength, then it must be equally sincere about giving Singaporeans the means and the space to tend that spirit themselves.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Too often, however, Singaporeans find themselves as mere spectators in the making of our national collective identity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Government recognises the importance of nurturing the shared bonds of civic friendships among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I hope to, however, convince the House that our national identity and sense of solidarity is something that is best fostered organically from the ground up in ways that affirm and reflect our citizens' lived experiences.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In the next few minutes, I will talk about heritage, history and human ingenuity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: First, I want to suggest the importance of heritage conservation, not out of sentimentality or nostalgia, but because these places have meanings for us as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Places and place memories are important to our identity and belonging.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Unrelenting change, including those brought about by rampant commercialisation, can degrade our sense of who we are.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will also suggest that the construction of our national history can be more democratised and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If Singaporeans are to be active participants in nation building, then we deserve to tell a Singaporean story that is brought forth by the collective memory making of the Singapore public.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My final point will address the Government's focus on AI.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I understand that we have to embrace advances in technology and seek to include these tools in our repertoire.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My concern is specific that we do not elevate AI to such a degree that we risk undermining the very thing that we are seeking to enhance: our human ingenuity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Government has made it a priority to renew and strengthen our Singapore spirit in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I especially welcome the Prime Minister's plans to strengthen our cultural and heritage institutions, which include the reopening of the revamped Malay Heritage Centre.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, even at the Istana Kampong Glam welcomes the public through its doors once more, it would be a pity if Kampong Glam itself loses its cultural character as a historical precinct which it has served and still continues to serve local communities.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I spent part of my early childhood in Bussorah Street which was once known as Kampong Kaji.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For me, Kampong Glam cannot be separated from the social and communal practices which are embedded within the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Kampong Glam thrives because the district remains a living heritage for the community who live, work and visit there.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am sure that the House shares my concern about how traditional and heritage businesses often with long standing roots in Kampong Glam are finding themselves displaced by the challenging operating environment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, this is not sufficient as an assurance that Kampong Glam will remain viable for heritage businesses.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We should also not understate the intimate connections between our sense of self, our sense of belonging and our sensing of the physical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To a large degree, our identity is anchored in places.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: People know who they are because they know where they were, where their grandparents brought them around to run errands, where they posed with their extended family around Sultan Mosque for a Hari Raya photo, or where they socialised over teh tarik with friends or brought their partner for a date.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Even when I grew older, I continued to bond with my father about Kampong Glam and our shared his interest in its history and heritage.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Born and raised in Kampong Kaji, my father would regale me with stories of Wak Cantuk and playing with his friends from Gedung Kuning and other parts of Kampong Glam.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While he is no longer here, our conversation still lived on fondly through my memories and every time I drop by Kampong Glam.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, such indiscriminate churn can carelessly sever the connective threads nested in Kampong Glam that intricately links people and places, history and memory, and identity and belonging.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A nasi padang stall that has operated for decades, or a textile shop that has served both grandmother and granddaughter – these are not merely commercial storefronts selling goods and services.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These are also precious repositories of cultural knowledge, community relationships and public memory.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These are simply gone when they are gone.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And no influx of souvenir shops, photo booths and Instagram-friendly cafes can compensate for such a loss.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We can still balance the forces of commerce and the imperatives of culture.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This includes helping the heritage businesses that carry the memory of many generations, supporting the families who have anchored this district through the decades and taming speculation so that the cultural heritage of the district is not hollowed out.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Urban Redevelopment Authority's (URA's) planning parameters for historical districts stipulate guidelines for building use.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Recently, I visited the Albatross Files exhibition at the National Library, which I thought was quite remarkable, since it is not often that the state offers a revisionist account of its own historical narrative.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As a student, the narrative of separation that I was taught was one of expulsion.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A Straits Times report from 21 December 2025 quoting a former secondary school history teacher confirms this.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: That aside, the declassification of the Albatross File is a good move.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Yet the existence of the file was only first revealed in 1996 by Dr Goh Keng Swee during an interview with Dr Melanie Chew.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And it took another 27 years for it to be fully declassified.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Must Albatross really wait for 30 years before its existence was to be publicly acknowledged and almost 60 years after Independence before its contents were to be fully revealed to the public?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Even then, the declassification process of Albatross seems tightly managed.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I refer to the 7 December speech by Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong, who shared how a specific team went through the material carefully, picked out the key documents and sections, annotated them and wrote up the editorial apparatus.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I do not mean to downplay the considerable work and effort of these scholars.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, was there a reason that the file was not released to the public domain in the first instance so that the wider community of scholars and the public can read, discuss, interpret and construct their understandings of a past in a more democratic and collective fashion?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As the Minister for Digital Development and Information stated in her written answer on 12 January, "A deeper appreciation of our history and how we got here will strengthen our national identity." I however doubt that our more mature and discerning citizens can truly have this deeper appreciation if the Government's approach to history remains didactic, where history is meant to be consumed by the people rather than constructed by the people and for the people.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Historical narratives gain resonance when it is written by the many, not dictated by the few.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Currently, even Government documents that have been transferred as public records to the National Archives Singapore (NAS), the so called "public archives", are not easily accessible.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, most of these records still require permission from the originating agency before they can be read.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I understand that a more transparent and open declassification policy may cause some anxieties.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, the Government can heed the advice of Senior Minister Lee, who once said, quote "In teaching the Singapore Story, you have to deal with delicate issues, especially race and religion, and sometimes relations with our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We must treat such issues sensitively, but we cannot gloss over them.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We cannot pretend that incidents involving race and religion never happened.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: They are part of our history", end quote.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To future-proof Singapore, amnesia is not an option.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If you want Singaporeans to be active participants in their own country, if you want our citizens to deepen their appreciation of our history and to strengthen our national identity, then the Government must believe that Singaporeans can be trusted to participate in the construction of our national history.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A focal point of the Budget speech was on harnessing AI as a strategic advantage for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister outlined the Government's commitment to strengthen AI literacy for our students in the institutes of higher learning (IHLs) and to help workers automate routine tasks so they can concentrate on performing higher value activities that would involve judgement, creativity and human insight.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These are pragmatic measures to familiarise Singaporeans with AI and integrate its use into our daily routines.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, I wonder whether we are in danger of becoming an AI-reliant society, rather than an AI-resilient society.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My worry is that such indiscriminate habituation to AI may risk undermining the very things that we want to augment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Those things that the Prime Minister talked about – judgement, creativity and human insight.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Had AI been available then, it would have been convenient and very tempting for me to have ChatGPT summarise the content or generate ideas for an essay or seminar discussion.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, there is value in undertaking the sometimes slow, often uncomfortable and always arduous task of reading a text and grappling to understand it on your own terms.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is the process through which we sharpen our cognitive skills.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is how we learn to decipher and interpret the meanings of the written word, and by extension, make sense of the world, which those words reflect and shape.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is how we develop our sense of judgement and our capacity for creativity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate the Prime Minister's reassurance that the Government will define how AI is developed and used in Singapore, including setting out clear rules for its responsible and safe implementation.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: One last point, Mr Speaker, I will reiterate what my WP colleague Dennis Tan raised, and his concerns about AI and the environment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We should remember that every AI query has a physical and environmental footprint.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We may think of AI as performing virtual magic on our computers, giving us answers in almost an instant, or even helping us to generate pantun for Parliament.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But this magic has to piggyback on a vast infrastructure of data centres that consume voracious amounts of electricity and water.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Globally, data centres are straining power grids and depleting water sources.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Needless to say, the energy and water demands of these data centres also have third party effects, such as increasing the utility cost for everyone else, including residents.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This has become such a serious issue in the US to the extent that the New York Times reported on 15 January, that the politicians and lawmakers have started mulling over legislation to oblige tech companies to pay their fair share for electricity consumption, including paying upfront for the cost of upgrading the power grid.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Given these circumstances, it seems only pragmatic for us in this House and as a country to consider the ethical and environmental trade-offs involved as we embark on a national quest to integrate AI into our personal, social and working lives.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I hope that the Government reads my remarks as I intend them to be: constructive amendments for the purpose of strengthening our civic endurance and collective resilience to navigate the challenging days ahead.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In such a world, resilience must be intentional.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Today, I will focus on three foundations that will determine whether we truly secure our future together: one, a workforce that can outrun disruption; two, families that experience structural assurance; three, a Singapore spirit strong enough to withstand fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: More than 600,000 individuals took up SkillsFuture-supported training last year.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Over 60,000 mid-career Singaporeans have benefitted from the Level-Up programme.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The merger of SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) and Workforce Singapore (WSG) into a single integrated agency is a decisive structural move.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It recognises that in an era of frequent job transitions, training and placement must operate as one system.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In the logistics industry, there have been many success stories of candidates undergoing career conversion or job reskilling and finding a newfound purpose in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I am very grateful to the various trade associations and chambers, as well who work hand-in-hand with the Government agencies in securing jobs for workers in their sectors.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In a slower growth environment, our edge will not depend on how many courses are taken, but on whether upgrading consistently leads to higher wages and better prospects.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The next step must be sharper outcome accountability.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I thus call on the Government to publish regular data on post-training wage progression and re-employment outcomes by sector.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Industry Transformation Maps should embed workforce mobility benchmarks, not just productivity metrics.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Firms that receive significant transformation grants should demonstrate clearly how local workers benefit in terms of career progression.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Resilience must mean that effort leads to advancement, visibly and measurably.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Yet even the most adaptable worker draws strength from stable family foundations.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Economic confidence cannot be sustained if households feel uncertain.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This year's Budget strengthens support across life stages.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Central Provident Fund (CPF) top-ups of up to $1,500 will support Singaporeans aged 50 and above with lower balances.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We begin this term on a strong fiscal footing.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In my interactions with residents in Canberra, many families have shared similar concerns.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: They are working hard, managing their responsibilities diligently and doing their best to provide for their children and care for their parents.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: What I hear consistently is not a demand for more but a desire for greater certainty, certainty that support will remain stable, that costs will not outpace incomes unpredictably and that the system will continue to stay behind them as they navigate different life stages.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But in an ageing society with structurally rising healthcare and retirement needs, assurance must be systemic.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We must hence move towards a clearer, consolidated family assurance framework – one that maps lifetime support across housing, childcare, healthcare and retirement in a transparent way.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I call on the Government to ensure that inter-agency support for families under multiple schemes is streamlined into a single digital interface, reducing administrative complexity.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Income thresholds for key schemes should also be reviewed regularly and pegged transparently to median income growth so that support evolves automatically with living standards.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: When families feel predictable stability, they make long-term decisions with confidence, and that confidence strengthens economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But every strong household and strong worker requires something deeper.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In 2025, global conflict remained high, with over 200,000 violent conflict events recorded across many regions and conflict-related fatalities rising to nearly 240,000, underscoring how geopolitical instability persists across multiple theatres and continues to affect millions worldwide.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The Budget invests deliberately in strengthening shared bonds through cultural institutions, expanded sports facilities, extended 250% tax deductions for donations and corporate volunteering, and a new $50 million SG Partnerships Fund.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In Canberra, we launched Project Sound Box, a sound mitigating box that reduces the sound generated from the lion dance troupes in the area by 40 decibels.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The troupes also work closely with various stakeholders to end training by 9.00 pm and to provide updates on their training schedules.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This information is disseminated to the resident chat groups so that they can be kept informed.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We have also organised learning journeys where residents of different races come and see the troupes train, and the troupes give a briefing on the significance of the various dance moves.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The troupes are seen as a member of the community and are invited to various events in the community.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The SG Partnerships Fund should incorporate clear multi-year community impact metrics so that cohesion outcomes are sustained, not symbolic.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Structured civic participation pathways, including youth policy internships and project incubators, should become a permanent feature of our governance landscape.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: When these three reinforce one another, we do not merely withstand uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That is how we secure our future together.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, last week was the Lunar New Year.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I had the pleasure of sampling a Xiangshan Hong Mei Ren mandarin orange.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The texture was extraordinary, the vesicles of the orange were very sweet, the skin almost paper thin.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It has been described as eating jelly, or jelly growing on a tree; 12% to 15% sugar content, low acidity, no floating skin.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Hong Mei Ren was once called the Ehime No 28, developed over 15 years at the Ehime Prefectural Fruit Tree Experiment Station in Japan, and prized for its jelly-like texture and ultra-premium positioning.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But due to the lack of intellectual property (IP) protection, it was lost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A handful of stem cuttings were carried to Xiangshan county in Zhejiang province in China in 2001.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Today, the Hong Mei Ren has expanded to over one million mu (亩) over 15 Chinese provinces, dwarfing Japan's 300 hectares over a hundred fold.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It was one of the most consequential agricultural IP losses in modern Japanese history, alongside the Shine Muscat grape and strawberry leakages.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That reminded me of something closer to home.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is well known that our research and development (R&D) ecosystem over the last 30 years has not produced impressive commercial outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Tens of billions of spending since 1990, more than 30 years.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The report card of significant commercial outcomes, high value initial public offerings (IPOs), globally competitive companies is bare.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is what I would have said up to 23 May 2025.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Coincidentally, also about 15 years of effort, like the Japanese breeding the Ehime No 28.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, the initial science came from Singapore, but commercialisation leaked offshore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If this is success, then what does failure look like?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is not the fault of the Chinese.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They optimise rationally within the realities of the system.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is our failure to capture value, our responsibility to anticipate, to get it right, to make sure Singaporean taxpayers reap the rewards of tens of billions ploughed into R&D.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, even when a success emerges, the system is naively vulnerable to value chain leakage.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To lose a one-billion-dollar IPO may be regarded as a misfortune.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But the question is not whether we are spending enough, it is whether the system converts that spending into commercial outcomes for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Why does the system produce these two outcomes: (a) a limited pipeline of commercially viable R&D companies; and (b) a failure to take advantage of successes when they come?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The structural flaw is that agencies like the Economic Development Board (EDB) and the Statutory Boards are structured as grant givers, not as investors or ecosystem builders.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If you are a grant giver, your job is to mark the market, to benchmark, to do due diligence against market rates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If you mark the market, you are then subject to the audit process, every decision scrutinised against whether you followed the benchmark.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If you are a civil servant in that position, there is absolutely no reason to stick your neck out.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Zero incentive for upside, only downside risk from audit.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, of course, you end up with super conservative civil servants who say, "I do not want to do any innovation." You end up with long meetings where senior officials agonise over $5,000 or $10,000 because they are worried about compliance.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Worse, annual key performance indicator cycles force officers to judge five- to seven-year bets on a 12-month horizon.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, promising ventures get culled before they can prove themselves.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Meanwhile, you miss the forest for the trees.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To take an ecosystem approach to funding so that the day-to-day operational environment for R&D startups is the best that it can be.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our agencies are structured to avoid losing money, not to make it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is why 30 years of spending has not produced 30 years of results.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I agree with the Prime Minister that R&D is a core imperative.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But there must be an honest reckoning with 30 years of limited commercial outcomes and value leakage.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The R&D ecosystem needs three things: money, speed and a market.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I tried to count Singapore's Government-linked startup funds.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There are eight sub-schemes under the Startup SG umbrella alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The National Research Foundation, A*STAR, the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the Monetary Authority of Singapore run their own programmes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is not an exhaustive list by any stretch of the imagination.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Of course, each was created for a reason.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: France has a public investment bank called Banque publique d'investissement (Bpifrance), a single institution combining innovation investment, SME lending, loan guarantees, export credit insurance and strategic equity stakes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is commercially viable, with a 2024 net income of 900 million euros.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
