text: Under Francois Hollande and economic advisor Emmanuel Macron, in 2012, France merged four fragmented investment bodies – one for SME loans, guarantees innovation, one for venture capital, one for strategic equity and one for regional equity – into a single entity, Bpifrance.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Export credit insurance was added later in 2017.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It now employs about 3,500 staff, centralising innovation investment, economy-wide strategic investment, SME financing, loan guarantees, export support and regional business development.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The diagnosis that prompted Bpifrance's creation was plain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Despite strong science and underlying dynamism, France's entrepreneurial culture was weak, risk-averse and fearful of failure.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Bpifrance also organised learning expeditions and export programmes to help French companies internationalise.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It became the anchor investor across French tech, not just deep tech.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We need to take a portfolio approach, thinking in 10-year cycles, 10-year cohorts, 10-year mandates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We had this in the early years with DBS and Temasek, but both have since drifted from that mission and today, no institution fills the gap.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The WP has argued before for an Export-Import (EXIM) Bank.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The French example shows a mandate wider still – innovation investment, SME lending, export credit, strategic equity, all under one roof.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is often said that we have a lot of capital in Singapore, but we have the wrong type of capital for R&D commercialisation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Excessive obsession with business metrics way too early.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Startups forced to jump through a thousand hoops for small cheques.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Family officers largely uninterested in our R&D ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: My colleague Jamus Lim has proposed requiring a modest domestic allocation as a condition for family office tax incentives, which I support.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What does success look like 25 years from now?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A flywheel, where private capital is sophisticated enough to understand deep tech.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Patient capital writing experimental cheques, less metric-obsessed early on.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is the ecosystem that we should be building towards.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Funders and regulators need to understand that two extra days of approvals or one month of delayed cash flow is life and death for a startup.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: You do not understand what it takes if you have not tried it yourself.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Fast capital deployment does not just save companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It trains a generation of entrepreneurs who will not waste 60% of their time fundraising.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should make peace with the fact that roughly 80% of bets on startups made in good faith will back a losing venture.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The real gain is often the entrepreneur's second and third startup.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But if the first attempt feels like pulling teeth, they drop out, and the compounding of iterated learning across business formation is lost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speed is not just about money, it is about people.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: MOM uses income as its proxy for talent: the Tech.Pass at $22,500 a month, the ONE Pass at $30,000.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It seldom works for deep tech, which due to their call-option nature, are unfashionable before they are fashionable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A strong biotech engineer in Thailand earns a quarter of Singapore wages.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To bring them here, a startup must triple their salary – not because their skills are worth less, but because MOM's threshold demands it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is startup cash burnt on regulatory compliance, not R&D.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We are asking founders to choose between the talent they need and the runway they cannot afford to lose.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The assumption that salary equals value breaks down where it matters most.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Deep tech talent is scarce, specialised and often transient.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A monthly review committee of mixed Singaporean and international entrepreneurs evaluating deep tech companies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There are perhaps 50 to 80 serious deep-tech companies formed here each year.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Companies meeting the criteria enter a special segment: flexibility for three to five visas in Year One, with annual portfolio reviews assessing whether the company is growing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Easy entry, progressively stricter requirements on each renewal, all strictly performance-based.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Are Singaporeans being hired and trained alongside foreign specialists?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Traditional organisations – banks, established corporates – can afford strict income rules.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But deep-tech startups need radical fluidity and the visa regime most suited to them should follow the company, not the person.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should also aim to make visa decisions snappy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is fine to say no to people.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But let us have the courtesy to do it fast, within a matter of weeks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Money and speed are necessary, but insufficient if no one is buying.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The system must be designed for offtake, structured so that when R&D produces something, there is a buyer on the other end.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Decision-making centres remain in New York, London, Paris and Shanghai.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When the regional executive who championed an innovation pilot rotates home, continuity goes with them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Corporate incentive structures often reward launching initiatives, not seeing them through, creating structural discontinuity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Tax incentives should require backing from both regional and global headquarters.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If there is no interlocutor in New York or Shanghai who has signed off, no incentive.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This ensures a direct link to decision-making and prevents projects from being forgotten when executives rotate home.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Beyond that, we should attach strategic buyer offtake commitments to grants.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Require multinational corporations (MNCs) to pilot, evaluate or procure from at least one local startup or SME, as part of grant conditions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the Government itself must practise innovation procurement.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Europe and China give SMEs quotas of contracts to help them gain scale, so we must do the same.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I said I would return to the question of protecting value.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Money, speed and a market can build a pipeline.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But pipeline alone is not enough if the value leaks out.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three countries have dealt with this question, and they are not peripheral economies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They are among the most successful R&D ecosystems in the world.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: No known prosecution has occurred, but the deterrent is powerful.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The critical feature was not any single restriction but a system: government ownership stakes in spin-offs, personnel who were Taiwanese nationals, incorporation in Taiwan, government funding giving the state structural leverage over deployment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Maximum prison sentences for overseas technology leakage reach 18 years, with punitive damages at five times actual losses.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some say we should adopt golden shares, IP retention conditions and protected technologies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: My view is the necessary and plausibly sufficient policy to adopt is an IP conditionality regime, designed for a small open economy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, we will be judged on the competitiveness of our ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Special Economic Zones that can scale up manufacturing at lower cost.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Risk capital from a consolidated policy investment bank, like Bpifrance.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Trade architecture that companies actually use, not headline ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement numbers or scarcely used Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), but reduced non-tariff barriers and the ability to incorporate once in Singapore and operate across key Southeast Asian markets.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When companies reach a certain size, the siren song of redomicile will prove irresistible for many.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The competition shifts to building a growth-capital ecosystem deep enough and catalysing a Southeast Asian market large enough that staying makes more sense than leaving.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, sunset such an IP conditionality regime once the ecosystem is strong enough.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This will crowd-in private R&D and take the burden of sustaining our headline R&D numbers off the Singaporean taxpayer.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Yes, fewer R&D startups may form under these IP conditions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But I say, it is better to have fewer startups with real upside capture than sexy headlines, nice public relations pieces in CNA and nothing to show from it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And it shifts R&D accountability to where it belongs, not on public servants approving a grant, but on the system retaining value.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: You may be very proud of your Ehime No 28.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But unless you take preparatory measures, unless you design for the upside, one day you will find your R&D being sold as a Hong Mei Ren mandarin.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Incubated in Singapore, harvested in Zhejiang and Hong Kong.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As expectations rise with regards to access to care, social support and well-being, and rightly so, we should not only be spending more, in terms of the help we give our people, but also spending to ensure that the help is received in a simple and dignified manner.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this regard, I have three reflections to share.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, how residents experience our systems on the ground; next, the progress Singapore has already made towards systemic integration; and third, how we can deepen integration so that care truly becomes seamless.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First reflection – when help exists, but feels hard to reach.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A senior elderly lady who comes monthly to collect her food packs from our weekly ground-up initiative called the Jurong Spring Food Cares programme.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For months she did not come, and we wondered what had happened to her.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One day, I received a phone call from her sister, saying that she had fallen, taken ill at the hospital and was now recuperating at home.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: She eventually returned to her home in our constituency and I visited her.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: She was overwhelmed – medical appointments, social service worker appointments and many other agencies that she had to visit.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, she was trying to cope with the new diagnosis of breast cancer, not knowing exactly how deeply this was going to affect her.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: She did not lack the services or the help.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What she lacked was just better coordination and integration.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our systems are robust and well-intentioned, but to a vulnerable senior, they can sometimes feel difficult to navigate.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As we move towards a "we first" society, we must design systems not just for efficiency, but also for human experience.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Reflection number two – the current progress we have made on integration as a nation.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These are important and commendable foundations, but we must be cognisant that integration succeeds, not merely when agencies connect, but when our people feel the connection.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A clinic visit may begin with diagnosis of diabetes or injury, but underlying issues may include loneliness, caregiver strain, financial stress or mental health concerns.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To truly integrate care, we must see the whole person and not just the diagnosis.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Reflection three – learning from international practice and adapting it for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One person coordinated services, one trusted point of contact.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Patients did not have to repeat their stories across agencies.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They experienced continuity, clarity, and most importantly, dignity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Singapore does not need to replicate another system, but we can adapt useful principles within our already strong healthcare and social care systems.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, as I have mentioned before, medical and social needs surface simultaneously most of the time.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, early intervention becomes possible, and fourth, support becomes proactive rather than reactive.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A senior visiting a primary care physician for follow-up for poorly controlled diabetes.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The doctor identifies several social vulnerabilities, a co-located or a nearby social worker or caseworker immediately responds and assist, with application for financial aid, mobility devices, befriending services and even social prescription.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In fact, this might achieve three of our national priorities of creating more jobs, providing seamless care, and even piloting AI solutions when we handle very complex health and social issues.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Stealing the words of my colleague, Dr Tan Wu Meng from last year's COS debates, this should not be seen as a cost, but as a forward investment, an investment in our people, for our people.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, let us invest more in integration and integration is not just about building new systems, but about making existing systems feel like one.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: (In Malay): Mr Speaker, before I continue, allow me to give some focus to our Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many Malay/Muslim seniors face challenges that not only relate to physical health, but also social, emotional and spiritual in nature.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In our culture, peace of mind, moral support and spiritual guidance are very important to age gracefully.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many of them come not just for financial or medical assistance, but because they seek support and guidance.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For our community, that place is usually the mosques and local asatizah networks.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The mosque is not just a place to perform their prayers, but also a centre for community support.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We already have a strong foundation in place through the M3 network, which combines the efforts of Government agencies and Malay/Muslim community institutions.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Based on this strong foundation, may I propose these three measures.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With these measures, Malay/Muslim seniors are not only cared for physically but are also strengthened spiritually and socially. : Mr Speaker, in Tamil, please.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: (In Tamil): Mr Speaker, at a time when we are debating on Budget plans with regard to ageing, we must also reflect on how we understand ageing.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Often, ageing is described only as a challenge.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They are repositories of wisdom, examples of patience, community leaders with skills and experience.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Also, they are strong pillars of families and society.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Therefore, it is now time for us to change the direction of our national conversation.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We are not a society that is ageing, we are a society that is active and that which has a long life.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We are not a society that is growing old, we are a society that is living well and maturing.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We are not only a society that supports the elderly, we are a society that empowers the elderly.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To implement this, we can advance in several key directions.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, we must create a platform where seniors serve as mentors to the youth.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Fourth, we must increase opportunities to utilise their experiences in community management, arts and traditional sectors.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As Singapore moves towards becoming a “we first” society, our task is not merely to build more programmes, but to ensure that every resident experiences care as one coherent journey – simple, humane and dignified.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because integration is not achieved when policies align on paper but when a senior no longer feels lost, when help arrives without confusion and when dignity is preserved at every step of life.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If we succeed, ageing will not be feared as decline but embraced as a stage of contribution, purpose and active longevity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, let us not just build a system that treats illness, health, social, or otherwise, but build a society that journeys with all our people together as one with clarity, compassion and care.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As the Prime Minister acknowledged in the Budget Statement, with longer lifespans, retirement adequacy is a major concern for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This is a sentiment that is echoed by the seniors in Potong Pasir.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If a senior retired in 2005 at the statutory retirement age of 62 years, he or she would be 82 in 2025 – a long retirement period of 20 years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For a retired senior, every dollar saved at the time of retirement, for retirement will be stretched with each passing year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In this Budget, seniors can look forward to benefiting from additional subsidies for CareShield life premiums via a top-up of the long-term care support fund, further CPF top-ups and changes to the CPF system to help build up retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The objective is to ensure that seniors age with dignity, security and peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: However, as the number of seniors continues to grow in the community, as we expect it to, it is inevitable that there will be seniors who fall between the gaps.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Others may have to grapple with challenges that extend beyond financial concerns.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Today, I wish to highlight the concerns of two such categories of seniors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The first are retired seniors who live in homes with higher Annual Value (AV).

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I had raised the issue of reviewing the use of the AV as a means test for healthcare subsidies in my maiden speech last year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This issue has also been raised by other Members of this House on other occasions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To address this, the Government had reviewed the AV threshold for means testing from time to time and raised it to allow more Singaporeans to benefit from higher subsidies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I agree with the Prime Minister when he explained in his response at the Budget debate last year that there is no perfect means testing regime to test both income and wealth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: However, the fact that this issue has been raised on a number of occasions by Members of this House reflects the ground sentiment that an increasing number of seniors living in homes with higher AV are either extremely concerned about their retirement adequacy in the future or already facing financial challenges in retirement.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To be clear, the means testing regime of PCHI and in its absence, the AV of one’s residence is, on the round, an objective measurement of one's income and wealth in the distribution of subsidies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I will posit, however, that retired seniors, who need to plan their retirement funds over a longer life span, own and live in homes with slightly higher AV purchased through pre-retirement income, or have residential arrangements that may not accurately reflect their level of wealth, are disproportionately more affected by this means testing regime than any other demographic of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Perhaps the deeper underlying issue is to consider whether there is a need to review holistically how we assess our retired seniors in the various subsidies and support mechanisms that we have in place.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Some of these mechanisms are applied nationally across all demographics of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The means testing regime of PCHI and AV is one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Other mechanisms are senior-centric, like silver support and the Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation Packages.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For those mechanisms applied nationally, in healthcare for example, some subsidies are tiered, like in hospitalisation ward subsidies, while others suffer a cliff-drop reduction of subsidies, like in the case of residential long-term care services.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The second category are seniors who live alone.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Based on the overall expectation that one in four Singaporeans will be over the age of 65 by 2030, we can certainly expect this trend to continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Through my pro bono LPA Programme over the past 10 years, I have had the opportunity to engage many seniors who make conscious choices on a very difficult and life-changing issue of the possible loss of mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It is abundantly clear to me that they are anxious, worried and unsettled about what could happen to them as they age, especially if they are single or choose to live alone due to complex family dynamics.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: A senior lived alone in a home that was in a state of disrepair.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Our volunteers in the neighbourhood observed that she needed help.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: She missed her bills and had her utilities turned off.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: She missed her meals, even though volunteers left cooked meals at her doorstep.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: She was friendly one day and extremely hostile the next.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Our grassroots team, the Social Service Office, AIC and other volunteer groups rendered assistance in whatever way possible.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Eventually, after almost a year, we were informed that some action had been taken to have her situation addressed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This may be an isolated case, one with a peculiar set of circumstances.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: But as the number of seniors living alone in Singapore grows, the expectation must be that more such cases will emerge.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The Public Guardian can work alongside the Public Trustee to manage the assets of such seniors and direct caregiving agencies to administer the care required.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I understand that in jurisdictions such as Australia, there exists a legal framework that allows for direct intervention in such cases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The concerns I raised today – from retirement adequacy to fair access to support and the vulnerabilities of seniors who live alone – remind us that no single framework can meet every circumstance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As we continue strengthening our systems, let us work together collectively to achieve the objective espoused in this year’s Budget: for every senior in Singapore to age with dignity, security and peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Much of the debates in this House has been dedicated to "national AI Missions" and our digital frontier.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the privilege of being the last speaker of the Budget debate, I want to speak about a different kind of infrastructure, one that does not run on silicon or servers, but on the time, heart and grit of our people.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we say "Care Economy," we are not just talking about a sector of work.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It refers to the unpaid labor of a daughter waking up at 3.00 am to check on the rise and fall of breath of her bedbound father.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The teacher conducting a welfare check in the evening at home of an absent child.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is the parent caring for an adult child of special needs worrying about the future when they pass on.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Or a retiree delivering lunch to a lonely neighbour unwell for the day.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Currently, the national accounting of our GDP struggles to see that work.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Behind every fiscal surplus is an "invisible surplus" provided by our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Their time is uncounted, but without it, our society would fracture.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must recognise that care has a cost, often paid in the currency of burnout by those who give the most.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, I would like to call for a flipping of paradigms.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The terms "silver tsunami" or "super-aged society" are used with a sense of gloom and burden.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us strive amidst a "silver opportunity" for a "super healthy society".

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us empower our active agers to be perceived not just as recipients of help, but mentors to youths and first-responders to frail neighbors in community.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us build a silver economy where products and services are designed by seniors, for seniors, allowing them to age with agency and purpose.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, as HDB supply gradually begins to meet demand, the anxiety of our residents shifts.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is moving from "Will I get a BTO?" to "What happens to my home in the long run?" And for those still on the margins – single unwed parents or Singaporeans with foreign spouses – the question remains, "Is there a place for me here, for me and my family?" We must reframe the narrative of home ownership.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: HDB should not be viewed through the lens of ticking depreciation or potential profit.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It must be seen as a home for life.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When a resident feels secure in the longevity of their community, they do not just live there.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They invest social capital and their generations after continue aspiring to remain as many generations have in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While we await the details of the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS), it is an opportunity to reframe and offer a vision of Singapore where HDB ownership provides psychological and social security through every transition of life.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Allow me to visualise what I have seen.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: You step into a flat with multiple children, up to eight or 10 people in a two-room.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The only room is typically wall-to-wall with mattresses with clothes piled, strewn all around. the living room doubles as a kitchen and a nursery.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Young children lie, occupied with screens while parents cook or rest after a long day of work, if they are even home.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sometimes, you find a charging personal mobility aid.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Within these four walls, a conducive environment is a state of mind, staying on the right track in life and keeping up with educational goals is a daily uphill struggle.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While our nation's commitment to education reform is a vital tool for social mobility, school only accounts for a fraction of a child's day.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What happens during the school holidays or the unsupervised hours after the bell rings?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have sat with primary school students who shared a cigarette, exchanging tips on which shop to shoplift.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And this is a friction of inequality that no Ministry alone can solve.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is heartening, though, is the organic resilience of our community.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Youths from the youth network have formed a kids club in Toa Payoh Central.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What started as weekly activities at the basketball court during school holidays have become homework sessions during school term.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These same children are now supervised at least for one night in seven days.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we truly believe that education is a vital tool for social mobility, let us reconsider and prioritise the design of spaces and rules in our homes and communities.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have the Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) Programme for retrofitting seniors' homes.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How about access as a ComLink scheme milestone?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Incentive for retrofitting modular furniture for families with young children in rental flats?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have even thought of the acronyms – ACCESS can stand for Adaptable, Compact, Child-centric Enhancements for Small Spaces, or Augmenting Conducive Childhood Environments for Student Success.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When a few accumulates significant assets, properties, equities and growing bank balances in an uncertain world, the instinct to secure one's future can easily transit into a cycle of accumulation where enough is always just beyond reach.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The gap between the haves and the have nots threaten to wedge society psychologically.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As President Tharman Shanmugaratnam reminded us at the Opening of this Parliament, we must resist the trend where wealth and trenches and inequality is passed down.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must be surgical in a moral division of resources to reinvest in our collective social capital, beginning with the stability of homes.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Workplace accommodations so that choosing to care for parent does not mean a blow to one's career for the sandwiched generation.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thousands battle autoimmune and invisible conditions that demand immense stamina.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must fund better diagnostic support and workplace flexibility, ensuring our infrastructure of care includes the struggles we cannot see.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The rising tide of youth mental health challenges is a cry for presence.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must divert resources to give parents the commodity of time, prioritising parenting over productivity during critical development windows and crisis.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Family must always be our first line of defence.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Offering these professionalising home-based services can extend ageing in place and provides our seniors dignity and our families a peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the vulnerable and persons with disabilities, we must move deeper for them.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This means moving beyond vouchers towards long term coordinated interventions that break the cycle of poverty, safeguard our children and ensure every Singaporean is an active contributor to our nation.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For large families with many children, costs do not merely add up.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They multiply: from space at home, food portions to educational expenses and transportation costs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unfortunately, childcare leave and Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers does not follow the same logic of proportionality.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Mandarin): Mr Speaker, the Government is investing heavily in artificial intelligence, but when I visit Toa Payoh, I often hear seniors express a complex sentiment about AI, in Hokkien: "Ai lai, Mai lai".

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first "Ai" is AI – artificial intelligence.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Chinese New Year, I believe many received AI-generated cartoon-style family portraits and even saw friends galloping with horses in the images.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This technology makes everyone's "good morning images" more interesting – this is the kind of AI application that everyone welcomes.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must harness AI's powerful organisational capabilities to handle complex administrative work.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Technology should not bring distance, but societal cohesion with love.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Because the second "Ai"; must be the "Ai" of "爱心" or love.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What seniors worry about is not how smart machines are, but that machines replace human warmth.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Technology should not bring distance, but societal cohesion with love. : In conclusion, Speaker, a rich Singapore is not defined by the size of surplus in our banks, but by the strength of the bonds in our community.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a place where a senior feels valued, a caregiver feels seen and our social fabric and cohesion remain strong.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us invest in the high touch human connection that no AI Mission can ever replace too.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And as Benjamin Kheng would sing in our 2024 National Day song, Not Alone: "If we just look to each other, then this house will feel like home." Mr Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And not surprisingly, we also have a record number of Members participating in this debate.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And I thank everyone who has spoken and supported the Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because it is not possible for any single Budget to be all encompassing.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, if your favourite item is not mentioned in this year's Budget, it does not mean that it has been overlooked or ignored.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because every Budget builds on the last, and lays the framework and groundwork for the next.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, in the debate, several Members highlighted that suggestions and points they raised on AI in previous years were taken up this year, in this year's Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, that is the spirit in which we craft and design every Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On that note, I have listened carefully to the many thoughtful suggestions that have been shared in the last few days, even on the occasions when I have not been in this Chamber, I have read your speeches.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will study your suggestions and give them due consideration.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And maybe, in a few Budgets from now, some of these suggestions will be highlighted thereafter.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The programmes, specific questions will be taken up during the COS debates.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For my response, I will focus on three broad issues that have been highlighted.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many Members spoke about this, including Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Victor Lye, Mr Kenneth Tiong, Dr Neo Kok Beng, Dr Wan Rizal, Ms Gho Sze Kee and Mr Vikram Nair, amongst others.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our economic strategies must adapt to a changed world.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is a world where power and strength increasingly shape outcomes where rules are more contested, where economic relationships are being rewired.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We felt these pressures acutely last year, especially after the US' Liberation Day tariffs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Now, fresh changes in US tariffs remind us that uncertainty and volatility is becoming the norm and in such a world, smaller countries, like Singapore, risk being bypassed or marginalised.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must deepen trusted partnerships, diversify our links and strengthen our resilience.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And crucially, we need to establish leadership positions in key domains, so that we create distinctive value that others cannot easily replicate.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And many Members talked about value capture for our economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And so, we are investing heavily in R&D, building up our enterprise ecosystem step by step and anchoring cutting-edge investments in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must stay at the frontier – in advanced manufacturing, finance, digital services and new growth sectors.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the past, growth and jobs moved more closely together.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When the economy expanded, firms hired more workers across the board.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Companies in these sectors compete globally and they create well-paying jobs, with strong career progression opportunities.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But precisely because they compete at the frontier, they have to be productive and operate efficiently, often with lean manpower.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: You look at leading companies around the world, some of them run highly automated facilities, including so-called "dark factories" that operate 24/7 with minimal human presence.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is one reason why manufacturing employment in many advanced economies has steadily fallen.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over that same period, employment in exportable services – areas like finance, information technology (IT) and professional services – has grown as we diversified our economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Yet, taken together, the manufacturing, finance, IT and professional services segments of our economy account for just around 30% of employment.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Does that mean that growth is no longer important?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It creates new opportunities, raises wages and generates the resources we need as a society.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They anchor our enterprise ecosystem and drive demand across the rest of the economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, without sustained growth and, especially, growth at the frontier, investments will go elsewhere, capabilities will erode, wages will stagnate and Singapore risks a real decline.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Growth alone will not automatically translate into job opportunities across the board.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must also uplift the broader domestic economy – raising productivity, wages and career pathways across the services sector.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is why we are taking sustained action in areas like education, healthcare and social services.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have put in place skills frameworks to articulate competencies, enable skills upgrading and support structured progression in these areas.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have increased salaries for workers in public healthcare institutions and Government-supported preschools.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have updated salary guidelines for the community care and social service sectors.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are not ad hoc or one-off moves.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because inclusive growth means more than developing frontier industries.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It also means ensuring that domestic services – services that Singaporeans rely on daily – become more productive, more professional and more attractive as careers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this regard, SMEs play a critical role.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They employ many Singaporeans and anchor economic activity across our island.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many members also shared their concerns about SMEs, including Ms Diana Pang, Mr Jackson Lam, Mr Fadli Fawzi, Mr Edward Chia, Ms Denise Phua, Mr Azhar Othman and Mr Sharael Taha.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, the two SME segments under greater pressure are retail and food and beverage (F&B).

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These sectors face structural headwinds – from e-commerce and changing consumer habits and from increased overseas travel by Singaporeans and perhaps also by the strong Singapore dollar.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Yet, even amid these challenges, the number of F&B and retail establishments continue to grow.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And with more players in the market, competition has intensified.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, how should we respond to these trends?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the immediate term, we have provided Corporate Income Tax rebates, including in this Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over the longer term, our support must be sustainable and should not distort market incentives.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For businesses in retail and F&B, what are their cost drivers?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The largest components of their operating expenditure are the costs of goods and materials, labour and rent.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In a small economy like ours, goods and materials are largely priced in global markets.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, there is little scope for us to influence these costs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On rental costs, at the macro level, rentals have broadly tracked economic fundamentals.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Rent increases for retail spaces have trended below nominal GDP growth and inflation in the last few years.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Rental costs have also declined as a share of total business costs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of course, market rents vary by property type and location.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Individual tenants may face higher rent increases at renewals, and we are mindful of these cases.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Where Government agencies are landlords, like HDB and JTC, and where we have direct oversight, like in hawker centres, we have frameworks to keep rents fair and competitive.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we will continue reviewing and updating these frameworks.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will also continue to monitor the situation closely to ensure that rentals remain sustainable and competitive.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, labour costs have increased in recent years.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Part of this reflects structural factors – an ageing population and tighter labour supply as well as market forces as firms compete for workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But part of this is also the outcome of policy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Through the Progressive Wage Model, we are raising wages for lower-wage workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That reflects our consistent approach to uplift workers while supporting firms to adjust.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to strike the right balance – sufficient flexibility for businesses without undermining Singaporean workforce development.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ultimately, the sustainable path forward is productivity improvement and business transformation.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We know that SMEs need more support to embark on such transformation.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members, including Ms Cassandra Lee, Mr Lee Hong Chuang and Mr Henry Kwek, have offered suggestions on what more we can do.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Mark Lee also highlighted the need to strengthen management capabilities, and he and several other MPs, including Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Victor Lye, spoke about the importance of internationalisation.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are all useful feedback and suggestions, and the Government will continue to take them onboard, study them and lean forward to enable our SMEs to innovate, upgrade and internationalise.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: SMEs that redesign jobs and transform their operations can offer higher wages and more meaningful opportunities to attract and retain Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many SMEs have done so successfully, including those in retail and F&B.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Enterprise Singapore and the Singapore Productivity Centre recently did a deep dive into F&B establishments in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The findings were reported in the media and they are very instructive because F&B establishments that benchmark themselves with productivity standards and knew that they were lower than the benchmarks could find practical and useful ways to raise their productivity.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And when they did do so, they have generally done better.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I mentioned HarriAnns on Budget Day as one example.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Other companies have done so too – restructured, transformed, digitalised and even expanded abroad.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we want to encourage many more SMEs to take that path.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It was founded in 1948 as a small shop on North Bridge Road.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over the decades, it grew into a household name.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A few years ago, the company embarked on a serious transformation.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These examples show that even traditional industries can reinvent themselves and in doing so, create better opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another powerful force reshaping our economy is AI.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And many Members spoke about this, including the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng, Mr Desmond Tan, Mr Desmond Choo, Dr Charlene Chen, Mr Darryl David, Ms Lee Hui Ying, Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Andre Low and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many also shared about the anxieties that workers and fresh graduates are feeling.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we must, and we will, take them seriously.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Historically, every major technological wave has displaced some jobs but also created new ones.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Computers displaced stenographers and typists but created new professions in ICT, in finance and services.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And over time, productivity gains expanded opportunities for workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, what we have seen in Singapore so far is that AI can augment jobs and help workers achieve more, even as it automates certain tasks.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Take the example of Ms Angeline Tan, who works at Nanyang Incorporated, a local event infrastructure company.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Her company adopted an AI chatbot to handle customer enquiries.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: She became a Chatbot Manager, assuming responsibility for auditing the system's responses and ensuring its accuracy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And today, she is an AI Tech Lead in her company, overseeing the implementation of AI tools, improving workflows and taking on more creative responsibilities.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is the pathway we want to encourage – workers moving up the value chain.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: AI can also make our workplaces more inclusive.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, they can support seniors and persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Mr Sharael Taha spoke about this, and we will step up efforts in this area too.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, thus far, the evidence does not point to widespread displacement.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But as many Members have highlighted, there are emerging pressures and we recognise that.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I mentioned earlier that the historical experience with major technological waves is that ultimately more jobs are created than lost.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But there is no economic law that says this will always happen or that this will happen in the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, many are concerned that this time may be different.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because AI is more powerful, advancing faster and affecting a wider range of occupations.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And many Members raised important concerns, for example, that companies may lean too heavily on AI and invest less in worker training.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That more workers could be displaced and the older ones will find it harder to re-enter the workforce.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that entry level jobs, the first rung of career ladders, may be hollowed out.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are alert to these risks and we will act early to prevent such outcomes from taking hold in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will invest more deliberately and more systematically in our people.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In that regard, I agree with NTUC Secretary-General Mr Ng Chee Meng's three calls: to empower every worker to be AI-ready; to strengthen support and safeguards for workers; and to strengthen the Labour Movement's ability to protect and uplift PMEs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will work closely with our tripartite partners, especially NTUC, to realise these shared goals.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, as we develop Champions of AI and implement our national AI Missions, we will not only just help companies transform.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will capture value in Singapore; we will pay close attention to how these companies apply AI; and, importantly, guide them to use AI to enhance human skills and expertise.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But skilled technicians remain essential and AI can help them make better diagnoses and perform their work more cost effectively.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Every sector is different, and how they use AI and the impact on workers in each sector will vary and that is why we are coordinating all of these efforts through the national AI Council, aligning industry transformation and workforce upgrading to ensure that AI uplifts our workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will exploit AI to grow the economy, and we will ensure that growth translates into good jobs and better wages.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is how we give every Singaporean confidence to progress in the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We achieved better than expected growth of 5% last year.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Yet, as many Members have highlighted, including Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, amongst others, Singaporeans continue to feel cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the question is this: what more must we do to ease cost pressures and ensure every Singaporean can continue to progress?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must first understand why affordability and cost concerns have surfaced – not just in Singapore, but across many economies around the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: After COVID-19 and the war in Ukraine, inflation surged globally.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Inflation has moderated, but price levels remain higher than before and that is what households are experiencing.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some have observed that the transfers in this year's Budget are smaller than last year.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But in fact, support in this Budget remains substantial and broader in scope: we are providing CDC Vouchers, cash support, utilities rebates, Child LifeSG credits and CPF top-ups for seniors.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A middle-income household with young children receives about $2,800, after you tote up all the different items.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Essentially, we give more to those with greater needs and we give more to seniors, especially our retirees, as they are not working and have to cope with higher prices on fixed incomes.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are meaningful sums and they are on top of substantial, broad-based subsidies for essentials, like education, healthcare and housing, as well as targeted support for lower-income families and workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Louis Chua said the Government’s primary response has been to rely on one-off and ad hoc handouts.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But regrettably, he has repeated this false claim again this year.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And in this Budget, we enhanced preschool and student care subsidies, as well as ComLink+ to support families with children.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our approach is not just to cushion costs because the durable solution to cost pressures is steady, sustainable wage increases.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Shawn Loh highlighted concerns that a decreasing proportion of Singaporeans benefit from economic growth.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, real incomes have gone up for both households and for workers across the entire income distribution.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Spending has increased in dollar terms, but expenditure as a share of income – that has either remained stable or fallen, across the income distribution as well.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Meaning Singaporeans generally are spending less as a share of their incomes even if their spending has gone up in dollar terms.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, the share of household income spent on essentials, like food, public transport and education, has declined across all income quintiles.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is one exception – that is, healthcare.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singaporeans are spending a larger share of their income on healthcare and health insurance.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That reflects our rapidly ageing population because as you get older, you will tend to spend more on healthcare, and that is why we provide significant and growing subsidies for healthcare services and for our national health insurance premiums.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is also why we have taken steps to rein in overly generous private riders and other practices that drive up medical inflation, especially in the private sector.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we will continue to ensure that healthcare remains affordable in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: No Singaporean will be denied the healthcare they need because of an inability to pay.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another reason for concerns about cost is that inflation for some frequently consumed services, especially F&B, has risen faster than general inflation.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Food consumption may form a smaller share of income which I mentioned just now.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we experience the higher prices each time we order something, or we dine out and the psychological impact is immediate and visible.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The domestic services, be it healthcare or F&B, are labour-intensive.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want wages for Singaporeans in these sectors to rise.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is the fundamental tension every economy must manage.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some countries choose to suppress service wages to keep prices low.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But then this traps a segment of workers in low-paying jobs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not what we want to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Others, like the European economies, have taken a different path.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: You go to any European country, you will know they are paid very well.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But that leads to higher prices overall and a heavier cost burden, which in turn has to be supported by a larger welfare state, financed by taxpayers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But wage increases have to be supported by skills upgrading and productivity improvements.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And at the same time, the Government bears a substantial share of the costs of essential services, through subsidies and transfers, with more support for lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Overall, this balance has delivered good and affordable services to Singaporeans at a sustainable cost.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we know that this is still a work in progress.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But as many Members have highlighted, the lived realities differ from household to household and the circumstances vary for specific segments.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, there are larger families with more children and they will face greater cost burdens, as Mr Pritam Singh and Mr David Hoe have highlighted.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That could be one way to help them.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we will continue to explore other measures to help those with larger families.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are also families caring for seniors or children, and especially those sandwiched with both.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Ms Jessica Tan and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin highlighted their concerns.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And in fact, we already provide more for them in the Budget, in every Budget, including in this year's Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are families with members who have special needs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Prof Kenneth Poon and Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim highlighted their concerns.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And caregivers too need to be supported, as Mr Cai Yinzhou and Ms He Ting Ru highlighted.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In recent Budgets, including this one, we have strengthened support for all of these groups.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we will continue to do so, and will consider the suggestions that Members have made.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Targeted support for specific groups requires means-testing, And we use different indicators to means-test.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The two key ones are the AV of dwellings and PCHI.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Quite a number of Members in this debate, including Mr Alex Yeo, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Gerald Giam, Ms Sylvia Lim just now, Mr Edward Chia suggested reviewing these indicators.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I suppose if you were to take a step back, most of us would agree that support should be given to households with less income and less wealth.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: How to measure income and wealth is the challenge.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But no measure is perfect and we will continue refining our criteria, especially when it comes to support for seniors.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Cost pressures can also feel sharper due to inequality.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Encouragingly in Singapore, income inequality has narrowed compared to a decade ago.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Lower- and middle-income workers have seen faster real income growth than those at the top.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Without this inclusive growth, I have no doubt that the cost pressures that we are feeling on the ground would have been far worse.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And in this Budget, we are raising the Local Qualifying Salary as well as enhancing and extending the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members, Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Sanjeev Tiwari, suggested further steps to support lower-wage and vulnerable workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will study your suggestions carefully – balancing wage increases with sustainable productivity improvements.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are also paying close attention to wealth inequality.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have begun publishing the data and will track this more systematically.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we are not starting from a weak base.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Through housing grants, homeownership and CPF top-ups, we enable lower-income households to accumulate assets in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Saktiandi and Assoc Prof Terence Ho suggested additional asset-based transfers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think someone called it a "Singapore Dividend" or other forms of putting together the measures that we do to help Singaporeans build assets.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, this is the approach that the Government has long taken.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We focus not just on income support, but on enabling Singaporeans to accumulate assets, because asset ownership gives families a concrete stake in our nation's success and allows them to share directly in Singapore's progress.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We do this through a range of different mechanisms like the CDA, Edusave, Post-Secondary Education Account, through CPF and our housing policies and most recently, we introduced the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) Progression Award which incorporates an element of CPF top-ups.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to strengthen pathways for Singaporeans to build savings and assets.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also have progressive taxes on wealth, through our property and vehicle taxes.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to study ways to moderate excessive wealth concentration – carefully and responsibly.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is very easy to say, "Let's tax the rich more!" But capital and talent are mobile and if we rely solely on ever-higher taxes for this segment, eventually, the broad middle will also have to shoulder the burden.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we risk undermining competitiveness, enterprise and job creation.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Redistribution alone cannot build a strong and resilient society.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We redistribute resources to those with greater needs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we complement that with heavy investments in human capital – early childhood education; quality schooling and tertiary education; as well as lifelong learning through SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Upward mobility remains central to our social compact.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because here in Singapore, your starting point should never determine your finishing position.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat has been championing this for many Budgets.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Poh Li San also mentioned this in the debate.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
