text: And in this Budget, we are indeed strengthening our CPF system because Singaporeans are living longer and we want them to retire with confidence and peace of mind.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our CPF system rests on sound and sustainable principles.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Each member saves for his or her own retirement.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we do not leave individuals to fend for themselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We boost those with lower balances through Silver Support, the Majulah Package and periodic CPF top-ups.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we continue to review the parameters of these schemes.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That keeps our system fiscally sustainable, while ensuring that those with less get more support.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members who wish to invest their savings for potentially higher returns can do so, today, through the CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS).

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But the experience with the CPFIS has been mixed.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, many would have been better off topping up their CPF SA and earning the guaranteed 4% return.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, they underperformed the SA rate, which is risk free.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the reality is that we all talk about investments.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But investing and earning consistently good returns is not that easy.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why we took some time to study how to implement a low-cost investment option within the CPF – it has to be simple, low-cost and effective.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are commercial lifecycle products available in the market, but up till now, the take-up has been limited, partly due to the high fees, which can go up to as much as 2%.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But in recent years, the market has matured.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why we now believe it is possible to offer well-diversified life-cycle products at lower fees.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is still a lot of work to be done – designing the scheme, the specific parameters that several Members talked about, building the IT system and ensuring a smooth and seamless user experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Beyond retirement, we have and will continue to strengthen support across life stages.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have initiated major moves as part of Forward Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In public housing, through the new HDB classification system of Standard, Plus and Prime flats.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In healthcare, through Healthier SG and Age Well SG.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have made SkillsFuture a key pillar of our social compact and we are strengthening this further.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have introduced the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support Scheme and we have enhanced ComCare and ComLink+.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have approached them, but some chose not to come onboard ComLink+ or could not be contacted.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With the enhancements to ComLink+, we will redouble our efforts to reach out to them and with stronger community support, we hope more of them will come onboard the scheme.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we will also extend ComLink+ to lower-income families beyond the rental blocks.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members have also offered many other suggestions to further strengthen our community and social support system.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, in healthcare delivery and integration with social support.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members, like Dr Choo Pei Ling, Mr Dennis Tan, Miss Rachel Ong and Dr Hamid Razak, just now spoke about this.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Suggestions around housing and neighbourhood rejuvenation – Mr Ang Wei Neng and Ms Joan Pereira touched on that.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: More support for the arts, culture and community initiatives – Ms Elysa Chen and Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh mentioned that in their speeches, as well as suggestions to review the income thresholds for the Jobseeker Support Scheme (JSS), which Mr Ng Chee Meng and Mr Patrick Tay had advocated.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, the JSS was launched only recently, about a year ago.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will review the scheme and its parameters once we have more experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many Members also asked for more support for families, especially for parents and would-be parents.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Foo Cexiang, Ms Hany Soh, Mr Shawn Loh, Ms Eileen Chong, Mr Gabriel Lam and others have highlighted this concern.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, our falling TFR is a serious concern.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is happening across all advanced and high-income economies.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we really should have some humility about this because no country has truly succeeded on a sustained basis to reverse this decline.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members offered practical suggestions around housing, cost pressures and the affordability of raising children.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some also asked for more work flexibility and leave provisions, so that parents can be present in their children's formative years.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a result of the recent enhancements, our expenditure on marriage and parenthood initiatives has increased – from $4 billion in FY2020 to $7 billion in this Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are already planning for the next tranche of measures to strengthen support for families.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And there will be an opportunity to discuss this at the COS debate and the Minister in the Prime Minister's Office will share more at that occasion.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will do this in a coherent and deliberate way – strengthening individual responsibility, reinforcing collective support and preserving long-term sustainability.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to strengthen our social compact and ensure Singapore remains a society where every citizen can progress with confidence.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Let us first look at the global context.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Since the start of this decade, countries have been tested in ways few could have anticipated.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many advanced economies are now carrying record high levels of public debt.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as debt rises, so will borrowing costs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Over time, this constrains fiscal flexibility and weakens longer-term growth potential for these economies.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Against this backdrop, Singapore's strong fiscal position is a strategic advantage.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many Members spoke about our fiscal position and public finances, including Mr Ang Wei Neng, Ms Valerie Lee and Mr Xie Yao Quan.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am glad they see our healthy fiscal position as a strength; a source of strength.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Given the surplus we have generated, in FY2025 and also the ones that we expect in FY2026, Mr Gerald Giam have asked whether the Goods and Services Tax (GST) hike should be re-evaluated.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the beginning of this decade, we knew that healthcare spending would rise sharply in line with our rapidly ageing population.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And healthcare was not the only area where spending pressures were increasing.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had estimated that healthcare alone would require additional funding of 0.6% to 1.2% of GDP and this would happen in the second half of this decade, which we are in right now.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We raised property taxes and motor vehicle taxes for luxury cars.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have increased the top marginal personal income tax rates.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But these moves were still not sufficient to close the structural funding gap.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we increase the cap to 60%, that can ease immediate pressures.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it will weaken fiscal discipline, reduce our buffer for future shocks and it will shift a heavier burden onto the next generation.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We enhanced the permanent GST voucher to further defray the tax paid by lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, we secured stable funding for healthcare while cushioning the impact of the increase for most Singaporean households.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Could we have relied instead on Corporate Income Tax collections?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But remember, back in 2022, when we made the decision on the GST, there was no sign that Corporate Income Tax collections would rise so significantly.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At that time, the discussions on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) were still evolving.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The eventual outcomes and their revenue implications were far from certain.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It would not have been responsible to fund permanent healthcare commitments using revenue sources that were uncertain and can yet dry up.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Corporate Income Tax collections only started rising towards the end of FY2023 and have stayed elevated until now.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It was due to GDP growth outperforming expectations in 2024 and 2025, as well as better-than-expected contributions from multinational enterprises (MNEs) in a few key sectors.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this brings us to the issue of fiscal marksmanship – Mr Alex Yam, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Louis Chua and Mr Xie Yao Quan touched on this.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have debated this before in the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is perhaps, my favourite topic, because I have shared before that I started work in the Ministry of Finance (MOF) doing precisely this – fiscal projections.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as I have explained, our forecast deviations are within a reasonable range – comparable to other advanced economies.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Within this range of variation, revenues in recent years have indeed come in above projections.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our projections are prepared by the MOF economists using the best available data at the start of each financial year, including GDP growth assumptions at that time.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But for a small open economy, like Singapore, growth outcomes can diverge significantly from forecasts, as global conditions evolve, Because we are so dependent on the external environment, forecasting Singapore's GDP growth is like forecasting the world's GDP growth; which is very, very difficult to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, revenues from property transactions or Certificate of Entitlement (COE) premiums are inherently difficult to predict.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Can you tell what the next year's property prices will be?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the case of COEs, we increased the quotas.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Yet the premiums continued to rise with sustained demand.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That explains the increase in revenue from Licences and Permits, which Mr Gerald Giam asked about.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, forecasting in such an environment will never be exact.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I assure everyone in this House and Singaporeans that our approach has been and will be responsible and professional.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A further insinuation is that the PAP Government deliberately painted a "doom and gloom" picture for electoral advantage.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Let us consider the facts and the context.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Actually, after the US Liberation Day tariffs, there was widespread uncertainty across the world, not just in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At that time, how many analysts projected 5% growth for Singapore in 2025?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The reason why things did not turn out as badly as we feared was partly due to factors beyond our control, but also partly because of the decisive steps we took.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Gan and the team moved quickly, engaging the US to safeguard our core interests, deepening links with other countries, forging new agreements that sustained investor confidence.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our agencies, our businesses and our workers adapted swiftly and worked tirelessly through a very uncertain period.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Let us not belittle these contributions just to score a political point.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The fact that we are in a better position today than our projections is something we should all welcome.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is good news for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we did not raise GST and had instead hoped for revenue upsides.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And then the economic situation did not turn out so well.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We would be having a very different debate today.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We would be scrambling to close fiscal gaps.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But because we made the difficult yet responsible decision, because we chose responsibility over convenience, we are now in a position of strength.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We made the hard call and that is why we can act with confidence today.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, let me turn to our medium-term revenue and expenditure outlook.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are expecting structural revenue increases from Financial Year 2027.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is when the first revenue collections from the BEPS Top-Up Taxes come in.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to firm up our estimates over the coming months as we get more up-to-date data on how firms are performing and adjusting their plans.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Since the BEPS revenue is coming, some may ask, well, how about rolling back the GST?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, the GST increase was introduced to fund rising structural healthcare expenditure for an ageing population.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These spending needs are permanent and will continue to grow.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They should be supported by a stable and reliable revenue base.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, as I have shared in the Budget, Government spending is rising in many other areas, aside from healthcare – for social needs, economic competitiveness, our energy transition, security and infrastructure.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The additional corporate tax revenues will strengthen our fiscal position and support these growing needs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But they do not replace the structural role of the GST and especially what we have done to fund permanent and rising healthcare costs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I mentioned that the Ministry of Defence's (MINDEF's) budget of 3% would be where it is for now and that the budget includes spending on cybersecurity by MINDEF and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), something Mr Giam asked about.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it does not include cybersecurity spending beyond MINDEF.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we do need to spend more on cybersecurity outside of the MINDEF family.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and the Cyber Security Agency, for example, will have to invest more.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will have to harden our critical information infrastructure, like our grids and our power system, against cyber threats.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why I said in the Budget that security spending will rise in the coming years.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In short, our aim is not to run high surpluses for the rest of this term of Government, something that Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our objective is a balanced Budget over the term of Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is clear from our historical records.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan very helpfully gave a speech yesterday outlining the historical data.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And if you look at the past years, we have had balanced Budgets in many years – balanced meaning within a range of plus/minus 0.5% of GDP, in terms of the overall fiscal balance.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have had years of surpluses, we have had good years, but we have also had years of deficits.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But on the whole, we plan for a balanced Budget over the term of Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If there are revenue upsides, when there are revenue upsides, we will deploy these to meet our growing needs.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Shawn Loh suggested giving back surpluses above 2% of GDP to all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But in practice, we actually do not wait to cross a mechanical threshold like that.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Whenever there are revenue upsides, we have shared some of the gains with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Last year, we used that to fund the SG60 package.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This year, we channelled them towards CPF top-ups and the Cost-of-Living Special Payment.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have also strengthened our national priorities by investing in our social support system – enhancing our connectivity, security and economic resilience.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For this FY2026 Budget, expenditure is at 18.4% of GDP.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I said just now, it is the largest Budget on record.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Earlier, MOF had projected that Government spending could reach 20% of GDP by 2030.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But if you look at the trends, since emerging from COVID-19, expenditure has grown by an average of $10 billion every year.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In light of our fiscal position, Mr Shawn Loh had asked if the Government can commit to not making further major revenue moves.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Aside from the GST, we continue to review our tax system regularly as part of prudent fiscal management.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will make revenue adjustments only when necessary – to fund structural spending needs or to achieve clear policy objectives like strengthening progressivity or addressing externalities.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Any tax change, I should say any tax increase, is a difficult decision.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We take them only after careful study and full consideration of the impact on households and businesses.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MOF had earlier published medium-term fiscal projections up to 2030.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But a word of caution is in order.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because in today's fast-changing world, assumptions can quickly become outdated.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The forward projections serve as a guide and will have to be continually updated.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ultimately, what matters most is maintaining fiscal discipline, together with the agility and nimbleness to respond swiftly as circumstances change.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That has long been our practice for property and motor-vehicle-related taxes.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The changes are announced and then applied immediately to ensure market stability and fairness.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A number of questions has been raised on this particular issue, and the Ministry of Transport will address them separately.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Saktiandi and Mr Louis Chua shared their views on the personal income tax regime.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will consider these suggestions around the personal income tax as part of our regular fiscal reviews.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There was a debate yesterday about what it means to run a fiscal surplus.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Does a fiscal surplus mean that the Government is taking more from the economy and leaving households and businesses to bear a deficit?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is an oversimplified and inaccurate characterisation of how our fiscal system works.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A surplus simply means that in a year, revenue exceeds expenditure.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, we are putting money back into the economy, not draining money from businesses and households.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, our Budgets in both 2025 and 2026 have been expansionary, with significant support for households and businesses.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: More importantly, we should look at who pays the tax and who benefits from the transfers.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And on that score, the picture is clear.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Pay a dollar in tax, you get 20 cents in benefits.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In contrast, the middle quintile receives around $2 in benefits.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, those who are better able to contribute, are the ones who generally pay more in taxes.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We use that revenue to strengthen our social compact and provide greater support to those who need it most.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I agree in-principle with the many comments and suggestions that Members have made, including Mr Pritam Singh, Dr Haresh Singaraju and Mr Yip Hon Weng, asking for more information to ensure fiscal accountability and value for money in Government spending.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is why we have been publishing the Singapore Public Sector Outcomes Review biennially since 2010.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That sets out the key outcome indicators across major policy areas and allows the public to track our progress over time.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to review the indicators in the report and ensure they are relevant and useful.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We continually look at refreshing and updating this document.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ministries on their own also conduct detailed reviews of major spending programmes to assess effectiveness and outcomes.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will ask all Ministries to provide clearer and more accessible information on major initiatives, so that Singaporeans can better understand how public resources are used and what results they achieve.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I have outlined our strategies to secure our future together in this changed world.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They may say they are not asking others to choose sides.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But in reality, they are using the full range of tools – from economic leverage to regulatory controls and technology restrictions – to advance their interests.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Others may be subtle – seeking to influence opinions, shape narratives, or even sow division among our people.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we have faced difficult external environments before.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have navigated uncertainty, preserved our sovereignty and independence, and emerged stronger because we remained one united people and acted with resolve.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we enter this new era with considerable strengths.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They are the result of decades of hard choices made by generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is a collective commitment that we will do what it takes to thrive in a more demanding world, that we will stand together when pressures mount and we will continue pushing forward to seize new opportunities on the horizon.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The world may be more uncertain, but we are prepared.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And together, we will shape our own destiny and secure a brighter future for every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call on hon Members for clarifications, I seek Members' understanding to keep them clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And if you have many clarifications, please raise all of them when called upon.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Knowing the Prime Minister, I know he will also keep his answers clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I actually did not have any clarification questions until Prime Minister reached the end of his speech, where he spoke of more information, more accountability, more sharing from the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I made some points in my speech about RIE.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just to make the point very clearly, the previous RIE plan had a simple pie chart, with a diagram telling people who are interested what $25 billion would be used for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The latest one does not have anything of that sort.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe there was a Member yesterday, also, who commented that he filed some Parliamentary Questions to MOE and he did not get the answers that he asked for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think there is quite a lot of work to be done there, and I hope in this term of Government, we see a new approach from the PAP Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I see the value of getting Ministries to put out more information, to share more about how their resources are being used and what outcomes they have achieved.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so, as I have committed in this Budget, or in the speech just now, we are getting Ministries to do more, certainly in the area of RIE as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More information and hopefully, that will encourage people, Singaporeans, to also look at the information and have a better understanding of what we have achieved.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, in the debate just now, I heard Mr Kenneth Tiong talk about the outcomes of our R&D spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that was rather one-sided, in talking about how poorly we have performed in terms of R&D spending and what outcomes we have achieved.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But hopefully, with more information, we can have a more holistic appreciation of the various outcomes we have achieved.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are not complacent, we are always looking at ways to do better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But having the information to provide more informed debate is always something we would encourage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have a question for the Prime Minister on what he said about BEPS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not an economist, so please forgive me if I do not frame it correctly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He appeared to say that we are expecting upside in the next few years due to BEPS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: From what I recalled in past debates, he was more cautious.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I mean, he said, well, we also have to consider the incentives that we need to give to businesses, and in the end, it might not be a net positive.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I wanted to know whether he has changed his view on this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we were concerned about revenue loss under Pillar One.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Pillar Two was about a minimum tax rate across the board.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It may be resurrected later on, but Pillar One has not been implemented.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not on the agenda for now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it does not change our broader assessment that even with the revenue upsides, we will have to spend more and we will have to find ways to strengthen our investment promotion toolkit, because notwithstanding the minimum corporate tax of 15%, which was supposed to give governments more negotiating power over the MNEs, the reality is MNEs still have considerable negotiating power.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And governments everywhere want to attract these strategic investments to their own countries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And they are continuing, notwithstanding a minimum corporate tax of 15% to offer other generous incentives, which are considered BEPS-compliant.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they are spending more, they are offering a whole range of different incentives to reshore or to attract strategic investments like that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what the competitive landscape is today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is facing indeed undue pressure, and something that we get as feedback as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Prime Minister emphasised how the Government has, where it can, looked to mitigate pressures that they face on rent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He spoke about how it hopes to try to limit hikes in properties that it controls.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet many business owners share that there is insufficient effort at restraining unbridled market forces and they hope that some form of a cap on the year-to-year rate of increase in rentals, without outright rent control via a fixed rent ceiling, may be helpful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder whether Prime Minister can share whether this is a possibility in future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On labour, I appreciate Prime Minister's explanation that foreign worker quotas and levies remain needed to ensure a Singaporean core.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the feedback we receive is that despite paying rather solid wages in these sectors, it is really hard to attract locals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I note that certain other sectors, like construction, actually have higher DRC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe the F&B is currently classified under services, which has a much lower DRC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given the unique work conditions within F&B, I am wondering if the Government will consider relaxing the ratio for this sector.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, as I mentioned just now, at the macro level, rental rates have moved in line with economic fundamentals – lower than GDP growth, lower than inflation rates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There may be localised issues, localised shortages, or a particular area, very popular, that kinds of things, these things can happen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, the experiences of jurisdiction everywhere when they impose such rental caps has been not so positive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because you end up with inadvertent consequences and you do not always achieve the objectives that you had wanted to do, which was to ensure competitive rentals.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On foreign worker levies and DRCs for the F&B industry, they are part of services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First of all, I would like to thank the Prime Minister for mentioning that he will be releasing fiscal projections beyond 2030.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just wondering whether I can get clarification from Prime Minister whether those projections will be accompanied with economic baseline assumptions, specific scenarios?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Within the same domain, thank you to Prime Minister for explaining the reassurance that the fiscal policy has been expansionary.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It helps to relieve concerns that it has been extracting and there is opportunity cost on that front.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second supplementary question, Mr Speaker, is on climate transition.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think Prime Minister in his speech and in his opening Budget speech touched a bit on climate and energy transition.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I was wondering whether the Prime Minister can share a bit more about climate transition, especially our plans to have those polders around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are those costs on our fiscal needs and our fiscal expenditure going forward, because those will be quite substantial beyond 2030 and beyond 2040 as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And thirdly, I would like thank the Prime Minister for mentioning my suggestion about changing the income tax thresholds, to help relieve lower-income and middle-income workers and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was wondering what is the possibility of that suggestion being implemented.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, yes, we will provide the economic assumptions underpinning our fiscal projections.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, on the climate transition, we will continue to provide more information on both our mitigation, as well as our adaptation plans, because we are moving on both.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the mitigation, it is really about pushing for decarbonisation and doing more in terms of clean energy, and there will be opportunities in due course to share more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Thirdly, on the personal income tax thresholds, as I said just now, we will take on board these suggestions as part of our regular fiscal reviews.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would also just want to mention again, on the point that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim talked about rental.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While I gave a macro picture about the overall rental rates, as I mentioned in my speech just now, I do recognise averages may not capture every single experience.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There will be instances where rental renewals end up with sharp increases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then we will have to study and consider what appropriate interventions might work for such circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just to very quickly clarify, I do not mean a rental cap in terms of the total amount that it can increase to, but just the rate of increase – precisely what the Prime Minister is getting at, which is when there is a surge, whether there is a cap on how much that surge can occur.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have two clarifications for the Prime Minister.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First of all, thank you so much for addressing the increase in capital intensity at some length.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have asked in two Parliamentary Questions yesterday about it that I did not get to ask a supplementary question for, so I am going to take the time to do it now.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, I am very heartened to hear the promise that in Singapore, we will not have jobless growth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I also am very heartened by the promise at the end of your speech on greater transparency on outcomes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I was wondering if you could share if capital intensity continues to increase, how will the Government's measures of outcomes change, if any?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My second clarification is, you talked about making the hard calls.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think it is very easy to talk about hard calls in terms of raising revenues, but let us also remember that hard calls are also in how much we choose to invest to grow the economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And so, I would like to just hear his thinking around how he will balance the need for immediate support, preserving fiscal space for unforeseen pandemics or higher than expected healthcare increases, but also importantly putting more into things that will grow the economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even though a billion dollars is being laid out for AI, for example, I would like to hear whether there is openness and preserving fiscal space for investing in growth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is a lot of concern that with AI you will see a disproportionate shift of returns to capital, and labour will suffer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are, as I said in my speech, I did not highlight that in such terms, but that is the risk we are very much alive to.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Not just capital owners, not just the companies that push out AI tools.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Singaporeans will always benefit from growth in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the question around our openness to using fiscal space and resources for growth, yes, of course we are.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will always want to grow the pie, because that is what our future is about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have to keep on expanding the pie for all to benefit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our investments in R&D are very much in that direction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With AI and all the moves we talked about in AI, we will also allocate more resources to pushing the frontier, so that we can continually expand opportunities, jobs and better incomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have three clarifications for the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I think the first is on the point he mentioned about the one-off, Sir, that I mentioned in my speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To me, the question is really, as I have shared in my speech, in light of our surpluses, are we then better off to put in place the structural levers and interventions, rather than having to decide on these on a one-off basis year after year?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I gave the example of personal income taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are we better off having that updating of the bracket rather than have varying personal income tax rebates year after year?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, on the corporate front, are we better off with revising, maybe some of our Partial Tax Exemption and Startup Tax Exemption schemes, which were last changed in 2018?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And I also gave the example of how for the Global Trader Programme, that was extended up till 2031.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second is in relation to the Occasional Paper that MOF has put out.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just wondering if the Prime Minister has given the MOF team perhaps a timeline as to when recommendations may be put forth to address some of the issues that were brought up, specifically when it comes to the taxing of wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I think it has always been mentioned that it is mainly via our system of property taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And the report has showed wealth, especially for the top 20%, to the extent that it is under reported.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would say that probably the share of non-property assets is likely to be larger than what we have found.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, in the context, wealth taxes beyond just property taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And last but not least, in terms of the TFR, on this front, again, to maybe borrow a phrase from the Ministry for Sustainability and the Environment, are we willing to have ambitious and realistic targets with regards to the TFR, even if for the medium to longer term to guide our policy interventions?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I hope we can banish this forever in this House.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have some, yes, 5% of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have much more allocation of resources on longer-term and structural schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And will there continue to be some one-off measures?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, we will, from time to time, it is not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the weight of our fiscal moves are really on the longer-term and structural schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And it is not just a mindset issue, it is not just a policy issue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I mentioned just now, policy changes, policy reviews, take some time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some suggestions we may not be able to do, and we explain our position, and there will be differences of views.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But there will be suggestions which we think are good and we will consider them carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And in time to come, we will make the changes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no specific timeline for this because we are always on a continuing basis, reviewing and updating our policies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On TFR and measures, will we be more ambitious?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would say we have always tried to be ambitious.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have pushed the boundary each time in terms of the moves we made.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And in this coming review we will be even more ambitious.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Name me a country which has succeeded on a sustained basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is a trend that is happening around the world.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If money can solve the problem, I will put the money down and solve the problem.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it is not just an economic issue, it is far more complex than that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Countries have spent far more than us and have not been able to achieve a meaningful, sustained improvement in their TFR.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And Minister Indranee at the COS debate will share more about how we can try to engender a whole-of-society reset around marriage and procreation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Just a quick point that my colleague just highlighted to me when Mr Singh talked about the RIE reports and what have been published.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, someone alerted me that there are additional reports, beyond what Mr Singh had shared.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the office, the National Research Foundation has put out more information already.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in any case, as I said, our commitment, whatever the baseline is today, we will do more.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I have two clarifications for the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When tariff shocks escalated last year, businesses were certainly genuinely uncertain.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It was the Government's swift and credible response that stabilised sentiment and positioned Singapore as a trusted base amid fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, as the tariff situation becomes uncertain again and supply chains continue to readjust, could the Prime Minister give assurance to businesses that we will have the fiscal space to support them, to respond decisively if volatility intensifies?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time as we move decisively into frontier industries like AI, quantum and space technologies, these are energy intensive and capital heavy sectors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Prime Minister clarify how the Government assesses our long-term fiscal headroom to support both frontier industry development and the sustainable energy infrastructure required to power it?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Whatever uncertainty and volatility we may face, the Government will certainly be there to walk with our businesses and our workers to navigate the changes ahead of us.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are not out of the woods yet.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The situation was better than expected last year, but there is new uncertainty now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I think uncertainty and volatility will now be the norm anyway.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will continue to work closely with our businesses and workers, and also as part of our tripartite system.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the frontier industries and the fact that they are energy intensive, it is a cause for concern.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Mr Dennis Tan had also spoken about this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are trying our best to manage this and the solution for us at the end of the day is to accelerate our efforts on decarbonisation to be able to harness even more clean energy sources than the limited sources we have today.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Prime Minister, our workers were very, very encouraged and inspired to hear that you will be personally overseeing the Singapore's AI transitions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: With autonomous vehicle (AV) bus services expected to commence this year, as well as pilot AV shuttle services already underway, it is clear that the pace of change is accelerating.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: My question is, how will we ensure that sectors such as our bus industry and point-to-point transport sector are given sufficient time and structured support for these transitions?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In particular, how do we sequence implementation so that technologies like AI and AV strengthen safety standards, uplift skills and enhance livelihoods, rather than become a source of disruption and anxiety for our workers?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, when I had the dialogue with union leaders, this was surfaced as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We want workers to benefit from new technologies.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The Prime Minister mentioned in his Budget speech that 1% of the GDP is dedicated to R&D expenses, commonly known as the gross expenditure on R&D (GERD).

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: For most of the European countries, it is about 3%.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: What is our target and how can we actually use part of the $15 billion surplus to give it a boost?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not think it is about saying that we just have to do more and spend more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As many have highlighted, we want to ensure good outcomes from our R&D spending as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will continue if the outcomes are good.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we also do not just track what the Government spends.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We want Government spending to catalyse more business R&D.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the other measure, aside from GERD is BERD or the business expenditure on R&D, which is commonly tracked as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we are heartened that on the business side, private sector R&D in Singapore has also gone up, corresponding or together with Government spending on R&D.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That bodes well for the future because that means that the private sector, too, is seeing the benefits of investing more in R&D and investing for the future.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: I, of course, respect the Prime Minister's prerogative to characterise my views on R&D as somewhat one-sided.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: So, I would like to offer him the opportunity for a fuller defence in light of, perhaps, three groups of facts.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: First, since 1991, the first National Technology Plan to RIE2030, the nominal amount committed is about $125 billion, of which I think there are indeed few visible commercial outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Mirxes in 2025 was the first and only billion-dollar IPO.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: I do not recall any other commercially significant companies out there.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Even if we were to give it to the Government that it is an MNC-driven strategy, the first phase of the Biopolis project was not a big success.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: For all the MNC R&D offices for these pharmaceutical companies – in 2010, we had the departure of Eli Lilly; in 2013, we had the departure of Pfizer; in 2014, the departure of GlaxoSmithKline; in 2016, the departure of Novartis.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: So, I do not really quite see where, perhaps, he is having his different view from.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: My second clarification is whether he will consider putting on a policy investment bank function or, rather, reconstituting it, given that it has been missing since Mdm Ho Ching took over Temasek in 2002.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is not just a narrow focus on a single measure of success but a wide range of different indicators.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the research part, mind you, which is also important because we do not only want commercialisation success, we also want to anchor strong basic research.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is also tracked with another set of different indicators, like publications, which we also track.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there are a wider range of outcomes we track in terms of our R&D spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no disagreement, in principle, in terms of that direction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We want to encourage more of an enterprise-building approach, in terms of how we grow our economy rather than just focus on specific individual grant schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are things we are already doing and will continue to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the question of an investment bank approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Well, I would also disagree with him that this has changed with the chief executive officer in Temasek.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Temasek, when it started, was always very clear about its mandate from the very beginning – commercial, not doing national service, focused on commercial outcomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If there are things that the Government wants to do and Temasek thinks it is useful to do from a commercial point of view, then, yes, we can partner Temasek to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are many instances even till today, including some of the equity funds which are done with a co-investment approach with Temasek, not because we forced Temasek to do these as national undertakings but because they see commercial value in growing enterprises and growing the enterprise ecosystem, and in achieving and securing better long-term returns for their portfolio.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This has been consistently the approach from the start and that is the same approach we will continue with Temasek going forward.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In this age of AI and growth, I asked about how the Government intends to strengthen the intermediaries who are actually advising the SMEs in this age, intermediaries, like the SME Centres, Singapore Business Federation, NTUC, the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) and the trade associations, for example.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: From where can these intermediaries tap on resources to advise and to be in a good position to advise as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second one is on the Prime Minister's comment on no jobless growth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wanted to hear his thoughts on the prognosis of those Singaporeans who are unlikely to catch up.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The vulnerable, for example, like some of the seniors, like persons with disabilities who have higher support needs, for example.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They might actually lose jobs in this time and age.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I wanted to hear his views on those who are likely to lose jobs and actually may not be able to take up or upgrade their skills, in that sense.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I think somebody mentioned it, but I am very relieved to hear from the Prime Minister that this is not a lost cause and that even if the Budget Statement does not cover it, Minister Indranee will cover that.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hopefully, what Elon Musk has predicted, that Singapore will become extinct, that will not be a reality.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But can the Prime Minister share a little bit more about strategies other than producing our own?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We know that many young people may not want to get married or even after they get married, some of them prefer pets to children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Are there other strategies that the Prime Minister will consider, like easier adoption procedures to have more people adopt, more of us Singaporeans adopting?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second is, in terms of immigration as well, to bring in people who are of the right profile and suitable profile to grow our Singaporean population?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: No easy answers now because when it comes to providing IT solutions that are AI-enabled, that is quite straightforward.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But when you talk about intermediaries who truly understand what it means to transform an enterprise using AI, in fact, there are very few.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mentioned this in my Budget speech, even the leading companies are grappling with this and looking at ways to do this better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is an area where we ourselves are looking to build capabilities and expertise and identifying experts who can help us and not just help us as in help the Government, but help the intermediaries within our economy, who can in turn help our businesses, especially our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, on jobless growth and the concerns that vulnerable groups may have.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continually review and strengthen our support mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, on the TFR and whether there are other ways in which we can encourage or we can maintain our Singaporean core, whether it is through adoption or immigration.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, indeed, we will have a multi-faceted approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Foo Cexiang gave a very good speech yesterday on adoption procedures and how it can be very complex and frustrating for parents who would like to adopt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Just like Member Denise Phua, I want to quote something the Prime Minister mentioned, which is that the starting point should never determine our finishing position.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I think that is a very high and inspiring principle to share.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But I bring this up because based on recent data – and I had asked a Parliamentary Question to MOE before about the difference in Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) scores across different income groups, we find that these differences are statistically significant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: While they are no different from other Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries, I think that we have that larger aspiration not just to match up to what other countries are doing, but to do better, regardless of what the other countries are doing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: So, I wanted to hear from the Prime Minister, what his thoughts are and what MOF is thinking is around this issue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Other concerns that I think Members raised in this House during the debate, for example, around digital screen time – Ms He Ting Ru talked about that, others too.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Access to social media for children, that is also on our agenda.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there are things that we are reviewing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Like I said, I cannot cover every single topic in a Budget or in a round-up speech, but these are things and priorities that we are looking at and we will have future occasions to address them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister said that Budget Estimates are prepared by MOF economists based on variable data, including GDP growth projections.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I accept that GDP is highly sensitive to external shocks and can deviate significantly from forecasts and this impacts the actual fiscal position, but in the interest of transparency, will MOF provide more disclosure regarding the methodology of its revenue projections?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, our GDP assumptions pegged to the mid-point of the official forecast range at the start of the fiscal year and what is the specific weighting of GDP growth in fiscal estimates?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this does not fully account for the systemic nature of the trend.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Could the Prime Minister explain why there is a consistent directional bias towards conservative fiscal marksmanship over the past 20 years, excluding the two years of exceptional circumstances of the COVID-19 pandemic and the FY2023 Majulah Package allocation?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For 18 of these 20 years, the actual surpluses have consistently exceeded original estimates by significant margins.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And the projections are done on those basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is a well-defined methodology used by many governments to project revenue, which often are tied to incomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is a certain buoyancy estimate of how buoyant the revenue is when incomes rise so the GDP is the most critical assumption in many revenue projections.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Why have we seen more revenue upsides than downsides over the years?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Perhaps, there is a simple explanation to this – which is that we have consistently performed better than expected.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: When we mentioned about space technology, quantum technology, AI technology and decarbonisation technology, if we look forward, it is very exciting to see all these coming.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: But, at the same time, we must also understand the capacity of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: At one point, they must be prepared to train towards a certain skill and these skills are somewhat, I would say, common across the board and these technologies need expert skills or those who are highly skilled.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: Having said that, how do we ensure that our workforce can keep up to the change?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: And furthermore, does our education allow that to happen as well?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: Because the speed of technology moves so fast; in other words, the speed of the education must also follow through as well.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: So, these are things that that become very clear and very apparent of what I think we must prepare the workforce for: the ability to learn, the ability to quickly learn become crucial.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: I am sad to say that the fundamentals of the citizens are not able to cope to the change where the country wants to go to.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: In other words, as a country move forward and get better and better, the workforce or the people still lag behind.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: At one form, they try to get better because of their own internal problems or their own family problems.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: Another section is that how do we improve, how we make them improve to keep up to the technology, to the change?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: So, Singapore in the context whereby we are moving quite rapidly; so does the world.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: But is the workforce, is the citizen able to do so?

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Memebr)
text: And how do we change the structure or allow the structure to be evolved, starting from education and looking at how the workforce can adapt to it because —

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman
text: So, this is the point I am saying: how do we prepare our workforce towards this technological change?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is key and that is why we have long invested in education.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And it is not just about the investments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is about updating our system so that at the school and tertiary levels, we help prepare our students well for new industries of the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But even that alone is not enough because, as Mr Azhar highlighted, the technology is changing so quickly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are mindful of all of these concerns – of the need to prepare our people well for the future and we will continue to invest heavily in every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But the Prime Minister has been answering our questions for close to an hour.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And I note the collective sigh of relief in the House.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I am glad to hear Prime Minister's round-up speech.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: To the Government's credit, the last few years of support have given that assurance to our retirees.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Would the Prime Minister now agree that we should assure this group of retirees that structural support should always keep up with the cost of living, not including the one-off measures that Prime Minister mentioned but that 95%?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Can Prime Minster promise our half a million retirees in Singapore that the cost of living should be not too much of an anxiety to all of them and that the current levels of support should stay the same in real terms?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are very mindful that retirees will face potentially the biggest concerns because they do not have incomes, they will not benefit from wage increases and the cost-of-living pressures would be felt more acutely by this segment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so our assurance to them is that we are watching out for them, we will take care of our retirees.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But at the same time, we will also take care of all Singaporeans, to make sure that we help wages go up, we help retirees who do not have wage increases ease their cost pressures across different areas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And everyone, everyone in Singapore can truly benefit from the nation's progress.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Prime Minister, you mentioned in your Budget speech on taking SkillsFuture forward and strengthening the assurance for mid-career workers and seniors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In my speech, I asked to help our young seniors stay relevant and employable for the long term.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I call for more fundamental revamp of the SkillsFuture and to retrain our workforce every 10 years or so, to counter the shorter economic cycles and the impact of AI.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I would like Prime Minister to share more about beyond merging WSG and SSG, and involving the IHLs and Institutes of Education (ITEs) more for continuing education and training, will the Government be looking at more measures to help our young seniors, especially the PMETs to stay effectively more relevant and more employable?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We know that at that mid-career level if you are made redundant, getting back into the workforce can be more challenging.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At that level, wage increases also may not be as high because there is a certain life-cycle to wages.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are many, many good ideas put forward by Members for many different segments: young seniors, retirees, disadvantaged groups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I wish I had a wand, a magic solution that can solve every problem and take care of every group overnight.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the realities of life are not like that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If these foundations are not present, we would be scrambling, we would be having a very different conversation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us also be mindful of the fundamentals – keep growth, keep our economy growing, keep on ensuring a dynamic vibrant economy, good growth and generate the resources we need in order to take care of all the different segments of society.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have had an hour of clarifications from 16 Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I do not see any more Members raising their hands.
